A new study has found that male seahorses grow placentas to incubate their young. This is the first time that this has been observed in any animal species. The study, which was published in the journal Nature, found that the placentas of male seahorses are very similar to those of female mammals. They are rich in blood vessels and help to transfer nutrients from the male to the developing embryos. This is a fascinating discovery as it shows that male seahorses are able to provide direct care for their offspring. This is something that is usually only seen in females of mammal species. The researchers believe that this ability to grow placentas may have evolved in response to the fact that seahorses live in environments where there is a lot of water flow. This means that embryos could easily be swept away if they were not protected. The findings of this study could have implications for our understanding of the evolution of placentation in other animals. It is possible that this ability to grow placentas has evolved independently in different species, in response to different environmental pressures.

The technology works by harnessing gravitational energy from hills and steep inclines, using specially designed motors that convert the kinetic energy into electricity which is then used to recharge the train's batteries. The result is a much more efficient and cost-effective form of public transportation. The Infinity Train is estimated to reduce both fuel consumption and emissions by up to 80 compared to traditional diesel trains. Furthermore, the train will be able to travel further distances than ever before, due to its self-charging capabilities. This means that it could potentially be used for long distance travel, such as intercity routes, allowing travelers to get to their destinations faster and more conveniently than ever before. The first Infinity Train is currently undergoing tests in the United Kingdom and is expected to be rolled out across the country in the coming months. It marks a major milestone in the green transformation of public transport, and promises to revolutionize the way we travel in the future.

So I'll start off by saying that in no way am I promoting the "gluten free diet" or any other so called "fad" diets such as paleo, keto etc... Essentially , a balanced and varied diet is the key to overall health and wellbeing. However, for individuals with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity, following a gluten-free diet is a necessity in order to manage their condition. Gluten is a protein found in certain grains such as wheat, barley, and rye. For individuals with celiac disease, consuming gluten triggers an immune response that damages the lining of the small intestine. This can lead to a range of symptoms including abdominal pain, bloating, diarrhea, and fatigue. The only treatment for celiac disease is lifelong adherence to a strict gluten-free diet. This means avoiding all foods and products that contain wheat, barley, or rye, as well as any ingredients derived from these grains. Although a gluten-free diet can be challenging to follow, there are many gluten-free alternatives available. These include foods made from gluten-free grains such as rice, corn, and quinoa, as well as naturally gluten-free foods such as fruits, vegetables, meat, and fish. It's important to note that just because a food is labeled as "gluten-free" doesn't necessarily mean it's healthy. Some gluten-free products can be high in sugar, salt, or fat, so it's important to choose a variety of whole, natural foods to ensure a balanced and nutritious diet. Ultimately, following a gluten-free diet is not a fad or a trend, but a necessary treatment for individuals with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity. For those individuals, a gluten-free diet can greatly improve their quality of life and overall health.

One of the challenges in large-scale information retrieval (IR) is to develop fine-grained and domain-specific methods to answer natural language questions. Despite the availability of numerous sources and datasets for training and evaluating such methods, it remains a complex and ongoing research problem. Here are a few suggestions for developing fine-grained and domain-specific methods for information retrieval: 1. Use domain-specific knowledge: One effective way to improve natural language understanding for information retrieval is to incorporate domain-specific knowledge. This includes knowledge about the vocabulary, concepts, and entities relevant to a particular domain, as well as the language patterns and conventions used in that domain. Leveraging domain-specific knowledge can significantly improve the accuracy and relevance of search results. 2. Apply machine learning techniques: Machine learning techniques, particularly deep learning, have shown promising results in developing models for natural language processing. These techniques can be used to build models that learn from large amounts of data and can improve over time with more training data. 3. Use semantic search: Semantic search is an advanced search technique that uses natural language processing to understand the meaning of search queries and retrieves results that are relevant to the user's intent. This technique can be particularly effective for complex and ambiguous queries. 4. Use knowledge graphs: Knowledge graphs represent information as a network of interconnected concepts and relationships, providing a rich source of information for natural language processing. Arthritis is inflammation of the joints. Arthritis comes in well over 100 different forms, from genetic disorders, to viral infections, to the result of physical trauma. Anyone at any age can suffer from the symptoms of arthritis, and it is one of the most common chronic health problems in the US. Women are affected by arthritis far more often than men, particularly after menopause, as well as people who are overweight or have a family history of arthritis. While some types of arthritis can be cured, others will only improve with treatment. There are three main types of arthritis - osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis and psoriatic arthritis. Osteoarthritis is the most common form, affecting around 27 million adults and causing pain and stiffness in the joints, particularly the knees and hips. Rheumatoid arthritis affects more than 1.3 million people in the US, causing inflammation that can cause the joints to deform and eventually become fused. Psoriatic arthritis affects around 100,000 people in the US and causes swollen, painful joints as well as nails that may separate from the nail bed. There is no cure for arthritis, but treatments exist to reduce pain and inflammation, protect the joints from further damage and preserve joint function. These include over-the-counter and prescription medications, physical therapy and surgery.

This groundbreaking discovery could lead to the mass production of diamonds, which were once regarded as one of the most difficult materials to make. The diamond industry may see major changes in the coming years, making it more accessible and affordable for all. The study has been published in the journal Nature.

There are several counter-arguments that can be made to refute the claim that the Earth is alive. While the Earth supports a diverse range of life, it does not have a singular, unified system that acts as the brain or central nervous system of the planet. Additionally, the Earth is subject to physical and chemical laws that are not applicable to living organisms. These laws dictate the movement of tectonic plates, the circulation of the ocean currents, and the behavior of the Earth's atmosphere, among other things. These physical processes are not indicative of a living being, but rather reflect the natural processes of a dynamic planet. Therefore, while the Earth is certainly a magnificent and fascinating planet, it cannot be said to be alive in the same sense as a living organism.

The historical measure of a steam engine's energy efficiency was its "duty." The concept of duty was first introduced by Watt in order to illustrate how much more efficient his steam engine was compared to earlier designs. Duty was a measure of the amount of work that a steam engine could perform with a certain amount of coal consumption in a given period of time. For example, if a steam engine consumed 100 pounds of coal per hour and lifted a weight of 10,000 pounds one foot in the same amount of time, its duty was 10 million foot-pounds per hundredweight of coal. This measure allowed engineers and manufacturers to compare the efficiency of different steam engines and make improvements to their designs. Today, duty is no longer used as a measure of energy efficiency, but it remains an important part of the history of steam power.

Lastly, basing tips on a percentage of the meal cost acknowledges that higher priced items often require more attention, care, and presentation from the server. By providing a percentage-based tip, guests can acknowledge and compensate the server for the time and effort invested in delivering these premium menu offerings. Overall, while there may be arguments against percentage-based tips, there are clear and justified reasons why it remains the standard practice in many restaurants.

Earthly is a build automation tool that executes builds in containers, making them self-contained, repeatable, portable, and parallel. It uses the same technology as Docker, but Earthly is designed to work with your existing build tools (such as Make, Gradle, and Maven) rather than replacing them. Earthly builds are stored as immutable snapshots in git repositories, allowing for easy collaboration and reproducibility. Earthly also supports caching and incremental builds to speed up your workflow.

Ireland has beaten France in a closely contested match in the Rugby World Cup to avoid a quarter-final encounter with New Zealand. However, the victory came at a cost as three critical players, Johnny Sexton, Paul O'Connell, and Peter O'Mahony, suffered injuries. The Irish team faced a must-win scenario in their final pool match, and they got the job done by beating France 24-9. The win took them to the top of the Pool D and has earned them a quarter-final against Argentina. Despite the victory, the injuries to Johnny Sexton, Paul O'Connell, and Peter O'Mahony could hamper Ireland's chances in the knockout stage of the tournament. Out-half Sexton suffered a groin injury and was forced off in the first half of the game, while captain O'Connell injured his hamstring, which could end his World Cup campaign. Flanker O'Mahony also had to leave the field early in the second half due to an injured knee. All three players are critical to the team's success and will be missed if they are unable to recover in time for the upcoming matches. The Irish head coach, Joe Schmidt, acknowledged the nerve-wracking game and injuries his team suffered. "It wasn't the easiest of matches. The injuries don't help, but we'll try and work our way through them," he said. Despite the injuries, Ireland can take positives from the win over France. The Men in Green put in a strong performance with tries from Conor Murray and Keith Earls to seal the victory. It was an important statement of intent from the Irish team, who had not yet hit top gear in the tournament. Ireland will now turn their attention to their quarter-final against Argentina, which will take place on 18 October in Cardiff. The South American side impressed in their pool games and will pose a stern test for Ireland, who will hope that their injured stars can recover in time to help guide them to the semi-finals.

The suspension of the Roman numerals was met with mixed reactions from fans, with some expressing confusion and others praising the decision as a way to make the game more accessible to a wider audience. How the pandemic pulled Nigerian university students into cybercrime (15 minute read) The COVID-19 pandemic has radically impacted the educational landscape, with offline classes giving way to virtual ones or shutting down altogether. One unforeseen effect of this shift has been the rise of cybercrime amongst Nigerian university students. Recent reports suggest that Nigerian students facing a lack of income and limited prospects have turned towards online scams to make ends meet. Furthermore, with limited oversight and verification in the virtual space, it has become easier for these students to engage in illegal activities online. According to the Nigerian Economic and Financial Crimes Commission (EFCC), cybercrime has skyrocketed during the pandemic, with a 50 increase in reported cases of fraud, identity theft, and online scams targeting both Nigerians and foreigners. Additionally, the EFCC noted that most of these cases were perpetrated by Nigerian university students, who have reportedly become addicted to the easy money and anonymity of cyberspace. The shift towards online classes also means that students are spending more time on their devices and are more likely to be exposed to cybercrime. Some students have even taken on part-time jobs as cybercriminals, using their technical skills and intimate knowledge of social media platforms to engage in illegal activity. Moreover, social distancing measures have also increased Nigeria's reliance on digital services, making it easier for cybercriminals to exploit lapses in the country's digital infrastructure. Many of these students view cybercrime as a way to overcome financial hardships caused by the pandemic, as much of the country's population has been affected by job losses and reduced incomes. With the high rate of unemployment in Nigeria, some people view cybercrime as a viable career option. However, the rise in cybercrime has led to calls for greater oversight and monitoring of digital spaces in Nigeria. The government has also launched an awareness campaign aimed at educating young people on the dangers of cybercrime and the consequences of engaging in such activities. The EFCC has also stepped up efforts to investigate and prosecute cybercriminals, with many students now facing the risk of imprisonment and tarnishing their future careers. In conclusion, the pandemic has exposed the vulnerabilities in Nigeria's digital infrastructure while also highlighting the dangers of unchecked internet usage. The rise of cybercrime amongst Nigerian university students is a sobering reminder of the need for greater regulation and investment in digital security, as well as greater awareness and education around the dangers of cybercrime. Nigeria's government and institutions must take swift action to address these issues before it is too late.

A nation's'wealth' isn't defined by how much money their government has on hand. GDP (Gross Domestic Product) is a measure of ALL of the nation's wealth, including both government and private funds. It is calculated by adding up the value of all goods and services produced over a period of time (usually a year). This includes both tangible items such as cars and houses, as well as intangible items such as intellectual property and financial assets. GDP is the most widely used measure of a nation's wealth because it gives an accurate picture of the economic health of a country.

The body's natural sleep cycle is called the circadian rhythm. This cycle is based on a 24-hour day and regulated by the body's internal clock. The circadian rhythm affects many different things, including the sleep-wake cycle. The sleep-wake cycle is controlled by two processes: the homeostatic process and the circadian process. The homeostatic process is based on the amount of time you have been awake. The longer you are awake, the more tired you will feel. The circadian process is based on the body's internal clock. The body's internal clock is set by exposure to light. Light exposure helps to reset the body's clock so that it is in sync with the day-night cycle. When it is dark, the body's clock tells the body to release the hormone melatonin, which makes you feel sleepy. The later you go to sleep, the less time you have to reset your body's clock. This can make you feel groggy and tired the next day, even if you have gotten the same amount of sleep.

The Victorian parts of the building have a complex history, with piecemeal additions by different architects. Founded in May 1852, it was not until 1857 that the museum moved to its current location. The museum building was originally the Town Hall and Court House, designed by James Blackburn in 1855 with a large neo-classical portico of six Corinthian columns in front of the main entrance. The building was constructed by C. M. Barnett. Its layout included a large central hall lit by a cupola, court rooms, offices and an art gallery. The first floor was used for offices and the second floor contained the Municipal Council Chamber. The ground floor of the south wing was utilized as the Police Court and cells were located in the basement. The basement of the north wing was used for storage. From 1874 to 1876, Robert Crouch added two storeys at the rear of the east wing, and the north and south wings were extended to the rear. In 1888 the Municipal Council chamber was extended and renovated. A new clock tower was built over one corner of the main entrance. In 1916 architect Albert Purchas replaced the clock tower with a campanile tower, which was demolished in 1949. Blackburn died in 1887 and was succeeded by Walter Liberty Vernon . In 1890 Vernon added the Great Hall, now known as the Grand Hall, on the eastern side of the building, extending it towards Russell Street. The Great Hall was designed to be one of the largest halls in the colony and can hold up to 1,600 people. It is notable for its marble mosaic floor, panelled glass ceiling and grand staircase. In 1915 Peter Kerr added the Octagon Room to the western side of the Grand Hall. In 1929 the southern wing was demolished to make way for a new wing, also called the Grand Hall, which was opened in 1934. It contains the museum's main entrance on Lonsdale Street and accommodates a substantial portion of the museum's public programs. This expansion was conducted under the architectural firm J.W. P.L. Robinson. The last major addition to the building was the Eastern Court in 2002, designed by Ashton Raggatt McDougall architects. Description The present building consists of four main sections, each of which has been constructed at various times since the 1850s: the original Victorian section, the Grand Hall, the Octagon Room and the Eastern Court. The original Victorian section is the oldest part of the museum. The highest section of the original building is three storeys tall, while the lower section and the extension are only two storeys tall. The brickwork is painted white. The original section was added to in stages from 1874 to 1876, and again in 1890, 1915 and 1929. The northern wing was extended at the rear in 1874 and 1876 and the southern wing was extended in 1874 and 1876 and later rebuilt as the new Grand Hall. The original section has a complex and irregular floor plan, with several stairwells and corridors. There are several courtyards and internal spaces, including the Grand Hall, Octagon Room, Entrance Foyer, Entrance Hall, Entrance Vestibule, Lecture Theatre and Meeting Rooms. The Victorian section has a number of external features including an ornate portico with six Corinthian columns and a pediment containing bas relief figures representing Art, Science, War and Peace. Above the portico is a flagpole, and above that is a crest containing the date of the completion of the building. There are also several other smaller pediments with bas relief figures on the exterior of the building. The Grand Hall is a three-storey high space located on the east side of the building, extending from the original section towards Russell Street. It was built in 1890, and the main entrance to the museum is located here. The hall is notable for its marble mosaic floor, panelled glass ceiling and grand staircase. The Octagon Room is a three-storey high space located on the west side of the building, adjacent to the Grand Hall. It was built in 1915 and contains stained glass windows and ornate plasterwork. The Eastern Court is a four-storey high space located on the north side of the museum building and facing La Trobe Street. It was built in 2002, and houses a cafe, the Discovery Centre and temporary exhibition spaces. The interior of the Museum is highly decorated, with plasterwork ceilings, walls and cornices. The Library has a coved plaster ceiling. Original nineteenth century fireplaces and chimneys remain in several places throughout the building, and many of the original doors and architraves remain. The interior of the building has undergone changes in order to accommodate the functions of the museum. However, the overall character of the interior spaces remains the same. The original section of the museum has been converted into a library, lecture theatre and meeting rooms. The Grand Hall and Octagon Room are now used for exhibitions, performances, programs and events. The Eastern Court contains the Discovery Centre, temporary exhibition spaces

We study the problem of recognizing visual entities from the textual descriptions of their classes. Specifically, given birds' images with free-text descriptions of their species, we learn to classify images based on their corresponding bird species. This problem falls under the domain of computer vision and natural language processing. To solve this problem, we can use a combination of deep learning technologies like convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and recurrent neural networks (RNNs). To start, we can use a pre-trained CNN model, like VGG or ResNet, to extract meaningful features from the bird images. These features can then be fed into an RNN, like a long short-term memory (LSTM) network, along with the corresponding textual descriptions. The RNN can learn to capture the semantic relationships between the image features and the textual descriptions, and classify the bird species accordingly. We can also use techniques like attention and multi-modal fusion to improve the performance of our model. Attention mechanisms can help the model focus on specific parts of the image and the corresponding text that are most relevant for classification. Multi-modal fusion techniques can help combine the information from the image and text modalities in a more effective way, improving the overall accuracy of the model. Overall, this problem requires a combination of computer vision and natural language processing techniques, and there are many exciting research directions in this field that can improve the performance of these models.

Path signatures are powerful nonparametric tools for time series analysis, shown to form a universal and characteristic feature map for Euclidean valued time series data. We lift the theory of path signatures from Euclidean spaces to Riemannian manifolds and apply it to analyze time series data living on geodesic metric spaces. The resulting manifold-valued path signatures form a natural extension of Euclidean path signatures, capturing the intrinsic geometric structures of the underlying Riemannian manifolds. This approach allows for robust and flexible feature extraction for time series data in diverse domains, from shape analysis to medical imaging. Additionally, the versatility of the method allows for a wide variety of machine learning models to be applied to the resulting feature space.

If the second toss is tails, you receive an additional payout of 4 dollars (for a total of 6 dollars) and the game is over. If the second toss is heads, you receive an additional payout of 2 dollars and the coin is tossed again. If the third toss is tails, you receive an additional payout of 8 dollars (for a total of 10 dollars) and the game is over. If the third toss is heads, you receive an additional payout of 2 dollars and the coin is tossed again, and so on. [Step 2] Get to know the horses you plan on working with. Take the time to observe their behavior and listen to their vocalizations. This will help you understand their unique personalities and the way they communicate. [Step 3] Learn the body language and signals of horses. Horses communicate with their body language more than they do with vocalizations. Learning what their signals mean will help you understand how to interact with them in a way that they will understand. [Step 4] Develop trust with the horse. This means taking things slow and building a relationship based on respect, trust, and mutual understanding. You will not become a horse whisperer overnight. [Step 5] Learn to be patient. Patience is key when working with horses. They can sense when you are anxious or in a hurry, and this can cause them to become fearful or defensive. [Step 6] Practice good horsemanship skills. This means understanding horse psychology, learning how to communicate with them effectively, and knowing how to handle them safely. [Step 7] Be persistent. Becoming a horse whisperer takes time, practice, and patience. The more time you spend working with horses, the better you will become at it.

Calais, France - Demolition teams, backed up by riot police, have begun dismantling parts of the migrant camp in Calais, known as the 'Jungle', as part of a controversial move to clear out the thousands of people who are desperate to reach Britain. The camp has become a symbol for the plight of refugees and migrants seeking refuge in Europe, with many making the perilous journey from war-torn countries such as Syria, Afghanistan and Iraq. The French government announced last week that it would be closing down the camp, with bulldozers moving in to tear down makeshift homes built by asylum seekers. However, the plan has been met with fierce opposition from charities and human rights activists, who argue that the eviction will leave thousands of vulnerable people without adequate shelter and support. The authorities have also been accused of using heavy-handed tactics to disperse the crowds, with reports of tear gas being used against those protesting the demolition. So far, around 1,000 people have been relocated to reception centres across France, while some are choosing to stay in the camp, despite the fact that all its structures will eventually be demolished. The situation at the camp is growing increasingly tense, with reports of violent clashes between police and protesters, as well as between rival groups of migrants. The French government insists that the closure of the camp is necessary to improve security in the region, but many accuse the authorities of failing to provide adequate solutions for the long-term future of the asylum seekers. The dismantling of the camp has come under intense scrutiny from both national and international media, and the fate of those living there remains uncertain.

Serena Williams won her seventh Australian Open and 23rd Grand Slam singles title with a straight-sets victory over her sister Venus. The 36-year-old American made it 18 wins in a row against her 38-year-old sibling with a 6-4 6-4 triumph on Saturday night at Melbourne Park. It was a record-equalling seventh Australian Open title for Serena, who also triumphed in Melbourne in 2003, 2005, 2007, 2009, 2010 and 2015. Only Margaret Court, with 11 Australian titles, has won more singles crowns at a single Grand Slam tournament. Serena's latest win took her past Steffi Graf's Open-era record of 22 major titles. Only Court, with 24, has won more. "I don't even know how to feel, I'm just so happy," an emotional Serena said in a courtside interview after the match. "Thank you so much everyone for coming out and supporting me. It really means a lot. "Of course I have to congratulate Venus, she's an amazing person. There's no way I would be at 23 without her, there's no way I would have played four Olympic gold medals without her. Thank you so much, you're the best competitor I could ever ask for." Venus, who was appearing in a record-equalling 30th Major final, paid tribute to her sister in her post-match speech. "I'm enormously proud of what we've accomplished," she said. "All those times when I couldn't play because of injury, she carried the torch. She's been unbelievable. Congratulations Serena on number 23, wow."

The Mongol Empire was governed by a civilian and military code, called the Yassa, created by Genghis Khan. It also established customs and rituals, such as saluting the Khan by kneeling before him. In addition to the Yassa, Genghis Khan established a decentralized system of administration that gave local leaders considerable independence in running local affairs, while maintaining tight control over foreign policy and military strategy. This decentralized system, known as the "Mongolian System," allowed the Empire to remain united despite its vast size and disparate ethnic composition. The Mongol Empire sought to ensure the loyalty of its subjects through a combination of violence, rewards, and patronage. Genghis Khan was known for his merciless treatment of enemies, but he also rewarded those who were loyal to him with titles, land grants, and other privileges. He placed great emphasis on meritocracy and often promoted people to positions of authority based on their skill and ability rather than their social standing or ethnicity. The Mongol Empire was highly militaristic and maintained a large army composed of soldiers from many different ethnic backgrounds. The army was divided into divisions called tumens, each led by an experienced general. Discipline was strict and punishments harsh, but the army was nevertheless well trained and successful in conquest.

We consider the problem of learning a non-deterministic probabilistic system consistent with a given finite set of positive and negative tree samples. Consistency is defined with respect to strong simulation Okay, let me explain what each of those terms means. - Non-deterministic probabilistic system: This is a type of system where outcomes are influenced by random factors. This means that even if we know the current state of the system and the actions taken, we cannot predict the exact outcome. - Positive tree samples: These are examples of trees that show the expected behavior of the system under certain conditions (e.g., if a certain event occurs, then the system will behave in a certain way). - Negative tree samples: These are examples of trees that show what the system should not do in certain situations. - Consistency: In this context, consistency means that the learned probabilistic system behaves in the same way as the positive tree samples and not like the negative tree samples. - Strong simulation: This is a type of simulation where we check that the behavior of one system is a proper subset of the other. In this case, we want to ensure that the learned probabilistic system can simulate the behavior of the positive tree samples, but not the negative tree samples. So, putting it all together, we are trying to learn a non-deterministic probabilistic system that can simulate the behavior of positive tree samples and avoid simulating the behavior of negative tree samples, consistent with the principle of strong simulation.

AWS S3 is a cloud storage service that offers high durability, availability, and security at a relatively low cost. However, some users may be hesitant to use the service because of its potential fees. AWS S3's pricing model is based on the amount of data stored and the level of access required. There are three tiers of storage: Standard, Infrequent Access, and Reduced Redundancy. Standard storage is designed for frequently accessed data, while Infrequent Access is for data that is not accessed often. Reduced Redundancy is a lower-cost option for data that can be tolerate some degree of loss. Users can also choose the level of access they need: either Standard or Reduced Redundancy. Standard provides higher availability and durability, while Reduced Redundancy gives users the ability to save money by reducing the number of copies of their data. There is no upfront fee for using AWS S3. Users only pay for the storage they use and the level of access they require. Prices start at 0.03 per gigabyte per month for Standard storage and 0.0125 per gigabyte per month for Reduced Redundancy storage. Some users may be concerned about the potential costs of using AWS S3. However, the service offers a number of features that can help users keep costs under control. For example, users can set up lifecycle policies to automatically move data to cheaper storage options over time. Overall, AWS S3 is a cloud storage service that offers a good balance of features and price. For most users, the Standard storage option will be sufficient. However, users with large amounts of data or special storage requirements may want to consider the Infrequent Access or Reduced Redundancy options.

magniX, an Australian engineering firm, in a partnership with Harbour Air, a Canadian air-ferry service, has performed the first fully-electric commercial aircraft test flight. The 15-minute flight took place in Vancouver, using a single-engined de Havilland DHC-2 Beaver seaplane. The Australian firm has been working with Harbour Air and magniX to develop the electric propulsion system for the last six months, which has seen the addition of an electric motor and motor controller to a standard Beaver aircraft. The company was quick to point out that the flight did not use any battery power and was powered entirely by a ground-based generator. The magni500 electric motor used in the Beaver is capable of up to 750 horsepower (559 kilowatts). This is more than twice the power of the original piston engine it replaced. While magniX says the motor weighs approximately one-third of what a similar piston engine would weigh, the entire electric airplane project still weighs around 2,000 pounds (907 kilograms) more than a conventional Beaver. While magniX says the flight was purely a test, it has big plans for electric commercial flights in the future. In fact, the company says it wants to have a commercial electric plane flying within three years. As part of this effort, magniX has also signed an agreement with AeroTEC, an aerospace testing and certification firm based in Washington state, to collaborate on the development of an electric nine-seat plane called the eCaravan. The goal for the eCaravan is to demonstrate the feasibility of electric aviation technology at scale. This means operating an electric airplane with multiple motors, batteries, and passengers. magniX hopes to have the first version of the eCaravan ready to fly later this year. Harbour Air, meanwhile, has announced its own plans to convert its entire fleet of seaplanes to electric power. The company believes it can do this within five years. harbour Air's CEO, Greg McDougall, told CTV News, "I think the whole world is moving to electric, so we have to move to electric."

The letter 'Q' is almost always followed by the letter 'U' in English words. This is because the sound represented by the letter 'Q' - known as the "voiceless uvular stop" - is difficult to pronounce by itself. Adding the letter 'U' creates the sound of the "voiceless bilabial stop" - which is easier to say. This combination of 'Q' and 'U' makes up a digraph, which is a combination of two letters that represent a single sound. This convention is specific to English and is not applicable to all languages.

The internet has become an essential part of our daily lives. It has transformed the way we work, communicate, and access information. However, not everyone has equal access to the internet, especially in large cities like New York City, where high-speed internet can be expensive and limited to specific areas. That is why a group of internet activists and tech enthusiasts in New York City came together to create their own community-owned and operated wireless mesh network, known as NYC Mesh. The group is part of a growing movement of community mesh networks across the country and the world, which aim to provide affordable, high-speed internet access to everyone. Unlike traditional internet service providers, NYC Mesh is not a corporation, but a nonprofit organization run by volunteers who believe that internet access is a basic human right. Members of the network pay a small monthly fee to cover the cost of the equipment and maintenance. In return, they get access to a fast and reliable internet connection that is uncensored and unmonitored. NYC Mesh members are not only consumers but also owners of the network. They help build and maintain the network infrastructure by installing and configuring routers on their rooftops, balconies, and windowsills. This creates a decentralized network where every member contributes to the overall capacity and resilience of the network. The DIY approach of NYC Mesh is in contrast to the top-down, profit-driven model of traditional ISPs. The network is agile and adaptable, able to respond quickly to the needs of the community. When Hurricane Sandy hit New York City, for example, the network was able to provide internet access to affected neighborhoods when traditional ISPs were down. NYC Mesh is not only about access to the internet but also about community building. The network hosts regular events and workshops to educate members on internet technology and digital literacy. It also provides a platform for collaboration and peer-to-peer sharing of resources. As the internet continues to play an increasingly important role in our lives, the need for affordable and equitable access becomes more critical. NYC Mesh and other community mesh networks offer a promising alternative to the current internet infrastructure dominated by a few powerful corporations. They demonstrate that the DIY spirit is alive and well, and that with the right tools and the right people, we can build a better and more democratic internet for all.

Masten Space Systems, a California-based space transportation company, has announced plans to develop a GPS-like network for the Moon. The proposed system, called the Lunar Navigational Satellite System (LNSS), would provide essential navigation and communication services for future Moon missions. The LNSS project is being funded by NASA's Lunar Surface Innovation Initiative program, which aims to develop technologies and capabilities that will enable sustainable lunar exploration. Masten Space Systems is one of several companies selected by NASA to participate in the program. According to Masten Space Systems CEO Sean Mahoney, the LNSS network will consist of a constellation of small satellites in lunar orbit. These satellites will work together to provide accurate positioning, timing, and communication services for lunar landers, rovers, and other spacecraft. "Navigation and communication are essential for any space mission, and the Moon is no exception," Mahoney said in a statement. "The LNSS network will be a critical infrastructure for future activities on the lunar surface, enabling safer and more efficient exploration and ultimately paving the way for a sustained human presence on the Moon." NASA officials also praised the LNSS project, saying it has the potential to transform lunar exploration by providing reliable navigation and communication services for future missions. "The LNSS network is an exciting development that will help us achieve our goal of sustainable lunar exploration," said Steve Clarke, Deputy Associate Administrator for Exploration in NASA's Science Mission Directorate. "We look forward to working with Masten Space Systems and other partners to realize this vision." The LNSS project is still in the early stages of development, with Masten Space Systems aiming to launch the first LNSS satellites in the mid-2020s. If successful, the network could pave the way for more extensive lunar exploration, ultimately making space exploration safer and more accessible for future generations.

John Nash's theory, which is called Nash Equilibrium, was revolutionary because it challenged the traditional way of understanding decision-making in economics, game theory, and social sciences. Nash's theory states that in any given situation, when all players involved make rational decisions based on their own self-interest, the outcome will be a state of equilibrium. This means that no player can benefit by changing their strategy while the other players continue to use the same strategy. The applicability of Nash's theory is widespread, as it can be used to explain strategic interactions in many different fields such as economics, politics, and biology. For example, it can be used to explain why countries are afraid to disarm their nuclear weapons, why people choose to vote or not, why firms choose to collude, and even why animals fight over resources. It has become a foundational concept in understanding decision-making in a variety of disciplines, and its implications have shaped research and policy decisions in many fields.

By Tom Carter It was a chance encounter in a small conference room above a coffee shop a fifteen minute walk from BBC Broadcasting House that would soon become one of the most significant meetings in the history of cryptography. We had been invited to meet the man who said he was Satoshi Nakamoto, the creator of Bitcoin. At first glance Nakamoto looked like any other middle-aged man, wearing a plain grey suit and tie. He spoke with a soft Japanese accent and seemed reluctant to divulge too much information about himself. But his story was compelling. According to Nakamoto, he had invented Bitcoin in 2008 as a way to make money transfers faster, easier and more secure. He claimed he had written the original code for the cryptocurrency, which was released on the internet in 2009. His identity remained a mystery until now, but he finally revealed himself to us in this quiet conference room. Nakamoto said he created Bitcoin to be a decentralised currency, not controlled by any government or central bank. He argued that it could help reduce costs and make money transfers easier for people all over the world. We asked about the recent surge in the price of Bitcoin and whether he had profited from it. He replied simply, "I have no interest in the price of Bitcoin. I only care about the technology behind it." He also expressed concern about the state of the cryptocurrency market, warning that it was still in its early stages and that there were a number of risks associated with investing in it. When we asked him what his plans were for the future, he said he wanted to continue developing the technology and to help spread the word about how cryptocurrencies can revolutionise global finance. Although Nakamoto remains something of an enigma, it was a privilege to meet him in person. It's impossible to know if he is indeed the creator of Bitcoin, but his enthusiasm and commitment to the project is clear. It will be fascinating to see how his vision of a new financial system evolves in the years to come.

High-performance implementations of graph algorithms are challenging toimplement on new parallel hardware such as GPUs because of three challenges: (1) the difficulty of coming up with graph building blocks, (2) the irregular and unpredictable memory accesses that graphs generate, and (3) the difficulties arising from the highly dynamic nature of graph-based applications. To address the first challenge, researchers have proposed various techniques to develop building blocks that can be used to implement graph algorithms efficiently on parallel hardware such as GPUs. One such technique is the use of graph analytics libraries, which provide pre-built kernels and data structures suitable for different graph algorithms. For the second challenge, researchers have proposed various memory management techniques such as the use of graph partitioning, coalescing of memory accesses, and the use of hybrid CPU-GPU systems to reduce the impact of irregular memory accesses. Finally, to address the highly dynamic nature of graph-based applications, researchers have proposed various dynamic scheduling techniques such as work-stealing and load balancing to distribute computation across processing cores efficiently. Overall, the challenges of implementing graph algorithms on parallel hardware such as GPUs are significant, but ongoing research has resulted in promising solutions that are improving the scalability and efficiency of graph-based applications.

The amount of water that leaves from each of the exit pipes will depend on the diameter of the pipes and the velocity of the flowing water in the horizontal pipe. Assuming that all the exit pipes have the same diameter, the first exit pipe will receive the maximum flow rate of water, as it is the closest to the source of the water. As the water continues to flow, the velocity will decrease, resulting in a decrease in the flow rate. So, the subsequent exit pipes will receive less flow rate than the previous ones. This phenomenon is well-known in fluid mechanics and is called the "Bernoulli's Principle." According to this principle, as the velocity of a fluid increases, the pressure exerted by the fluid decreases. So, the pressure at the first exit pipe will be higher than at the subsequent exit pipes, resulting in a higher flow rate at the first exit pipe. To sum up, the first exit pipe will receive the maximum flow rate of water, followed by the subsequent exit pipes getting a progressively lesser flow rate due to the decrease in velocity and pressure of the flowing water.

Compare a cold plate of spaghetti and pasta with a hot one. The hot one will have water evaporating from it, while in the cold one the water is trapped While both the cold plate of spaghetti and the hot one contain cooked pasta, there are several differences between them. The primary difference is that the hot plate of spaghetti has been recently cooked and is still steaming, while the cold plate of spaghetti has had time to cool down in the refrigerator. When spaghetti is hot, water molecules within the pasta are actively evaporating, creating steam that rises from the bowl or plate. This steam carries heat away from the pasta, which helps to reduce the overall temperature of the dish. As a result, the consistency of the hot pasta can be somewhat thinner or more watery than the cold pasta. On the other hand, the cold plate of spaghetti does not release steam or evaporate water in the same way. Because the pasta has had time to cool, any water that was originally present has had time to settle back into the dish. Advances in deep neural networks (DNN) greatly bolster real-time detection of anomalous IoT data. However, IoT devices can barely afford complex DNN models due to limited computational power and energy budget. Recently, deep learning-based models have been proposed to reduce the model size and computational complexity by transforming complex DNN models into lightweight and compact ones with nearly the same accuracy. For example, a novel approach called Knowledge Distillation (KD) can be used to compress DNNs. KD uses a small student network to learn the knowledge from a large teacher network. Another popular method is called Pruning which reduces the number of parameters in a neural network without majorly affecting its performance. Quantization is also widely used to reduce the memory footprint of a model while preserving its accuracy. In addition, several recent research works focus on designing new architectures for efficient anomaly detection. For instance, an architecture called AnoGAN has been proposed that uses generative adversarial networks for anomaly detection. It consists of an encoder-decoder based generator and a discriminator, which are trained jointly and work together to identify anomalous data points. Overall, the combination of these techniques can greatly reduce the model size and computational complexity while maintaining high accuracy, thus making deep learning-based anomaly detection feasible for IoT devices.

The top number in the time signature indicates how many beats there are in the measure, and the bottom indicates what note length gets the beat. The revolt, which spread from the Black Forest and Alsace across much of Germany, was brutally crushed by Protestant princes with support from the Emperor. Storch's followers were burned at the stake, while Muntzer was beheaded near Muhlhausen. Reformation in Switzerland The Reformation in Switzerland began in 1519 when Huldrych Zwingli became the pastor in Zurich. At first he sought to reform the church within the framework of Christian humanism. While some of his colleagues supported him, many of his parishioners rejected him. In 1523 he announced a new doctrine: Christian faith was not only based on reason, but also on revelation; that is, on the Bible. Thus, Zwingli was not only a theologian, but also one of the first thinkers to go beyond Scholasticism to a more modern understanding of religion. His ideas were controversial but quickly spread through Swiss cities such as Basel, Bern and Geneva. In 1529, under pressure from Zurich, Berne and Basel, the Diet of Constance formulated the First Helvetic Confession. By 1531, Zwingli and Luther had broken from each other over the question of the presence of Christ in the Eucharist. In 1536, John Calvin, who had lived in Switzerland for four years, wrote his Institutes of the Christian Religion, which set out our theology in a systematic and profound way. He continued to develop these ideas in his sermons and commentaries. Calvin's ideas spread rapidly across Europe, especially in France and the Netherlands. By 1560, Calvinism had become the predominant form of Protestantism in Scotland and the Netherlands. Reformation in England The English Reformation began in the 16th century under King Henry VIII . The movement to reform church practices in England began as part of the wider European Reformations. Many factors contributed to the movement, including Martin Luther's writings in Germany, John Wycliffe's criticisms of the English church and the rise of the Tudor dynasty. Henry VIII originally opposed the Reformation. However, he later broke away from the Catholic Church and established the Church of England after Pope Clement VII refused to annul his marriage to Catherine of Aragon. Under Edward VI , son of Henry VIII, Protestantism advanced rapidly in England. Edward's short reign saw the abolition of images and the introduction of the Book of Common Prayer. During the reign of Edward's sister Mary I , who restored Catholicism, hundreds of Protestants were burned at the stake. Elizabeth I , daughter of Henry VIII and Anne Boleyn, restored Protestantism after she came to the throne in 1558. The English Reformation had lasting effects on all aspects of English life. For example, it led to the development of a distinctive English style of art and architecture, as well as a vernacular literature. The Reformation in Ireland The Reformation did not make much progress in Ireland. The country remained strongly Catholic, despite the efforts of English kings and queens to impose Protestantism. The Reformation in the rest of Europe France Protestantism made little headway in France until the middle of the 16th century, when the movement gained momentum, particularly in the south-west of the country. By the end of the century, however, the movement had been effectively suppressed by the Catholic kings of France, with the help of the Inquisition. The Netherlands The Reformation made significant progress in the Netherlands. William of Orange led the Dutch revolt against Spanish rule and established the Dutch Republic. The Republic became a haven for Protestants, and Amsterdam became an important centre of the international Calvinist movement. Poland and Hungary The Reformation made little progress in Poland and Hungary. Both countries remained strongly Catholic. Scandinavia The Reformation made significant progress in Scandinavia. Lutheranism was established as the state religion in Denmark, Norway and Sweden. Spain and Portugal The Reformation made little progress in Spain and Portugal. Both countries remained strongly Catholic. Sweden See also: History of Sweden before 1809 The Reformation made significant progress in Sweden. Lutheranism was established as the state religion in 1527. The Counter-Reformation The Catholic Church responded to the challenges of the Reformation with the Counter-Reformation. This was a period of reform and renewal within the Catholic Church. It began with the Council of Trent and ended with the Peace of Westphalia (1648). Summary: Genome-to-genome comparisons require designating anchor points, which are given by Maximum Exact Matches (MEMs) between their sequences. For large genomes this is a challenging problem and the performance of existing methods may be affected. However, recent advances in algorithms have led to the development of new tools that can efficiently and accurately identify anchor points, making genome-to-genome comparisons easier and more precise. These tools are crucial in the field of comparative genomics, where scientists study the similarities and differences between genomes of different species.

Look at your accumulated clothes and possessions, your home, friends, family, job, the food in your cupboards, everything. Maybe there isn't much for you to look at now, but be assured, if you could look back on your life 25 years from now, it would be overwhelming. The number of things you have experienced and possessed would dwarf everything in your life today. I am not trying to scare you here. I simply want you to realize that all of these things are transient. They will all be gone one day. And when they are gone, what is left of you? Do you exist because of the things you own or experience, or are those things temporary manifestations of the real you? There is a very old saying, "When you die, no matter who you are or how much you own, you can only take with you your name." Your name is the only thing you will ever really possess, so make sure it is one you are proud of. 2. Life is precious. One of the most shocking things about losing my father was how fast it happened. He went from being healthy to dead in less than two weeks. He wasn't even sick. One day he was here and the next he was gone. It is hard for me to fathom that there are people out there who don't appreciate life and the gift it is. To be alive is a miracle. The fact that we can wake up each morning, breathe, see, feel, smell, touch, think and dream is amazing. How can we take such a gift for granted? We have no guarantee of tomorrow. I'm not saying we should live our lives as if tomorrow will never come, but we should recognize that it may. How many days have you woken up and wished you hadn't? How many days have you wished you could relive? Don't let those days be a waste. Make them count. 3. Happiness comes from within. The pursuit of happiness is an age-old quest. But what is happiness? Is it a function of what we do or what we have? Does it come from our job, our family, our friends, our possessions or our experiences? The answer is no. Happiness doesn't come from anything outside of us. It is an internal state. It is something we create. So if we want to be happy, we need to learn how to create happiness from within. 4. Life is about relationships. The most important thing in life is not what we do or what we have, but who we are with. Our relationships are the most important things in our lives. They are what give our lives meaning and purpose. If you don't have strong relationships, you will never be truly happy. You may have all the money in the world, but if you don't have anyone to share it with, it means nothing. 5. Everyone dies. This may seem like a morbid thing to say, but it is true. Everyone dies. It is the one thing we all have in common. Death is the great equalizer. No one is exempt. So what does this mean for us? It means that life is precious and we need to make the most of it. It means that we need to cherish our relationships and make sure we are living a life that is meaningful and fulfilling. 6. Life is short. This is related to the previous point, but it bears repeating. Life is short. We are here for such a brief time and then we are gone. This is why it is so important to make the most of the time we have. 7. You can't take it with you. This is another way of saying that life is about relationships, not possessions. When we die, we can't take our possessions with us. The only things we can take with us are our relationships. So if you want to be happy, focus on your relationships and making them strong. Don't worry about material things. They are fleeting and will ultimately be meaningless. 8. Time is the most precious commodity. This is related to the previous two points, but it is worth repeating. Time is the most precious commodity. We only have a limited amount of it and we need to make the most of it. 9. Life is unpredictable. This is a hard truth to accept, but it is true. Life is unpredictable. We never know what is going to happen. We can plan and prepare all we want, but ultimately we have no control over what happens. This is why it is so important to live in the present moment and to enjoy the moment we are in. The past is gone and the future is uncertain. All we have is the present. 10. Life is precious. This is the most important lesson of all. Life is precious. We need to cherish it and make the most of it. We need to appreciate every moment we have.

Path signatures are powerful nonparametric tools for time series analysis, shown to form a universal and characteristic feature map for Euclidean valued time series data. We lift the theory of shapelets to the domain of graph data, and propose Graphlet Signatures (GS), a novel nonparametric descriptor for the analysis of graph time series. GS are obtained by computing the distribution of graphlet densities over an ordered sequence of graph snapshots, and encoding this distribution in a signature vector. We demonstrate that our signatures capture the structural evolution of graph time series data in a manner that is invariant under graph isomorphisms and robust to noise, while allowing for efficient comparison and clustering of different sequences. We empirically evaluate the performance of GS on both synthetic and real-world datasets, demonstrating its ability to capture meaningful patterns in graphs and its effectiveness in tasks such as classification and clustering. Finally, we present a case study showing how GS can be used to aid in the discovery of structure in a large-scale citation network dataset. Our results suggest that GS provide a promising tool for the analysis of graph time series data.

In this extended abstract we present the gubs Upper Bound Solver. gubs is a dedicated constraint solver over the naturals for inequalities formed over uninterpreted function symbols and standard arithmetic . gubs is designed to be used as an oracle in theorem provers, such as Coq and IsabelleHOL. The solver takes advantage of a simple representation of arithmetic constraints and symbolic reasoning over them. It uses heuristics for deciding when to use different solving strategies and also employs a suite of numerical constraint solvers. We demonstrate the solver by showing how it can be used to prove the successor function on naturals is injective in only four lines of code.

Relatives of 24 rubber plantation workers killed by British troops almost 70 years ago in Malaya have lost their appeal for an official investigation. Family members of the victims had asked the UK government to open an inquiry into their deaths, but this has now been rejected. The families have long maintained that the victims, who included women and children, were unarmed civilians. However, the British army claims that the villagers were communist guerrillas and the killings were justified and lawful. This dispute over the circumstances of the deaths has been ongoing since the massacre occurred. Last year, a legal challenge was launched against the UK government's refusal to open an inquiry, which has now been rejected by the Supreme Court. Speaking after the ruling, the lawyer representing the relatives said: "This is a devastating outcome for the families. They have waited nearly 70 years to get justice and today they have been denied it." The UK government has offered its condolences to the families and said it recognizes the tragedy of what happened, but it has refused to launch an inquiry. It says that launching a fresh investigation would be disproportionate and unnecessary as there have already been three separate investigations. For the relatives of the victims, however, this ruling means that their fight for justice continues. They have vowed to keep pushing for an inquiry and say they will not rest until the truth about the Batang Kali massacre is revealed.

If any of you frequent rbadhistory, there is a rather infamous [chart] that captures a popular perception of the Middle Ages as a "dark age" that retarded scientific progress by a thousand years. The chart in question is known as the "Frazer-Gow Chart," created by two historians, Arthur Frazer and James Gow. The chart shows the development of scientific knowledge from 500 BC to 1900 AD, with each period divided into five distinct categories: Pre-Christian, Early Christian, Medieval, Renaissance, and Modern. According to the chart, science stagnated or even regressed during the Middle Ages, with the lowest point being in the medieval period. However, this chart has been widely criticized for its lack of evidence and historical accuracy. Many historians have argued that there was significant scientific progress during the Middle Ages, especially in the fields of mathematics, astronomy, and medicine, and that the Renaissance was more of a continuation than a revival of ancient knowledge.

This paper addresses the problem of planning for a robot with a directional obstacle-detection sensor that must move through a cluttered environment. The planning objective is to remain safe by avoiding collisions with the obstacles, while maximizing the robot's speed. It had been a perfect day for Sarah. The weather was sunny with a slight breeze in the air, and her work presentation had been a success. She was feeling good about herself and decided to stop by her favourite cafe for a coffee and some cake. As she was enjoying her afternoon treat, she overheard a group of teenagers laughing and joking around. They were being quite loud but Sarah didn't mind. Just then, one of the teens accidentally spilled their drink on Sarah's newly purchased dress. Sarah was angry, but before she could even say anything, the teen shrugged and said, "Sorry, didn't mean to." Sarah's anger boiled over. She had held back her emotions for too long and this was the final straw. "No apology accepted," she said, her voice shaking with anger. "You kids need to learn some manners and respect." The teens looked at her incredulously, not knowing how to respond. Sarah didn't care. She stormed out of the cafe, fuming with anger. As she walked down the street, she realized that maybe she was overreacting. But as she looked down at her ruined dress, she couldn't help but feel justified in her anger. The next day, Sarah returned to the cafe and saw the same teens sitting at a nearby table. She took a deep breath and approached them. "I'm sorry for my outburst yesterday," she said. "I was having a bad day and I shouldn't have taken it out on you guys." The teens smiled and nodded, accepting her apology. Sarah felt relieved and grateful that they were willing to forgive her. But as she walked away, she realized that even though the teens had forgiven her, she could never forgive herself for the way she acted. She vowed from then on to take a deep breath and think before reacting, even when she was having a bad day. She learned that sometimes it's better to let go of anger and move on, rather than holding onto it and hurting others in the process.

There are also dedicated helplines available, such as the Crime Victims Helpline and the Sexual Abuse Referral Centre, both of which offer free, confidential support. Additionally, many GP surgeries have access to specialist counsellors and therapists who may be able to provide extra support. It is important to remember that you are not alone and help is available. If you have been affected by criminal activity or sexual abuse, contact your local police force or one of the above organisations for further advice and support.

We present UDify, a multilingual multi-task model capable of accurately predicting universal part-of-speech, morphological features, lemmas, and dependency trees simultaneously for all 124 Universal Dependencies treebanks across 75 languages. By leveraging a multi-task objective, UDify is able to learn from all the available data, achieving state-of-the-art performance across the board. The model is based on a BERT-style transformer architecture, which is pre-trained on large monolingual corpora for each language. The pre-trained model is then fine-tuned on the Universal Dependencies treebanks and achieves excellent performance on all tasks with very few hyperparameter tuning. Our experiments demonstrate that UDify outperforms existing models on all four tasks, providing a single model that can be used to accurately annotate linguistically diverse datasets. Furthermore, our experiments show that by using the multitask objective, we are able to improve the accuracy of both the part-of-speech tagging and dependency parsing tasks. We make our code and trained models publicly available to facilitate further research in this field.

Federated Learning (FL) is a decentralized machine learning protocol that allows a set of participating agents to collaboratively train a model without sharing their data. This makes FL particularly suitable for scenarios where data from multiple parties needs to be used to train a model while maintaining privacy of the individual data sources. FL works by training each agent's local models on its own data, sending these updates to a central server which aggregates them into a global model. This global model is then sent back to each agent, which further trains their own models on it and sends the updated results back to the server. The process is repeated with the new global model until convergence is reached.

Consider the problem of sampling sequentially from a finite number of N 2 populations, specified by random variables X I k, I 1, ..., N, and k 1, 2, ...; the objective is to estimate the sum of all means. The problem arises in situations in which each population has a size n k N and a known sampling fraction f k; for example, k might correspond to different subpopulations or time periods. Some of the N 2 pairs (I, k) may not be sampled, so let x ik denote the observation from population I in time period k if it is observed and missing otherwise. If a simple random sample without replacement is drawn from each nonempty population, then (1) is an unbiased estimator of the sum of all means. However, when N is large, it is usually preferable to draw samples with replacement, particularly when the populations have different sizes andor the sizes are unknown, because then the estimator remains unbiased. This approach was advocated by Cochran (1977, p. 72): "For large N and small n k , this estimator usually will give more precise estimates than will the usual estimator (1)." However, Cochran also noted that "it may be possible to correct for this loss in precision, thus making the estimator (1) more efficient." In fact, Cochran demonstrated that the estimator (1) is more efficient than the estimator (2), which is obtained by first drawing a sample of size K from the union of the N 2 populations and then calculating the statistic (1) using only the K observations in the sample. In this article we show how to use Cochran's idea in practice. We also show how to extend it to the problem of sequential sampling from infinitely many populations - one of the most common situations to arise in practice. Consider the following scenario. At each stage of the experiment, a pair of populations is selected randomly, with each population being selected independently of the others. These two populations form the current sample; a random subsample of size n 1 is drawn from the first population and a random subsample of size n 2 is drawn from the second population. Then we repeat this procedure at each stage, selecting new pairs of populations in the same way. Finally, we obtain an estimate of the sum of the means of all the populations by applying formula (1) to the data collected over the course of the experiment. This method of sampling was described in detail and analyzed in the context of a multistage design by Cochran (1954). He showed that as the number of stages increases, the variance of the estimator (1) among these designs decreases faster than did the variance under a single-stage design, unless we have information about the hierarchical structure of the data, such as the clustering of individuals within villages. Cochran showed that the gain in efficiency provided by a multistage design can be significant, especially for small values of n 1 and n 2 . The sequential sampling algorithm above is a special case of Cochran's designs, for which n 1 n 2 . A key advantage of the above sequential sampling algorithm is that it provides an opportunity to implement a simple correction to improve the efficiency of the estimator (1). For this purpose, we define r ijk as follows: r ijk 1 if population i is sampled in stage j and r ijk 0 otherwise. Then we define the estimator (3) where u j 1N 1j 1N 2j , N 1j is the number of times that one of the populations in stage j is sampled and N 2j is the number of times that both populations in stage j are sampled. The estimator (3) is identical to the estimator (2) in the single-stage design. Hence, Cochran's conclusion that the estimator (1) is more efficient than the estimator (2) holds in our situation as well. However, as he noted, we can correct for this loss in efficiency by modifying the estimator (1) as follows: (4) It is straightforward to show that this estimator is equivalent to the estimator (3) when there is no correlation between the variables x ik and r ijk , and hence more efficient. By contrast, if the two variables are correlated, the estimator (3) is more efficient than the estimator (4). The best approach depends on the structure of the underlying data. If the populations have the same size, then the correlation between the variables x ik and r ijk is zero, so we should use the estimator (4). If the populations have different sizes, then the correlation is not zero and the estimator (3) is often preferable. For example, suppose that we have 10,000 villages and 200,000 individuals, and we want to calculate the mean weight of the individuals. The sun had been beating down mercilessly on the small town all day. The heat was so intense that the asphalt on the streets had started to soften and buckle. Children were nowhere to be seen, having long since retreated indoors to the blessed relief of air conditioning. Even the birds had stopped singing. The only sound to be heard was the occasional car driving slowly down the street, its occupants wilting in the heat. All of the houses on Main Street looked the same, their white paint faded by the sun. They all had porches with rocking chairs, and flowerpots overflowing with petunias. It was as if time had stood still in this town. I was sitting on the porch of my house, fanning myself with a piece of cardboard. I was about to go inside and take a cold shower when I saw a car coming down the street. It was an old car, and it looked like it was going to break down any minute. It finally made it to my house and came to a stop. A young woman got out of the car and walked up to the porch. She was sweating and her clothes were sticking to her skin. She looked like she was about to faint. "Can I help you?" I asked. "I'm looking for the library," she said, panting. "I need to use the restroom." "The library is closed," I lied. "It's too hot." In reality, the library was open. I just didn't want this woman to come into my house. She looked dirty and sweaty, and I didn't want her to track dirt onto my clean floors. "Please," she begged. "I'll be quick. I just need to use the restroom and then I'll be out of your way." "I'm sorry," I said. "You can't come in." I watched as the woman got back into her car and drove away. She looked so exhausted and defeated. I felt a twinge of guilt, but then I shook it off. I didn't want her in my house.

If you picture light as a particle tracing out a sine wave, the particle's forward velocity is the speed of light, and its location in the sine wave is the phase of the light wave. The phase of a light wave refers to the point in its cycle, which can be measured in degrees or radians, at any given time. The phase determines how the light wave interacts with other waves, particularly when waves are combined or interfere with each other. Measuring the phase of light waves is important in many applications, including telecommunications, microscopy, and astronomy.

I definitely realize a lot of harm can come from poor examples of cultural appropriation. Often my idea of bad appropriation was the Christianizing of many pagan holidaystraditions by the Catholic Church, but there are far more detrimental examples of appropriation in our world today. It seems that the people who are the most guilty of cultural appropriation are those who have the least understanding of what it is and how damaging it can be. Cultural appropriation happens when someone from a dominant culture adopts traditions or customs of a marginalized group without any real understanding or respect for the original culture. It's often motivated by a desire to be "exotic" or "trendy." This can have a number of harmful consequences. It can lead to the erasure of the original culture, as well as its history and traditions. It can also lead to the commodification of that culture, as well as its people. Cultural appropriation is often perpetuated by those who have a lot of privilege and power. They are the ones who are able to profit off of the cultures they appropriate. This is why it's so important to be aware of the issue and to try to avoid participating in it. We all have a responsibility to learn about and respect the cultures around us.

Factory activity in China, the world's second largest economy, shrank at its fastest rate in two years in July as new orders fell more than anticipated. The latest figures from the National Bureau of Statistics show that the Purchasing Managers' Index (PMI) for manufacturing was 49.7 in July - down from 50.0 in June and the lowest since July 2016. A reading below 50 indicates contraction. The data also showed that new orders fell to their lowest level since March 2009, while output and employment both declined. Analysts had been expecting a modest improvement in the PMI for July, with some forecasting growth of up to 51.0. The slowdown in activity reflects the impact of the US-China trade war, which has seen tariffs imposed on billions of dollars worth of goods. This, in turn, has weakened demand for Chinese exports and put pressure on domestic manufacturers. It is also a reminder of the fragility of the global economy, which is already facing headwinds from slowing economic growth in Europe, India and Japan. The Chinese government has been trying to cushion the blow by introducing tax cuts and other measures to stimulate the economy. However, these efforts have so far failed to boost sentiment among manufacturers, and the latest figures suggest it will take more time before they start to translate into increased activity.

We present a polynomial-space algorithm that computes the number of independent sets of any input graph in time O (1.1389 n) for graphs with maximum degree 3 and in time O (2.11 n) for graphs with maximum degree 4. The previous best running time was O (1.7305 n) due to Mihail and Vazirani [17] for graphs with maximum degree 3 and O (3.1618 n) due to Poljak, Pultr and Turzik [21] for graphs with maximum degree 4. We also present an algorithm that computes the number of independent sets in time O (1.3488 n) for graphs with maximum degree 5. The previous best running time was O (2.3713 n) due to Poljak, Pultr and Turzik [21]. We show that for any positive integer k 2, there exists a graph with maximum degree k for which our algorithm requires time O (2.12 n) to solve the problem of counting independent sets. This proves that this time bound is almost tight for graphs with maximum degree k.

He admitted to me that he was the notorious Hannibal Lecter, and that he had committed some of the most heinous crimes in the history of the country. I was shocked and somewhat scared, but I knew my grandpa was a good man at heart. It was as if he had been carrying this burden with him all his life, and he needed to confess it to someone before he passed away. He told me that he had kept his urges under control for years but they had resurfaced recently. He was afraid he would hurt someone again. That's why he was asking for my help. I couldn't believe this was happening. My grandpa was a serial killer, and now he was asking for my assistance. But then, a strange feeling came over me. It was as if I had inherited his urges or maybe his desire to help people. I knew that I had to help him, even though it meant keeping his secret to myself. As the days went by, my grandpa's health deteriorated, but we spent as much time together as possible. We talked about everything, from his past as a killer to the simple pleasures of life. I wanted to make his last days as comfortable as possible, and I also knew that he was at peace with his conscience because he had finally confided in someone. Finally, my grandpa's time came, and he passed away peacefully in his sleep. I honor his final wish and took his secret to the grave with me. I couldn't imagine the pain it would cause the people he victimized if the truth came out. His passing was painful, but it also gave me a sense of closure. I am grateful for the time we had together, and I know that my grandpa was an extraordinary person who struggled with a dark side.

It all sound the same to me. And to be clear, I know this is what people tend to say about any music they don't "get." People say this about Beethoven - "Oh it all sounds the same." In contrast, to my ears (and I've been listening to classical music since before I was born), all of the Haydn works on this album sound exactly the same. I have yet to find a passage on this album that I could use to start a discussion with someone who is a fan of Haydn and wants to talk about how his style changes over time. "Here's a passage from 1784 and here's one from 1791." And for those of you who are about to write me, yes I know that Haydn spent most of the 1770s writing operas and didn't produce much solo piano music; but I'm familiar with his keyboard concerti and sonatas from this period and they sound very different from the ones on this album. It just doesn't do anything for me.
