While the idea of police using tranquilizer guns to subdue suspects without causing harm may seem appealing in theory, it is not a practical solution in real-life situations. Tranquilizer guns are typically used on animals and can take several minutes to take effect. In a high-pressure situation, such as a potential armed confrontation or a suspect fleeing on foot, waiting for the tranquilizer to take effect can delay the capture of the suspect and put both law enforcement and the public at risk. Additionally, the dosage of the tranquilizer needed to subdue a suspect can vary depending on their size and other factors, making it difficult to determine the appropriate amount to use. In contrast, firearms discharges are quick and can immediately neutralize a threat, allowing law enforcement to swiftly resolve a dangerous situation. Therefore, while non-lethal options such as tasers and pepper spray can be effective in some scenarios, firearms remain an essential tool for law enforcement to neutralize serious threats quickly and efficiently.

In a remarkable breakthrough, scientists have successfully detected brain waves emanating from lab-grown "mini brains." This marks a significant step towards understanding the mysteries of the human brain and could pave the way for revolutionary treatments for neurological disorders. For years, researchers have been growing mini-brains - also known as cerebral organoids - in the lab to better understand the complex workings of the brain. These miniature organs are created by coaxing human stem cells to develop into brain tissue, which then self-organizes into three-dimensional structures that resemble the developing brain of a fetus. Although mini-brains have been useful in certain types of research, scientists have been limited in their ability to study their activity, as they are too small and fragile to be implanted with electrodes to measure their electrical signals. However, in a new study published in the journal Cell Stem Cell, a team of researchers announced that they had detected brain waves in the mini-brains for the first time, using advanced techniques to monitor their activity. The brain waves were strikingly similar to those seen in the human brain, and they occurred in a highly synchronized pattern, suggesting that the organoids are capable of transmitting information across different regions, just like the human brain. The researchers say that this finding could provide a new tool for studying neurological disorders, such as epilepsy and Alzheimer's disease, and open up new avenues for developing treatments. While the study is still in its early stages, the researchers are excited about the potential of their discovery. "Being able to study the activity of these mini-brains in such detail could give us a better understanding of how the human brain works, and could ultimately help us to develop better treatments for a range of neurological conditions," said one of the study's authors. The discovery of brain waves in mini-brains is a remarkable achievement that could have far-reaching implications for neuroscience and medicine. With further research, it may be possible to unlock the secrets of the human brain and find new ways to treat the most complex and devastating neurological disorders.

The names of Nazi SS commanders and guards who operated at the infamous Auschwitz death camp during World War II have been made public by Poland's Institute of National Remembrance (INR). The move is aimed at increasing accountability for those who committed crimes against humanity during the Holocaust. Auschwitz, which was located in German-occupied Poland, was the largest of the Nazi concentration camps and was responsible for the deaths of more than 1.1 million people, mostly Jews. The names, which were compiled by the INR over a period of several years, are searchable on the institute's website. They include the names of more than 9,000 SS officers and guards, along with information about their duties and the time periods they served at the camp. The release of the names is significant because it marks the first time that a comprehensive list of Auschwitz personnel has been made publicly available. Historians and Holocaust researchers have long sought access to such information in order to better understand the inner workings of the camp, which has become a symbol of the atrocities committed during the Holocaust. Many of the guards and commanders named by the INR have already been convicted of war crimes and crimes against humanity. However, there are likely still many who have not been held accountable for their actions. The INR hopes that the release of the names will encourage further investigations and prosecutions, and will also serve as a warning to those who would commit similar crimes in the future. "We believe that in a democratic state, the citizen has the right to know who was responsible for these crimes," said Jarosaw Szarek, president of the INR. The move to release the names has been praised by Jewish organizations and Holocaust survivors, who see it as a step towards justice and accountability for the victims of the Auschwitz death camp. However, some have questioned whether the release of the names could lead to witch hunts or retribution against the families of those named. The INR has said that it has taken measures to protect the privacy of those who are still alive and that it will not tolerate any form of vigilante justice. Overall, the release of the names is seen as an important milestone in the ongoing effort to remember and honor the victims of the Holocaust, and to ensure that the atrocities committed during that dark period of human history are never forgotten.

Uber is having a very public fight right now with NYC Mayor Bill de Blasio, basically arguing that they should be allowed to compete with yellow cabs in a free market. This fight is interesting for a couple of reasons. First, Uber has all the money in the world to hire lawyers, lobbyists, and ad agencies to make a big public argument about this. They're rich and powerful enough to fight entire cities. Second, even though they have lots of money, they actually don't seem to be winning this particular battle. It's been a PR disaster for them. Third, I think it highlights some important issues about what the internet does to business competition. Here's the basic story. Uber is a ride-sharing service that uses an app to connect people who need rides with drivers who are willing to give them. You can use the app to get a ride anywhere, anytime, and it will tell you how long it will take and how much it will cost. The service is very convenient, and it's often cheaper than a traditional taxi. Yellow cabs are regulated by the city, and there are only so many of them. They're expensive, and they're not always available when you need them. Mayor de Blasio wants to limit the number of Uber cars on the road, because he says they're causing traffic problems. Uber says that's not true, and they should be allowed to compete in a free market. The issue here is that the internet is changing the way we do business, and it's not always clear what the rules should be. Should traditional businesses be allowed to operate the same way they always have, or should they have to change to compete with new, internet-based businesses? It's a tough question, and there's no easy answer. But I think it's important to remember that the internet is making it easier for new businesses to enter markets and compete with established businesses. And that's generally a good thing.

As I sat in the waiting room, I couldn't shake the feeling that I was alone in the world. In my mind, there was no doubt that I was the last surviving member of the human race. It didn't matter that there were people in the room with me or that I had just passed by hundreds of people on my way to the clinic. They were all just figments of my imagination. When the therapist called me into his office, I tried to explain my situation to him. But the words wouldn't come out. How can I make him understand that I feel like I'm living in a world that only exists in my mind? He asked me a few questions about my life and my mental state, but I knew his questions were pointless. How could he possibly relate to my situation? After a few more minutes of speaking, he stopped me and asked, "Do you truly believe you are the only human left on this planet, or do you just feel alone?" I stared blankly at him, my mind racing. Was there a chance that I wasn't the only one left? Could there be others out there? The therapist continued. "Your thoughts and feelings are valid, but they may not be based on reality. It's possible that your mind is playing tricks on you, and it's important that we work together to figure out what's going on." I didn't quite believe him, but I agreed to attend regular therapy sessions to try and work through my feelings of isolation. Over the next few weeks, we talked about my childhood, my relationships, and my thoughts about the future. Slowly, I began to realize that my beliefs were irrational, and that there were indeed other people in the world. I'll never forget the moment when I stepped outside of the clinic after one of my appointments, and I saw people walking by. For the first time, I truly saw them. They were real, and they were here. It took some time, but I was able to let go of my beliefs and start living in the real world. I still see the therapist occasionally, but mostly in gratitude. He was able to help me see the world for what it truly was, and for that, I will always be thankful.

Recently I've heard a lot about mandatory vaccination schemes in public schools. I don't see any problem with them. I've heard a few counterarguments, but they seem unsatisfying to me, Mandatory vaccination schemes in public schools have been implemented to protect the public from the spread of infectious diseases. Vaccines have been shown to prevent diseases and save lives. They are also cost-effective because they prevent individuals from getting sick and requiring medical treatment. Some of the counterarguments against mandatory vaccination include concerns about the safety of vaccines, personal freedom and individual rights, and religious or philosophical objections. However, the safety of vaccines has been extensively studied and verified by scientific research, and the benefits of vaccination far outweigh the risks. As for personal freedom and individual rights, it's important to remember that these rights come with responsibilities. We are responsible for not putting others at risk of infectious diseases. By getting vaccinated, we are fulfilling our responsibility to protect others. In terms of religious or philosophical objections, exemptions are usually available, but these exemptions should not be misused to put others at risk. Overall, mandatory vaccination schemes in public schools are an important public health measure to prevent the spread of infectious diseases and protect the health of the community.

Wireless communications are vulnerable against radio frequency (RF) jamming which might be caused either intentionally or unintentionally. A particular subset of wireless networks, vehicular ad-hoc networks (VANET) which incorporate a large number of vehicles, are particularly vulnerable to RF jamming attacks. The attackers can disrupt the communication between the vehicles as well as between the vehicles and the roadside infrastructure (RSI). Jamming is a serious threat to VANETs as it results in degraded performance, denial of service and even life-threatening situations. To mitigate these threats, a variety of countermeasures have been proposed. These include using spread spectrum techniques such as frequency hopping, direct sequence spread spectrum, and orthogonal frequency division multiplexing. Additionally, high gain antennas and multi-hop communication protocol can be used to increase the communication range and reduce the effects of jamming. Authentication schemes can also be employed to ensure the integrity of data transmitted through the network. Furthermore, power control techniques can be used to adjust the transmitted signal power so as to avoid jamming. Finally, appropriate physical and MAC layer protection methods can be used to detect and prevent jamming attacks.

Loops and other very specific shapes are made by extrusion: they are squeezed out of a shaped nozzle and then cut off. So Froot Loops come out as a hollow tube, which is then cut into individual Froot Loops. The top and bottom of the Froot Loop has slightly different shapes, so there's a top and bottom to each Froot Loop. Marshmallows are also extruded, but they are extruded as a solid tube, which is then cut into pieces. The top and bottom of the marshmallow have the same shape, so there's no top or bottom to each marshmallow.

This spell would ensure that if any kingdom were to attack another, they would all suffer the consequences. At first, the rulers were hesitant. They had been taught to believe that war was the only way to settle conflicts, and the idea of using magic to maintain peace seemed like a dangerous gamble. However, Zoltar was persuasive and, seeing the potential for peace and prosperity, many of them ultimately agreed to his proposal. Remarkably, the spell worked. For years, the kingdoms lived in peace, and battles were a thing of the past. No one dared to wage war, knowing the catastrophic consequences of such actions. The spell acted as a deterrent that ensured all disputes were resolved peacefully, and trade flourished as a result. As time went on, the kingdoms grew closer together, becoming allies and friends rather than adversaries. They shared their resources and magical knowledge, and the people of the kingdom prospered. The legacy of Zoltar's spell lived on, and the rulers of each passing generation maintained the pact, ensuring that their kingdoms remained peaceful and prosperous. Years later, as a new age dawned, the crystal that held the mutually assured destruction spell was placed in a museum, a testament to the power of magic to create peace. The once-warring kingdoms that had joined together were now all part of a great union, and they enjoyed an era of prosperity and harmony that lasted for ages. And although no one dared to touch the crystal or the spell it held, the mere presence of it served as a reminder of the power of cooperation and the dangers of war.

While the intention of ensuring equal education for every child may seem noble, making private schooling and homeschooling illegal would ultimately do more harm than good. Many parents choose private schools or homeschooling because they believe that their children will receive a superior education or because they have religious or philosophical objections to certain aspects of the public school system. By taking away these options, students may have to attend schools that do not meet their individual needs or beliefs, which could have adverse effects on their education and overall well-being. Additionally, private and homeschooling families pay taxes that support public schools, even though they don't use them. It would be unfair to force them to financially support a system they do not believe in, while also limiting their educational freedoms. Instead of banning these options, we should work towards improving the public school system to provide a high-quality education that meets the needs and interests of all students.

Shoppers in the United Kingdom had an early Christmas present this November, as retail sales rose by more than expected. Figures released by the Office for National Statistics (ONS) show that UK retail sales increased by 4.6 percent in November, compared to the same month last year. This was far above the 1.2 percent rise that analysts had predicted, and is the highest rate of growth since April. The figures are being attributed to shoppers taking advantage of discounts and promotions at the end of the month ahead of Black Friday. The event, which sees retailers offering deep discounts on a range of products, has become increasingly popular in recent years, and is seen by many as the start of the Christmas shopping season. Analysts believe that shoppers took advantage of the discounts and promotions on offer, leading to a surge in sales. Clothing stores saw their sales increase by 7.3 percent, while department stores saw sales jump by 5.4 percent. Commenting on the results, ONS statistician Rhian Murphy said: "Retail sales increased in November, boosted by strong demand in the clothing and department store sectors, likely due to Black Friday promotions." While the figures are encouraging, there is still some uncertainty over the future. With economic uncertainty continuing due to Brexit, shoppers may be cautious about spending over the coming months. Nevertheless, the figures suggest that shoppers were willing to splash out in November, with retailers likely to be thankful for the extra boost during the busy festive period.

Nazism is an ideology that was developed by Adolf Hitler and his followers in the early 20th century, during his reign as the leader of Nazi Germany from 1933 to 1945. The principles of Nazism were based on a set of beliefs that emphasized the supremacy of the Aryan race, the need for an authoritarian government, rejection of democracy and socialism, and the exaltation of violence and militarism. Some of the key principles of Nazism include: 1. A belief in racial superiority: The Nazis believed that the so-called Aryan race, which was composed of light-skinned people of European descent, was superior to all other races. They saw Jews, Romani people, homosexuals, and people with disabilities as "inferior" and sought to eliminate them. 2. Authoritarian government: The Nazi regime was characterized by a dictatorship in which all power was concentrated in the hands of Hitler and his close associates. The Nazis believed in a strict hierarchy of power, with the Fuhrer (leader) at the top. 3. Opposition to democracy and socialism: The Nazis rejected democratic forms of government and saw socialism, especially of the Marxist variety, as a threat to the purity of the Aryan race. 4. Militarism and expansionism: The Nazis believed in the power of military might and saw war as a means of expanding their influence and territory. They sought to establish a "Greater Germany" through conquest and annexation of neighboring countries. 5. Propaganda and censorship: The Nazis used propaganda to promote their ideology and suppress dissenting views. They also censored books, films, and other forms of media that did not conform to their worldview. Overall, Nazism was a dangerous and destructive ideology that led to the deaths of millions of people during World War II. It is widely regarded as one of the darkest periods in modern history.

The Rankine cycle is sometimes referred to as a practical Carnot cycle because, when an efficient turbine is used, the TS diagram begins to resemble the Carnot cycle. The main difference between the Rankine cycle and the Carnot cycle is that the Carnot cycle is an ideal cycle that operates under perfect conditions, while the Rankine cycle operates under real-world conditions where there is always some loss of heat and energy. However, the Rankine cycle is still an effective method for power generation and is widely used in power plants. It consists of four basic components: a boiler, turbine, condenser, and feed pump. The cycle begins with liquid water being pumped into the boiler, where it is heated until it becomes high-pressure steam. The steam is then directed into a turbine, where it expands and generates mechanical energy. The turbine is connected to a generator, which converts the mechanical energy into electrical energy. After the steam has passed through the turbine, it is then sent to the condenser, where it is cooled and condensed back into liquid form. Finally, a feed pump is used to return the liquid water back to the boiler, and the cycle begins anew. Overall, the Rankine cycle is an efficient and reliable method for power generation, although there is always room for improvement and optimization.

While it's understandable to have concerns about animal welfare and ethical treatment, stating that "meat is murder" isn't an accurate or fair depiction of the complex relationship between humans and animals. First of all, it's important to acknowledge that not all meat production involves killing animals in cruel or inhumane ways - there are many farms and producers who prioritize animal welfare and sustainability. Additionally, many cultures and societies have long-standing traditions around hunting and eating meat, and for some people, it's a key source of nutrition and sustenance. Finally, it's worth noting that not everyone can or wants to adhere to a vegetarian or vegan lifestyle, so claiming that meat is inherently immoral or murderous can come across as dismissive or judgmental towards those who don't share that worldview. Rather than demonizing meat entirely, it's more productive to focus on promoting ethical and sustainable farming practices, reducing food waste, and considering the impact of our dietary choices on both human and animal welfare.

Behavioural economists have shown that people are often averse to inequality and will make choices to avoid unequal outcomes. In this paper, we consider how to allocate indivisible goods fairly in the presence of averse-to-inequality preferences. We start by discussing existing models of fairness, outlining their limitations and then propose a new model which allows us to define fairness in terms of individual preference satisfaction and social welfare. We then develop an algorithm for allocating indivisible goods fairly when preferences are averse-to-inequality. Finally, we test our algorithm on a set of numerical examples and show that it is able to effectively identify fair outcomes in a variety of scenarios.

In processing human produced text using natural language processing (NLP) techniques, two fundamental subtasks that arise are (i) item (i) item Item items Items (i) item (i) segmentation of the text into individual units, such as sentences or words, and (ii) tagging or labeling these units with appropriate semantic categories, such as parts of speech or named entities. One common approach to segmentation is to use punctuation marks, such as periods, question marks, and exclamation marks, as sentence boundaries. For word segmentation, techniques such as word tokenization are used to split the text into individual words. Tagging or labeling can be done using various techniques, such as rule-based systems, statistical models, or machine learning algorithms. These techniques analyze the contextual information around each unit to determine its semantic category. For example, a part of speech tagger may use surrounding words to determine whether a word is a noun or a verb. Named entity recognition (NER) systems can be used to identify entities such as persons, organizations, or locations in a text. Overall, segmentation and tagging are crucial components of NLP systems, as they provide the foundation for many downstream tasks, such as sentiment analysis, text summarization, and machine translation.

The rise of TikTok has been unprecedented. It's become one of the most popular social media platforms, especially among teens and young adults. But why is it so addictive? It turns out, there are several psychological factors at play that contribute to its success. First off, TikTok's algorithm is designed to keep users engaged. By monitoring user behavior and interests, the app can curate a personalized feed tailored to each individual user. As a result, users consistently find new content they're interested in, which keeps them coming back for more. Second, TikTok also takes advantage of our natural tendency to be curious and explore new things. The "For You" page features an ever-changing selection of videos, which encourages users to keep scrolling and watching to see what's next. This helps keep the feed fresh and exciting, and it prevents users from getting bored or losing interest. Finally, the platform also taps into our need for social validation. Every time someone likes or comments on a video, the user feels seen and heard, which reinforces their desire to keep engaging with the app. TikTok's success is no accident; the platform was deliberately designed to be as addictive as possible. By understanding the psychology behind its popularity, we can better understand why it's so successful.

The pound-force has a metric counterpart, less commonly used than the newton: the kilogram-force (kgf) (sometimes kilopond), is the force exerted by standard gravity on one kilogram of mass. The kilogram-force is equal to 9.80665 N. The pound-force and the kilogram-force are both units of force in the imperialcustomary and metric systems, respectively. The two units are not directly equivalent, as the pound-force is a unit of weight (or mass) whereas the kilogram-force is a unit of force. To convert between them, one must use a conversion factor that takes into account the difference between mass and force.

When faced with learning a set of inter-related tasks from a limited amount of usable data, learning each task independently may lead to poor generalization performance. exploits the latent relations between different tasks to learn a more efficient representation of the data. This approach, called multi-task learning, aims to improve generalization across tasks by learning shared representations that capture similarities and differences across the tasks. In this way, the model can better generalize to new and unseen situations, leading to more robust and accurate predictions. Multi-task learning can be applied in various fields, including computer vision, natural language processing, and speech recognition.

In a groundbreaking study led by Dr. Jane Thompson, a team of medical researchers discovered that the appendix actually plays a crucial role in the immune system. Contrary to prior beliefs, the organ is not a worthless remnant of human evolution. It seems that the appendix functions as a safe harbor for beneficial gut bacteria. However, the discovery is not all good news. The study also found that during the course of certain diseases, such as severe gastrointestinal infections, the appendix can become a deadly liability. The organ can become a breeding ground for harmful bacteria and can ultimately burst, leading to widespread infection and even death. Dr. Thompson's team is now working on developing new treatments to mitigate the risks associated with appendicitis. The findings have caused some controversy within the medical community, as the practice of removing the appendix has long been considered a routine procedure. However, with this new understanding of the organ's function, it may be time for doctors to reconsider their approach. In conclusion, the discovery of the appendix's role in the immune system is a significant breakthrough in medical science. While the knowledge of the organ's importance is cause for celebration, the discovery of its potential risks highlights the importance of further research and understanding. Doctors must now take a more thoughtful approach to the treatment of appendicitis, and the medical community as a whole must come to grips with the new reality that the appendix is not just some redundant organ after all.

He added that M.C. was "relieved and happy" to have been pardoned by the Pope. This is not the first time that Pope Francis has intervened in a Vatileaks case. The pardon of M.C. is seen as an indication that the Pope is willing to take a stand against those who abuse their power within the Church. It also shows that he is committed to transparency and accountability within the institution. If you picture light as a particle tracing out a sine wave, the particle's forward velocity is the speed of light, and its location in the sine wave is the phase of light. The particle's motion, then, is a direct manifestation of the wave nature of light. But what if we could reverse this process and use the wave nature of light to control the particle's motion? This is the basic idea behind a new type of "light-matter interface" developed by researchers at MIT, Harvard University, and elsewhere. The device consists of a laser beam that is split into two beams with slightly different colors, or frequencies. When these beams are focused on a tiny nanoparticle, they create a standing wave - an interference pattern in which the two beams reinforce each other in some regions and cancel each other out in others. The resulting interference pattern creates a kind of potential landscape for the nanoparticle, sort of like a set of hills and valleys. And just as a marble rolling down a hilly landscape will eventually come to rest in the lowest valley, the nanoparticle will migrate toward the region of lowest energy in the interference pattern. The researchers can control the direction and speed of this migration simply by changing the relative frequencies of the two beams. This gives them a way to steer and focus the nanoparticle on demand. The system can be used to transport nanoparticles along arbitrary paths inside a liquid medium. The researchers have demonstrated this capability by steering nanoparticles through a complex maze, and they believe it could have applications in nanofabrication, optogenetics, and other areas. "You can envision a future where you have these little robots that you can control very precisely in three dimensions," says Marin Soljacic, the Robert N. The paper's lead authors are former MIT postdoc Xin Zhang, who is now an assistant professor at Boston College; former graduate student Wei Zhu, who is now a postdoc at Harvard; and Siyuan Lin, a graduate student at MIT. "It is a very versatile approach to nanomanipulation," says Zhang. "You can change the shape and size of the nanoparticles you're manipulating, and you can also use different materials. There are lots of possibilities here." The two beams are combined into a single beam, which is passed through a microscope objective and focused onto a 1.5-micron-diameter silica sphere suspended in a liquid solution. In the absence of the AOM beam, the system functions as an ordinary microscope, allowing the researchers to track the position of the nanoparticle. The relative frequencies of the two beams are then adjusted so that the nanoparticle is located at a point of maximum interference between the two beams. The result is a standing wave, whose peaks and troughs produce a potential landscape for the nanoparticle. The steeper the gradient of this landscape, the more rapidly the nanoparticle will roll downhill. The researchers can adjust the gradient of the potential landscape simply by changing the relative frequency of the two beams. The system can also be used to separate different types of particles based on their size. Courts have distinguished between two types of civil disobedience: "Indirect civil disobedience involves violating a law which is not, itself, the object of protest, whereas direct civil disobedience involves protesting the law itself. Also, sometimes the distinction is made between civil disobedience and conscientious objection; the difference being that civil disobedience is a political act and conscientious objection is based on moral or religious grounds." The two main examples of civil disobedience are the American Civil Rights Movement led by Martin Luther King, Jr., and Mahatma Gandhi's struggle for Indian independence. The former was largely based in indirect civil disobedience, as protesters were violating Jim Crow laws and regulations, while making a point about the immorality of such laws. The latter was based in direct civil disobedience, as Gandhi himself was the one breaking the law. "The term 'civil disobedience' has often been used to describe protests which involve acts of violence. However, the general consensus is that the use of violence does not make the protest civil disobedience. Rather, the use of violence would disqualify it from being civil disobedience." In short, civil disobedience is a protest against an unjust law, where the protester is willing to accept punishment for breaking the law. The use of violence does not make the protest civil disobedience, but rather disqualifies it.

Prince Louis de Conde, along with his sons Daniel and Osias,[citation needed] arranged with Count Ludwig von Nassau-Saarbrucken to establish a Huguenot community in present-day Saarland in 1604. The Count 's sister, Elizabeth Charlotte, married the German King Charles I Louis, Elector Palatine. The descendants of the barons de Cosse became some of the most important nobles in France and Italy during the 17th and 18th centuries, as well as prominent finance ministers, such as Etienne Francois, duc de Choiseul and Jacques Necker.[citation needed] Jean-Baptiste Colbert was the son of a Huguenot, who founded the French East India Company and served as its director for many years. His mother was the daughter of another Huguenot, who had fought at Rocroi in 1643. Louis, Duke of Montpensier , a prince of the blood, converted to Catholicism on his marriage to Elisabeth Charlotte d'Orleans in 1626. He remained a Catholic until his death. In 1655, he disowned his only daughter La Grande Mademoiselle, after she announced her own conversion to Catholicism. In 1668, Henry of Navarre IV (Henry IV of France), grandchild of Antoine of Navarre and Jeanne d'Albret and heir to the throne of France converted to Catholicism. The last king from the House of Valois (the same dynasty as Joan of Arc) was Henry III of France, who died in 1589 without an heir. One branch of the Bourbons, the House of Conde, became Protestants, while the other, the House of Conti, became Catholics. After the accession of the House of Bourbon - which united the two branches of the family - three more Bourbons also converted to Catholicism: Henry IV of France , King of Navarre and later King of France as Henry IV; Louis XIII of France ; and Louis XIV of France . During the reign of Louis XIV, the Crown granted the order of Saint Esprit to the last of the Huguenots. During the early days of the Reign of Terror, Protestants were again subjected to terrible persecutions; many Huguenots fled to Switzerland or to England. Huguenot refugees from France settled in London and Ipswich in the late 17th century, and many Huguenots settled in New York City during the eighteenth century. Many Huguenots emigrated to the Netherlands in the early 18th century and established churches there. After the defeat of Napoleon Bonaparte in 1814, many Huguenots returned to France, but few went back to their former homes in the south. In the 20th century, the last Huguenots lost their language. In the 21st century, a new generation is learning it. France today While Huguenot numbers have declined over time, they are still estimated to have between 1 million and 1.5 million living in France (2 of the population). Most live in the region of Alsace-Lorraine. A Huguenot museum is located in the historic center of Nimes, in the old bishopric. It is called the Musee du Desert. The museum was started by several Huguenot families and opened to the public in 1958. Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) have emerged recently as a promising application of deep neural networks to the numerical solution of nonlinear partial differential equations (PDEs). However, the original PINN algorithm is highly sensitive to the initialization of the weights of the neural network and often results in unstable training. In this work, we propose a novel algorithm for training PINNs that is based on a trust region method. The proposed algorithm is significantly more robust to initialization than the original PINN algorithm and leads to stable training. We apply our algorithm to several test problems, including the Burgers' equation and the nonlinear Schrodinger equation, and demonstrate the superior performance of our algorithm compared to the original PINN algorithm.

Python autocomplete is a project that experiments with using an LSTM model to autocomplete python code. Test results show that it can save users between 30 to 50 percent of the time they spend typing. Dataset The training set consists of 1,000,000 samples of python code. The validation and test sets contain 10,000 and 100,000 samples of python code respectively. Model The model consists of an embedding layer, followed by a Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) layer and a dense layer. The model is trained using the Adam optimizer and categorical cross entropy loss. Results The model achieves a validation accuracy of 97.87 percent and test accuracy of 97.90 percent.

Researchers at MIT have created a rechargeable lithium-ion battery in the form of a 460-foot-long fiber. The batteries can be manufactured to arbitrarily long lengths. They can be 3D-printed into any shape, and are only about three times thicker than a human hair. The battery is made up of an anode and a cathode, with a solid electrolyte in between. This combination allows the lithium ions to move back and forth between the anode and the cathode as the battery is charged and discharged. The fibers can withstand temperatures of up to 250 degrees Celsius (482 degrees Fahrenheit). Because they are so thin and lightweight, these batteries could be used in many applications, such as powering medical implants, wearable electronics, or even robots. They could also be woven into fabrics to provide power for smart clothing. The researchers believe that the batteries could be a potential alternative to traditional batteries due to their flexibility and small size.

Importance of visual context in scene understanding tasks is well recognized in the computer vision community. However, to what extent the computer vision models for image classification and semantic segmentation can accurately understand the visual context depends on various factors, including the complexity of the scene, the diversity of objects and their interactions, and the quality of the training data. In simpler scenes, where the objects and their relationships are clearly defined, a computer vision model can accurately predict the object classes and their locations. However, in complex scenes where multiple objects are present and their relationships are intricate, the accuracy of the models decreases. This is because the models require not only visual cues but also contextual cues such as spatial relationships and semantic relationships to determine the correct object class and its spatial location. Hence, the importance of visual context increases in such cases. Furthermore, the quality of the training data is crucial as the computer vision models rely on labeled data to learn the object classes, their semantic relationships, and their spatial locations. Inaccurate or insufficient training data can lead to poor performance of the models. In conclusion, while the recognition of the importance of visual context in scene understanding tasks is well-established, the accuracy of the computer vision models for image classification and semantic segmentation depends on various factors, including scene complexity, diversity of objects, quality of training data, and the ability of models to incorporate contextual cues.

When animations in CSS conflict, only one of them will occur. The Web Animations API allows developers to mix up animation behavior using the composite option. This article discusses how to use the composite property to create complex animations with the Web Animations API. The composite property in the Web Animations API allows you to control how multiple animations should interact with each other. By default, only the animation with the highest z-index will play. But with the composite property, you can create complex animations that blend together and produce unique visual effects. There are several values for the composite property: - replace (default): This value replaces any animations currently playing with the new animation. - add: This value adds the new animation to any animations currently playing, creating a cumulative effect. - accumulate: This value accumulates values from all animations currently playing and applies them to the new animation. This creates a more complex animation, as each animation affects the others. To use the composite property, you need to create multiple animations and specify their composite value. Here's an example: " 'javascript const element document.querySelector .box; const animation1 element.animate transform: 'rotate (0deg) ' }, { duration: 1000, composite: 'add' ; const animation2 element.animate transform: 'translateX (100px) ' }, { duration: 1000, composite: 'add' ; const animation3 element.animate transform: 'scale (2) ' }, { duration: 1000, composite: 'add' ; " ' In this example, we create three different animations for the same element. The composite property is set to 'add' for each animation, which means they will blend together to create a cumulative effect. You can also use the composite property to create complex animations that react to user input or events. Here's an example of an animation that changes color based on a user's click: " 'javascript const element document.querySelector .box; Initial animation element.animate backgroundColor: 'red' }, { duration: 1000, composite: 'replace' ; Click animation element.addEventListener click', { element.animate backgroundColor: 'blue' }, { duration: 1000, composite: 'accumulate' ; ; " ' In this example, we create an initial animation that sets the element's background color to red. When the user clicks on the element, a new animation is created that changes the background color to blue. The composite value is set to 'accumulate', which means the animation blends with the existing animation to create a more complex effect. Overall, the Web Animations API's composite property allows developers to create complex and dynamic animations that react to user input and events. Using this property, you can create unique visual effects that would be difficult to achieve with CSS alone.

We give an algorithm that for an input n -vertex graph G and integer k 0, in time 2 O (k) n either outputs that the treewidth of G is less than or equal to k, or outputs a tree-decomposition of G of width at most 2k1. 1. If k0, output "treewidth of G is 0." 2. If G is already a tree, output "treewidth of G is 1." 3. Otherwise, choose a vertex v with degree at least 3 in G and let N (v) be its neighborhood. 4. Compute the connected components of G - N (v) and recurse on each component with parameter k-1. 5. For each recursive call, check if the returned tree-decomposition has width at most k. If all recursive calls have returned a tree-decomposition of width at most k, output "treewidth of G is at most k." 6. Otherwise, let T be the smallest tree-decomposition returned by a recursive call with width at most 2k1. 7. Construct a tree-decomposition of G as follows: - Let T' be the tree obtained from T by adding a new root node r and edges connecting r to each bag of T that contains a vertex in N (v). - Update the bags of T' so that each bag containing a vertex in N (v) also contains v. - Finally, add bags B1 and B2 to T', such that B1 contains v and all vertices in N (v) not already included in bags of T', and B2 contains all remaining vertices in G not yet in T'. 8. Output T' as the tree-decomposition of G. The running time of the algorithm is 2 O (k) n, as in each recursive call the parameter k is decreased by 1, so there are at most O (k) levels of recursion. At each level, the algorithm computes connected components of G, which takes at most O (n) time. The check of the returned tree-decompositions takes at most O (kn) time. Constructing T' takes at most O (n) time. Therefore, the total running time is 2 O (k) n. Note that if the algorithm outputs a tree-decomposition, it is guaranteed to have width at most 2k1, since T was chosen as the smallest tree-decomposition returned by a recursive call with width at most 2k1, and T' was constructed by adding bags and vertices to T.

Courts have distinguished between two types of civil disobedience: "Indirect civil disobedience involves violating a law which is not, itself, the object of protest, whereas direct civil disobedience involves protesting by specifically breaking the law that is being challenged. Both types of civil disobedience involve breaking the law as a means of political protest or dissent, but the distinction lies in the target of the disobedience. Indirect civil disobedience may involve breaking a law or regulation that is related to the issue being protested against, but is not the main focus of the protest. For example, blocking traffic to draw attention to a discriminatory housing policy. Direct civil disobedience, on the other hand, involves breaking the specific law or regulation that is being protested against. For example, refusing to obey a law mandating segregation in public schools. Both forms of civil disobedience can be effective in drawing attention to a cause and inspiring change, but they carry different risks and consequences for the protestors.

Indonesia - the World's Largest Muslim Population and Southeast Asia's Biggest Economy Spread across a chain of thousands of islands between Asia and Australia, Indonesia is a beautiful and diverse country. It boasts of stunning landscapes, fascinating cultures, and a rich history. But beyond its enchanting scenery, Indonesia is also home to the world's largest Muslim population and Southeast Asia's biggest economy. Indonesia is known as the fourth most populous country in the world, with over 260 million people. Of that number, about 87 of Indonesians follow Islam, making it the world's most populous Muslim country. Indonesia's history with Islam dates back to the 13th century when traders from the Middle East and India introduced the religion to the archipelago. Today, Indonesia's significant Muslim population represents a mix of Sunni and Shia Muslims. While Islam plays a crucial role in the lives of many Indonesians, it does not define the country's identity. Indonesia is a diverse nation with over 300 ethnic groups, each with its unique customs, traditions, and languages. The country's heterogeneity is a source of pride for Indonesians and adds to its charm as a tourist destination. Beyond its cultural heritage, Indonesia has a booming economy, ranking as Southeast Asia's largest economy in terms of GDP. Its economy has grown exponentially over the past decade, driven by the rising middle-class population and strong domestic consumption. The country's natural resources, including oil, gas, and minerals, have helped it secure a spot as a globally significant player. Indonesia has also made strides in developing its tourism sector, with its pristine beaches, volcanoes, and lush forests attracting millions of visitors every year. The government has invested heavily in developing the country's infrastructure, including expanding its airports, building new highways, and improving connectivity. Despite its challenges, including inequality and political instability, Indonesia has maintained steady economic growth and remained an important regional ally, cooperating with other Southeast Asian countries to promote stability and growth. Indonesia is a country of contrasts that has managed to blend tradition and modernity seamlessly. Its mix of cultures, religions, and landscapes makes it an ideal place to explore and discover. Its large Muslim population is a testament to its diverse heritage, while its booming economy showcases its potential as an emerging market. Indonesia is indeed a fascinating land of unique experiences awaiting exploration.

Okay, little one, let me explain some big words to you! Knowledge means knowing something. It's what you learn from books or from asking questions. For example, if you know the capital of your country or how to add 22, that's knowledge! Intelligence means being able to think and learn quickly. It's how smart you are - like if you can solve a puzzle or understand a difficult book. When you use your brain to figure out something, that's intelligence! Wisdom means having good judgement and knowing what's right or wrong. It's what happens when you use your knowledge and intelligence to make the right decision. For example, if you know not to touch a hot stove and you don't do it, that's wisdom! Now, let's talk about information vs. data. Data is just a bunch of numbers or facts by themselves. For example, if you have a list of names and ages, that's data. But when you use that data to learn something, that becomes information. So if you look at the list of names and ages and figure out which age group is the biggest, that's turning data into information. Does that make sense to you now?

This group is now thought to have played a critical role in shaping the genetic diversity of modern-day Europeans. The Basal Eurasians are believed to have brought with them traits such as light skin and blue eyes, which have since become common in Europe. The researchers also suggest that these ancient peoples were the first to bring agriculture to Europe, a pivotal event which transformed human societies. The discovery of this fourth ancestral group follows years of genetic research which has uncovered the complexity of European ancestry. Previous studies have found evidence of three main groups which have contributed to the gene pool of modern-day Europeans: hunter-gatherers, farmers and pastoralists. However, this new research has demonstrated that there is yet another layer to this complex story. The Basal Eurasians are thought to have interbred with the other ancestral groups, resulting in the unique mix of DNA that characterises modern Europeans. The study also highlights the importance of using ancient DNA to understand the origins of human populations. This is particularly important in Europe, where there was a constantly shifting landscape of human populations and a rich history of migration and cultural exchange. The findings have significant implications for our understanding of human evolution and our shared history as a species. They also emphasise the need for further research into ancient DNA, which has the potential to reveal even more insights into our past. Overall, the discovery of the Basal Eurasians represents a major breakthrough in our understanding of European ancestry. It challenges traditional notions of European origins and forces us to reconsider our understanding of human history.

A quantum effect called superabsorption allows a collection of molecules to absorb light more efficiently than if each molecule were acting individually. Researchers have used this phenomenon to create a variety of applications, including more efficient solar cells and sensors. Superabsorption occurs when multiple molecules are in close proximity and act together to amplify the absorption of photons. Essentially, the molecules combine their energy levels to create a larger, more effective energy trap, allowing for better energy transfer from the photons to the molecules. This effect has been observed in organic molecules, like those found in plant pigments, and in inorganic materials, like semiconductors. Harnessing the power of superabsorption could lead to new breakthroughs in energy and sensing technology.

Since the embedding is derived from speech signals and therefore contains information about the target speech, we expect that this embedding can provide some clues to help recover the target speech. Structural geologists use microscopic analysis of oriented thin sections of geologic samples to observe the fabric within the rocks which gives information about strain within the crystalline structure of the rock. The orientation of the rock is observed using a petrographic microscope, in which the light shines through a thin slice of the rock and is projected onto a screen by glass lenses. The anisotropy of the minerals within the rock can be observed using polarized light, because each mineral has different optical properties depending on its crystalline structure. In addition to observing the fabric of the rock, structural geologists may also use X-ray diffraction to determine the crystal structure of minerals within the rock. This information can be used to calculate the amount of strain that has been applied to the rock.

This paper investigates a general framework to discover categories of unlabeled scene images according to their appearances (i.e., textures and structures). We jointly solve the two coupled tasks in an unsupervised manner, which are the discovery of visual features and the clustering of images. The proposed framework utilizes a deep convolutional neural network (CNN) to extract high-level features from the images, and then applies a clustering algorithm to group the images with similar features into the same category. The CNN is trained in an unsupervised manner with a clustering loss function to encourage grouping of similar images. The proposed framework has been evaluated on several benchmark datasets, and achieved state-of-the-art performance in discovering scene categories. This framework has potential applications in image retrieval, image classification, and scene understanding.

Researchers from the California Institute of Technology have verified a theory that could lead to quantum batteries - a new form of energy storage technology. The breakthrough, published in Nature Materials, revolves around a concept called 'quantum coherence', which is the ability of an electron to maintain its quantum state over a long period of time. The researchers found that it was possible to store electrical charge in a semiconductor material for an extended period without the electrons losing their quantum state. This finding could have profound implications for the development of quantum batteries - a type of energy storage device that would be much more efficient than traditional batteries. The team tested the concept using a nanostructured aluminum oxide film that was placed between two electrodes. When a voltage was applied to the electrodes, the electrons in the film were able to maintain their quantum state for up to one millisecond, which is much longer than the fraction of a nanoseconds it takes for them to lose their quantum state in normal conditions. This proof of concept could pave the way for further research into the development of quantum batteries and other related technologies. "The fact that we can now see that this kind of coherence can last for milliseconds is really important, because now it's worth looking into devices that take advantage of this," said Caltech professor Jelena Vuckovic in a press release. While the research is still in its early stages, the findings could potentially revolutionize the way we store and use energy. If successful, quantum batteries could enable us to create far more efficient energy storage systems than what exists today.

[header] How to control weeds [title] Refrain from disturbing the soil. [step] Heavy digging and cultivation can cause weed seeds to come to the surface and begin growing. Only disturb the soil when you have to, so that you don't inadvertently raise weed seeds. [step] Mulch heavily around plants to suppress weed growth. A layer of mulch (such as bark, leaves, or compost) several inches deep can block sunlight and prevent many weed seeds from germinating. [step] Hand-pull weeds as soon as you spot them. Be sure to remove the entire weed, including the roots. This is most effective when the soil is moist - after rainfall or after watering. [step] Use weed barriers. If weeds are a persistent problem in a particular area, consider laying down a weed barrier - a layer of landscape fabric or plastic - to smother existing weeds and block sunlight. [step] Consider using natural alternatives to herbicides. You can create a natural weed killer by mixing vinegar, salt, and dish soap, and spraying it on weeds. Some gardeners also use boiling water to kill weeds in cracks in sidewalks and driveways.

This paper investigates a general framework to discover categories of unlabeled scene images according to their appearances (i.e., textures and structures). We jointly solve the two coupled tasks in an unsupervised manner: (i) feature representation learning and (ii) categorization of scene images. Specifically, we propose an end-to-end generative model that learns a low-dimensional latent space to represent scene features and simultaneously clusters the scene images into categories from the learned feature space. The generative model is a combination of convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and Gaussian Mixture Model (GMM). To regularize our model for better clustering results, we introduce a novel self-supervised task, which ensures that the latent space encodes meaningful representations for different scenes. We evaluate our approach on three widely used scene datasets, i.e., 15Scenes, LabelMe and SUN, and demonstrate that it can discover discriminative scene categories with superior performance comparing to state-of-the-art methods.

Relatives of 24 rubber plantation workers in Malaya who were killed by British troops almost 70 years ago have suffered a setback in their quest for justice. A recent appeal for an official investigation into the incident has been denied, leaving the families feeling let down by the authorities. The tragedy occurred in December 1948, during the Malayan Emergency, a conflict between the British colonial authorities and communist insurgents. The 24 workers were suspected of being communists and were rounded up by British soldiers at the Batang Kali village in Selangor state. The workers were led to a nearby rubber plantation and executed, with their bodies left in a ditch. British authorities claimed they were killed while attempting to escape, but this account has been challenged by survivors and eyewitnesses. The relatives of the 24 victims have long sought an official inquiry into the incident, which they believe was a massacre. They say that successive British governments have failed to acknowledge the wrongdoing of their soldiers and have refused to offer compensation to the families. The families launched a legal battle in 2019, arguing that the killings constituted war crimes and that British authorities should be held accountable. However, on 24th June, the High Court of England and Wales dismissed the relatives' appeal for a public inquiry. The judge ruled that the incident was outside the time limit for an investigation and that there was insufficient evidence that any individuals involved were alive and could be held accountable. The ruling was a blow to the families, who say they will continue their fight for justice. Many human rights campaigners and historians have supported the families' demands for an inquiry. They argue that the Batang Kali massacre is one of the most egregious examples of British atrocities during the Emergency and that it has been covered up for too long. They say that an official investigation is necessary for the victims' families to find closure and for the truth to be established about what really happened. The ruling by the High Court is a setback, but it is unlikely to deter campaigners from continuing to press for justice for the 24 victims. For them, the memory of their loved ones and their desire for accountability and closure remains as strong as ever.

Tensor completion is a challenging problem with various applications. Many related models based on the low-rank prior of the tensor have been proposed. However, the low-rank prior may not be able to capture all the underlying structures of the tensor, which can negatively impact the accuracy of tensor completion. Therefore, researchers have proposed more advanced regularizations, such as sparsity and smoothness constraints, to improve the performance of tensor completion models. Some applications of tensor completion include image and video processing, recommendation systems, and neuroscience. In image and video processing, tensor completion is used for image and video inpainting, which involves filling in missing or corrupted parts of an image or video. In recommendation systems, tensor completion is used to predict missing ratings in user-item matrices. In neuroscience, tensor completion can be used to reconstruct 3D images of brain structures from 2D image slices. Overall, tensor completion is an important problem with numerous applications, and researchers continue to develop new models and algorithms to improve its accuracy and efficiency.

lettrine Lesion segmentation from the surrounding skin is the first task for developing automatic Computer-Aided Diagnosis of skin cancer. Variant features of lesion like uneven distribution of color, irregular shape, and varying texture make the segmentation task challenging. There are various methods developed for lesion segmentation such as thresholding, region-growing, edge detection, and machine learning-based approaches. Thresholding is a simple and easy-to-use technique where a threshold value is selected to separate the lesion from the surrounding skin. However, thresholding might not work well for lesions with complex textures or color variations. Region-growing is a technique that starts from a seed point inside the lesion and grows the region by adding adjacent pixels that have similar properties. This method can segment complex irregular shapes, but the selection of seed point can be crucial. Edge detection techniques segment lesions by detecting the boundaries between lesion and skin. However, this method may fail to segment textured or homogeneously colored lesions. Machine learning-based segmentation techniques use algorithms to learn from given training data and make predictions on new data. These techniques have shown promising results in lesion segmentation but require a significant amount of training data. Overall, lesion segmentation is a challenging task requiring expertise and specialized techniques.

With each passing hour, The Beast grew increasingly agitated as it sensed the presence of the teenagers nearby. As it began to close in on the cabin, one of the teens, named Jake, began to feel a strange sensation in his body. He knew that he was a werewolf, and that the full moon was rising. Jake knew that he had to use his powers to protect his friends from certain death at the hands of The Beast. As The Beast closed in, Jake transformed into a powerful werewolf, his fur bristling with energy and his claws at the ready. The monster launched itself at the cabin, clawing at the walls and windows. But Jake was ready, and he charged at The Beast with all his might. Claw met claw in a fierce struggle that lasted for what felt like hours. Finally, though, Jake emerged victorious, the mighty werewolf having slain The Beast. As the sun rose on the forest, the teenagers emerged from the cabin, stunned and a little worse for wear. They had no idea what had just transpired, but Jake knew that he had saved their lives. From that day forward, the teenagers were never again so reckless, and they learned to respect the power of the supernatural.

The UK retail sector has seen a boost in sales for November, according to the latest figures released by the Office for National Statistics. The increase in sales is attributed to the promotions offered by shops in the lead up to Black Friday, which fell on the last day of the month. Retail sales rose by 1.1 in November, which is higher than the 0.4 projected by economists. This marks a significant increase compared to the 0.6 decline in October. Sales in the three months to November also saw a 0.8 increase, which is not only above expectations but also the highest level in a year. The boost in sales was driven by the clothing and footwear sector, which saw an increase of 3.8, as well as household goods, which saw a 2.2 rise. Online sales also saw significant growth, with a 3.3 increase in the share of sales made online. Experts say that the increase in sales is due to the promotions and discounts offered by retailers in the lead up to Black Friday, as well as the rise in consumer confidence. The uncertainty surrounding Brexit has had a significant impact on consumer confidence, causing many shoppers to hold back on spending. However, the recent announcement of a Conservative majority in the general election has given some consumers more confidence to spend. The Black Friday period has become a key event for retailers in recent years, with many offering discounts and promotions in-store and online. The success of this year's Black Friday period is expected to boost sales for the entire holiday season. While the boost in sales is a positive sign for the retail sector, experts warn that the uncertainty surrounding Brexit and the upcoming general election could impact consumer confidence and spending in the coming months. Retailers will need to carefully manage their pricing and promotions strategies in order to continue to see growth in sales.

The two companies have been working together since March to retrofit the 62-year-old aircraft with a 750-horsepower electric motor. The successful test flight marks a major milestone in the development of electric aviation, showing that it is possible to operate commercial aircraft without relying on fossil fuels. The aircraft is expected to be certified for commercial use within two years and could transform the way people travel in the future. "This is history in the making," said McDougall after the flight. "I'm incredibly proud of Harbour Air's leadership role in redefining safety and innovation in the aviation and seaplane industry." The world is watching as this new technology is making waves in the aviation industry, and many are excited to see what the future holds for electric commercial aviation.

Recent years have seen big advances in the field of sentence-level quality estimation (QE), largely as a result of using neural-based architectures. However, the majority of these methods work only on sentence-level data and do not take discourse-level information into account. In this paper, we present a novel neural-based QE system that uses discourse-level information to identify and correct errors in long text documents. Our method employs a hierarchical recurrent neural network (HRNN) to capture both sentence-level and discourse-level information, and then uses an attention mechanism to focus on the most relevant parts of the text. We evaluate our system on a corpus of student essays annotated with error tags, and show that it outperforms existing state-of-the-art systems. We further analyze the system's performance on different types of errors, demonstrating its effectiveness in detecting both grammar and style errors. Our results suggest that incorporating discourse-level information can lead to more accurate predictions of sentence-level quality, and give promising directions for future work.

Once, there was a cheerful yellow lamp that was always happy to provide light to its owners. It was a simple task but it brought joy to the lamp to be useful in such a way. One day, the lamp noticed something strange. The usually busy household became eerily quiet. The lamp was puzzled and wondered what was happening. Suddenly, a loud noise interrupted the silence. The lamp's cheerful glow flickered as someone entered the room. It was a man the lamp had never seen before. He was covered in blood and had a knife in his hand. The man walked towards the lamp and stopped right in front of it. The lamp's bulb shone brighter, illuminating his face. The man's eyes glimmered as he stared at the lamp, almost as if he was admiring its beauty. Suddenly, the man plunged the knife into the lamp's cord, cutting the electricity supply. The lamp's cheerful glow began to fade away. It could see everything that happened in the room, but it was powerless to do anything. The man then proceeded to do the unimaginable. He murdered someone in the same room, right in front of the lamp's eye. The lamp was a witness to the murder but was helpless to stop it. It watched in horror as the man picked up his knife, wiped it clean and walked away. The cheerful yellow lamp, now shattered and broken, lay motionless on the floor, unable to process what had just happened. From that day on, the lamp's light never shone again. It remained silent, as if it had lost its cheerfulness and its purpose in life. It was forever haunted by the image of the murderer and the horror of what it had witnessed.

A pizza company in the UK has caused outrage after referring to a hospital as a "looney bin" in a promotional email. The comment left mental health workers "horrified and distressed" and sparked a flurry of complaints on social media. The email was sent out by local pizza chain 'Pizza Pals', advertising a new opening in the area. It featured a graphic of a pizza with toppings arranged in the shape of a straitjacket, along with the caption "Looney Bin Special - because our pizza will drive you crazy!" Several staff at the hospital, which offers psychiatric care to patients with a range of mental health problems, received the email and were quick to voice their dismay. "It feels like a terrible insult," said one nurse, who wished to remain anonymous. "We work hard to create a safe and supportive environment for people with mental illness, and to be labelled a 'looney bin' is incredibly hurtful." Other mental health workers echoed these sentiments, taking to social media to express their anger over the insensitive language used in the email. "This is appalling," wrote one Twitter user. "Using derogatory terms to describe people with mental health conditions is deeply harmful and only adds to the stigma they already face." Pizza Pals has since issued an apology for the incident, claiming that the email was sent out without the knowledge or approval of senior management. "We are deeply sorry for any offence caused by the inappropriate language used in our promotional material," they said in a statement. The company has also pledged to make a donation to a mental health charity in the local area, and to review their advertising policies to ensure that similar incidents do not occur in the future. While some have accepted the apology, others remain unconvinced that Pizza Pals has truly learned its lesson. "It's not just about this one email," said mental health campaigner Sarah Smith. "It's about the wider culture in which we use words like 'looney bin' to describe people with mental illness." She added: "Companies need to understand that there are real people behind the diagnoses and the labels. If we want to build a society that supports and values mental health, we need to start by respecting people's dignity and humanity."

Researchers at Stanford University and the SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory have discovered a way to transform a substance found in fossil fuels into diamonds with pressure and low heat. Diamond is a highly valuable material that has many applications in various industries, such as electronics, jewelry, medicine, and more. This new discovery could potentially offer a sustainable way to create diamonds without the need for mining or environmentally harmful practices. The substance that the researchers used to create diamonds is called "buckyballs," which are small, spherical carbon molecules that are found in petroleum. They placed the buckyballs in a diamond anvil cell, which is a device that can apply immense pressure to materials. They then heated the buckyballs with a laser to a temperature of 2,200 to 2,600 degrees Fahrenheit. Under these extreme conditions, the buckyballs transformed into a type of diamond called "lonsdaleite," which is only found naturally in meteorites. The lonsdaleite diamonds created in the experiment had a hardness that approached that of natural diamonds. While this discovery is still in the experimental phase, it has the potential to provide a more sustainable and ethical way to create diamonds. It also shows how the study of materials at the atomic level can lead to innovative solutions for industrial and societal problems.

An Australian inquest has heard that a mother was suffering from "forgotten baby syndrome" when her young son died in a hot car. The inquest, which took place in the Supreme Court of Victoria, heard that in January 2019 the mother had left her two-year-old son in the car while she attended work. She told the court that she had intended to drop him off at daycare but had forgotten and driven to work instead. When she returned to the car after an eight-hour shift, the boy was unresponsive. He was taken to hospital but pronounced dead on arrival. The inquest is investigating whether the mother could have been suffering from "forgotten baby syndrome," a condition where a caregiver becomes distracted and forgets about their child in the car. The court heard evidence from experts who said this can happen to even the most attentive parents, and that the tragedy was likely due to a lapse in memory rather than negligence. The coroner will now consider the evidence before determining the cause of death. The case has sparked a debate in Australia around the issue of leaving children unattended in cars and the potential for similar tragedies. The mother's name has not been released and the outcome of the inquest is yet to be determined.

We study the problem of learning a real-valued function that satisfies the Demographic Parity constraint. It demands the distribution of the predicted output to be independent of the sensitive attribute. We propose a novel approach to enforce the demographic parity constraint while learning the underlying function. Our method is based on a regularized minimax optimization problem which uses a convex-concave procedure to solve the problem. We provide theoretical analysis of our method and establish generalization guarantees for the learned function. In addition, we empirically demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed approach on real-world datasets.

There was a man, we'll call him Tim, who had a strange problem that no one could quite explain. For as long as he could remember, his stomach would make a loud and continuous gurgling noise. It sounded like a distant thunderstorm all day, every day. The strange thing was, nothing seemed to help the noise. No matter how much he ate or drank, it kept on going. He tried drinking peppermint tea, eating mints, and even lying down in different positions - nothing worked. One day, out of desperation, he decided to see a doctor. After an extensive examination, the doctor concluded that the sound was coming from his intestines. It turns out that Tim had a condition known as borborygmi, or stomach rumbling. The good news was that the condition wasn't serious. The bad news was that there was no cure. However, the doctor did prescribe certain lifestyle changes that would help reduce the noise. He advised Tim to eat smaller meals more frequently throughout the day and to avoid foods that could cause gas or bloating. Tim followed the doctor's advice and slowly but surely, the noise began to fade away. He still hears it occasionally, but now it's only a faint reminder of his past problem. From then on, he was able to enjoy life without the constant hum of his stomach.

In this paper, we provide details of a robotic system that can automate the task of picking and stowing objects from and to a rack in an e-commerce fulfillment warehouse. The system includes a robotic arm with sensory and gripper hardware for picking items from a rack, an item conveyor for transporting picked items to a packing station, and a vision-based sorting system for identifying objects at the conveyor. The robotic arm is mounted on a linear stage that can move along the length of the rack. The gripper is equipped with suction cups and pressure sensors to enable it to pick up a variety of different objects. The item conveyor is used to transport picked items to a packing station. The vision-based sorting system uses a camera to identify objects at the conveyor and sort them into bins. The system has been designed to be scalable and modular. It can be configured to work with different types of racks and objects, and can be expanded to include additional robotic arms and conveyors as needed.

Lily had no choice but to accept that it was a no-show date and move on. She tried to forget Jack and channel her energy into other things. Several weeks later, Lily received a text from Jack apologizing for his behavior. He explained that he had suffered from a severe anxiety attack and couldn't bring himself to show up. He apologized for not calling her earlier and for any pain he had caused. At that point, Lily had already moved on and knew that she deserved someone who would respect her enough to show up on time. She decided not to respond to Jack's message, and instead, she went out with her friends to celebrate the lesson she had learned - that she deserved better than a no-show date.

Once upon a time, there was a little boy named Timmy. Timmy was always scared of the monster that lived in his closet. Every night, he would hear strange noises coming from the closet, and he knew the monster was waiting to grab him and take him away. One night, Timmy couldn't take it anymore. He decided to confront the monster and see what it wanted. Slowly, he opened the closet door and peeked inside. To his surprise, there was no monster. Just a dark, empty space. "Well, that's strange," Timmy thought to himself. Just as he was about to close the door, he heard a faint whisper coming from inside the closet. "Come in, come in," the voice said. Timmy was hesitant at first, but he was curious. He stepped inside the closet and looked around. It was dark, but he saw a soft glow coming from the back of the closet. Intrigued, he decided to follow it. As he got closer, the glow grew brighter, and he saw shapes moving inside the light. But as he got even closer, he suddenly felt a cold chill run down his spine. The monsters in the closet weren't monsters at all. They were shadows, flickering and twisting in the light. Something was very wrong. Immediately, Timmy turned and tried to run back to the door, but it was gone. The darkness had swallowed it up. Panic set in as Timmy realized that he was trapped. Suddenly, he felt something wrap around his ankle. The shadows were pulling him down, dragging him into the darkness. But just before he was consumed by the darkness, a bright light appeared. The closet door had opened again, and his mother's smiling face appeared, asking him what he was doing in there. Trembling, Timmy realized that the monster in the closet wasn't real. It was just a figment of his imagination. But now, he knew that darkness held secrets that shouldn't be explored. He hugged his mother tightly, happy to be safe once again.
