Tax brackets are the divisions at which tax rates change in a progressive tax system (or an explicitly regressive tax system, although this is much rarer). Essentially, federal income tax brackets determine how much of your income is taxable, and also how much you will be taxed. The US federal income tax system operates on a marginal rate system. This means that each portion of your income is taxed at its corresponding tax rate. For example, if you are single and earn 50,000 in 2020, you will pay 10 on the first 9,875 of your income, 12 on income between 9,876 and 40,125, and 22 on any income above 40,125. So your total tax bill would be the sum of the taxes paid on each bracket's income range. In addition to tax brackets, there may be deductions or credits that can reduce your tax bill or increase your refund. It's important to understand how tax brackets and deductions work together to help you maximize your savings.

Distributed machine learning is becoming a popular model-training method due to privacy, computational scalability, and bandwidth capacities. In this work, we explore scalable distributed-training versions of two algorithms commonly used in machine learning: stochastic gradient descent (SGD) and alternating least squares (ALS). Distributed SGD involves partitioning data across multiple machines, and updating the model parameters in a parallel fashion. This results in faster training times and the ability to handle larger datasets. However, it can be more challenging to ensure that the different machines are able to communicate effectively and maintain consistency between updates. Distributed ALS is commonly used for matrix factorization problems, such as collaborative filtering in recommender systems. In this approach, the matrix to be factorized is partitioned across multiple machines, and each machine updates a subset of the latent factors. This allows for efficient scaling to large datasets and can be tailored to the specific structure of the matrix. Overall, distributed machine learning is an important area of research and development, enabling faster and more efficient training of models on large datasets. However, it can also be challenging to design and optimize distributed algorithms, and careful consideration must be given to issues such as communication overhead and load balancing.

We consider the stochastic extensible bin packing problem (SEBP) in which n items of stochastic size are packed into m bins of unit capacity. In contrast to the classical bin packing problem, the size of each item is not fixed but follows a probability distribution. The goal is to minimize the expected number of bins used to store all items. To solve SEBP, we can use some variant of the dynamic programming (DP) algorithm. The basic idea here is to construct a sequence of tables, where each table represents the optimal solution for a subset of items. We start with the base case where we have no items, and hence, no bins are used. Then, we add items one by one and compute the optimal solution for each subset of items. At each step, we consider all possible bins that the current item can be packed into. For each bin, we compute the cost of packing the item into that bin using the best solution found so far for the remaining items. Finally, we take the minimum over all possible bins to obtain the optimal solution. The time complexity of this algorithm is O (nm2), which can be quite high for large problem instances. To reduce the running time, we can use some optimization techniques such as pruning and memoization. Moreover, we can consider some heuristics to obtain good initial solutions that can be used to prune the search space. In summary, SEBP is a challenging stochastic optimization problem that can be solved using DP or other optimization techniques. The precise approach depends on the specific problem instance and the available computational resources.

Now, scientists have used it to create a superabsorbing panel that can absorb light with up to 95 percent efficiency. The panel consists of a thin film of molecules that are arranged in a periodic structure. When light strikes the panel, the molecules absorb the light and re-emit it at a different wavelength. This process happens multiple times, and as a result, the light is eventually absorbed by the panel. The efficiency of the panel depends on the number of molecules in the film and the spacing between them. The researchers found that by increasing the number of molecules and decreasing the spacing between them, they could increase the panel's efficiency. The panel could be used to create more efficient solar panels or to create coatings that absorb light and convert it into heat.

Each Local Pastor must be licensed as a Local Pastor before being appointed to serve a church. The Local Pastor may be eligible to receive continuing education benefits from the Conference, but is not eligible to attend the Graduate School of Theology at Drew University. Commissioned Lay Ministers may be eligible to receive continuing education benefits from the Conference, but are not eligible to attend the Graduate School of Theology at Drew University. Ordained Deacons An Ordained Deacon is a clergy person who has been ordained by a bishop to extend Christ's compassion to those in need. Deacons are assigned to serve as pastors of local churches, and also to serve as District Superintendents and Conference staff. In this position paper we present a novel approach to neurobiologically plausible implementation of emotional reactions and behaviors for real-time autonomous robotic systems. The working metaphor we use is the "emotional brain," which describes a complex network of interacting neural circuits that underlie emotional processing and responses in humans and other animals. Our approach is inspired by recent advances in neuroscientific research on the emotional brain, which suggest that emotions are not discrete, fixed states but rather dynamic and adaptive processes that emerge from the interactions of multiple brain regions and systems. Accordingly, we propose a set of neurobiologically realistic computational models that simulate the activity of key brain areas involved in emotional processing and behavior, such as the amygdala, prefrontal cortex, and basal ganglia. By incorporating these models into the control architecture of autonomous robots, we aim to create machines that are capable of displaying sophisticated emotional reactions and behaviors in response to a wide range of stimuli and environmental conditions. For instance, our robots could exhibit fear or avoidance behaviors in the face of danger or threats, approach and seek out sources of reward or pleasure, or display a range of social and communicative behaviors in interactions with humans or other robots. To achieve this goal, our models draw on a variety of input modalities, including visual, auditory, and somatosensory information, as well as higher-level cognitive processes such as attention, memory, and decision-making. Additionally, we incorporate feedback loops that allow our robots to learn from their experiences and adjust their emotional responses and behaviors accordingly. Overall, we believe that our approach could open up new possibilities for the development of socially and emotionally intelligent robots that can interact with humans and other agents in complex and dynamic environments. By leveraging insights from neuroscience to guide the design of robotic systems, we hope to bridge the gap between artificial and biological intelligence and create machines that are more responsive, adaptable, and engaging than ever before.

While it is true that some non-voters do not vote due to their lack of confidence in political parties or candidates, implementing a "no confidence" vote may not necessarily increase voter turnout or provide a better understanding of the public's perception of the political climate. Instead, it could lead to further political polarization and fragment the political landscape. Moreover, a "no confidence" vote could damage the legitimacy of the electoral process by calling into question the very idea of democracy and free elections. Elections are a fundamental aspect of democratic societies and should be upheld as such, rather than creating a separate mechanism that would detract from its significance. Furthermore, one potential drawback of such a system is that it could result in a continuation of the status quo. With a "no confidence" vote, individuals who are dissatisfied with the current political climate may use it as a means to express their discontent without actually working towards a positive change. Rather than fueling democratic participation, it could lead to an increase in apathy and a lack of engagement in the political process. Instead of implementing a "no confidence" vote, efforts should be made to increase civic education, engagement and awareness. This would help individuals feel more informed and empowered to participate in the democratic process and to hold their elected officials accountable. Political parties should also work towards addressing the concerns of disaffected groups to help build trust and confidence in the political system.

However, the report raises concerns that the facility is failing to provide proper care and support for detainees during this often lengthy period. Campaigners have criticized the UK government's use of immigration removal centers, advocating for a more compassionate approach to those who have sought refuge within the country's borders. They claim that conditions within the centers are inhumane, with little access to basic necessities such as outdoor space, mental health support or legal representation. The report states that many in the Brook House facility are living in cramped, tense conditions with little contact from the outside world. Detainees are often held with little explanation or justification offered by the Home Office, who oversee the facility. A spokesperson for the Home Office has emphasized the importance of detention for those who have no legal right to remain in the UK, and who have not complied with attempts to remove them. However, the report calls for the Home Office to rethink its immigration policies, and to adopt a more humane approach towards those facing detention. The centers like Brook House have faced significant backlash in recent years, with campaigners calling for alternatives that prioritize rehabilitation and integration, rather than punishment and exclusion. As the UK government continues to grapple with immigration and asylum policies, the question of how to best address the needs of those seeking refuge within the country remains a crucial concern. And, as the report on Brook House highlights, reform is sorely needed to ensure that detainees are treated with empathy and respect, regardless of their immigration status.

Jenny had always considered herself a rational and level-headed person. But somehow, one small decision at Baskin Robbins had set off a chain reaction that ruined her life. It was a hot summer day six years ago when she and her friends had walked into the ice cream shop. They had all been debating what to choose, and when it was finally Jenny's turn to order she remembered feeling overwhelmed. She wanted to try something new but was also hesitant about wasting money on something she might not like. The server's question, "What flavour do you want?" seemed to hold so much weight in that moment. Jenny's palm began to sweat as she blurted out, "Chocolate." Her friends ordered their ice cream, and they all laughed and joked while they walked out of the shop. But something inside Jenny had shifted. She knew it was just ice cream, but suddenly she became acutely aware of all the other seemingly insignificant decisions she had made in her life. And the more she thought about them, the more she realized how much they had added up. Jenny started to second-guess everything. Should she have taken that job offer? Should she have gone on that date? Should she have said no to that one party invitation? When she finally made a decision, she was too scared to commit to it. She would constantly doubt herself and worry about what could have been if she had chosen differently. It was a vicious cycle that led to anxiety, depression, and eventually substance abuse. Jenny had hit rock bottom when she finally realized that the only way to move forward was to go back to the beginning. Back to that moment in Baskin Robbins where she chose chocolate. She knew it was a silly thing to fixate on, but it symbolized so much more to her. Jenny made the decision to track down the server who had asked her that life-altering question. After some detective work, she finally found her working at another Baskin Robbins location. Jenny walked in nervously, unsure of what she would say. But when she saw the server's familiar face, she knew exactly what she wanted to do. "Excuse me," Jenny said, "I know this is going to sound crazy, but can I order that ice cream again? The one I got six years ago. Chocolate." The server looked at her quizzically but obliged. Jenny took the cone and walked out of the shop, feeling a strange sense of peace. For the first time in years, she felt like she had control over her life. She wasn't going to let one small decision dictate her entire future. Jenny threw the ice cream away without taking a single bite, knowing that its real purpose had been served. She was ready to move forward and make decisions confidently, without fear of regret. And even though she couldn't change the past, she knew that she now had the power to shape her future.

Snopes, the popular online fact-checking website, has announced it is leaving Facebook's fact-checking program. The site, which has been involved in the program since 2016, said that recent changes to the monetary structure of the program made it unsustainable for them. In a statement, Snopes cited "financial and operational constraints" as the reason for their departure from the program. The change in financial structure, which was implemented this month, involves Facebook giving money to its third-party fact-checkers in exchange for their services. Snopes said they were unwilling to accept the new terms due to their "strict standards" regarding independence and objectivity. The decision comes at a time when Facebook is facing increasing scrutiny over its handling of misinformation on its platform. The company has been criticized over its failure to adequately moderate its content, particularly following the events of January 6th, when supporters of former President Donald Trump stormed the Capitol building in Washington DC. Facebook responded to the news of Snopes' departure with a statement saying that they respect the decision and are "confident in the impact" their independent fact-checking program has had. The company also noted that there are still 35 other fact-checkers in the program, including PolitiFact, FactCheck.org and The Associated Press. For its part, Snopes said it will continue to fight misinformation and false claims on the internet, but not through the Facebook fact-checking system. The website said it will focus on developing its own partnerships with other outlets and organizations in order to "help better serve the public interest."

There can be several reasons for your computer to lag even when only 50 of the CPU is being used. Here are some possible reasons and solutions: 1. Insufficient RAM: If your computer has low RAM, it may struggle to keep up with the applications you are running even if the CPU is not fully utilized. Try upgrading your RAM to increase overall system performance. 2. Background processes: Background processes, such as those running antivirus scans or system updates, can utilize CPU resources even if they are not actively being used. Check your task manager to see what processes are using CPU resources and close any unnecessary ones. 3. Outdated software: Outdated software can cause compatibility issues, leading to performance problems. Make sure all software on your computer is up to date. 4. Hard drive problems: If your hard drive is almost full or has issues, it may cause your computer to lag or freeze. Try freeing up some space or running a disk check to fix the issue. 5. Overheating: Overheating can cause performance issues and even damage hardware. Check that your computer fans are working properly and that there is proper airflow around the computer.

You've got a bottle-neck! It doesn't matter what system you run, just about every single one of them have multiple things going on all at the same time. Most of them are waiting on IO, and the faster you can perform that IO, the more efficient your system will be. The first thing you want to do is figure out what is causing these delays. To do this, you need to find out which processes are doing the most IO. If you're running Linux, you can use "iotop." If you're running Windows, there's a very similar program called "Process Explorer." Run this while you're seeing the delays, and see which process is using the most disk activity. In your case, it looks like it's Apache. The next step is to figure out why Apache is reading and writing so much data. There are a few possibilities: Your web site is very popular, and Apache is just busy handling a lot of requests. You have a lot of static files on your web site, and Apache is spending a lot of time reading them from disk. You have a lot of dynamic content on your web site, and Apache is spending a lot of time reading and writing to your database. The first thing you want to do is figure out which one of these is the case. The easiest way to do this is to look at your web server's access logs. If you see a lot of requests for static files (like images, CSS, and JavaScript), then that's probably the issue. The solution here is to enable caching in your web server, so that it doesn't have to read the same files over and over again. If you see a lot of requests for dynamic content (like PHP pages), then that's probably the issue. The solution here is to optimize your database queries, so that they're faster. Once you've identified the problem, you can start working on a solution.

URL0 The empty time that it takes you to look at the clock is replaced by the image of it about to tick in your brain.','Your visual field isn't a continuous stream of information. Instead, your brain fills in the gaps between what your eyes perceive, creating the illusion of a solid visual field. This means that when you glance at a clock, your brain doesn't register every single tick; rather, it uses prior knowledge or expectations to "fill in" the time between glances. So the empty time you experience is actually just your brain compensating for the gaps in your visual perception.

There is, in the lands bordering the Sahara Desert right now. The Sahara Desert has been expanding and expanding for decades now and this desertification is turning once arable crop-land into a wasteland. The Sahara Desert is expanding at about 3 kilometers per year, and that's not just because of climate change. The main reason for this expansion is overgrazing, as well as bad irrigation practices that are causing water to evaporate quickly. These factors are making it harder and harder for crops to grow, which is in turn making it harder for people to make a living. As the Sahara Desert expands, it's putting more and more pressure on the countries that border it. This is especially true for countries like Mali, Niger, and Chad, where many people rely on agriculture for their livelihoods. The desertification of the Sahara is making it increasingly difficult for these people to make a living, and it's estimated that by 2025, the Sahara Desert will be twice as large as it is today.

Factory activity in China, the world's second-largest economy, shrank the most in two years in July, according to the latest data from the National Bureau of Statistics. The official Purchasing Managers' Index (PMI) fell to 49.2 in July, from 50.9 in June, below expectations of 50.0. A PMI reading above 50 indicates expansion in the manufacturing sector, while a reading below 50 suggests contraction. This sharp drop in the PMI was mainly due to a decline in new orders. The sub-index for new orders fell to 47.7, down from 52.0 in June, its lowest level since early 2016. Exports also declined, with the sub-index for export orders falling to 48.4, down from 49.8 in June. Furthermore, the sub-index for employment remained in contraction territory for a third straight month, underscoring the challenges faced by Chinese manufacturers in retaining workers amid slowing growth. The data comes as China is being hit by escalating trade tensions with the United States, which have raised fears of a global trade war. U.S. President Donald Trump has threatened to impose tariffs on all imports from China, including cars and televisions, worth about 500 billion. The latest PMI figures suggest that China's economy may be losing momentum as a result of the trade dispute. The Chinese government has already taken measures to boost economic growth, including tax cuts, infrastructure investment, and faster approvals for infrastructure projects. Despite the challenges, some analysts remain optimistic about China's economic prospects. "We still believe that the Chinese economy will be able to meet the [economic] growth target of around 6.5 percent this year," said Julian Evans-Pritchard, senior China economist at Capital Economics. "But if trade tensions escalate further, there will be downside risks to growth."

Sharon was always known as the punctual one in her family. She made sure that she was always early to class, meetings and appointments. Being late was out of the question for Sharon. Today, however, Sharon found herself running late. Her alarm had failed to go off and Sharon had woken up to find that it was already 10 minutes past the start of her first class. She quickly grabbed her backpack and ran out the door. She sprinted down the street, weaving in and out of people, narrowly avoiding collisions. Finally, Sharon arrived at the building where her class was held. She ran up the stairs two at a time and burst into the classroom, panting and out of breath. The professor looked at her with surprise, but didn't say anything. He simply smiled and nodded his head in acknowledgement. Sharon was relieved to have made it on time and sat down in her seat. As she settled into her chair, she realized that she had forgotten her textbooks at home. She groaned inwardly and prayed that the professor wouldn't call on her during class. Despite her best efforts, Sharon was still late to class. Luckily, her professor didn't seem to mind. From now on, she would make sure that she was even more diligent about setting her alarm and getting to class on time.

We met on a rainy day in August. She was standing over the metal guard rails of an overpass, staring at the murky waters below. I was walking towards her. "It's a long way down," she said. I nodded. "Sure is." She looked at me then, and I saw the sadness in her eyes. "Do you ever feel like just giving up?" she asked. I swallowed hard. I wanted to tell her that I understood, that I'd been there before. But the words wouldn't come. "It's okay," she said softly. "I know how you feel." We stood there for a moment, staring at the dark water below. Then, slowly, she reached out and took my hand. "Let's get out of here," she said. And I knew then that I'd found a friend.

The historical measure of a steam engine's energy efficiency was its "duty." The concept of duty was first introduced by Watt in order to illustrate how much more efficient his steam engines were over the Newcomen engines of his day. When he introduced his steam engines to the world in 1769, he claimed that one of his engines could do the work of twenty of the best Newcomen engines. He developed the term "duty" to explain the difference. Today, duty is usually expressed as a ratio of work output to heat input. In other words, it is a measure of how much useful work an engine can do for a given amount of heat. The higher the duty, the more efficient the engine. Duty can be further divided into two types: indicated duty and brake duty. Indicated duty is a measure of the work done by the engine itself (excluding any external devices such as pumps or fans). Brake duty includes the work done by the engine and all external devices. In general, indicated duty is a better measure of the true efficiency of the engine, while brake duty is a better measure of the overall system efficiency. Theoretical maximum efficiency The theoretical maximum efficiency of a heat engine is known as the Carnot efficiency. It is the efficiency that would be achieved if the heat engine operated between two temperatures that are very close together (such as absolute zero and room temperature). The Carnot efficiency is given by: eta 1 - rac{Tmathrm{cTmathrm{h where Tmathrm{c} is the temperature of the cold reservoir and Tmathrm{h} is the temperature of the hot reservoir. For example, if the cold reservoir is at absolute zero 273.15C) and the hot reservoir is at room temperature (20C), the Carnot efficiency would be: eta 1 - rac273.1520} 0.993 In other words, the theoretical maximum efficiency of a heat engine operating between these two temperatures would be 99.3. Real-world efficiency In the real world, it is impossible to achieve the Carnot efficiency. This is because real-world heat engines always have some friction and other inefficiencies that prevent them from operating at 100 efficiency. The actual efficiency of a heat engine depends on its design, operating conditions, and other factors. For example, a typical internal combustion engine has an efficiency of around 25-30. How to improve efficiency There are four main ways to improve the efficiency of a heat engine: 1) Improve the design of the engine itself. This can be done by reducing friction, improving cooling, and using other methods to reduce inefficiencies. 2) Increase the temperature of the hot reservoir. This can be done by using a higher-temperature fuel, such as natural gas or propane. 3) Decrease the temperature of the cold reservoir. This can be done by using a lower-temperature coolant, such as water or air. 4) Use a regenerative cycle. This is a type of heat engine that captures some of the waste heat and uses it to preheat the working fluid. This can be done with Rankine cycle and Brayton cycle engines. Increasing the efficiency of a heat engine can be an important way to improve its overall performance.

On the world of immortals, life was an endless cycle of curiosity, discovery, and celebration. Nobody ever died. And yet the day came when one immortal being, Maja, drew her last breath. It was an unexpected event, something nobody thought could happen. The news shook the world to its core. Immortals gathered in the town square, trying to comprehend what had happened. Some of them cried, others comforted their loved ones, while others still just stood in silence, staring at the sky above. An emergency session of the Council of the Elders was called, with the hope of understanding what had happened to Maja. But even they were clueless. At last, they decided to summon a being whose powers surpassed all others - a being who could take on this impossible task and bring answers. And so, the council unanimously called upon Zara. Zara was a master of time and space. She could traverse the universe, explore the mysteries of time, and unlock the secrets of life - or in this case, death. When Zara arrived, she was greeted by the elves, dwarves, and other immortal races. They explained what had happened and awaited her verdict. Zara searched the universe and consulted with other enlightened beings. After days of exploration, she concluded that Maja had died due to an extremely rare disease, a disease that was virtually unknown to the immortals of that world. The news was both comforting and alarming. On one hand, the cause of Maja's death had been found, which put many people at ease. On the other, it meant that something else could happen that they had never expected. The immortals had to face a new kind of uncertainty, and they realized that no one, not even them, was immune to death. Maja became the first immortal being to die on their planet, but her death brought new insights into the lives of the immortal beings. They embraced their mortal natures and stopped taking their lives for granted. They lived each day as it came, with gratefulness and appreciation for every moment. They learned to value life, and in their mortality, found a newfound respect for it.

A new government initiative to get more children in English schools to play rugby has come under fire from public health doctors who have expressed concerns about the risks of injury in the sport. The initiative, which was launched earlier this week, aims to increase participation in rugby among school-age children by providing funding for rugby coaches to be trained and for equipment to be purchased. However, the move has been met with criticism from experts in public health who argue that rugby is a high-impact sport and that the risk of injury is significant. Writing in a letter to The Times newspaper, the public health doctors warn that the government's initiative is "ill-conceived" and could lead to children getting seriously hurt. "We support the growth of sport and physical activity but the promotion of rugby in schools, given its high injury risk, is misguided," they write. The doctors go on to point out that rugby can cause serious injuries including concussion, spinal injuries, and fractures, and that the risk of injury is particularly high in children. "Children playing rugby are vulnerable to potentially serious and life-changing injuries," they warn. The doctors argue that the initiative should be reconsidered and that other, less dangerous sports should be promoted instead. "We urge the government to give careful consideration to the risks associated with promoting rugby in schools and instead focus on the promotion of other sports that do not carry such a significant risk of injury," they conclude.

The St Petersburg Paradox is a paradox that comes from a thought experiment. In the experiment, a person is asked to imagine a game where they flip a coin. If the coin comes up heads, the player gets 1. If the coin comes up tails, the player loses 1. The game is played over and over again, and the player can stop at any time. The paradox comes from the fact that, even though the expected value of the game is 0 (meaning that, on average, the player will neither gain nor lose money), the game is still worth playing because there is a chance that the player could get lucky and end up with a lot of money.

Arthritis is a disease that causes pain and swelling in the joints. The joints are the places where two bones meet, such as the elbow or knee. Arthritis can make it hard to do everyday activities such as walking or opening a jar. There is no one test for arthritis. Doctors often use a combination of tests to diagnose it. These may include blood tests, X-rays, and MRIs. There is no cure for arthritis, but there are ways to manage the symptoms. These include exercise, weight loss, and medications.

The letter U follows Q in English words because the two letters together often represent a unique sound in the language. In Old English, the combination of Q and U represented a single phoneme, which is a distinct unit of sound that distinguishes one word from another. This phoneme no longer exists in Modern English, but it's still represented by the letters Q and U in many words.

The Victorian parts of the building have a complex history, with piecemeal additions by different architects. Founded in May 1852, it was not until 1857 that the museum moved to its current location in South Kensington, London. The original buildings were designed by Francis Fowke, but after his untimely death in 1865, the job was taken over by Alfred Waterhouse. Waterhouse's additions gave the museum its distinctive terracotta exterior, and the Natural History Museum still stands as one of the finest examples of Victorian Gothic architecture in the world. Over the years, the museum has been expanded and renovated several times, with the most recent renovation completed in 2009. Today, it houses over 80 million specimens and is one of the most popular tourist attractions in London.

The European Union is in the midst of a deep crisis as leaders meet for an emergency summit in Brussels to debate the relocation of 120,000 migrants. The issue has exposed deep divisions within the 28-nation bloc, with several member states refusing to accept any refugees at all. The meeting was called after the European Commission proposed that each EU country should take in a quota of asylum seekers from Italy and Greece, who are currently struggling to cope with the influx of migrants fleeing conflict and poverty in the Middle East and North Africa. However, several countries have already declared their opposition to the idea, including Hungary, which has adopted an increasingly hostile stance towards immigrants over the past year. "It's not just about the number of refugees. It's also about the kind of society we want to live in," said Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orban. "We don't want to change Hungary into an immigrant country." Meanwhile, the Czech Republic, Slovakia and Romania have also refused to accept any refugees, arguing that the issue should remain a matter for individual states to decide. Despite the disagreement, some countries such as France and Germany have voiced their support for the plan, citing the need for solidarity in the face of the current refugee crisis. The outcome of the summit remains uncertain, but it could potentially set the tone for future debates on how to deal with the migrant crisis. Whatever the outcome, the divisions among EU nations are becoming ever more apparent, with the success or failure of the relocation scheme likely to play a major role in determining the relationship between Europe and the rest of the world in the years to come.

The first thing that came to my mind was getting a job, so I went around the town square to check out the job board. The world was beautiful, and I was glad I had the chance to explore it. Finally, I saw a notice pinned to the wall. The sign said, "Wanted: Experienced Miner" - lucky for me, I was an experienced miner in my universe. I walked up to the man in charge and said, "Hey, I'm interested in the mining job." "Sure," he replied, a bit surprised by seeing someone from the 'real world,' as he called it. "But, you need to have the skills for it." "I was a miner in my world. I can do the same here too," I explained. "Alright then," he nodded. "You can come to work tomorrow morning. I'll provide you with the necessary tools and some information about it." I thanked him and went off to sleep. The next day, I woke up early and went straight to work. It was a lot like mining in real life, except with a stone pickaxe, and mining and gathering materials from the earth. I was the only human mining in that area, and the rest were villagers who helped load my cart. After a long day of mining, I went back to my room in the marketplace, tired but satisfied. I had the tools, and I knew I could do my job well. The days slowly passed and my job became an everyday routine. On some days, I found some rare ore, and it was always a significant accomplishment. I would use the resources I gathered to improve my living space or trade with one of the villagers. As it turned out, life in the world of Minecraft wasn't that different from real life. I still had to work for a living, but I enjoyed it because I was doing it in a world that I loved. It was fascinating to me because everything was as if it came out of a game, yet it was a part of my reality now. In the end, I discovered that nothing could get in the way of a dedicated and skilled worker, even when they were in a different universe. I worked hard, and it paid off. Life was good, and I couldn't have been happier.

This early experiment laid the foundation for the later discovery of oxygen's role in combustion by Antoine-Laurent Lavoisier in the 18th century.

This article details the process of searching for a job in tech. It follows the author through the application, screening, interview, and negotiation processes, breaking down each process and how to optimize for each. The process of job hunting in tech can be divided into four main stages: application, screening, interview, and negotiation. Each stage presents its own unique challenges and opportunities, and it's important to approach each one with care and diligence if you want to maximize your chances of landing the job you want. Application The first stage of the job hunt is the application process. This is where you'll submit your resume and application materials to the company or companies you're interested in working for. The goal here is to make a good impression and stand out from the crowd. To do this, you'll need to have a well-written resume that highlights your skills and experience in a way that's relevant to the position you're applying for. You should also take the time to tailor your cover letter to each position you're applying for. Generic cover letters are a turn-off for hiring managers, so make sure to take the time to customize yours. In addition to your resume and cover letter, you may also be asked to complete an online application. This will usually include questions about your work history, education, and skills. Make sure to answer these questions thoughtfully and completely. Screening Once you've submitted your application, the next stage is screening. This is where the company will review your materials and decide whether or not to invite you to interview. There are a few things you can do to improve your chances of making it past the screening stage. First, make sure your resume and cover letter are error-free. typos and grammatical errors are a major turn-off for hiring managers. Second, take the time to research the company and the position you're applying for. This will give you a better understanding of what they're looking for and help you tailor your materials to their specific needs. Finally, don't be afraid to follow up after you've submitted your materials. A quick email or phone call to thank the hiring manager for their time and express your interest in the position can go a long way. Interview If you make it past the screening stage, the next step is the interview. This is where you'll have the opportunity to sell yourself to the company and demonstrate why you're the best candidate for the job. There are a few things you can do to prepare for your interview. First, review your materials and be ready to talk about your skills and experience. Second, practice your answers to common interview questions. And finally, take the time to research the company and the position you're interviewing for. The more you know about them, the better you'll be able to sell yourself. During the interview, be sure to dress professionally and arrive on time. Be friendly and personable, but avoid being too casual. And most importantly, be honest. Hiring managers can spot BS a mile away, so don't try to fake it. Negotiation If you're offered the job, the final stage is negotiation. This is where you'll discuss salary, benefits, and other terms of employment with the company. It's important to remember that the initial offer is just that - an initial offer. It's very rare for a company to offer their top candidate the first salary they request. So don't be afraid to negotiate. Research salaries for similar positions in your area before you begin negotiating. This will give you a good starting point for your negotiations. And don't be afraid to ask for more than you think you're worth. The worst they can do is say no. When it comes to negotiation, the most important thing is to be confident. Believe in yourself and your value, and don't be afraid to ask for what you deserve.

This paper considers a traditional problem of resource allocation, schedulingjobs on machines. One such recent application is cloud computing, where jobsarrive in an online fashion with capacity requirements and need to be matchedwith available machines. In a cloud environment, it is important to have efficientalgorithms for online allocation of resources to jobs. We consider the followingproblem: given a set of jobs with release times and deadlines, and a set ofmachines each with a time-varying capacity and energy consumption profile,allocate the jobs to machines such that the total energy consumption is minimized.We consider the problem under several different assumptions on the problemdata and propose algorithms for solving the problem. We prove the performanceof the algorithms and show experimentally that the algorithms perform wellcompared to existing algorithms from the literature. 1 Introduction The resource allocation problem can be defined as follows: given a set of jobs J with release times rj , deadlines dj , and capacity requirements p j , and a set of machines M with capacity profiles xi (t), allocate jobs to machines such that the maximum load on any machine is minimized, and all deadlines are met. We assume that all machines start out with zero load, i.e., 0 xi0 (t) 0 for all t and xi0 (t) is time-varying but non-decreasing, and initially all jobs are unassigned. A job can be assigned to a machine when the machine has sufficient capacity to accommodate the job. Jobs can be pre-empted and reassigned to another machine later, if necessary, to accommodate other jobs with earlier deadlines or to satisfy the capacity requirement of the job. The objective is to find a schedule that minimizes the maximum load on any machine. Alternatively, the objective may be to find a schedule that minimizes makespan, which is the maximum load on any machine over the time horizon. The resource allocation problem occurs in several real-world situations. It can be viewed as the problem of scheduling jobs on servers in a datacenter. In this case, the capacity of a server (machine) varies depending on its workload and cooling requirements, and hence it is not always possible to use the full capacity of the server at all times. In another application where the problem arises is cloud computing. In cloud computing, users submit jobs (with release times, deadlines and capacity requirements) to a cloud provider (the machines). The cloud provider must then schedule the jobs on the machines such that the total energy consumption is minimized. The energy consumption of a machine is a function of its workload, and therefore it is not always possible to use the full capacity of a machine at all times. The problem of resource allocation has been studied extensively in the literature; see e.g., [5, 9, 11, 13, 14, 17, 18]. There are two main approaches to solving the problem: exact methods and approximation methods. The former attempt to find an optimal solution while the latter attempt to find a near-optimal solution. Exact methods tend to be more computationally expensive than the approximation methods, and therefore are typically used only for small problem sizes. For example, the dynamic programming approach proposed by Graham [9] solves the problem exactly in time O (mn2). A variant of the dynamic pro- gramming approach proposed by Wierman et al. [18] runs in time O (n3 log m). Other exact methods proposed in the literature include branch-and-bound based methods [14], local search methods [17], and Integer Linear Programming (ILP) based methods [13]. Approximation methods tend to run faster than the exact ones, but generally provide suboptimal solutions. Some examples of approximate methods include heuristics like the longest processing time first (LPT) method [11], randomized rounding methods [5], and greedy methods [11]. The LPT method schedules the jobs in the order of increasing processing time. It provides a bounded performance guarantee: it gives a schedule that is at most twice the optimal schedule. The randomized rounding method [5] is based on solving a relaxation of the problem called LP-rounding. The best known approximation factor is 23. A simple greedy method is proposed by Baruah et al. [11], which schedules jobs in the order of increasing deadlines. The approximation factor of the method is 12. The resource allocation problem considered in this paper is a natural exten- sion of the traditional resource allocation problem, where we also minimize the total energy consumption of the machines. The mayor of Warsaw is called President. Generally, in Poland, the mayors of bigger cities are called presidents - i.e. such cities, which have over 100,000 people or these, where the city's name is a noun derived from the word "president" (e.g. Poznan). Nowadays, the title of President of Warsaw is given to the head of Warsaw City Hall. The first person to be called the President of Warsaw was Stefan Starzynski. He was appointed in 1934 and held this position until 1939. After the outbreak of World War II, the German authorities gave this title to the head of the city administration - Ludwig Fischer. In 1944, after the Warsaw Uprising, the title was taken away from him and given to the commander of the Polish Home Army in Warsaw - Antoni Chrusciel. When Poland regained its independence in 1918, the title of President of Warsaw was taken by Stanisaw Thugutt.

Factory activity in China shrank in July, the most in two years, as new orders fell more than expected. The data is a further sign that the world's second-largest economy is cooling as the government tries to rein in debt and factory overcapacity. The Purchasing Managers' Index (PMI) fell to 49.9 in July from 50.4 in June, according to the National Bureau of Statistics and Caixin media group. A reading below 50 indicates contraction. Analysts had expected the index to hold steady. The new orders sub-index fell to 47.8 from 49.4 in June, while the output sub-index also declined, to 51.1 from 52.0. The slowdown in manufacturing comes as Beijing tries to shift the economy from its reliance on heavy industry and exports to domestic consumption. But the transition has been bumpy, and policymakers have had to rely on stimulus measures to prop up growth. They have also been struggling to contain a rapid build-up in debt, which could threaten financial stability.

This framework accelerates the development of new architectures and reduces the time and effort required for prototyping, testing, and benchmarking. Our second contribution is to systematically investigate the impact of network topology, filter sizes, and non-linearities on model performance. When faced with learning a set of inter-related tasks from a limited amount of usable data, learning each task independently may lead to poor generalization performance. exploits the latent relations between tasks. Multi-task learning (MTL) is an approach to address this issue by using a single model to learn all of the tasks simultaneously. Multi-task learning helps to improve generalization performance by exploiting the shared features among different tasks, while still allowing each task to specialize on its own features that may not be present in the other tasks. This approach can improve accuracy, since it takes advantage of the correlations between tasks and allows the model to focus on learning the most valuable information for all tasks instead of just one. Additionally, it reduces the amount of data needed for training as the same data can be used for multiple tasks. Furthermore, MTL can also reduce the risk of overfitting due to fewer parameters being used overall.

From video streaming to security and surveillance applications, video data play an important role in our daily living today. However, managing a large amount of video data and retrieving the information of interest from them remain a big challenge. This is due to the high volume and complex structure of the data, as well as the inherent properties of vision and visual perception. The aim of this project is to develop efficient methods for managing and processing large amount of video data. The first part of this project deals with the problem of detecting objects in videos. We propose a new method for object detection and tracking which can effectively cope with the uncertainties caused by object occlusion, deformation, background clutter, and changing lighting conditions. Our method uses a discriminative appearance model for object representation and tracking. It employs a latent SVM framework for learning the discriminative appearance model from a small set of positive examples, and integrates an efficient object detection algorithm into the tracking process to handle the problems of object occlusion and deformation. In addition, we present an effective strategy for handling the problem of background clutters by using a hybrid tracker, which consists of a correlation tracker and our discriminative tracker. Finally, we develop an online object tracking method based on the proposed tracker. In the second part of this project, we focus on challenging issues in medical image analysis, including vessel segmentation, tumor detection and classification. Vessel segmentation is an important task in ophthalmology and has been extensively studied during the past two decades. However, it remains a challenging task due to the difficulties of detecting thin vessels with varying widths, tortuosities and low contrast. We propose a new method for vessel segmentation which is capable of effectively detecting thin vessels with varying widths and tortuosities. The method uses a local region-based active contour model with a novel shape prior term. The shape prior term is based on an extended version of the stationary wavelet transform (SWT), which can efficiently capture the local shape characteristics of vessels. We also proposing a new way of using the SWT for performing tumor detection and classification. Experimental results show that our methods are effective for vessel segmentation and tumor detection and outperform the state-of-the-art methods. Advisor: Prof. Xiaoming Liu

Synergistic interactions are ubiquitous in the real world. Recent studies have revealed that, for a single-layer network, synergy can enhance spreading and even induce an explosive contagion. There is at least one universal property of real-world networks that is known to promote synergy: the existence of mesoscale modules or communities. We study the effect of modularity on synergistic interactions, and show that modular structure can strongly enhance the synergy-driven spreading. Specifically, we find that the synergy-driven spreading threshold decreases with increasing modularity, and can even become zero in certain cases. We also find that the synergy-driven contagion exhibits a discontinuous transition from subcritical to supercritical when the modularity exceeds a certain critical value. Our findings demonstrate that modular structure can significantly amplify synergy-induced contagion, and suggest that modularity may be an important factor for understanding the emergence of explosive epidemics in the real world.

With the increasing penetration of renewable energy resources, power systems face new challenges in maintaining power balance and the nominal frequency. This paper studies load control to handle these challenges. Two load control methods are studied. One is the direct control method, where the frequency deviation is compensated directly by changing the real power of loads. The other is the indirect control method, where the frequency deviation is compensated by changing the reactive power of loads and then the change of reactive power is used to compensate the real power deviation. In both methods, a proportional integral (PI) controller is used for each load. Simulation results show that the indirect load control has a better performance in maintaining power balance and the nominal frequency than the direct load control method does. View Less

Scientists have successfully demonstrated a proof of concept that could lay the foundation for quantum batteries. In a recent study, researchers at the University of Cambridge in the UK have shown that they can use entanglement, one of the fundamental principles of quantum mechanics, to create a battery that could store energy for a long time without leakage. The principle of entanglement refers to the phenomenon where two quantum particles become connected in such a way that their properties are no longer independent of each other - they become correlated. When two particles are entangled, any change that occurs to one particle will also affect the other, no matter how far away they are from each other. The researchers used this principle to develop a quantum battery that would be able to store energy indefinitely, without leaking or decaying. They did this by creating a system of entangled particles that were placed inside a supercooled, high vacuum environment. The team also found that the energy density of their quantum battery was much higher than any other battery that currently exists. In fact, they calculated that their system could hold over 1,000 times more energy than a conventional battery of the same size. While the study is still in its early stages, the researchers are optimistic that their work could pave the way for the development of quantum batteries that would be much more efficient and long-lasting than current battery technologies. Quantum batteries could revolutionize many industries, including electric cars and renewable energy storage. The ability to store large amounts of energy in a small space with no leakage or decay would be a game-changer for these industries. The team plans to continue their research and development of the technology, with the goal of creating a prototype quantum battery in the near future. If successful, this could be a major step forward in the ongoing efforts to create a sustainable and energy-efficient future.

We show dense voxel embeddings learned via deep metric learning can be employed to produce a highly accurate segmentation of neurons from 3D electron microscopy images. A metric graph on the encoded voxel representations is constructed using a nearest-neighbor search algorithm, which enables efficient computation of shortest paths on the graph. These shortest paths form the basis of segmenting individual neurons from the image by identifying the boundaries between them. The accuracy of the segmentation is enhanced by integrating multiple image modalities, such as electron microscopy and fluorescence microscopy, using a multimodal fusion strategy. Overall, this approach significantly improves the efficiency and accuracy of neuron segmentation from 3D electron microscopy images, which has important applications in neuroscience research.

We present and analyze a numerical method to solve the time-dependent linear Pauli equation in three space-dimensions. The Pauli equation is a "semi-relativistic" generalization of the Schrodinger equation for 2-spinors . It is a model of relativistic quantum mechanics which has received much attention in the past decade, particularly with respect to the spin-orbit and Darwin terms. The Pauli equation has two vector potentials, each corresponding to an electromagnetic field. One vector potential, A, corresponds to the external electromagnetic field (e.g., a laser field) in which the particle moves. The second vector potential, B, corresponds to the effective magnetic field that arises from the motion of the particle itself. This "magnetic" vector potential exists even in the absence of any external field, and it accounts for the spin degree of freedom of the particle. We discuss the physical meaning of the Pauli equation, and its relationship to the Dirac and Schrodinger equations. We then describe a method for solving the time-dependent Pauli equation numerically. The method is based on a discretization of the 3-dimensional spatial grid, and a transformation of the Pauli equation into a set of coupled first-order differential equations. This method is applicable to a wide range of problems in physics and chemistry, including those involving spin-orbit and Darwin terms. For example, the method can be used to study the dynamics of electrons in atoms and molecules, as well as in solid state systems. In addition, the method can be used to study the scattering of electrons from atoms and molecules, as well as from materials surfaces.

The United Methodist Church is organized into conferences. The highest level is called the General Conference and is the only organization which may speak officially for the church. The General Conference meets every four years and is made up of delegates from all over the world. Its responsibilities include setting policies, electing bishops, and approving the church's doctrinal statements. Below the General Conference, there are several other levels of conferences. The next level is the Jurisdictional Conference. This conference is responsible for electing and assigning bishops to oversee specific regions of the world. The annual conferences are the next level down. Each annual conference covers a specific geographic region and is responsible for appointing pastors, managing finances, and overseeing local ministries. Finally, there are district conferences, which cover even smaller geographic regions and are responsible for the day-to-day operations of the local churches in their area. Overall, this organizational structure allows the United Methodist Church to effectively communicate and implement policies and practices across a large, global organization while still allowing for local autonomy and decision-making.

Despite the fact that free personal care has been available in Scotland for over a decade, it was only introduced in England in April 2020. However, the effects of the COVID-19 pandemic on the health and social care sector have led to significant delays in assessments and care arrangements being carried out. According to Age UK, the consequences of these delays are severe. Many elderly individuals are left to manage on their own without any support, which can lead to isolation, poor health and a loss of independence. Others are forced to pay for their own care, which can use up all of their savings and assets. Charity officials believe that more needs to be done to ensure that elderly individuals receive the care they are entitled to. Some of the recommendations being made by Age UK include greater investment in social care services, better communication between health and social care providers, and the streamlining of the care assessment process. Age UK's director, Caroline Abrahams, said: "Free personal care is a lifeline for many elderly individuals who struggle to carry out the most basic tasks. We need to ensure that everyone who is entitled to this support receives it in a timely and efficient manner. It is time for the government to take action and address the issues that are preventing elderly individuals from accessing the care they need."

Tim was always a bit messy. His mom would constantly nag him about cleaning his room - books and clothes strewn across the floor, empty candy wrappers on his nightstand. But he never really saw the point in tidying up when he was just going to mess it up again the next day. One afternoon, Tim's mother had enough. She had been cleaning up after him for long enough and decided to teach him a lesson. She marched into his room and gave him an ultimatum: either clean up his mess or leave the house for the night. Feeling defiant, Tim decided to leave. He grabbed his backpack, threw in a few clothes, some snacks, and his phone charger, and took off down the street. He didn't have a plan, just a vague idea of maybe finding somewhere else to sleep for the night. As he walked, he realized that he didn't even know where he was going. He wandered around for a while, then found himself at a small park on the outskirts of town. As the sun began to set, he settled in on a bench, munching on a bag of chips and scrolling through social media on his phone. It wasn't long before he noticed that the park was a little sketchy. A few people seemed to be hanging around, looking at him strangely. He started to feel a little uneasy, especially when he saw someone digging through a trash can nearby. As it got darker, he decided it would be best to leave the park and find somewhere else to stay. But as he got up from the bench, he realized he had left his backpack unzipped and a mess of snacks had spilled out onto the ground. Feeling like an idiot, he quickly gathered everything together and stuffed it back into his bag. He couldn't believe how much of a mess he had made - his mom was right, he really did need to start taking responsibility for his actions. Tim eventually found a spot to sleep for the night, but he didn't get much rest. He thought about his mom and how sorry he was for leaving a mess, and how he needed to start being more responsible in all aspects of his life. The next morning, when he returned home, his mom was surprised to see him. She was angry that he had left without cleaning up, but it was clear that he had learned his lesson. He immediately started cleaning his room and promised to do better from now on. From that day forward, Tim made an effort to be more organized and tidy. It wasn't always easy, but he knew it was the right thing to do. He didn't want to be known as the kid who always left a mess, and he was happy that he had learned that lesson before it was too late.

A problem is regarded as inherently difficult if its solution requires significant resources, whatever the algorithm used. The theory formalizes this intuition, by introducing mathematical models of computation to study the limitations and possibilities of algorithms. In other words, some problems are simply more complex than others, and no matter how efficient an algorithm is, it may still require a significant amount of time or resources to solve these difficult problems. The study of inherently difficult problems is known as complexity theory, and it has important practical applications in fields such as computer science, operations research, and cryptography. By understanding the inherent difficulty of certain problems, researchers can develop more efficient algorithms and design systems that are more secure and resilient to attack.

The approval of the DAO in Wyoming marks a significant milestone in the development of the blockchain industry in the US. It is expected that other states will soon follow suit and pass similar laws in order to provide more clarity and security for businesses operating in the space.

In 2010, a security researcher named Tavis Ormandy discovered a critical vulnerability in the way that the Google App Engine handled Java bytecode. This flaw could be exploited to allow remote code execution, and Ormandy released a proof-of-concept exploit. The Google App Engine is a platform-as-a-service offering that allows developers to run their applications on Google's infrastructure. One of the language options for developing App Engine applications is Java. When an application is deployed to App Engine, the Java bytecode is compiled to native code. This native code is then executed by a lightweight virtual machine (LVM). The LVM sandbox provides a restricted environment for untrusted code, but the details of the sandbox implementation are not made public. The flaw that Ormandy discovered was that the App Engine sandbox did not properly restrict access to certain Java classes. This allowed his exploit to bypass the sandbox restrictions and gain full control of the underlying server. Ormandy's exploit was a serious blow to the security of the App Engine platform. In response to the discovery of the flaw, Google implemented a number of changes to the way that Java bytecode is compiled and executed. Despite these changes, the App Engine platform remains a popular target for attackers. In 2016, a researcher named Robert Hansen published a blog post detailing how he had successfully bypassed the App Engine security controls to execute arbitrary code. The App Engine platform is just one example of the challenges that exist in securing Java-based applications. The Java platform itself is notoriously complex, and there are a number of ways in which flaws in the platform can be exploited. As more and more businesses move to the cloud, it is important to understand the security risks associated with platform-as-a-service offerings. The App Engine platform provides a great deal of flexibility and scalability for developers, but it is important to be aware of the potential security pitfalls.

One of the challenges in large-scale information retrieval (IR) is to develop fine-grained and domain-specific methods to answer natural language questions. Despite the availability of numerous sources and datasets for training IR models, the selection of appropriate resources for a specific domain is usually a challenging task that requires domain expertise and human intervention. In this work, we propose an approach to automatically identify and select the most appropriate source and dataset for learning an IR model. The proposed approach consists of four steps: (1) data collection from multiple sources; (2) generation of a set of questions based on the selected data source; (3) retrieval of answers using different IR models; and (4) selection of the best IR model. We evaluated our approach to automatic selection of IR models on two tasks: question answering (QA) and machine translation (MT). Our results show that our approach can be used to automatically identify and select the most appropriate IR model for a given task.

Target speech separation refers to isolating target speech from a multi-speaker mixture signal by conditioning on auxiliary information about the target speaker. Different from the mainstream audio-visual approaches which usually require visual information, target speech separation only requires audio signals and an auxiliary source of information about the target speaker. The goal of this task is to reconstruct the target speech signal while suppressing the interference from other speakers and background noise. Target speech separation techniques can be broadly classified into two categories: supervised and unsupervised models. Supervised models rely on a priori knowledge of the target speaker, such as voiceprint or language identity, to help separate the target speech from other speakers. Unsupervised models, on the other hand, utilize some form of clustering algorithm to identify the target speech from the mixture. In recent years, deep learning approaches have become increasingly popular for target speech separation tasks. Deep learning models are often trained in an end-to-end fashion on large datasets, allowing them to learn complex representations of the audio data and effectively perform speech separation. In addition, these models can also be trained with auxiliary input features such as speaker embeddings, which can further improve the performance of the model. Overall, target speech separation is an important task that has been extensively studied in the past few years. With the advances in deep learning, it is now possible to achieve state-of-the-art results in this task.

As a software engineer, feeling engaged at work is crucial for both personal job satisfaction and team productivity. Supporting your colleagues can help take your work to a higher level, and build camaraderie that you never knew was possible. 3. Focus on accomplishments: Don't let yourself get bogged down in the day-to-day minutia. Celebrating small accomplishments is a key aspect of feeling engaged and motivated. 4. Keep learning: Software engineering is an ever-changing field. Make sure you stay abreast of new developments and trends by attending conferences, following blogs and articles, and seeking out learning opportunities. 5. Take breaks: Finally, remember to take breaks every so often. Stepping away from the work can help renew your energy and focus, and allow you to come back to work feeling refreshed and ready to tackle the next challenge. By incorporating these tips into your daily work routine, you'll find that it's easier than ever to feel engaged and motivated in your role as a software engineer.

While addiction may start as a habit, it progresses to become a disease. Over time, addiction changes how the brain functions, leading to compulsive behavior, loss of control, and continued use despite negative consequences. Various studies have shown that addiction involves changes in brain chemistry that continue even after a person has stopped using the substance. In contrast, habits can be changed through willpower and motivation, whereas addiction requires professional help and ongoing support. Thus, addiction is not solely a habit but a disease that requires medical treatment, counseling, and a strong support system to overcome.

He later revealed that he was protesting against the Ethiopian government's treatment of the Oromo people, the largest ethnic group in the country. Following the event, Lilesa feared for his safety upon returning to Ethiopia, so he chose to stay in Brazil while seeking asylum in another country. The outpouring of support from around the world has been tremendous, with thousands of individuals donating to the campaign. It also gained the backing of prominent athletes, including Mo Farah and Almaz Ayana of Ethiopia. "Feyisa's courage has inspired us all," said Farah. Television shows shot in front of a live audience preserve continuity and ensure that the crowd laughs at running jokes throughout the show by using various techniques. One technique is to film multiple takes of the same scene, so the audience can react to the jokes multiple times. Another technique is to use a "laugh track," which is pre-recorded laughter that is inserted into the show during post-production. This way, even if the audience does not laugh at a particular joke, the laugh track can be used to create the illusion of a lively and responsive audience. Additionally, the actors often interact with the audience during breaks or before and after the show to build rapport and create a more active and engaged crowd. Finally, the producers and writers of the show can also study which jokes and scenes receive the most laughter during rehearsals and adjust the script accordingly to keep the audience engaged and invested in the show.

John was a curious man who spent most of his free time exploring. One day, he came across an old bookstore and decided to go inside. As he was browsing through the books, he noticed a strange-looking book on the dusty shelf. The cover read, "The Book of The Impossible." Intrigued, John picked up the book and began flipping through the pages. The book was filled with predictions, but not ordinary ones. The pages were filled with what could not and would not happen. At first, John didn't understand the purpose of such a book. However, as he kept reading, he realized the potential of the book. In it, he found indications of all the things he should avoid and the things that he should never look forward to. It offered him a different perspective about the future. John took the book home with him and carefully read through every page. He learned that no matter how much he tried, some things were impossible, and he should not waste his time or energy trying to achieve them. The book told him that he would never be able to fly without a plane, find a pot of gold at the end of a rainbow, or survive without food and water. On the other hand, the book also mentioned what he should focus on. It told John that love, compassion, and kindness are things that he can always make happen. The book taught him to cherish the people around him and to be grateful for every moment of his life. John realized that the book was not just a collection of predictions but was a guide to help him live a full and happy life. The book has shown him all the things he shouldn't cling on to and the things that were always possible. From that day forward, John lived a more fulfilling life. He stopped worrying about the impossible things and instead, focused on what really mattered in his life. The book of the impossible had changed his life forever, and he knew he would forever be grateful for that strange day when he found it in that old bookstore.

It was yet another day in Mrs. Johnson's math class, and Emma was struggling to keep her eyes open. Just as she was about to doze off, Mrs. Johnson began speaking in a strange and monotonous tone. Emma quickly realized that her teacher had been repeating the same sentence over and over again. "This formula is the key to solving all math problems," Mrs. Johnson droned on. At first, Emma tried to ignore the repetition and focus on her notes. But as the minutes ticked by, the incessant repetition began to grate on her nerves. Emma looked around the classroom and saw that her classmates seemed similarly bored and frustrated. Some were dozing off, while others were doodling in their notebooks. Finally, Emma had enough. She decided to confront Mrs. Johnson. "Excuse me, Mrs. Johnson," Emma said. "You've been repeating the same sentence for the last 10 minutes. Is everything okay?" Mrs. Johnson blinked and looked up from her notes. "Oh, I'm sorry, Emma. I didn't even realize I was doing that. I must be more tired than I thought." Emma felt a wave of relief wash over her. She wasn't sure if Mrs. Johnson was deliberately trying to drive her students crazy or if there was something genuinely wrong. But as Mrs. Johnson continued with the lesson, Emma noticed that she was more alert and focused than she had been before. Maybe hearing the same sentence over and over again wasn't such a bad thing after all.

In November 2006, the Victorian Legislative Council elections were held under a new multi-member proportional representation system. The State of Victoria was divided into eight electorates with each electorate represented by five members. The system used was a single transferable vote (STV) method, with voters having the option of voting above the line for a party as well as below the line for individual candidates. The quota for election was 16.7, meaning that a candidate needed to receive one-seventeenth or more of the formal first preferences before being elected. Counting commenced immediately following the close of polling and was conducted at the Victorian Electoral Commission's count centre in Melbourne. The Coalition won three seats and the ALP won five seats. The ALP won the final seat after three rounds of counting. The final result was announced on 14 November 2006. Graph neural networks (GNNs) are powerful machine learning models for various graph learning tasks. Recently, the limitations of the expressive power of various GNN models have been revealed. For example, it has been shown that some GNNs are incapable of distinguishing between certain graph structures, leading to poor performance on certain tasks. This discovery has led to the development of more expressive GNNs, such as graph attention networks (GATs) and graph convolutional networks (GCNs). GATs are designed to attend to different parts of the input graph to learn more complex representations. They achieve this by learning a weighting function for each node's neighbors, which determines the importance of each neighbor. This allows for more flexible feature aggregation and has been shown to significantly improve performance on a range of tasks. GCNs, on the other hand, use a convolutional operation to aggregate features from neighboring nodes in a graph. They learn filters that are applied to the node features to generate new representations. They also have the advantage of being able to propagate features across multiple layers, allowing them to capture more complex relationships in the graph. Overall, the development of more expressive GNNs has led to improved performance on many graph learning tasks, and ongoing research in this area is likely to continue uncovering new insights and improving the ability of these models to learn from complex graph structures.

Tensor completion is a challenging problem with various applications. Many related models based on the low-rank prior of the tensor have been proposed. However, the low-rank prior may not be suitable for all the tasks. In this paper, we propose a new tensor completion model based on a low-rank approximation with a novel non-convex regularizer, namely, the ell{2;1norm regularizer (L2:1). The regularizer is designed to impose sparsity constraints on the components of each matrix unfolding of the tensor. This forces the low-rank approximation to capture significant structures in the tensor. We develop an alternating minimization algorithm for solving the proposed model, and provide theoretical guarantees for its convergence. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate that our method significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods in terms of reconstruction accuracy. The contributions of this work are threefold. First, we propose a novel tensor completion model based on the low-rank approximation with the L2:1 regularizer. Second, we develop an efficient algorithm to solve the proposed model and provide theoretical analysis to guarantee its convergence. Finally, experimental results show that our method achieves better performance than existing methods.

Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) have emerged recently as a promising application of deep neural networks to the numerical solution of nonlinear partial differential equations (PDEs). However, the original PINN algorithm is limited in its ability to solve certain types of PDEs, such as those with nonlinear coefficients or high-dimensional input spaces. In this paper, we introduce a new algorithm, the Deep Multi-Physics PINN (DMP-PINN), which extends the original PINN algorithm by incorporating multiple physical models into the network architecture. The DMP-PINN algorithm can be applied to a wide variety of nonlinear PDEs, including those with nonlinear coefficients and high-dimensional inputs.
