Throughout the Middle Ages, Newcastle was England's northern fortress. Incorporated first by Henry II, the city had a new charter granted by Elizabeth in 1589. A 25-foot (7.6 m) high town wall was built around the city in 1370 and completed in 1400. The main gateway, the "Black Gate" was built in 1450 and has been successfully restored. Newcastle also had the first recorded City Council in England, established in 1216. The medieval castle, now incorporated into the city walls, was built by Henry II on the site of an earlier 11th-century fort and extended by Richard I, John and Henry III. It was the scene of many sieges during its history; the most notable being that led to its capture by the Scots in 1346. By 1834, the town had become a county borough independent of Northumberland. The town developed rapidly during the Industrial Revolution, particularly in shipbuilding and coal mining. Tyneside's steel industry also rose to prominence. During this period, Newcastle became a major centre for banking and insurance. In the early 20th century, its port was amongst the world's busiest. The Great Depression hit the city hard, particularly between 1929 and 1934. After the Second World War, Tyneside's traditional industries declined, leaving high unemployment and social deprivation across the area. The city was a target for German V-1 flying bombs during the later stages of the conflict. Newcastle expanded greatly in the latter half of the 20th century, especially towards the west of the city centre. Much of the housing stock in central Newcastle was demolished during the 1960s and 1970s, and replaced with modern office blocks and business parks. Significant regeneration has taken place since the 1990s, and a new residential area, Spital Tongues, was built near the city centre. Newcastle University is a member of the Russell Group, an association of research-intensive British universities; it is also ranked among the top 200 universities in the world by QS World University Rankings. The city is also home to Northumbria University, one of the largest universities in the country. Newcastle's economy includes commercial shipping, retail, tourism and public administration. In 2009, Newcastle was ranked as the fourth most visited city in England by overseas visitors. edit] History Main article: History of Newcastle upon Tyne Built on the River Tyne, Newcastle began life as a Roman settlement called Pons Aelius or 'Bridge of Aelius'. Pons is Latin for bridge and Aelius was the family name of the Roman Emperor Hadrian, who founded it in about AD 122.[4] Hadrian's Wall passed through the present day city centre and it is thought that the Roman military settlement remained there well after the wall was constructed. A number of fragments of Hadrian's Wall have been excavated in Newcastle, especially along the West Road. The course of the "Roman Wall" can be traced eastwards to the Segedunum Roman fort in Wallsend - the "wall's end" - and to the supply fort Arbeia in South Shields. After the Romans left, Newcastle was part of the Anglian kingdom of Bernicia. The first recorded mention of the castle of Newcastle was in 1080 when William the Conqueror ordered its construction. The castle was built to protect the northern approaches to London and the settlements along the River Tyne from the expected invasion by the Scots. The village of Newcastle probably grew up around the castle and it was known as Novum Castellum or New Castle. The castle was rebuilt in stone in 1087, and it was eventually destroyed by fire in 1344.[5] The name 'Newcastle' has been used since the Norman Conquest (1066), and because of its strategic position at the furthest accessible point up the River Tyne from the sea, it became important as a trading hub. The first recorded coal shipment from Newcastle dates from 1200, and the town was soon exporting coal to the Netherlands and parts of France. In the 14th century, Newcastle became increasingly involved in the wool trade and later became a major centre for the manufacture of cloth, particularly linen. The town's merchants were instrumental in the establishment of the Guild of the Holy Trinity in 1326, which was granted a royal charter eight years later. Newcastle was successfully defended against the Scots three times during the 14th century, and was created a county corporate with its own sheriff by Henry IV in 1400. The French attacked Newcastle twice during the Hundred Years' War; in December 1421, and again in May 1424, but they were repulsed both times. In 1436, Henry VI granted Newcastle a charter founding the town as a county corporate, granting the corporation sole responsibility for the governance of the town and trade within it. The charter also granted Henry VI the right to appoint the mayor. In 1446, the town was made a county of itself. The Black Gate was built in 1450 and added to the town walls. I made my way around the store, keeping an eye out for anyone who could help me. The first hour or so passed in a daze as I explored the store's many sections. I watched customers and employees alike go about their day, behaving as if there wasn't a floating shirt and pants hovering from aisle to aisle. Finally, I decided to approach a Walmart employee hoping they could help. "Excuse me," I said, hovering in front of them invisible. "I need some help, please." They looked around confused, but then their eyes rested where I was. A look of both fear and fascination crossed their face. After a few moments of explaining my situation, the employee finally put the pieces together, telling me I could use the phone at the customer service desk. I made my way there feeling a little relieved. However, as I waited for help, I couldn't help but notice that people were treating the floating items showing no concern for the possibility of theft. Two hours passed in near silence, though it was surreal. Finally, a security guard arrived. After checking to see if I was insane or on drugs, the officer took me to the store manager. The manager listened attentively to my story, explaining that he couldn't see me either but could hear me talking. He took my details and called the police who showed up not long after. In the end, the police helped me find a way to become visible once more. It was one of the strangest experiences of my life, and a great example of how people don't always notice what's right in front of them.

We show dense voxel embeddings learned via deep metric learning can be employed to produce a highly accurate segmentation of neurons from 3D electron microscopy images. A metric graph on the voxel embeddings is used to construct a segmentation of neurons from the raw image. The resulting segmentations are shown to be highly accurate compared to manually-annotated ground truth data, with a mean Intersection-over-Union scoring of 0.90 on our test set. We also show that these embedding-based segmentation models can be used to accurately detect small-sized neurons, which are difficult to identify using traditional algorithms. Our approach provides a powerful and flexible method for neuron segmentation in 3D electron microscopy images. Our results demonstrate that deep metric learning can be used to learn dense voxel embeddings that can be employed to obtain accurate neuron segmentations from EM images. This approach could potentially be extended to other types of biomedical images.

Knowledge graphs capture entities and relations from long documents and can facilitate reasoning in many downstream applications. Extracting compact knowledge graphs containing only salient entities and relations is important but challenging. To address this challenge, we propose an unsupervised method to select salient entities and relations by modeling the context of each entity-relation pair in a given document. Our method is based on a simple but effective insight that the more frequently a pair of entities appears in the same context, the stronger their relation is. We use a vector representation of contexts to capture the occurrence and co-occurrence of entities and relations in a document, and then apply a graph-based clustering approach to select the most relevant pairs. Experiments show that our method outperforms existing approaches for knowledge graph summarization in terms of both coverage of salient relations and compactness of the output graphs. The proposed method for knowledge graph summarization is based on an intuitive insight that the frequency of co-occurrence of entities and relations in a given document reflects the strength of the relation between them. We model this insight with a vector representation of contexts, which captures both the occurrence of each entity-relation pair and their co-occurrences. We then apply a graph-based clustering approach to select the most relevant pairs based on their vector representations. The output of our method is a compact knowledge graph containing only the most salient entities and relations. Experiments show that our method outperforms existing approaches in terms of both coverage of salient relations and compactness of the output graph.

We devise a distributional variant of gradient temporal-difference (TD) learning. Distributional reinforcement learning has been demonstrated to outperform the regular one in the recent study (,). In the policy evaluation step, instead of estimating the expected value of the state-action pair, we estimate the distribution of possible returns for each state-action pair. This distribution is then used to update the Q-values instead of a single value. This approach allows us to capture the variance in possible returns for each state-action pair and can lead to more accurate value estimates and improved performance. To perform the distributional update, we first discretize the range of possible returns into a set of probability mass functions (PMFs) over a set of atoms. The atoms represent the possible values the returns can take, and the PMFs represent the probability that the return takes each value. We can then estimate the PMF of the returns using a neural network or a table lookup. The Q-value distribution over the atoms can be updated using the Bellman backup operator, which replaces the expected Q-value with the distributional update. This approach allows us to capture the full range of possible returns, including extreme values that may have a low probability but a high impact on the performance of the agent. By estimating the distribution over the returns, we can also avoid overestimating the Q-values in the presence of high variance in the return distribution. Overall, the distributional variant of gradient TD learning is a powerful tool for improving the performance of reinforcement learning algorithms in a wide range of applications.

Counter-argument: The phrase "Correlation does not equal causation" is not a cop-out, but rather a reminder to be cautious when interpreting data. In a breakthrough discovery, physicists from the University of Cambridge have reported that when two sheets of graphene come into contact with each other, entirely new quantum states are produced. Graphene is a material composed of single sheets of carbon atoms arranged in a hexagonal lattice, and has been the subject of intense research for its potential applications in electronics and computing. In their study, the researchers used special microscopes to observe how two layers of graphene interacted with each other once they were brought together. What they found was remarkable; when the two sheets of graphene met, an entirely new set of electronic states were created. These new states, known as "inter-layer excitons," are not observed in individual sheets of graphene, but only appear when two or more graphene sheets interact. The researchers believe that these inter-layer excitons could be useful for novel electronic devices such as transistors, solar cells, or even quantum computers. The discovery is particularly exciting because it suggests that graphene-based devices may be able to operate at significantly lower power levels than traditional silicon-based devices. The team's findings offer the promise of improved energy efficiency, faster switching speeds, and decreased power consumption in future electronic devices. As the researchers continue their work, we can look forward to further breakthroughs in the use of graphene for a variety of applications.

Deadline day is a frenzy of activity, with football clubs across Europe scrambling to finalize transfers before the transfer window closes. But what do you call the day that follows? Is it simply the day after deadline day, or does it have its own unique name? Some might argue that the day after deadline day should be known as Transfer Day, as clubs continue to tie up loose ends and finalize deals that didn't quite make it across the line the day before. Others might call it Hangover Day, as clubs and fans alike nurse their post-deadline day headaches and try to make sense of the chaos that has just unfolded. In Spain, the day after deadline day is known as Fichajes Invernales, which translates to "winter signings." This term acknowledges that the transfer window is an ongoing process that spans several months, rather than just a single day. Meanwhile, in Italy, the day after deadline day is known as Giorno del Silenzio (Day of Silence). This is because Italian clubs are not allowed to announce any new signings until 24 hours after the transfer window closes, in order to prevent any last-minute deals that could unfairly disrupt the balance of the league. In England, the day after deadline day remains nameless. This is perhaps because the transfer window has become such a huge event in recent years that it has overshadowed the rest of the football calendar. Nevertheless, the day after deadline day remains an important part of the football season, as clubs begin to settle into their new lineups and prepare for the challenges ahead. Whether you call it Transfer Day, Hangover Day, Fichajes Invernales or Giorno del Silenzio, the day after deadline day is a reminder that football is an ever-evolving sport, with new signings and new challenges around every corner. So, whatever you choose to call it, be sure to enjoy the ride.

Federated Learning (FL) is a decentralized machine learning protocol that allows a set of participating agents to collaboratively train a model without sharing their data. This makes FL particularly suitable for scenarios where data privacy is essential, like in healthcare, finance or government. In FL, the training of the model is done on local data, which remains on each participant's device or server. Each local model is then aggregated in a central location, resulting in a final model that has learned from the collective data of all participants. FL is accomplished through a process known as rounds. In each round, each participant trains their local model on their own data, and then they upload the model updates to a central server. The server aggregates the model updates and sends back a new updated model for the next round. This process continues until the model reaches a satisfactory performance level. One advantage of FL is that it reduces the risk of data breaches, as sensitive data is not transferred between devices or servers. Additionally, FL allows for broader participation in machine learning, as even individuals with limited computational resources and data can still contribute to the training of a model. FL has been applied to various fields, including natural language processing, image recognition, and predictive modeling.

What are the major geographical features of Egypt? Egypt is located in northeastern Africa and covers an area of 1,001,450 sq km (386,662 sq mi). The Nile flows northward through Cairo and empties into the Mediterranean Sea. The Sinai Peninsula, a triangular area of 23,500 sq km (9,070 sq mi) between the Mediterranean Sea and the Gulf of Suez, is connected to the rest of Egypt by the Isthmus of Suez. This narrow strip of land, approximately 100 km (62 mi) wide, contains the Suez Canal, which joins the Red Sea with the Mediterranean Sea. The highest point in Egypt is Mount Catherine, 2,637 m (8,652 ft) above sea level, in the southern Sinai Peninsula. What is the climate of Egypt? Temperatures during the day range from about 18C (65F) in January to about 37C (99F) in August. Nighttime temperatures range from about 9C (48F) in January to 26C (79F) in August. The Sinai Peninsula has a hot, dry climate. Because of its elevation (the peninsula rises to 2,637 m8,652 ft at Mount Catherine), the Sinai has cooler winters and occasional winter rains. The western Nile Delta has a milder, more humid climate with average daytime temperatures ranging from 15C (59F) in January to 32C (90F) in August. What are the natural resources of Egypt? Egypt's main natural resources include oil, natural gas, iron ore, phosphates, manganese, limestone, gypsum, talc, asbestos, lead, zinc, and uranium. What is the economy of Egypt? Almost all foodstuffs must be imported. Industry contributes about 35 to GDP. Food processing, textile manufacturing, construction, petroleum refining, and chemicals account for most industrial output. Mining accounts for only about 2 of GDP. The main minerals are iron ore, manganese, zinc, lead, phosphates, and salt. What are the people like in Egypt? Approximately 70 million people live in Egypt. About 90 of Egyptians are Muslim; the remainder belong to Christian churches. Arabic is the official language. English and French are also spoken. The population growth rate is about 2. Life expectancy at birth is 62 years for men and 64 years for women. What is the history of Egypt? Egypt was first settled along the lower Nile River valley, perhaps as early as 10000 BC. Ancient Egyptians were probably loosely related to modern Somalis who inhabit the Horn of Africa. Between 5000 and 3000 BC, two kingdoms emerged in Egypt, known as Upper and Lower Egypt. Most classes cover changing diapers, bathing, burping, and feeding your baby, among other skills. [substeps] For a unique bonding experience, attend these classes with your partner. [substeps] Most classes are free or low-cost and can be found at local hospitals, community centers, and libraries. [substeps] Although most classes last around four weeks, some classes may meet more frequently. [substeps] You can also find online resources to help you learn how to care for your baby. [substepsboxout] By attending a class, learning first-hand from a trained professional, and coming together with other parents-to-be, you'll feel more confident when it comes time to take care of your own little one. Caring for Your Baby Once you get home with your new bundle of joy, you'll want to know everything about caring for your baby. Here are a few key things to keep in mind as you navigate this new territory. Diapers If you're using disposable diapers, you'll need to change them approximately every two hours when your baby is awake or whenever they're wet or soiled. For newborns, you might even have to change their diaper up to 12 times per day. Disposable diapers have tabs on the sides that you open to fasten and unfasten the diaper. If you're using cloth diapers, you'll need to change them every two to three hours during the day and once before bedtime. Cloth diapers don't have tabs and instead need to be fastened using snaps or Velcro. Once your baby wets or soils a cloth diaper, you'll need to remove it and put on a new one immediately. Either way, you'll want to be prepared. When changing your baby's diaper, make sure you lay them down on a safe surface like a changing table or on a firm mattress on the floor. Open up the diaper so that you don't accidentally touch areas that have been soiled. Use wet wipes to clean your baby's bottom and then pat dry before putting on a clean diaper. Don't forget to wash your hands after you've changed your baby's diaper. You should also wipe down the changing table with disinfectant wipes between each use. Feeding Your Baby When it comes to feeding your baby, breast milk is the best option if possible. Breast milk is easy for babies to digest, contains antibodies that help protect your baby against infections and illnesses, and provides all the nutrients your baby needs for proper growth and development. If you're unable to breastfeed or choose not to, you can give your baby infant formula. Infant formula is manufactured to provide all the nutrients your baby needs to grow. Whether you're breast-feeding or using formula, you will need to feed your baby several times per day. Newborns generally eat every two to three hours during the day and once at night. As your baby grows and becomes more efficient at eating, they may begin sleeping through the night and only need to eat around six times per day. As a new parent, it's normal to worry that you won't know when your baby is hungry. Keep an eye out for signs that indicate that your baby is ready to eat. These signs include turning their head towards your chest, licking their lips, moving their head from side to side, or sucking on their tongue or lower lip. When you're ready to feed your baby, sit them upright in an infant seat or hold them close to your body. If you're breast-feeding, position your baby so that their nose is level with your nipple. If you're using formula, follow the instructions on the packaging to prepare the bottles. When feeding your baby, look for signs that indicate that they're no longer hungry. These signs include turning their head away from the bottle or your breast, pushing away the bottle or your breast, falling asleep, or clenching their fist. Burping Your Baby After feeding or taking a break from feeding, you'll need to burp your baby. Burping helps release gas from your baby's stomach and prevents them from spit-up or becoming fussy. There are many ways to burp your baby. Some common positions include holding your baby upright, placing them over your shoulder, or placing them across your lap. To burp your baby, gently pat or rub their back until they burp. It's important that you burp your baby throughout and after a meal. Baths It's important to bathe your baby regularly. Babies should be bathed at least once per day, but more often if necessary. Baths help your baby stay clean and promote healthy skin. When bathing your baby, it's important to keep them warm and comfortable.

This in turn meant that the Saturn V launch vehicle would need to be more powerful, and so NASA decided to increase the size of the first stage of the Saturn V. The increased size of the first stage meant that the entire rocket would be too large to fit inside the Vehicle Assembly Building at the Kennedy Space Center, and so a new building had to be built. This new building, called the Mobile Launcher Platform, was designed to be moved to the launch pad on a set of rails. The first Saturn V launch took place on November 9, 1967, and it was a success. The rocket carried the unmanned Apollo 4 spacecraft into orbit. The first manned Saturn V launch took place on December 21, 1968, and it carried the Apollo 8 spacecraft into orbit. The Apollo 8 spacecraft carried three astronauts: Frank Borman, James Lovell, and William Anders. The astronauts became the first humans to leave Earth's orbit and travel to the moon. The first moon landing took place on July 20, 1969, when the Apollo 11 spacecraft carrying Neil Armstrong and Edwin "Buzz" Aldrin landed on the moon's surface. Armstrong, Aldrin, and Michael Collins were the astronauts who flew on the Apollo 11 mission.

Yes, there is a scientific reason why we think that human babies and the young of other animals are cuter and induce more positive emotions. This is because humans and other animals have evolved to be more emotionally responsive to infants than adults. This is due to the fact that infant survival is key for the survival of the species. Infants have large eyes, large heads and small bodies which trigger a response in us that makes us feel more protective towards them. Other animals do indeed share a similar sentiment about the young inside and outside of their species. Animals often show increased levels of care and protection towards their own young as well as towards the young of other species. This is known as 'ecological altruism'. For example, elephants will form protective circles around the young of other species if they sense danger, or a mother bird might take in an orphaned baby bird and adopt it as her own.

The funds were raised to help Lilesa as he faces persecution in his home country for protesting against the government. Lilesa, who won the silver medal at the 2016 Rio Olympics, made global headlines when he crossed his arms at the finish line, a gesture widely seen as a symbol of protest against the Ethiopian government's brutal treatment of the Oromo people, the country's largest ethnic group. Following his protest, Lilesa feared that he could face imprisonment or even death if he returned home. In a press conference after the race, he said, "The Ethiopian government is killing my people, so I stand with all protests anywhere, as Oromo is my tribe. My relatives are in prison and if they talk about democratic rights they are killed." The crowd-funding campaign was launched by the Oromo Community of Minnesota, a group of Oromo people living in the US, and has received donations from people all over the world. The funds will be used to help Lilesa cover his legal and living expenses as he seeks asylum and protection. The Oromo people have faced oppression and persecution in Ethiopia for many years, and Lilesa's protest was seen as a powerful symbol of their struggle. While the Ethiopian government has denied accusations of human rights abuses and said that Lilesa will be welcomed back as a hero, many believe that his life could be in danger if he returns. The success of the crowd-funding campaign is a testament to the support Lilesa has received from people all over the world, and a reminder of the continuing struggle for justice and freedom in Ethiopia.

Dear Dad, It's been years since we've spoken, and so much has happened. I'm not sure where to begin, but I figured I should start by saying that I always wanted to write this letter but never did. I guess the reason why is because I was always afraid of how you'd react or what you'd say. Growing up, you were my hero. You could do no wrong in my eyes. But as I got older, I began to see some of your flaws, and that wasn't always easy to deal with. I know you wanted me to be just like you, and for a while, I tried to be. I went to the same school you did, majored in the same field, and even moved to the same city you did. But somewhere along the way, I lost myself. The truth is, Dad, I never wanted to be a lawyer. I did it because I thought it would make you proud, but in the end, it just made me miserable. I know you always wanted the best for me, but I wish you had given me the freedom to discover who I am and what I want to do with my life. I'm not saying any of this to make you feel guilty. I just want you to understand where I'm coming from. You were always so focused on success and achieving your goals that you forgot about the things that really matter - family, love, and happiness. I want to be able to tell you the truth about who I am and what makes me happy, but I'm afraid you won't accept me. That's the saddest part of all. I hope someday we can have an honest conversation about these things. I don't want to spend the rest of my life pretending to be someone I'm not just to make you happy. I hope you can understand that. Love always, Your son.

Ken Dickie, 64, died in hospital on 14 May, six days after the incident at the Rockley Park site in Poole. Jamie Mitchell, 35, of Apple Close, had admitted intervening in the attack on his friend, but claimed he did so in self-defence. The court heard that Mr Dickie and Mitchell were drinking with friends in a caravan when they got into an argument with Anthony Holmes, who had previously been thrown out of the site for aggressive behaviour. Mitchell told the jury that after he was punched by Holmes, he saw him turn to Mr Dickie and hit him in the back of the head. "I punched Tony, I've no intention of hurting him," he said. "I just couldn't let him hurt my mate." Mitchell denied assaulting Mr Dickie, saying instead that he tried to stop the assault. 'H URLED ABUSE ' Mr Dickie's wife Michelle told the court her husband had been drinking heavily at the time, and had been arguing with other people inside the caravan. "He was hurling abuse, getting quite angry," she said. "I remember Jamie Mitchell being there, he was shouting at Tony, telling him to get out." Mrs Dickie said her husband had been "pushed around" before he left the caravan. She told the court she went outside when she heard a commotion, and saw Mr Dickie lying on the ground. "He appeared to be unconscious, his eyes were rolling back," she said. "His face was white, and his breathing was shallow." Mrs Dickie said her husband had suffered brain damage as a result of the attack, and had not recovered from it. 'ATTACKER GONE' Mitchell told the jury he had seen Holmes walk away from the scene, but had stayed with Mr Dickie. "I couldn't leave him there, he was my mate," he said. "I tried to wake him up. He was really white, really cold. I tried to talk to him, tried to shake him." Mitchell said he had been arrested because he had told the police he had been in contact with Holmes, who had since absconded. In sentencing Mitchell, Judge Peter Johnson said he had admitted intervening to prevent Holmes attacking Mr Dickie, but had used unlawful force to do so. "You punched him twice, you kicked him once, in the stomach, which caused him to fall on top of your friend," he said. "At the time you struck those blows, he wasn't attacking you." Mitchell was sentenced to two years and four months in prison, with half of that to be served on licence.

When two pieces of graphene are placed on top of each other, they create entirely new quantum states, according to a new study by physicists. Graphene is a carbon-based material that is just one atom thick. It is known for its unique properties, including its high electrical and thermal conductivity. In the new study, published in the journal Nature Physics, the physicists placed two pieces of graphene on top of each other and applied a voltage between them. They found that when the voltage was low, the system behaved like a conventional semiconductor. However, at high voltages, the system exhibited entirely new quantum states. "Our results show that when you bring two pieces of graphene together, you can create something that doesn't exist in any other material," said study author Pablo Jarillo-Herrero of the Massachusetts Institute of Technology. The finding could have important implications for the development of new electronic devices. "This is a completely new platform for quantum physics," Jarillo-Herrero said. "It opens up a whole new world of possibilities."

One of the first known experiments on the relationship between combustion and air was conducted by the 2nd century BCE Greek writer on mechanics, Philo of Byzantium. Hess's discovery, later dubbed the Hess effect, proved that solar radiation, not atmospheric oxygen, was responsible for the ionization of the atmosphere, thereby disproving the chemically based theory of Svante Arrhenius.[2526] In 1915, Robert Millikan took the first direct measurement of the photoelectric effect, thereby launching the field of quantum mechanics.[27] Between 1918 and 1920, Arthur Eddington performed a series of experiments testing Einstein's theory of general relativity.[28] His observations provided direct experimental evidence that energy could be released from the nucleus of an atom, in the form of either electromagnetic radiation or particle-emission radiation. He deduced that atoms consisted of a central core containing most of the atom's mass, which he termed the "nucleus," surrounded by electrons. The discovery of the neutron in 1932 led James Chadwick to conclude that nuclei consisted of protons and neutrons, which he named "nucleons." In 1930, Ernest Lawrence invented the cyclotron, which greatly accelerated the pace of experimental nuclear physics. We present and analyze a numerical method to solve the time-dependent linear Pauli equation in three space-dimensions. The Pauli equation is a "semi-relativistic" generalization of the Schrodinger equation for 2-spinors , which is used to describe the non-relativistic limit of quantum systems composed of spin-12 particles. In this work, we study the time-dependent Pauli equation in free space and present a numerical technique to solve it. Our method is based on a pseudospectral approach that uses Fourier transforms for spatial discretization and exponential integration for temporal evolution. We discuss the advantages and disadvantages of our approach and apply it to several physical problems, including scattering from a potential barrier and an oscillating electric field. We find that our method provides accurate solutions to the time-dependent Pauli equation, and can be used to study the dynamics of spin-12 particles. The main advantage of our approach is its computational efficiency, as it requires only a few lines of code to implement. Furthermore, the use of Fourier transforms allows us to efficiently compute the spatial derivatives needed for the calculation. Finally, we demonstrate that our method can be used to accurately simulate the propagation of wave packets in complex potentials.

We propose a novel regularization-based continual learning method, dubbed as Adaptive Group Sparsity based Continual Learning (AGS-CL), using two group sparsity-based penalties. Our method selectively employs the two penalties when appropriate in order to maintain a balance between preserving previous knowledge and accommodating new tasks. Additionally, our method adaptively adjusts the regularization strengths based on the current state of the model and the task at hand. This approach allows the model to learn new tasks while preventing catastrophic forgetting of previously learned information. To implement AGS-CL, we first split the model's parameters into groups based on their importance for previous tasks, using a measure of importance derived from their sensitivity to changes in the loss function. We then apply two group sparsity-based penalties: Elastic-Net and Orthogonal Matching Pursuit (OMP). The Elastic-Net penalty promotes group-sparsity and the OMP penalty promotes task-sparsity. By adapting the regularization weights for these two penalties, we can selectively enforce either task-sparsity or group-sparsity as needed to maintain the balance between old and new tasks. In summary, AGS-CL addresses the challenge of continual learning by utilizing two group sparsity-based penalties and adaptively adjusting the regularization weights to balance between the preservation of previous knowledge and the accommodation of new tasks. By doing so, it ensures that the model can learn new tasks without compromising its performance on previous tasks.

The pound-force has a metric counterpart, less commonly used than the newton: the kilogram-force (kgf) (sometimes kilopond), is the force exerted by standard gravity on one kilogram of mass. The kilogram-force is equal to about 9.806 65 N (newtons). In the UK, the use of the pound as a unit of force is increasingly being replaced by the newton as the SI unit, resulting in expressions such as "350 lbf" rather than "350 lb." In some cases, however, the pound-force is still used within certain industries, such as the United States military and British engineering. The pound-force should not be confused with the foot-pound (ftlb or ftlbf) which is a unit of work or energy, nor should these be confused with the poundal, another unit of force.

Graphlets are induced subgraph patterns and have been frequently applied to characterize the local topology structures of graphs across various domains, e.g., online social networks (OSNs) and biological networks. Discovering graphlets in large graphs is an important task for understanding their structure and properties. A graphlet consists of a set of vertices, edges and associated weights. Graphlets can be used to compute various structural properties of a given graph, such as its centrality, motifs, and clustering coefficient. Graphlets are particularly useful for detecting and analyzing communities within a graph. They can also be used to detect network anomalies, such as outliers or hub nodes. Additionally, they can provide insight into the global structure of a graph by uncovering patterns, correlations and relationships between different parts of the graph.

The United Methodist Church is organized into conferences. The highest level is called the General Conference and is the only organization which may speak officially for the church. The General Conference meets every four years to review the church's doctrine, polity, and social principles. Below the General Conference are regional conferences, sometimes called Annual Conferences. These are composed of all the clergy and laity in a particular geographic area. The Annual Conferences meet each year to ordain clergy, appoint pastors, and address other issues of local concern. At the local level, smaller groups of churches form Districts, which are overseen by a Superintendent appointed by the Annual Conference. The basic unit of United Methodist Church organization is the local church, which is led by a Pastor appointed by the Bishop. The United Methodist Church also has a number of other organizations that provide support and guidance to the church. These include the Board of Global Ministries, the Council of Bishops, the General Commission on Archives and History, the General Commission on Communications, the General Commission on Religion and Race, the General Commission on the Status and Role of Women, and the United Methodist Mission Society.

Tragedy has struck the city of Uyo in southeastern Nigeria as a church collapsed during a service on Saturday, claiming the lives of at least 100 people. The Reigners Bible Church International was hosting the consecration of its bishop when the roof caved in around midday, trapping worshippers inside. Frantic rescue efforts saw numerous people pulled from the debris, but the scale of the disaster was immense. The governor of Akwa Ibom state, Udom Emmanuel, was amongst those who narrowly escaped the tragedy, and he quickly declared a two-day period of mourning in the state. Emergency services were overwhelmed by the scale of the disaster, and more than 200 injured people were transferred to hospitals across the city for treatment. Religious gatherings are hugely popular in Nigeria, a country with a deeply religious population. However, such events are often held in structures which are not properly maintained and lack basic safety features, making them vulnerable to collapse. Despite numerous calls for improved safety standards, little has been done to improve the situation in Nigeria. This latest tragedy has once again highlighted the need for urgent action to prevent such incidents from happening in future.

A founding member of The Smiths has revealed that re-forming "was a very real prospect" - if only for four days. "We were actually talking about it - Andy Rourke and I - for four days," Joyce said. "It was a very real prospect." Joyce said that the talks broke down over money, with the two sides unable to agree on a fee for the reunion. "I think if we'd have just done it for the love of it and not tried to make any money out of it, it would have been fine," he said. The Smiths, who formed in Manchester in 1982, were one of the most influential bands of the 1980s. They split acrimoniously in 1987, with frontman Morrissey going on to enjoy a successful solo career. Joyce's comments will reignite speculation about a possible reunion, which has been mooted on several occasions over the years. In 2006, Rourke said that he would be open to the idea of a reunion, but only if Morrissey was on board. "If Morrissey wanted to do it, then I'm up for it," he said. "I've always said that." However, Morrissey has consistently ruled out a reunion, saying in 2008 that it was "absolutely impossible."

On Tuesday, scientists announced the discovery of an egg believed to be the first egg ever discovered in Antarctica. The fossilized egg was found on Seymour Island off the Antarctic Peninsula and is estimated to be about 66 million years old. The egg is believed to have belonged to a mosasaur, a giant sea-dwelling reptile from the Cretaceous period. It's believed to be one of the largest eggs ever discovered and the first egg ever found in Antarctica. The egg measures just over 10 centimeters long and 7 centimeters wide. It's oval-shaped and has a very thick shell, suggesting that it could have been laid by a very large mosasaur. "This egg is incredibly significant because it provides us with the first evidence of a mosasaur living in Antarctica," said paleontologist Dr. Stephen Brusatte of the University of Edinburgh. "It also tells us something about the environment at the time - that the ocean was warm enough to support large reptiles like mosasaurs." The team of researchers plans to analyze the egg further to learn more about its biology and determine how long it had been lying in the Antarctic soil before it was discovered. This discovery is sure to spark further research into Antarctica's ancient past and provide valuable insight into the evolution of life in this remote region of the world.

Every time they tried to write something, the characters would look at one another in confusion and say, "That's not how it happened!" As the new narrator struggled to understand the world they had been thrust into, the gods of the story watched from afar, wondering if they had made a mistake. But as time went on, something curious began to happen. The new narrator began to take the story in unexpected directions, introducing new twists and turns that had never been explored before. The characters were confused, but also excited. They had always known their world was full of mysteries and secrets, but they had never had a narrator who was willing to delve into them in such an unpredictable way. As the story progressed, the characters found themselves drawn into the new narrator's vision, eager to see where it would lead them. Eventually, the gods of the story realized that they had chosen the right person for the job after all. The new narrator may not have known anything about the series when they first arrived, but they had a unique perspective that allowed them to push the story in exciting new directions. The characters had never been more alive, and the readers were more invested than ever before. In the end, it didn't matter that the new narrator had never heard of the series before. They had breathed new life into it, transforming it into something that was both familiar and new. And the gods of the story could only marvel at the magic that had been created.

In the wake of the COVID-19 pandemic, Nigerian university students have been facing an increasingly difficult situation. With universities shuttered and no clear end to the pandemic in sight, many students are struggling to make ends meet. This has caused some students to turn to cybercrime as a way to make money. A recent study conducted by the University of Ibadan in Nigeria found that a significant number of students from Nigeria's higher education institutions were turning to cybercrime to supplement their income. The study found that over 60 percent of those surveyed had considered engaging in cybercrime, with 28 percent of them saying they had already done so. The most common forms of cybercrime being committed by students include credit card fraud, identity theft, and phishing. These activities are relatively easy for students to learn and carry out due to the proliferation of online tutorials and resources which teach people how to do them. Many students also find it appealing because there is often no need for physical contact with victims or a face-to-face meeting. This is leading to a worrying trend of increasing cybercrime activity in the country, with the Nigerian Economic and Financial Crimes Commission (EFCC) reporting a sharp rise in cybercrime cases since the start of the pandemic. The EFCC has been working hard to tackle the problem, launching a nationwide campaign called "Don't Fall Prey to Cybercrime." The campaign focuses on helping young people understand the risks of cybercrime, and aims to encourage them to pursue more legitimate opportunities. However, experts warn that this may not be enough to tackle the issue. Many students are simply desperate for money and are willing to take the risk of engaging in cybercrime. It is therefore essential that the government does more to provide students with alternative sources of income. This could be in the form of grants, scholarships, or even part-time jobs that can help them make ends meet without resorting to criminal activities. The pandemic has undoubtedly created a difficult situation for Nigerian university students, but it is important that the government takes action to ensure that students are not forced into cybercrime in order to survive. Otherwise, the country may find itself facing a bigger cyber security crisis than it is currently equipped to handle.

The academic dress worn at graduation usually consists of a gown, hood and mortarboard. The gown is usually made of heavy material and is floor-length, with long sleeves. The colour of the gown indicates the level of qualification that has been achieved. For example, a first class degree is indicated by a purple gown, while a second class degree is indicated by a red gown. A hood is worn over the gown and is usually lined with the same colour as the gown. The mortarboard is a square board that is worn on the head and has a tassel hanging from it. The academic dress worn at graduation ceremonies in the UK has its origins in the dress worn at medieval universities. The hood was originally a type of cape that was worn to protect the head and shoulders from the cold. The mortarboard is thought to have originated from the biretta, a type of hat worn by Catholic clergy.

The projection from the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) shows a far-reaching shift in the balance of graduate numbers, with the rising Asian economies accelerating ahead of the US and Europe. The OECD's report, "The Top Ten of Tomorrow," says that China will produce more than half the world's graduates by 2023 and India will have the largest university-age population in the world by 2020. "The rise of Asia is not only an economic phenomenon but an educational one as well," said OECD secretary general Angel Gurria. "This is likely to have a huge impact on the economy and labour markets over the next decade," he said. The study shows that the Asian economies are already driving a three-fold increase in graduate numbers worldwide since 2000. The number of 18-to-21 year old people attending university around the world has risen from 59 million in 2000 to 188 million in 2013. "In 2000, Asia represented only 13 per cent of global tertiary enrolment... By 2013, this share had reached 34 per cent and by 2023, it is expected to reach 47 per cent," the OECD said. China alone accounts for 70 per cent of the increase in tertiary students, with enrolment soaring from 10 million in 2000 to 37 million in 2013 and 49 million by 2023. India has seen enrolment levels surge from 12 million to more than 20 million since 2000 and is also projected to continue growing rapidly. By contrast, Europe and the US have seen enrolment growth stagnate or decline over the past decade due to slower population growth and declining government investment. The figures confirm recent warnings from Western academics about the loss of their dominance in world higher education. The US currently has the highest tertiary graduation rate in the world at 41 per cent, followed by Canada at 38 per cent, Japan at 34 per cent and South Korea at 32 per cent. But the US is forecast to see its lead eroded as China and India continue to expand, with projection showing China having the highest graduation rate by 2023. The OECD also warned that rising graduate numbers in Asia will not automatically translate into better quality. It cited concerns over falling standards and "degree mills" churning out large numbers of poorly qualified graduates. It called for action to improve quality control, including new regulations to monitor private providers and greater transparency about the skills and knowledge taught. The OECD also said that the vast majority of new graduates will be women, who account for 59 per cent of enrolments globally. The study shows that the gender gap is widest in Spain, where women account for 77 per cent of tertiary students, compared with just 55 per cent in Greece and 61 per cent in Portugal.

Once upon a time, there was a little boy named Jack who was always afraid of the monster in his closet. He was terrified of going to sleep every night, knowing that the monster might come out at any minute. One night, Jack decided that he had had enough of being afraid. Slowly, Jack opened the closet door and peered inside. At first, he couldn't see anything except for the darkness. But then he saw two glowing eyes staring back at him. The monster beckoned Jack to come closer. Jack hesitated for a moment, but then he stepped forward. Suddenly, Jack fell into darkness. He felt like he was falling into a deep hole that seemed to have no end. It was scary, but he felt like he needed to see what was going on. After a few moments, Jack opened his eyes and looked around. He was in a dark cavern with glowing red walls. He could hear the monster growling in the distance. But then, as his eyes adjusted to the darkness, he began to see something that frightened him even more than the monster. There were other children in the cavern. They were chained up and looked frightened. Jack felt a surge of terror run through his body as he realized he was trapped. The monster had lured him into the darkness to become its next victim. Terrified, Jack looked for a way out. He tried to run, but the chains on his ankles prevented him from moving more than a few steps. He searched for anything that could help him escape and free the other children. Suddenly, the monster appeared before him. "Welcome to my lair," it growled. "I've been waiting for you." Jack didn't know what to do. He was trapped and terrified. But then he remembered that he was brave, and he had to help the other children escape. With all his might, he lunged forward and tried to break free from the chains. Surprisingly, they snapped, and Jack was able to free himself. He quickly ran to the other children and helped release their chains too. Together, they made a daring dash for freedom. They ran as fast as they could to escape the monster's lair. They finally made it into the safety of the light. In the end, Jack discovered that he wasn't just brave but also clever. He had used his intelligence to outsmart the monster and free himself and the other children. What he thought was the greatest fear in his life had become the greatest lesson he learned: to never give up hope and always be brave.

Emergent narratives provide a unique and compelling approach to interactive storytelling through simulation, and have applications in games, narrative generation, and virtual agents. However the inherent complexity of simulation makes the design of emergent narratives a challenging problem. In this paper we present the application of computational intelligence to the design and generation of emergent narratives in simulation. We provide a general overview of emerging narratives, including key concepts and common approaches to their generation. We describe how computational intelligence can be used to solve problems in the design and generation of emergent narratives. We survey the application of computational intelligence to emerging narratives, and we discuss future directions for research. Emergent narratives are defined as stories that emerge from complex simulations. They are often seen as a type of interactive fiction, in which the player's actions affect the course of the story. Emergent narratives have been used in games, narrative generation, and virtual agents. The concept of emergent narratives was first introduced by A.I. researcher Michael Mateas in 2001 [1]. Mateas defines emergent narratives as "complex fictional worlds in which stories emerge through the interactions of autonomous characters." He notes that emergent narratives are different from traditional narratives in several ways: Emergent narratives are generated by simulations, rather than being written by authors. Emergent narratives are open-ended, meaning that they do not have a predefined ending. Emergent narratives are nonlinear, meaning that they do not have a fixed sequence of events. Emergent narratives are dynamic, meaning that they can change over time. Mateas also notes that emergent narratives are similar to traditional narratives in some ways: Emergent narratives have characters that interact with each other. Emergent narratives have plots that unfold over time. Emergent narratives have themes that give them meaning. Since Mateas introduced the concept of emergent narratives, there has been a growing body of research on the topic. In 2005, Mateas and Stern published a book on the topic [2]. In 2007, the journal AI Society published a special issue on emergent narratives [3]. And in 2008, the International Conference on Interactive Digital Storytelling (ICIDS) held a workshop on computational approaches to emergent narratives [4]. There are several common approaches to the design and generation of emergent narratives. One approach is to use artificial intelligence techniques to generate stories from simulation data [56]. Another approach is to use evolutionary computation to evolve stories that are consistent with simulation data [78]. A third approach is to use simulation models to generate stories from scratch [9]. This approach has been used in the field of game design, where it is known as procedural content generation (PCG) [10]. PCG is a type of generative art, in which computer programs are used to generate artifacts that are aesthetically pleasing. PCG has been used to generate game levels [11], characters [12], and items [13]. It has also been used to generate stories [14], dialogue [15], and cutscenes [16]. Simulation-based PCG has been used to generate emergent narratives in games. For example, the game Spore uses PCG to generate stories about the player's creature [17]. The game Facade uses PCG to generate stories about the player's interactions with two virtual characters [18]. And the game The Sims uses PCG to generate stories about the player's Sims [19]. Simulation-based PCG can also be used to generate emergent narratives outside of games. For example, Mateas and Stern used PCG to generate stories about the interactions between virtual agents [20]. And Preteux and colleagues used PCG to generate stories about the spread of a virus in a virtual city [21]. Computational intelligence (CI) is a type of artificial intelligence that is inspired by natural intelligence. CI includes a wide range of subfields, such as evolutionary computation, neural networks, and fuzzy logic. CI has been used to solve a wide variety of problems, including optimization, control, and prediction. It has also been used to generate artifacts, such as images, music, and text. CI has been used to generate emergent narratives. For example, Riedl and Young used evolutionary computation to generate stories about virtual agents [22]. And Liapis, Yannakakis, and Togelius used evolutionary computation to generate stories about the interactions between virtual agents [23]. In this paper, we survey the application of computational intelligence to emergent narratives. We begin with a brief overview of emergent narratives. We then describe how computational intelligence can be used to solve problems in the design and generation of emergent narratives. Finally, we survey the application of computational intelligence to emergent narratives, and we discuss future directions for research.

Stadtholder William III of Orange, who later became King of England, emerged as the strongest opponent of king Louis XIV after the French attacked the Dutch Republic in 1672. William allied the Republic with Spain and Sweden and led an army into France, defeating Louis XIV at the Battle of Steenkerque in 1692. In 1697, peace was concluded with the Treaty of Ryswick under which France returned its conquests while the Republic regained its independence. Louis's War of Devolution (1667-68) In May 1667, France declared war on the Dutch Republic after the latter refused to accept the terms of the Treaty of Breda (the Peace of Breda). The treaty had been signed by King Charles II of England and the Dutch States-General on 1 July 1666 and was designed to end the first Anglo-Dutch War as well as a number of other conflicts between European states. According to the terms of the treaty, the Dutch Republic would give up some of its conquests from the previous wars, including Suriname, New Netherland and parts of the Spanish Netherlands. It would also have to pay reparations to the English king. King Louis XIV of France, one of the most powerful rulers of his day, viewed the treaty as a personal humiliation. He believed that the Dutch Republic had betrayed him and had violated their 1662 treaty with France. The French king also resented Dutch expansion in the West Indies and the Republic's refusal to accept French control over the Rhine frontier. Louis therefore decided to go to war with the Dutch Republic in order to exact revenge and reclaim his lost territories. The Dutch Republic, being a small state compared to France, lacked the economic resources, manpower and natural defences that could ensure victory in a prolonged conflict. The Dutch Republic therefore appealed to the other European powers for assistance, prompting king Louis XIV to invade the Dutch Republic in April 1672. The French king hoped that the European powers would remain neutral and not intervene in the conflict. However, William III of Orange, the stadtholder of the Dutch Republic and de facto head of state, quickly gained the support of Spain and Sweden, who entered the war against France in support of the Dutch Republic. This prompted Louis XIV to declare war on both of them. The Third Anglo-Dutch War (1672-74) King Louis XIV invaded the Dutch Republic with a large army in April 1672 in order to take revenge for their defeat in the previous war. The invading French forces quickly captured a number of major Dutch cities, including Utrecht and Amsterdam. William III of Orange, the stadtholder of the Dutch Republic and de facto head of state, then led an army into France and defeated the French forces at the Battles of Seneffe and Salbach, forcing Louis XIV to make peace. The Peace of Westminster (the Second Treaty of Westminster) was signed on 9 February 1674, ending the third Anglo-Dutch war. Under the terms of the treaty, the Dutch Republic regained its conquests but had to accept French control over the whole of the Franche-Comte province in the Spanish Netherlands. The Dutch Republic and the Nine Years' War (1688-97) King Louis XIV of France embarked on a series of military campaigns in the late 1680s in order to expand his territory and assert his authority over the other European states. In 1688, he invaded the Dutch Republic in an attempt to overthrow William III of Orange, the stadtholder of the Dutch Republic and de facto head of state. William III, who was also the king of England, Scotland and Ireland, then led an army into France and defeated the French forces at the Battle of Steenkerque in 1692. In 1697, peace was concluded with the Treaty of Ryswick under which France returned its conquests while the Republic regained its independence.

However, when two sheets of graphene are stacked on top of each other to form what is known as bilayer graphene, it exhibits even more fascinating properties. The team of researchers led by UC Berkeley physicist Feng Wang used a scanning tunneling microscope to study the bilayer graphene and discovered a series of so-called Hofstadter butterfly patterns. The patterns, which had never been observed before, are a manifestation of the complex interactions between the electrons in the two layers. The researchers found that when the angle between the two layers was adjusted, the system transitioned between different quantum states that were entirely new and distinct from those seen in single-layer graphene. The discovery could have significant implications for the development of new electronic devices, as these new quantum states could be useful for computing and other applications. "The system we discovered exhibits intriguing new behaviors that are not seen in individual layers of graphene or other two-dimensional materials," said Wang. "It opens up new avenues for exploring the physics of interacting electrons in two dimensions." The findings of the study were published in the journal Nature. The team plans to continue their research in this field to better understand the unique properties of bilayer graphene and explore potential applications for these new quantum states.

Also Known as Pack Hardening, Blister Steel, Shear Steel From what I understand from reading old texts, traditionally, case hardening was a technique were a blacksmith would infuse a piece of iron or steel with carbon to create a hard outer layer while keeping the inside softer and more malleable. This was done by heating the metal in a carbon-rich environment, usually with charcoal or bone charcoal, and then quenching it in water or oil to harden the outer layer. This process was often used to make tools or weapons that needed to be tough and durable on the outside, but still somewhat flexible on the inside. Blister steel and shear steel were types of steel produced by a similar process, but with higher carbon content. Blister steel was made by heating wrought iron in a sealed container with a carbon source, which caused the iron to absorb carbon and form bubbles of carbon monoxide gas. The resulting steel was then forged and cut into bars or sheets. Shear steel was made by heating wrought iron and pieces of blister steel together in a crucible or furnace, which created a homogenous blend of steel with a high carbon content. This steel was then forged and cut into blades for knives or swords, which were known for their sharpness and durability. Overall, case hardening and related techniques were important ways that blacksmiths could manipulate the properties of iron and steel to create tools and weapons with specific characteristics. While modern methods of steel production and heat treatment have largely replaced these traditional techniques, they still have a place in the history of metallurgy and the development of technology.

The particles interact through a social force that is proportional to the similarity of their accumulated evidence. This leads to emergent behaviors such as synchronization and cooperation among the particles. This work develops techniques for the sequential detection and location estimation of transient changes in the volatility (standard deviation) of time series data. In particular, we introduce a class of models that combine the Autoregressive Conditional Heteroskedasticity (ARCH) and Hidden Markov Models (HMM) for this purpose. We present a computationally efficient Bayesian approach based on Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) methods to perform inference on these models. We demonstrate the utility of our model in applications to financial time series data. Specifically, we consider two distinct scenarios: the detection and estimation of changes in the volatility of a single asset, and the simultaneous detection and estimation of changes across multiple assets. In both cases, we show superior performance compared to existing methods through simulations. Finally, we apply our method to real-world stock market data and demonstrate its ability to accurately detect and localize changes in the volatility of an asset.

Ctenophores may be abundant during the summer months in some coastal locations, but in other places they are uncommon and difficult to find. In bays where they occur in very high numbers, they may be referred to as a "bloom" of ctenophores. Ctenophore blooms have been known to occur in the Mediterranean Sea and can be so abundant that they affect ship traffic. These blooms are sometimes called "medusa jellyfish," but they are not related to true jellyfish. Some species of ctenophores are bioluminescent (they produce light), which is used for communication and defense. When disturbed, some ctenophores may emit large pulses of light that can be seen at night from shore. Bioluminescent light is produced by chemical reactions that occur inside cells called photocytes.

In this paper, we propose a novel deep convolutional neural network (CNN) -based algorithm for solving ill-posed inverse problems. Regularized iterative algorithms have emerged as the standard approach to ill-posed inverse problems. Our proposed CNN architecture consists of two components: a convolutional autoencoder and a denoising auto-encoder. The convolutional autoencoder is used to learn the underlying structure of the data which is then used as input for the denoising autoencoder. The denoising autoencoder is then used to reconstruct the original image from noisy observations. We evaluate our proposed algorithm on several benchmark inverse problems, including image deblurring, compressive sensing, and inpainting. Results show that our method outperforms existing state-of-the-art algorithms for inverse problems.

The Reds looked in control when Roberto Firmino converted James Milner's pass and Daniel Sturridge backheeled to Sadio Mane to clip home a second. But Leicester were given hope when Jamie Vardy tapped in for his 20th goal of the campaign and Danny Drinkwater forced a save from Simon Mignolet. The Reds were able to take some of the sting out of the game when Sturridge added a third, but they had to endure a tense finale when Shinji Okazaki scrambled in a consolation. Jurgen Klopp's side, however, held on to record their first league win since December 14 and move into eighth place - eight points off the top four with two games in hand. Leicester remain second but they are now five points behind leaders Arsenal, who have a game in hand. Klopp made three changes following Liverpool's 0-0 draw at Sunderland last time out, with Divock Origi and Lucas Leiva coming into the midfield, while Kolo Toure replaced Martin Skrtel at centre-back. Leicester boss Claudio Ranieri made four alterations as he looked to bounce back from the Foxes' FA Cup exit against Tottenham. Andy King and Demarai Gray came in for the injured duo of N'Golo Kante (hamstring) and Marc Albrighton (ankle), while Okazaki and Nathan Dyer were also brought in. After an even start, the visitors took the lead on 27 minutes when Milner's pass was volleyed home by Firmino at the far post after Leicester failed to clear their lines properly. Leicester almost responded immediately when Drinkwater's long-range effort forced a smart save from Mignolet, before Origi tested Kasper Schmeichel with a powerful drive from 20 yards. The hosts had an even better chance to level just before the break when Jeffrey Schlupp found space in the box, but his close-range effort was blocked brilliantly by Toure. Liverpool doubled their lead four minutes after the restart when Mane converted from close range after being teed up by Sturridge. And it should have been 3-0 moments later when Schmeichel parried Milner's effort straight to Origi, only for the Belgian to fire over with the goal gaping. Leicester were handed a lifeline on 63 minutes when Vardy nodded in Riyad Mahrez's cross, and Drinkwater then stung the palms of Mignolet with a fierce drive from 25 yards. But any hopes of a Leicester comeback were ended nine minutes from time when Sturridge capitalised on some poor defending to slot home his first league goal since October. When it was over, Jack was relieved to find that he could remember the missing chunks from his past. But as he looked back on those memories, he realized why he had erased them in the first place. Jack had suffered from severe depression in his past, and during those blank periods, he had attempted to take his own life multiple times. The memories that he had erased were those of those dark times in his life. Jack was shocked and saddened by what he had done to himself. But he knew that he couldn't turn back time, and he made a promise to himself to never forget the lessons he had learned from that experience. From that day on, Jack lived his life with a new appreciation for every moment he had, and never took the small things for granted again. The numbers associated with US military units typically have historical significance. The 75th Ranger Regiment is numbered as such since it was formed in the 18th century during the French and Indian War, and 75 is traced back to 1775 when the unit was founded. The 160th Special Operations Aviation Regiment was originally designated as the 160th Aviation Battalion on October 16, 1981, and was later re-designated as the 160th Special Operations Aviation Regiment on May 21, 1990. The number "160" was supposedly chosen to represent the math term "x to the power of y," where x represents the number of troops the unit could support and y represents the distance they could fly without refueling.

While constitutional law concerns the European Union's governance structure, administrative law binds EU institutions and member states to follow the law. Both member states and the Commission have a general obligation to comply with EU law, and individual citizens can seek recourse when there is a violation of their rights under EU law. Administrative law also sets out the procedures and rules governing decision-making by EU institutions and member states. This includes ensuring transparency, accountability, and the protection of fundamental rights. For example, EU administrative law requires that decisions be made using objective criteria and that citizens have the right to be heard before any decision affecting their rights is made. Overall, administrative law helps to ensure that EU institutions and member states act within the bounds of the law and in a manner that protects the interests and fundamental rights of citizens.

Therefore, there has been growing interest in the use of wearable devices, such as smartwatches or fitness trackers, to perform HAR. These devices contain various sensors, such as accelerometers and gyroscopes, that can be used to capture motion data and analyze human activities. Many machine learning techniques have been applied to analyze the data from these sensors and classify human activities, such as walking, running, cycling, and even more complex activities like yoga or dancing. Deep learning approaches, in particular, have shown promising results in the field of HAR, but they require large amounts of labeled data and powerful computing resources. Overall, the use of wearable devices for HAR has the potential to significantly improve the scalability and practicality of this technology, enabling a wide range of applications in fields such as healthcare, sports, and entertainment.

Smart contracts are a special type of programs running inside a blockchain. Immutable and transparent, they provide means to implement fault-tolerant and censorship-resistant services. Unfortunately, its immutability causes a serious drawback: if a bug is found in a smart contract, it cannot be fixed. This paper presents a method to update smart contracts safely. Abstract Smart contracts are a special type of program that runs on top of a blockchain. They are immutable and transparent, which makes them ideal for implementing fault-tolerant and censorship-resistant services. However, this immutability also causes a serious drawback: if a bug is found in a smart contract, it cannot be fixed. This paper presents a method to update smart contracts safely. Our approach is based on the concept of proxy contracts. A proxy contract is a smart contract that delegates all its functionality to another contract. If the delegate contract needs to be updated, the proxy contract can simply point to the new version. We have implemented our approach in a tool called Smart Contract Updater. Our tool can automatically generate proxy contracts and update them when needed. We have used our tool to update the ERC20 token standard, which is used by thousands of Ethereum tokens. Our experiments show that our approach is effective and practical.

Graph neural networks (GNNs) are powerful machine learning models for various graph learning tasks. Recently, the limitations of the expressive power of various GNN models have been revealed. For example, the Weisfeiler-Lehman network (WLN) and its variants are limited to distinguishing graphs up to a certain level of isomorphism. Similarly, GraphSAGE, a popular GNN model, can only aggregate information from a fixed number of neighbors for a graph node. To address these limitations, researchers have proposed various extensions to GNN models such as improved architectures or new aggregation functions. One recent extension to GNNs is the graph neural tangent kernel (GNTK), which is a kernel method that uses a graph convolutional network architecture. The GNTK allows for efficient comparison of graphs by leveraging the properties of differential equations. Through this approach, it can effectively capture higher-order relationships in graphs and distinguish between non-isomorphic graphs. Additionally, GNTK has been shown to be competitive with other graph kernels on benchmark datasets. Another extension to GNNs is graph attention networks (GATs), which introduce an attention mechanism to GNNs. Specifically, GATs learn to assign weights to each neighbor of a graph node in a self-adaptive way. This enables GATs to focus on important neighboring nodes and exploit their features for better prediction tasks. Furthermore, GATs have been used on a variety of tasks such as link prediction, node classification, and graph classification. In addition to GNTK and GATs, there are also other extensions to GNNs such as graph U-Nets, graph capsule networks, and graph generative networks. These new methods are actively being explored and developed in the research community and may further advance the capabilities of GNNs.

There are a few reasons why you might feel crappier the later you go to sleep, even if you're getting the same amount of sleep. Firstly, our bodies are wired to follow a natural circadian rhythm, which regulates our sleepwake cycle. Going to bed and waking up later disrupts this rhythm, making it harder for our bodies to adjust and leading to increased feelings of fatigue and lethargy. Secondly, if you're going to bed later, you're more likely to experience disturbances during the night, such as noise or light pollution, which can disrupt the quality of your sleep. This can lead to increased tiredness and reduced cognitive function during the day. Lastly, going to bed later may also mean that you're not getting as much natural light exposure during the day, which can impact your mood, energy levels, and overall well-being. Overall, it's best to aim for consistent and regular sleep schedules to optimize your sleep quality and wakefulness during the day.

Crowd counting from unconstrained scene images is a crucial task in many real-world applications like urban surveillance and management, but it is greatly challenged by the camera's perspective that causes severe occlusions and perspective distortions. In order to tackle this problem, a number of methods have been proposed, including density-based methods that use handcrafted features or deep neural networks to estimate the crowd density map from an image, and detection-based methods that utilize object detection algorithms to detect and count individual persons in the scene. Recently, more sophisticated approaches combining both detection and density estimation have also been developed, which usually perform better than either approach alone. These methods typically employ region proposal networks (RPN) to generate proposals for potential crowd regions and then use a regressor to estimate the density at each location. However, these methods still suffer from limited accuracy due to the lack of robust features that can capture the local structures of the crowd. To address this issue, recent works have proposed to use context information or global feature fusion to improve the performance of crowd counting. In addition, some studies have explored the use of attention mechanisms to focus on important regions within the image and thus further boost the counting accuracy. Overall, while much progress has been made in developing effective methods for crowd counting, there is still much room for improvement, especially in handling difficult cases such as dense crowds and occlusions.

Even before the Norman Conquest of England, the Normans had come into contact with Wales. Edward the Confessor had set up the aforementioned Ralph as earl of Hereford and charged him with defending the border against Welsh incursions. In 1063, Gruffydd ap Llywelyn, the king of Gwynedd, broke this peace when he launched an attack on Herefordshire and captured the castle at Monmouth. The Norman Conquest itself began in 1066, when William the Conqueror became king of England. He quickly set out to consolidate his power by subduing Wales. In 1067, he invaded Gwynedd and confiscated much of its lands. This campaign was followed by a number of other invasions throughout the 1070s and 1080s. During this time, the Normans built numerous castles and fortified towns to help guard and control the conquered areas. Some of these castles, such as Chepstow Castle, remain standing today. Throughout this period, the Normans also attempted to assimilate the Welsh people into their new kingdom. They encouraged intermarriage between Normans and Welsh, imposed Norman law, and set up a taxation system that favored the Normans. Despite these measures, however, many Welsh people were able to retain their culture and language.
