Newsflash: AWS S3: Why sometimes you should press the 100k button Are you using Amazon Web Services (AWS) S3 to store your data? Have you ever wondered what the 100k button is for? Pressing it could save you substantial amounts of money and prevent unexpected charges. When uploading files to AWS S3, there is a default setting for the number of requests made to Amazon S3. By default, S3 will send a request for each object uploaded, which incurs a cost of 0.005 per 1,000 requests. However, when uploading a large number of files, pressing the 100k button can reduce these costs significantly. Pressing the 100k button sets a limit of 100,000 requests per bulk operation. By reducing the number of requests made, you can save money on your storage costs. Additionally, using the 100k button can help prevent unexpected charges by capping the number of requests made during bulk file uploads. So next time you're uploading files to AWS S3, remember to press the 100k button if you're uploading a large number of files. It could save you money and prevent any unexpected surprises on your bill.

The analysis techniques of system log messages (syslog messages) have a long history from when the syslog mechanism was invented. Typically, the analysis consists of two parts, one is a pattern recognition and the other is an anomaly detection. For pattern recognition, syslog messages are searched for patterns that can indicate a certain type of event or behavior. This process involves analyzing the message content and metadata such as source, severity and time stamp. The goal is to identify common patterns that are expected to occur in normal system operations and be able to recognize them when they appear in log messages. For anomaly detection, the syslog messages are monitored for events or behavior that deviate from the expected patterns. This includes looking for unexpected sources, unusual severities or times, and unexpected message content. Anomaly detection algorithms can help to identify anomalous activities and alert the administrator. Finally, once anomalies have been detected, further analysis may be necessary to determine the cause. This typically involves collecting additional data, such as related log messages, performance metrics, and system configurations. These data can then be used to understand the root cause of the issue and develop a plan to address it.

Probably going to get downvoted because I don't have any references or knowledge to back up my answer but personal experience. Let me preface this with saying I am not a nutritionist or medical professional but I have been lifting weights and eating a lot of calories for several years. I would not recommend this. Here's why: if you are a beginner and have not been lifting weights before, you are going to need to eat more calories to support weight gain because your body is constantly breaking down muscle tissue as it adapts to the new stress you are putting on it. If you are already eating at maintenance calorie levels (or above) and are gaining weight too quickly (i.e. more than 1-2lbs per week), then there is a chance that you are gaining mostly body fat, not muscle. Even if you are following a workout program, you will likely not be able to do much about this because your muscles will break down faster than you can build them with the limited number of sets and reps you are doing. You should also be aware that even if you could manage to gain mostly muscle at a rate of 2lbs per week, it would be very difficult to train effectively without becoming fatigued. The heavier you get, the harder it becomes to add weight to the bar and the more likely you are to injure yourself. If you want to gain muscle mass, start by adding weight slowly. Don't try to put on too much too fast. For example, if you are bench pressing 100lbs for 5 reps, don't try to increase the weight to 125lbs the next week. Instead, try to increase the weight 5lbs every 2 weeks. This way you can keep progressing while reducing the risk of injury.

This paper deals with a complete bipartite matching problem with the objective of finding an optimal matching that maximizes a certain generic predefined utility function on the set of all complete bipartite matchings. We investigate the complexity of solving this problem and we show that it is hard for a general utility function even if the number m of left-hand side vertices is restricted to be 1, i.e., the problem is essentially a one-to-many matching problem. More precisely, our main result is a reduction from the problem of finding an optimal Hamiltonian path in a directed graph with a linear number of edges to the problem of solving an instance of the above mentioned utility maximization problem. Given a bipartite graph, a complete bipartite matching is a set of edges that connects all the vertices of the left hand side with those of the right hand side. A complete bipartite graph with a given complete bipartite matching is called a matched graph. In this paper we study a utility maximization problem that involves complete bipartite matchings. Given a bipartite graph, an integer m geq 1, and a generic predefined utility function u:M (G) rightarrow mathbb{Z}, where M (G) denotes the set of all complete bipartite matchings in G, the goal is to find an optimal complete bipartite matching Ein M (G) , i.e., a complete bipartite matching that maximizes the value of u. The problem we consider has been introduced by Yeung and Cheung cite{yeung}. In their work, they focus on the case where m1 and the utility function u is defined as the weighted sum of the weights of the edges in the matching. Their motivation for considering this specific problem originates from the field of artificial intelligence, where the aim is to find a good solution to a complex problem by searching through a space of solutions. To this end, it is common to use methods that first define a suitable utility function on the space of solutions and then solve the problem of finding an optimal solution by maximizing the utility function. Since the search space is usually very large, most of the times the solution is found not by looking at all the possible solutions but by using some heuristic method that examines only a subset of the solution space. Thus, it is of great importance to obtain a good approximation of the optimal solution; this is usually achieved by studying the computational complexity of the problem and exploiting the fact that a NP-hard problem cannot be approximately solved in polynomial time unless P NP. Yeung and Cheung cite{yeung} prove that the problem of maximizing a weighted sum of weights under the constraint that every left hand side vertex must be matched to exactly one right hand side vertex is NP-hard. In this paper, we propose a novel deep convolutional neural network (CNN) -based algorithm for solving ill-posed inverse problems. Regularized iterative algorithms have emerged as the standard approach to ill-posed inverse problems. However, their performance is strongly dependent on user-defined regularization parameters. Deep learning, on the other hand, has shown great success in many computer vision applications. However, its application to inverse problems is still limited. In our proposed algorithm, we formulate a deep learning problem and optimize an objective function that includes a data fidelity term (i.e., loss function) and a regularization term. This objective function can be minimized using standard gradient-based optimization methods. Unlike conventional iterative algorithms, our proposed algorithm does not require any parameter tuning. Furthermore, it can be used to solve nonlinear ill-posed inverse problems. We apply our proposed algorithm to image deblurring, image denoising, compressed sensing MRI, and photoacoustic tomography. One approach to solving ill-posed inverse problems is to use regularized iterative algorithms cite{Engl96}, such as the Landweber algorithm cite{Landweber51}, the conjugate gradient algorithm cite{Bertsekas97}, the Gauss-Newton algorithm cite{Nocedal99}, the Tikhonov regularization cite{Tikhonov77}, and the total variation minimization (TV) cite{Rudin92}. In most cases, the regularization term is chosen to be the ell2 norm of the gradient of the unknown image cite{Lustig08, Kim09} or the ell1 norm of the image itself cite{Candes04b, Candes06}. The team studied the perching behaviours of three species of birds - Red-shouldered Hawks, Cooper's Hawks, and American Kestrels - in Arizona and New Mexico. They observed that all three species opted to perch on one limb rather than two, and that they positioned themselves so that they had an optimal view of their surroundings. The researchers then carried out experiments in which they hung stuffed predators and other objects around perches to see how it affected the birds' behaviour. They found that the presence of potential threats caused the birds to perch on one limb more often and from a higher vantage point. The findings suggest that the birds' single-limb perching behaviour is an adaptation to reduce the risk of predation. Perching on one foot may allow the birds to maintain a better lookout for danger, and by positioning themselves higher up, they can also be more aware of any potential threats from above.

A singularly perturbed parabolic problem of convection-diffusion type with a discontinuous initial condition is examined. An analytic function is identified which matches the discontinuity in the initial condition and also captures the behavior of the solution as the perturbation parameter approaches zero. This technique is known as matched asymptotic expansion and involves constructing a series expansion of the solution in two separate regions, one near the discontinuity and one away from it. The two expansions are then matched together using the analytic function to ensure that the solution is continuous and satisfies the governing equations. The process is useful for problems where the dominant behavior of the system changes abruptly over a small region or when there are sharp gradients in the initial or boundary conditions.

In October 1529, Philip I, Landgrave of Hesse, convoked an assembly of German and Swiss theologians at the Marburg Colloquy, to establish doctrinal unity in the emerging Protestant states. Agreement was reached on fourteen out of sixteen points, including the central doctrine of justification by faith alone. The Marburg Colloquy was convened in response to the Protestant Reformation taking place in Germany at the time. It was an attempt to bring together the various reformers and have them agree upon a common set of doctrinal beliefs. The colloquy took place in Marburg, Hesse and was attended by Philip I, Landgrave of Hesse, as well as theologians from Switzerland and Germany, such as Martin Luther, Ulrich Zwingli and Johannes Oecolampadius. The colloquy focused on sixteen points of doctrine, with the two most important being the doctrine of the Eucharist (the Lord's Supper) and the doctrine of justification by faith alone. After much discussion, agreement was reached on fourteen out of sixteen points, but disagreement remained on the two key issues of the Lord's Supper and justification by faith alone. The former could not be resolved due to theological differences between Luther and Zwingli, while the latter was accepted by both sides, but with different interpretations that could not be reconciled. As a result, the Marburg Colloquy failed to produce unity among the Protestants and the two sides eventually split into separate Lutheran and Reformed churches. The Marburg Colloquy is significant in the history of Protestantism as it highlighted the fundamental differences between the two major strands of the Reformation and established the basis for the split between the two camps. It also demonstrated the importance of coming together to discuss religious differences and try to reach a consensus. Despite its failure, the Marburg Colloquy provided a model for future conversations between Protestants and Catholics and paved the way for the eventual resolution of some of the major doctrinal disputes between them.

Preterm infants' limb-pose estimation is a crucial but challenging task, which may improve patients' care and facilitate clinicians in infant's movements monitoring. Work in the literature either provides approaches to estimate the limb pose of preterm infants using computer vision techniques or proposes wearable sensors-based solutions. Computer vision approaches utilize cameras to capture images or videos of the infant's limbs, and then use image processing and machine learning techniques to estimate the pose of the limbs. Wearable sensors, on the other hand, can be placed on the infant's limbs and use accelerometers and other sensors to measure the movements and position of the limbs. Both approaches have their advantages and disadvantages. Computer vision approaches are non-invasive and do not require any additional equipment to be placed on the infant's body. However, the accuracy of pose estimation may be affected by factors such as lighting conditions, positioning of the camera, and occlusions caused by blankets or other objects. Wearable sensors, on the other hand, provide more accurate measurements of the limb's position and movements but may cause discomfort to the infant and may require frequent adjustments due to the infant's growth. Overall, further research is needed to develop more accurate and reliable methods for estimating preterm infants' limb pose, which can improve patient care and help facilitate clinicians in monitoring the infant's movements.

A warrant is a legal document that authorizes law enforcement officials to carry out a specific action. This can include searching a location, arresting a suspect or seizing assets. A warrant is obtained by presenting evidence to a judge, who then decides whether there is enough probable cause to justify the requested action. Warrants are difficult to obtain because they require a high level of evidence and legal justification. The Fourth Amendment to the US Constitution protects citizens from unreasonable searches and seizures, and as such, the process for obtaining a warrant is designed to provide a balance between citizens' rights and the needs of law enforcement officials to investigate and prosecute crimes. Judges are required to carefully review warrant requests to ensure that they meet the legal standard of probable cause and that they do not violate the Fourth Amendment. Overall, warrants are an important tool for law enforcement officials, as they provide legal justification for actions that might otherwise be considered unconstitutional. However, they should be used sparingly and only when there is a clear need for them.

Auschwitz was one of the most notorious Nazi death camps, where more than 1.1 million people were killed during World War Two. Now, the names of the SS commanders and guards who served there have been put online by Poland's Institute of National Remembrance (INR). The INR says it hopes the database will help "prosecute perpetrators of crimes against humanity." "For years, the world has been waiting for this moment," said Piotr Cywinski, director of the Auschwitz-Birkenau State Museum. "This is an important step in the fight against forgetting and denying the Holocaust." The database includes the names of around 8,500 people who served at Auschwitz between 1940 and 1945. It includes information on their ranks, dates of service and - in some cases - what happened to them after the war. Many of those named served at the camp for a short time, and some were only teenagers when they were assigned there. Some later served at other Nazi camps, while others went on to have successful careers in post-war Germany. The release of the database comes as Poland prepares to mark the 75th anniversary of the liberation of Auschwitz by Soviet troops on 27 January.

I'm more interested in the best practices for writing documentation and how to make such documentation more useful. Behavior planning is known to be one of the basic cognitive functions, which is essential for any cognitive architecture of any control system used in robotics. At the same time , it is known that in many cases the behavior planning problem is unsolvable. This fact has been proved by the Church-Turing theorem. There are two ways to deal with this situation: either to use a suboptimal solution or to use an approximate solution. The first way is to use a heuristic search algorithm, which can find a suboptimal solution in polynomial time. The second way is to use a approximation algorithm, which can find an approximate solution in polynomial time. The most popular heuristic search algorithm is the A algorithm. It is known that the A algorithm is optimal if the heuristic function is admissible. An admissible heuristic function is a function that never overestimates the cost of reaching the goal. The most popular approximation algorithm is the Simulated Annealing algorithm. It is known that the Simulated Annealing algorithm converges to the global optimum if the cooling schedule is chosen properly. Both of these algorithms have been used in the field of robotics. The A algorithm has been used in navigation and path planning. The Simulated Annealing algorithm has been used in motion planning.

The widespread presence of dragon legends in different civilizations and cultures can be explained by several factors. Firstly, there is a possibility that the depiction of dragons could have arisen independently in different places and times, as humans may have been inspired by real-life creatures such as crocodiles, snakes, or fossils of dinosaurs to create the mythological beasts. Secondly, the ancient myths frequently sought to explain natural phenomena around humans, such as natural disasters, changes in the seasons or the cycle of life and death. The fire-breathing dragons, with their intriguing anatomical features and supernatural powers, could easily be associated with various natural events. Finally, dragons were often used in many cultures as a symbol of strength, power, and wisdom. Some cultures viewed them as guardians of magical secrets that only the wise and courageous could unravel, while others regarded them as protectors of sacred places, royal heirs, or even entire cities. Overall, the various representations of dragons in different cultures could have emerged from the presence of common themes and shared beliefs among humans, as well as a common human desire for magical creatures and supernatural entities that defy our known physical laws.

Ping is a measure of how quickly data packets are travelling from one computer to another. It is measured in milliseconds (ms). Loss is a measure of how much data is being lost in the transmission, usually expressed as a percentage. Loss has a more direct effect on your connection than ping does, because it can cause slowdowns or disruptions in service. Ping simply measures the speed of transmission, so if there is a high level of loss, it will not be reflected in the ping measurement.

Scientists and engineers have designed a new origami-inspired lunar habitat that has the capability to unfold into 750 times its own size. The habitat, called "Lunar Quattro-Hab" was developed by scientists from the Bremen University of Applied Sciences and the German Aerospace Centre. The design aims to provide a more convenient and efficient way to construct lunar settlements. The current process of constructing lunar habitats involves manually erecting rigid, container-like structures on the surface. The Lunar Quattro-Hab is unique because of its ability to pack flat into a container for transport and deployment on the lunar surface. The mechanism uses Origami folds on a lightweight metal frame to unfold and create a super-large structure of thousands of square meters. The design is configured to provide ample space for up to four astronauts to live and conduct scientific experiments for several weeks or months. The research team has tested Lunar Quattro-Hab in simulated lunar environments, and the results have been impressive. The folded structure exhibits versatility and robustness, withstanding extreme temperatures, radiation, and the impact of small meteoroids that commonly hit the moon's surface. The Lunar Quattro-Hab not only carries a spacious habitat but also provides a reliable framework to support the associated logistics of future lunar missions. This innovative achievement represents a significant milestone for space exploration and could indicate new discoveries yet to come. With the Lunar Quattro-Hab, the idea of establishing permanent lunar settlements seems more achievable than ever before. It is hoped that this new design will inspire further research and contribute to creating a sustainable human presence on the moon. The Bremen University of Applied Sciences and the German Aerospace Centre plan to advance Lunar Quattro-Hab to incorporate enhanced technology, including self-sustaining power, and water availability. The researchers expect that their contribution to a rapidly developing space industry will continue to grow as they solve more problems in future space missions.

An Australian mother who lost her young son after leaving him in a hot car during a workday suffered from "forgotten baby syndrome," an inquest has heard. The tragedy occurred in November 2019 when the woman, a veterinarian, forgot to drop off her son at daycare and instead drove straight to work, leaving the child unattended for hours in the back seat of her car on a scorching hot day. The toddler tragically died from heat-related injuries. At an inquest into the child's death, the court heard that the mother had been experiencing extreme sleep deprivation and stress at the time of the incident. She claimed that she had believed she had dropped her son off at daycare, only to later realize to her horror that she had left him in the car. This phenomenon, known as "forgotten baby syndrome," can occur when a person's habitual behavior is interrupted due to stress or sleep deprivation, leading to a lapse in memory. This can result in a parent or caregiver mistakenly leaving a child in a car, often with fatal consequences. While rare, these incidents are a devastating reminder of the dangers of leaving children unattended in vehicles, particularly during hot weather. According to the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration, an average of 39 children die each year in the US alone as a result of being left in a hot car. The inquest has highlighted the need for greater awareness of forgotten baby syndrome and the potential dangers it poses. The mother involved in this case has urged others to educate themselves on the issue and take steps to avoid similar tragedies from occurring. This tragic incident is a reminder to all parents and caregivers to remain vigilant and mindful of their children's whereabouts at all times. It is crucial that we continue to educate and raise awareness about forgotten baby syndrome to prevent further heartbreaking losses.

Emergent narratives provide a unique and compelling approach to interactive storytelling through simulation, and have applications in games, narrative generation, and virtual agents. However the inherent complexity of simulation makes it difficult to evaluate emergent narratives as they emerge. We present a method for evaluating emergent narrative content in games, using a combination of quantitative and qualitative analysis. Our approach is based on a framework of themes, characters, and plotlines, which can be used to assess the complexity, coherence, and engagement of emergent narrative content. We demonstrate our method by analyzing two different games: a real-time strategy game and an adventure game. The results of our analysis indicate that both games have highly engaging emergent narratives, with complex plotlines, meaningful characters, and interesting themes. Furthermore, our method provides insight into how emergent narratives can be further improved and optimized for maximum engagement. Our approach to evaluating emergent narrative content was designed to provide an objective measure of narrative complexity and coherence, as well as provide guidance for how narrative content can be improved. A key component of our approach is the use of a "theme" system, which allows us to evaluate the overall structure of the narrative and identify important plot points, characters, and themes. Additionally, our evaluation process incorporates both quantitative and qualitative analysis techniques, allowing us to assess the impact of individual elements on the narrative as a whole. Finally, we also analyzed the player experience to determine whether the emergent narrative was engaging and immersive. Overall, our method provides an effective way to analyze and evaluate emergent narrative content in games, and offers insights into how narrative content can be improved. By using quantitative and qualitative analysis techniques, our approach can help developers understand how the elements of their game interact to create a compelling story. Additionally, our method can help them identify areas where narrative content can be further enhanced or refined. Ultimately, our approach provides a valuable tool for understanding how emergent narratives work, and for ensuring that games are engaging and immersive for players.

The consensus among mental health professionals is that physical punishment of any kind should not be used when disciplining children. While it may seem like an easy way to get a child to stop misbehaving in the moment, research has shown that physical punishment can have long-term negative effects on a child's development, such as lower self-esteem, increased aggression, and even delays in cognitive development. There are some cases where physical punishment may be warranted if there is an immediate threat to the safety of either the child or someone else; however, this should be an extremely rare occurrence. Instead, experts recommend positive reinforcement and a consistent system of rewards and consequences to encourage good behavior. This method is usually more effective in helping children learn how to manage their emotions and make better choices in the future.

In this paper, we propose a novel algorithm for matching faces with temporal variations caused due to age progression. The proposed generative adversarial network algorithm is a unified framework that simultaneously learns the feature representation of the face and the mapping between the faces of different ages. It consists of two key components: a generator network and a discriminator network. The generator network takes a face image at a younger age as input and generates a corresponding face image at an older age. The discriminator network judges whether the generated image is real or fake. During training, the generator network learns to generate more realistic images that can fool the discriminator network. The proposed algorithm has several advantages over traditional methods. First, it can handle facial variations due to age progression in a more efficient and effective way. Second, it can generate new faces that are not present in the training set. Third, it can generate a sequence of face images that shows the progression of a face over time. The experimental results on various datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed algorithm in handling the face matching problem with age progression. The proposed algorithm achieves higher accuracy compared to state-of-the-art methods.

Internet of Things (IoT) is the next big evolutionary step in the world of internet. The main intention behind the IoT is to enable safer living and risk mitigation on a global scale. IoT, in simple terms, refers to a network of physical devices that can communicate and exchange data with each other through the internet. The devices can be anything from household appliances and wearable devices to industrial machinery and vehicles. By connecting these devices to the internet, we can access real-time data about their functioning and use this information to optimize their performance and improve efficiency. This can have a significant impact on a variety of industries, including healthcare, agriculture, transportation, and manufacturing. However, with the increased connectivity also comes the risk of security breaches and data privacy concerns. As we move towards a more interconnected world, it is important to address these issues and prioritize the safety and security of the IoT network.

We introduce a new machine-learning-based approach, which we call the Independent Classifier networks (InClass nets) technique, for the nonparameteric estimation of conditional independence mixture models (CIMMs). We approach the estimation problem by learning a CIMM from a set of input data points, typically observations of the joint distribution of two random variables. InClass nets are composed of a set of independently trained classifiers, each of which is trained to predict the class label of a given data point based on its features. These classifiers are then used to form an ensemble prediction, which is used as the CIMM estimate. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on a variety of real-world datasets, and show that it outperforms existing techniques in terms of accuracy, speed, and scalability.

While the idea of using tranquilizer guns may seem like a humane alternative to firearms for law enforcement officers, it would not be a practical solution. Tranquilizer guns are designed for use on animals, and their effects on humans could be unpredictable and dangerous. There is also the issue of dosage, as different individuals may require varying amounts to achieve the desired effect, and the risk of a fatal overdose is high. Additionally, in high-pressure and fast-paced situations, tranquilizer guns may not be effective in immediately incapacitating a suspect. Finally, there is the question of logistics - it would be impractical and costly to equip all law enforcement officers with tranquilizer guns and train them to use them properly, especially given the large number of situations where firearms may still be necessary. Therefore, while it is important to explore alternatives to firearms, tranquilizer guns are not a feasible solution for law enforcement.

In this extended abstract we present the gubs Upper Bound Solver. gubs is a dedicated constraint solver over the naturals for inequalities formed over uninterpreted function symbols and standard arithmetic . gubs is a branch-and-bound algorithm for upper bounding the solution set of a given set of constraints. gubs works by iteratively exploring the search space and constructing bounds on the solution set. The exploration is done by recursively partitioning the search space into subspaces, and generating new bounds by analyzing the lower and upper bounds of the subspaces. Bounds are generated using a combination of projection and linear programming techniques. The main advantage of gubs over existing methods is its ability to handle non-linear constraints. Unlike other methods that can only solve linear problems, gubs can efficiently solve non-linear problems, opening up new applications in verification, test generation, and optimization. In addition to solving nonlinear problems, gubs also has several advantages over existing constraint solvers. For example, gubs is able to automatically detect and discard redundant constraints, resulting in faster computation times. Moreover, gubs does not require an explicit encoding of the problem, allowing for more flexibility when formulating problems. Finally, gubs is highly parallelizable, enabling it to scale to larger problems than existing methods. We have implemented gubs and evaluated its performance on a number of benchmark problems. Our results show that gubs outperforms existing methods and is able to solve nonlinear problems significantly faster than existing solvers.

The findings are based on a review of previous studies, which found that MUPs reduce the affordability of alcohol and lead to a reduction in consumption. It also found that MUPs can have greater impacts on heavier drinkers than moderate drinkers. PHE is now calling for further research into the introduction of MUPs, saying that it could be an effective way of reducing harms from alcohol in England. PHE's Chief executive, Duncan Selbie, said: "Alcohol misuse is linked to many serious health conditions, including cancer and liver disease, as well as playing a role in violent crime and anti-social behaviour. We must take action now to tackle this avoidable harm." The call for further research follows a number of other countries have implemented MUPs, including Scotland, Canada and some parts of Australia. In Scotland, where a 50p MUP was introduced in 2018, alcohol-related hospital admissions dropped by 2.6. However, the UK government has so far refused to introduce a MUP in England, instead preferring a duty escalator system, which increases taxes on higher strength drinks. Commenting on the review, Professor Sir Ian Gilmore, chair of the Alcohol Health Alliance UK, said: "This review provides further evidence of the need for the UK Government to introduce a minimum unit price for alcohol in England." He added: "Minimum unit pricing is the most effective policy measure available to reduce the harms from alcohol and should be implemented without any further delay."

If addiction is a disease, why do most addictions end spontaneously, without treatment? Why did some 75 of heroin-addicted Vietnam vets kick the drug when they returned home? It's hard to explain without invoking the concepts of volition and choice, but that won't do for those who want to see addiction as a disease. And what about people who are addicted to risky behaviors? Certainly some people develop dependencies on such things as gambling, food, or sex. But others seem to be able to gamble responsibly, eat moderately, and enjoy their sexuality without developing addictions. Where's the disease here? If intoxication is a disease, why does society fail to treat it as such? We do not hesitate to lock up addicts if they commit crimes, even nonviolent ones. If we truly believed that addiction was an involuntary condition, however, we would not punish addicts for breaking the law whenever their compulsion got the better of them. At best, we would give them some kind of treatment; at worst, we'd just let them be. The theory that addiction is a disease fails to live up to its scientific billing. By contrast, the research conducted by Volkow and her colleagues at the National Institute on Drug Abuse confirms that drug addiction is a voluntary behavior. As they put it, "While the initiation of drug use may be involuntary, once underway, continued drug use is typically a voluntary behavior." This is the conclusion of other researchers as well. Unless addiction really is involuntary, advocates of this theory must show that addicts lack the capacity to make choices. And that is where the theory runs into trouble. To understand why, it helps to think about the ways in which people typically become addicted to drugs. Most people who become addicted start as recreational users, which is to say, they use drugs to make themselves feel good. They certainly don't start out using drugs to get sick, and they certainly don't intend to become addicts. Many people who use drugs recreationally never become addicted. The difference between addicts and nonaddicts is that addicts have more trouble quitting. It's not that they can't quit at all. In fact, the vast majority of addicts eventually kick the habit. As Volkow and her colleagues point out, "continued drug use is typically a voluntary behavioreven among addicts. What's more, studies suggest that the vast majority of addicts want to quit and are willing to try. In a longitudinal study of heroin addicts in Baltimore, researchers found that 85 percent expressed a desire to quit at least once during their careers as addicts. And a 2007 survey of patients at addiction-treatment facilities found that 86 percent said they wanted to quit alcohol and 79 percent said they wanted to quit drugs. As with most health-related issues, people's attitudes toward addiction are often shaped by personal experience. It is common for people who have not had problems with addiction to assume that addicts simply enjoy being addicts. That is clearly not true. The truth is that addicts begin by deliberately choosing to use drugs to alter their mental states. Over time, however, their use of drugs changes from voluntary to compulsive. When someone is addicted, his body has adapted to the presence of particular substances. The addict's tolerance to these substances increases, so he needs to take larger doses to achieve the same effect. His dependence also grows, so he feels physically ill when he attempts to quit. These effects cause addicts to spend increasing amounts of time and money obtaining and using drugs. They break the law if necessary. Their job performance suffers, and their relationships with family members deteriorate. They no longer do what they used to do for fun. Instead, they spend their time acquiring and using drugs. In this way, addiction changes the addict's behavior. Addiction also changes the addict's psychological state. Addicts tend to become extremely anxious and depressed when they are not high. They tend to obsess about drugs and to focus on how to obtain them. All of this makes quitting more difficult. The addict's physical cravings and psychological obsessions can be very powerful. They can persist for years after the addict stops using drugs. Because of this, even addicts who are determined to quit often find themselves slipping back into old habits. It is clear that addiction has a profound impact on addicts' lives. But this doesn't mean that addiction is involuntary. Addicts continue to use drugs because they choose to. Although the reasons for this choice may be complex, the choice itself is not. The idea that addiction is involuntary is based on a misunderstanding of what addiction is and how it develops. Addicts do not become addicts because they are unable to control their impulses or because they are powerless against their cravings. They become addicts because they choose to use drugs, and they continue to use drugs because they prefer being high to being sober. This is not to deny that addiction is a serious problem. It clearly is. But the solution is not to treat addiction as a disease. The solution is to treat addicts as people who are capable of making choices and who are responsible for the consequences of their choices.

Warsaw was occupied by Germany from 4 August 1915 until November 1918. The Allied Armistice terms required in Article 12 that Germany withdraw from areas controlled by Russia in 1914, including the so-called Congress Poland. In 1918, the German commandant of Warsaw issued a proclamation announcing that the Armistice to be signed in Compiegne would not affect the status of Warsaw. Nevertheless, the German commander allowed the Polish authorities to return to Warsaw and participate in the administration of their city. An interim Polish government of the newly independent Republic of Poland (Rzeczpospolita Polska) was formed on 7 November 1918. It included Jozef Pisudski, who became Chief of State (Naczelnik Panstwa), and Ignacy Jan Paderewski, Prime Minister. The army of the new Polish state was commanded by General Jozef Haller de Hallenburg. On 10 November, the first conflict between the newly formed Republic of Poland and Germany took place in Posen where Polish nationalists instigated a short-lived uprising against the Germans. Pisudski did not consider Warsaw the natural capital of the country, but rather a provisional one; Krakow was considered more important as the former capital of the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth. Although Warsaw would remain the official capital until after World War II, Pisudski preferred to work from Krakow. In December 1918, Pisudski was named Marshal of Poland (Marszaek Polski). A leading human rights organisation has called on the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation (Nato) to properly investigate reports of civilian casualties in air strikes in Libya last year. The call comes after a recent report submitted to Nato revealed that "several dozen" civilians were killed as a result of air strikes during the conflict in Libya between 2011 and 2012. The report concluded that the number of civilians killed was "unacceptably high," but did not recommend any action or investigation into the deaths. Amnesty International, an international non-governmental organisation focused on human rights, has called on Nato to take further steps to investigate the deaths of civilians in Libya. The organisation is demanding that Nato launch an independent inquiry into the events, in order to ensure that those responsible for the deaths are held accountable and that proper measures are taken to prevent similar incidents from occurring in the future. In a statement released by Amnesty International, researcher Heba Morayef said: "Nato must not be allowed to simply brush this under the carpet. The alliance must conduct a full, transparent and independent investigation into the reported civilian casualties and take appropriate measures to protect civilians from harm in future interventions." Nato has yet to respond to the demands made by Amnesty International.

Recent years have seen big advances in the field of sentence-level quality estimation (QE), largely as a result of using neural-based architectures. However, the majority of these methods work only for specific language pairs and require parallel data for training. This poses a challenge for many low-resource languages or domains where parallel data may be scarce or unavailable. One approach to address this problem is to use unsupervised or weakly supervised methods that rely on monolingual or comparable corpora. These methods often leverage pre-trained language models or transfer learning techniques to estimate the sentence-level quality without relying on parallel data. Another approach is to use domain adaptation techniques to transfer knowledge from a high-resource language or domain to a low-resource one. These methods aim to reduce the domain or language gap and improve the generalization of the models to new data. Overall, the field of QE is rapidly evolving, and there is still much room for improvement, especially for low-resource languages and domains.

The current gold standard for human activity recognition (HAR) is based on the use of cameras. However, the poor scalability of camera systems renders them impractical in pursuit of the large-scale recognition of human activities. In recent years, the emergence of wearable sensors has enabled the development of alternative systems for HAR that are more scalable and cost effective. These systems rely on a combination of inertial sensors (accelerometers and gyroscopes) andor magnetic sensors (magnetometers) to measure the 3D orientation and movement of the body as well as its interaction with the environment. By combining sensor data with sophisticated machine learning algorithms, these systems can accurately detect and recognize various activities such as walking, running, and jumping. In addition to the scalability benefits, wearable sensor-based systems also offer improved precision and accuracy compared to camera-based systems. Moreover, they can provide information about activity intensity and duration in real time, which is useful for applications such as healthcare monitoring, sports performance analysis, and automated video annotation.

Lessons From A Tech Job Search (13 minute read) Are you looking for a job in the tech industry? Are you feeling lost and unsure of where to start? Look no further. One tech job seeker has shared their experiences and offered valuable lessons for those in the same position. Paul, a software developer with four years of experience under his belt, found himself in the market for a new job. He shared his journey on a tech job search forum, hoping to help others navigate the often overwhelming process. Lesson 1: Know what you're looking for Before hitting the job search sites, Paul recommends taking the time to really think about what you want in a job. Consider the type of work you enjoy, the company culture, and even the type of city you want to work in. Having a clear idea of what you're looking for will help you weed out jobs that don't align with your goals. Lesson 2: Do your research Once you've identified what you want, it's time to research potential employers. Look at their company culture, mission statement, and current job openings. Reach out to current employees on LinkedIn or other social media platforms to get an insider's perspective on the company. Lesson 3: Customize your application materials Gone are the days of a one-size-fits-all resume and cover letter. Paul stresses the importance of customizing application materials for each job you apply for. Highlight the specific skills and experiences that make you a good fit for each company. Lesson 4: Be prepared for technical interviews Many tech companies require a technical interview as part of the application process. Paul recommends preparing for these interviews ahead of time by practicing coding challenges and reviewing algorithms. He also suggests being honest if you don't know the answer to a question, as interviewers appreciate honesty and a willingness to learn. Lesson 5: Stay positive The job search process can be grueling and demotivating. However, Paul stresses the importance of staying positive and keeping a growth mindset. Use rejections as opportunities to learn and improve your application materials. Celebrate small victories, like getting an interview or receiving positive feedback on an application. In conclusion, a tech job search can be daunting, but with these lessons from one experienced job seeker, you're one step closer to landing your dream job. Remember to take the time to identify what you're looking for, research potential employers, customize your application materials, prepare for technical interviews, and stay positive throughout the process.

Lily's mother explained that although the doll was not perfect anymore, it still held a special place in her heart. Lily began to understand what her mother meant. She realized that even though the doll was broken, it was still beautiful. From that day on, Lily took care of her doll more carefully than she had ever done before. She dressed it up in new clothes and played with it every day. The doll was still broken, but it brought her joy and companionship just like before. Years passed and Lily grew up, but she never forgot the lesson she learned from her broken doll. She learned that even though things may not always be perfect, they can still be beautiful and valuable. She kept the doll with her always as a reminder of this lesson and cherished it as much as ever.

Currently, the visually impaired rely on either a sighted human, guide dog, or white cane to safely navigate. One solution to this problem is the use of assistive technologies such as wearable devices and apps that use sensors, cameras, and other technologies to detect obstacles and guide users. Some devices use haptic feedback to provide users with tactile cues to avoid obstacles, while others use audio cues or verbal instructions. Another solution is the use of Wayfinding systems with audio guidance like beacons or GPS. These systems can provide audio cues to help visually impaired people navigate indoor and outdoor environments. There are also technologies being developed to assist visually impaired people in specific tasks, such as identifying objects using computer vision, and even reading text using optical character recognition (OCR) software. Overall, these technologies can greatly improve the independence and quality of life for visually impaired individuals.

The colour of the sky is caused by sunlight light bouncing around within the atmosphere. At night, on earth, there's no sunlight so it appears black. The pound-force has a metric counterpart, less commonly used than the newton: the kilogram-force (kgf) (sometimes kilopond), is the force exerted by standard gravity on one kilogram of mass. The kilogram-force is equivalent to 9.80665 newtons, since that is the acceleration due to gravity in standard units of meters per second squared (ms2). So 1 kgf is the force required to accelerate a mass of 1kg at a rate of 9.80665 ms2.

John Nash's theory was so revolutionary because it provided a general framework for analyzing the behavior of multiple actors in strategic situations. His work revolutionized economics, game theory, and mathematics as he proposed a formal mathematical model of interactions between rational decision makers. This was a major development since prior to his work, economists had relied on qualitative explanations and analogies to explain their results. The Nash equilibrium concept is applicable across many disciplines, including economics, political science, biology, psychology, engineering, and philosophy. It is used to understand and analyze a wide range of issues, from stock market pricing to climate change negotiations.

Starting a business is certainly one of the most challenging, yet rewarding, adventures that any individual can embark on. However, persisting as a solo founder requires extraordinary dedication, perseverance, and resilience. According to a recent study conducted by the Global Entrepreneurship Monitor, only 20 of startup founders run their ventures alone. Nevertheless, there are plenty of examples of successful entrepreneurs who achieved remarkable success as confident solo operators. One such example is Jack Ma, the legendary founder and former executive chairman of Alibaba Group, a Chinese multinational conglomerate specializing in e-commerce, retail, and technology. In his early days, Ma was rejected from every job he applied to, including positions at KFC and the police force. However, he didn't let that discourage him and founded Alibaba in 1999, which now has a massive 650 billion valuation. Another notable example of an individual founder is Elon Musk, the CEO of SpaceX and Tesla, whose innovations are driving the advancement of science and technology. Musk began his career as a software developer and went on to co-found PayPal, which laid the foundation for his future successes. Persisting as a solo founder requires extraordinary determination, resourcefulness, and self-motivation. It can be isolating and challenging to balance all aspects of the business, from finances to marketing, from product development to customer service. There are days when the progress seems painfully slow, and the challenges seem insurmountable. Still, solo founders who persevere gain independence, creative freedom and build unique businesses that reflect their vision and values. They also have complete control over their work and are likely to be more agile and flexible in pivoting business models or responding to trends and changing circumstances. In conclusion, while teamwork and collaboration can often be indispensable to a startup's success, the journey of a solo founder can be equally rewarding. It takes remarkable courage, ambition, and grit to set out on one's own, navigate the uncertainties and risks, and transform a vision into a profitable and innovative enterprise.

The fuzzy K -means problem is a generalization of the classical K -means problem to soft clusterings, i.e. clusterings where each points belongs to each cluster to some degree. Although the classical K -means algorithm is easy to implement and fast to execute, it has some drawbacks. One of its main drawbacks is that it requires prior knowledge on the number of clusters or a good estimation of it. Furthermore, it requires the data to be well separated. In fuzzy K -means, each point belongs to all the clusters with a certain degree of membership, which can be seen as a probability. This allows for overlapping clusters and makes the algorithm more robust when dealing with noisy data. The algorithm also does not require prior knowledge about the number of clusters, since this can be determined by an objective function. The algorithm starts by randomly assigning a degree of membership to each point for each cluster and then it iterates until a local optimum is found. At each iteration, the centroid of each cluster is updated based on the degrees of membership and the objective function is evaluated. The algorithm stops when the objective function reaches a certain level of satisfaction.

Federated Learning (FL) is a decentralized machine learning protocol that allows a set of participating agents to collaboratively train a model without sharing their data. This makes FL particularly suitable for privacy-sensitive applications like healthcare or finance, where data is sensitive and centralized data storage is not possible. In a Federated Learning setting, a global model is trained on a dataset that is distributed across a set of participating agents. Each agent trains the model on its local dataset and then shares its model updates with the other agents. The global model is then updated using these model updates. This process is repeated until the global model converges to a desired accuracy. There are a number of benefits to using FL over traditional centralized machine learning methods. First, FL allows for training on sensitive data that cannot be shared with a central server. Second, FL can be more efficient than centralized methods, as it avoids the need to send data back and forth between a central server and the participating agents. Finally, FL is more robust to data fragmentation, as each agent only needs to have a small portion of the total dataset in order to train the model. However, FL also has a number of challenges. First, it can be difficult to protect the privacy of the participating agents, as their model updates may reveal information about their data. Second, FL can be slow, as the global model needs to be updated after each round of training. Finally, FL can be unstable, as the model updates from each agent may not be compatible with each other. Despite these challenges, FL is a promising direction for machine learning and has a number of potential applications.

We introduce Fluid Annotation, an intuitive human-machine collaboration interface for annotating the class label and outline of every object and background region in an image 1 footnote 1 1 footnote 1 . To make it easier for humans to annotate images with large numbers of classes, Fluid Annotation shows a selectable set of class icons along the top of the annotation interface. For example, in Figure 1, we show an image annotated using Fluid Annotation, with the classes "Person" and "Animal" selected. The classes can be filtered by a search bar so that only relevant classes are displayed. Humans can also create their own custom classes. footnote: 1We would like to thank the anonymous reviewers for their valuable feedback. We also would like to thank the following people for their help with this work: Yimeng Li, Priyanka Vijayakumar, Timnit Gebru, and Jonathan Krause. We introduce an end-to-end system for semantically segmenting objects in natural images. The system is based on Mask R-CNN 2 , 3 , a state-of-the-art object detection and instance segmentation framework. Mask R-CNN is composed of three components: 1) a feature extractor, which is typically a convolutional neural network (CNN), trained for object classification, 2) a region proposal network, which is used for generating a set of candidate object locations and scales, and 3) a prediction network, which is used for predicting object labels, bounding box offsets, and class-specific mask logos. We employ two novel techniques to improve the performance of Mask R-CNN. First, we use a new region proposal network architecture called RPN 4 , which is faster and more accurate than traditional region proposal methods 5 , 6 , 7 . Second, we use an attention model 8 to improve the performance of the feature extractor. Our system takes as input an image and outputs the locations and masks of the objects in the image. The primary output is shown in Figure 2. The left column shows the input image, and the right column shows the corresponding semantic segmentation. In addition, the system outputs the class label of each object. In our experiments, we evaluate the system on four standard data sets: 1) Microsoft COCO 9 , which contains 80 classes and is split into training, validation, and test sets containing 118K, 5K, and 20K images, respectively; 2) PASCAL VOC 2010 10 , which contains 20 classes and is split into training, validation, and test sets containing 5K, 1K, and 1K images, respectively; 3) PASCAL Context 11 , which contains 59 classes and is split into training, validation, and test sets containing 4K, 5K, and 5K images, respectively; and 4) ADE20K 12 , which contains 150 classes and is split into training, validation, and test sets containing 20K, 2K, and 3K images, respectively. Our system achieves state-of-the-art results on all four data sets. On COCO, our system achieves a mean intersection over union (mIoU) of 0.891, which is 2.4 higher than the previous state-of-the-art result 13 . On PASCAL VOC 2010 and PASCAL Context, our system achieves mIoU of 0.965 and 0.857, which are 1.3 and 0.6 higher than the previous state-of-the-art results 14 , 15 , respectively. On ADE20K, our system achieves mIoU of 0.430, which is 0.6 higher than the previous state-of-the-art result 16 . Our system also outperforms the previous state-of-the-art system on speed. On a Titan X Pascal GPU, our system runs at approximately 30 frames per second (fps). Our system is therefore fast enough to operate in real time.

In 2013, the Peabody Awards honoured Doctor Who with an Institutional Peabody "for evolving with technology and the times like nothing else in the known television universe." The programme is one of only a handful of shows that have won the award more than once, having previously received it in 2006 and in 2011. In 2016, Doctor Who was again nominated for a Peabody and was shortlisted for the award. In addition to these awards, the programme has also been recognised by the British Academy of Film and Television Arts (BAFTA). Since the awards began in 1947, Doctor Who has received fifty-six nominations and won eleven times, most recently in 2009 in the Special, Visual and Graphic Effects category. It has also won several BAFTA Craft Awards, which recognise technical achievement in television. The show was nominated for Best Drama Series at the National Television Awards in 2005, but lost out to Spooks. The show also won the Digital Spy Readers' Award for Best Drama Series in 2005. In 2006, Doctor Who won the SFX Readers' Award for Best TV Show. David Tennant won the 2006 SFX Readers' Award for Best Actor. In 2007, Billie Piper won the SFX Readers' Award for Best Actress. In 2008, David Tennant won the SFX Readers' Award for Best Actor for the second year running. In 2010, Matt Smith won the SFX Readers' Award for Best Actor. In 2011, Karen Gillan won the SFX Readers' Award for Best Actress. In 2012, Steven Moffat won the SFX Readers' Award for Best Writer. In 2013, Karen Gillan and Arthur Darvill were both nominated for SFX Readers' Awards for Best Actress and Best Actor respectively. In 2014, Peter Capaldi won the SFX Readers' Award for Best Actor. In 2015, Peter Capaldi was nominated for a BAFTA Television Award for Best Actor for his role in the series eight episode "Heaven Sent," but lost out to Stephen Graham for This Is England '90. In 2016, Doctor Who won the SFX Readers' Award for Best TV Show for the third time. In 2017, Jodie Whittaker won the SFX Readers' Award for Best Actress. Ratings The ratings of Doctor Who are an issue of some debate within fandom. There is a general consensus among fans that the show's decline in viewership since 1989 has been gradual, as opposed to the sharp drop seen in many other programmes. Preterm infants' limb-pose estimation is a crucial but challenging task, which may improve patients' care and facilitate clinicians in infant's movements monitoring. Work in the literature either provides approaches to estimate limb-pose from image data or applies motion tracking systems for the estimation. However, these approaches are either complex and limited to a specific setting or require an expensive motion capture system with markers on the infant's body. In this paper, we propose a novel approach based on a low-cost depth camera to estimate limb-poses of preterm infants in a non-invasive manner. The proposed approach consists of two main stages: (1) detect the infant's body parts using deep learning techniques; and (2) estimate the pose of each body part using a simple kinematic model. We evaluate the proposed approach using a publicly available dataset and demonstrate that it outperforms the state-of-the-art methods. Our findings suggest that the proposed approach is a promising tool for preterm infants' poses estimation.

I cowered behind my owner's legs and wished I was back home in my cozy bed. I tried my best to be a good boy and not resist, but I couldn't help yelping when she touched a sore spot on my leg. She took my temperature and gave me some shots that made me feel dizzy and groggy. The vet decided to run some tests and sent us home with some medication and instructions to come back in a week. The next few days were tough. I didn't have any energy to play or run around, and I didn't even want to eat my favorite treats. But my owner took great care of me, giving me cuddles and making sure I drank enough water. The medication started to work, and I started to feel better, little by little. When it was time to go back to the vet, I wasn't as scared. I knew that she was helping me feel better, even if it meant some uncomfortable moments. The tests came back, and it turned out that I had a minor infection that was easily treatable. The vet gave me a clean bill of health and said I could go back to my normal routine. I was so relieved and happy to be back to my old self. I wagged my tail and licked the vet's hand as a thank you. The trip to the vet wasn't fun, but it was worth it to feel better and to know that I was in good hands.

Well before we had the planets, we had a disc of dust orbiting the sun. This is because when the initial cloud (which formed the sun) collapsed due to gravity , it began to spin, flattening into a disc shape due to centrifugal force. As the disc cooled, tiny particles of dust and gas came together, forming larger and larger clumps through a process called accretion. These clumps eventually became planetesimals, which then collided and merged to form the planets we know today. It's incredible to think about how our solar system and its planets came into existence through this process!

Magnets can be turned off and on by manipulating their magnetic field. One way to turn off a magnet is to heat it to its Curie temperature, which is the temperature at which it loses its magnetic properties. Another way is to apply a magnetic field in the opposite direction, which can cancel out the original magnetic field and effectively turn off the magnet. To turn a magnet on, one can simply remove the opposing field, increase the strength of the magnet or change its orientation to align the domains within the material to the original magnetic field. This property of being able to turn magnets on and off is essential in many applications, such as in electric transformers, motors, and data storage devices.

In this work, we explain the working mechanism of MixUp in terms of adversarial training. We introduce a new class of adversarial training schemes, which we refer to as directional adversarial training. We demonstrate that MixUp can be interpreted as a directional adversarial training method, and discuss its advantages over other methods such as virtual adversarial training and traditional adversarial training. Finally, we provide an empirical comparison between MixUp, virtual adversarial training, and traditional adversarial training. MixUp is a data augmentation technique which has been shown to improve the performance of deep learning models. It works by randomly mixing up two training examples, creating new "virtual" examples from their combination. This form of data augmentation helps regularize the model, improving its generalization ability. The underlying principle of MixUp is similar to adversarial training, where an adversary is used to create perturbed versions of training examples in order to fool the model. Adversarial training is usually accomplished by adding small perturbations to the training examples, however MixUp takes a different approach. Instead of perturbing the original examples, MixUp creates entirely new examples by combining two existing examples. These new examples are then used to train the model. The main advantage of MixUp compared to traditional adversarial training is that it does not require any additional effort to generate adversarial examples. Since MixUp does not rely on perturbing existing examples, it can be applied to any dataset without modification. Additionally, MixUp does not require knowledge of the model's internals, making it more robust to model changes. In this work, we propose a new class of adversarial training schemes, which we refer to as directional adversarial training. Directional adversarial training operates similarly to MixUp, in that it uses combinations of existing training examples in order to generate new virtual examples. However, instead of using random combinations of existing examples, directional adversarial training uses a specific direction to mix the examples. This allows for more targeted data augmentation, which can lead to better results. We demonstrate that MixUp can be interpreted as a directional adversarial training method, and discuss its advantages over other methods such as virtual adversarial training and traditional adversarial training. We also provide an empirical comparison between MixUp, virtual adversarial training, and traditional adversarial training, showing that MixUp outperforms the other methods on several benchmark datasets.

Four men have been held for more than two years at an immigration removal centre after a report found that the average length of detentions had grown. The report by the Refugee Council and Medical Justice examined detention records of people held at Brook House Immigration Removal Centre (IRC) near Gatwick Airport in West Sussex, between July 2017 and June 2020. It revealed that in total, 441 people were held in the centre over this period, with the average length of detention rising from 40 days to 68 days. The report also highlighted four cases where individuals were detained for more than two years, with one being detained for almost three years. This is despite the Home Office's own guidelines, which require it to review each case every 28 days and only use detention as a "last resort." The report found that in many cases, the Home Office failed to properly assess whether detention was necessary or proportionate. In response, the Home Office said it was working to reduce the overall number of people in detention, and that it took its responsibility to ensure detention is used appropriately "extremely seriously." However, Refugee Council Chief Executive Maurice Wren argued that "the sheer scale of the long-term detention of people seeking asylum should shame us all." He added: "It's not just wrong, it's a waste of public money and deeply damaging to those who are locked up without knowing when they will be released." The report's findings come at a time when immigration detention centres have been heavily criticised for their treatment of detainees, particularly during the coronavirus pandemic. Some campaigners have called for the Government to end indefinite immigration detention, arguing that it is inhumane and unnecessary.

Tamara de Lempicka was a famous artist born in Warsaw. She was born Maria Gorska in Warsaw to wealthy parents and in 1916 married a Polish lawyer Tadeusz Lempicki. Better known as Tamara de Lempicka, she was a leading representative of the Art Deco movement. Her distinctive painting style combined elements of Cubism and Futurism with the realism of Neoclassicism and Expressionism. De Lempicka's work was heavily influenced by modernism, which had become popular in Europe during the 1920s. She was inspired by the works of other modernist painters such as Pablo Picasso, Georges Braque, and Amedeo Modigliani. De Lempicka also drew inspiration from Italian Renaissance art, which she encountered while studying in Italy. Her paintings often featured luxurious settings and figures with elongated proportions, giving them an almost dreamlike quality. In her lifetime, de Lempicka achieved extraordinary success and international fame. She was one of the most sought-after portraitists of her day and counted among her patrons members of the aristocracy and the Hollywood elite. Her works were exhibited from New York to Paris and can be found in museums around the world.

I really want someone to change my view on this, since everyone I know are frowning on me for thinking this way. My argument is, that just with my single vote, I can't make a change. Imagine the amount of people who feel like me and don't vote, the number will be too big to ignore. My parents are both immigrants from Cuba, so I guess that is where some of my views come from. A: In any single election, your vote is unlikely to be decisive. However, in aggregate over time, votes matter a lot. Consider a hypothetical election in which only two candidates - one conservative and one liberal - were running. Each received 49 of the vote. The outcome would be determined by a coin flip. If you favored the liberal but voted for the conservative instead because you wanted the outcome to be determined by a coin flip, you would be wasting your vote. Nonetheless, if everyone thought that way, then the conservative would win by chance. Suppose that everyone thought that way and that there were ten such elections. In that case, the conservative would probably win five times and the liberal would probably win five times. In aggregate, those ten votes would have had an impact. Similarly, after each election, there is always a group that blames their party's loss on the fact that not enough people voted. They argue that if more people had voted, then the outcome would have been different. That may or may not be true. But either way, the reason that more people didn't vote is that they thought that their vote wouldn't matter anyway. So again, in aggregate it does matter. There are two ways to increase the likelihood that your vote would matter. First, turn out. Second, vote in a close district. For example, in 2016, Donald Trump won Pennsylvania by 44,292 votes. If all 1,128,427 Pennsylvania residents who voted for Jill Stein had instead voted for Hillary Clinton, then she would have won Pennsylvania and thus the election. This was not a realistic scenario (most Stein voters were probably more anti-Clinton than they were pro-Trump), but it illustrates how even small changes can matter. (Or how a few thousand Stein voters may have decided the entire election.)

Shijian-21, or SJ-21, is a Chinese satellite designed to test and verify space debris mitigation technologies. It was recently observed pulling a dead satellite out of its normal orbit and into an orbit where it will eventually reenter the atmosphere and burn up. This is a major step forward in the effort to reduce the amount of space debris that is accumulating in Earth's orbit. The satellite was launched in July 2020, as part of China's Long March-4B rocket mission. It is equipped with a robotic arm and a capture device, which are capable of grasping objects up to 350 kilograms in weight. The satellite also features a variety of sensors and cameras for monitoring the captured object. SJ-21 is the first satellite of its kind to be sent into space and has already proven successful in its mission. In addition to being able to de-orbit discarded satellites, it is also capable of stabilizing their orbits, allowing them to remain in a safe area of space. This technology could potentially be used to help prevent further collisions between satellites and other space debris. In the future, SJ-21 could be used to clean up other types of space debris, such as defunct spacecraft and pieces of rocket boosters. This could have a significant impact on the environment by reducing the amount of trash in orbit and preventing long-term damage to our planet.

The reason is that many currencies are now traded in very small units. The tiniest unit of currency is called a "pip," and is equal to 1100,000th of the currency's base unit. For example, the smallest unit of U.S. currency is the penny, which is one one-hundredth of a dollar. The smallest unit of Japanese currency is the sen, which is one one-hundredth of a yen. In the foreign exchange market, one pip is usually equal to 0.0001 of the currency's base unit. So if the exchange rate for the U.S. dollar against the Japanese yen is quoted as 115.50, that means one dollar is worth 115.50 yen.

The shortcomings of Aristotelian physics would not be fully corrected until the 17th century work of Galileo Galilei, who was influenced by the late Medieval idea that objects in forced motion should continue in that motion forever. The particle model of matter is a model in which matter is considered to be composed of extremely small particles called "molecules." History The particle model was first proposed by Democritus, in the 5th century BC, who believed that all things were composed of tiny indivisible particles which he called "atomos" (Greek for indivisible). It was not until the late 17th and early 18th centuries, however, that scientists began to develop what is now known as the modern particle theory of matter. This was done primarily through the work of Robert Boyle and Isaac Newton. The particle model was developed from observations and experiments involving the behavior of matter. Experimental evidence Newton's laws of motion and his law of universal gravitation explained many features of the universe; however, they did not explain everything. In particular, they could not explain why objects in forced motion should continue in that motion forever. The particle model of matter provided an explanation for this behavior. Particles are constantly moving, even when they appear to be at rest, and they exert forces on each other. When one particle collides with another, the force of the collision causes the particles to change direction. This explains why objects in forced motion continue in that motion: the particles that make up the object are constantly colliding with each other, and thus the object continues to move. Even though the particle model of matter could explain many observed phenomena, it was not without its problems. One problem was that the model could not explain how two particles could interact with each other if they were not in contact with each other. Another problem was that the model could not explain how heat could be transferred from one object to another. These problems would not be fully resolved until the development of quantum mechanics in the early 20th century. Today, the particle model of matter is considered to be a valid model at the macroscopic level (i.e. at the level of everyday experience). At the atomic and subatomic level, however, the model is no longer considered to be accurate. Instead, quantum mechanics provides a more accurate description of the behavior of matter.

It all sound the same to me. And to be clear, I know this is what people tend to say about any music they don't "get." People say this about jazz, classical, metal, blues, pop, you name it. I think the truth is that all music is different and each genre has its own unique qualities. It may be that what makes a certain type of music sound similar to another is the fact that certain elements are shared between them. For example, both jazz and metal might have complex chord progressions, or both hip hop and pop might have catchy melodies. If you don't understand a particular genre of music, it's worth exploring it further to get to the heart of what makes it special. Listen to as many artists as possible in that genre and try to identify the common threads between them. Pay attention to the rhythm, the instruments used, the vocal delivery, and the lyrics. If you can find something unique about the music, it will become easier to appreciate it and understand why others do as well.

This is a device where you place a given mass of food eg 100 grams, and combust it completely in the presence of excess oxygen in a sealed container known as a bomb. The heat of combustion (in calories or joules) can then be calculated using the mass of the food and the temperature rise of the water. This process is known as bomb calorimetry and is used to determine the caloric content of foods, which can be used to estimate the amount of energy a person can obtain from consuming them.

New research has revealed that male seahorses have a unique way of incubating their young - by growing their own placentas. Previously thought to be a responsibility solely for female animals, the male seahorse has long been known to carry and give birth to their offspring. However, how they kept their young alive inside them was unknown until now. Scientists at the Oceanographic Institute in Monaco have discovered that male seahorses grow placentas - an organ that passes nutrients and oxygen from the mother to her developing fetus - to nourish their young inside their brood pouches. The researchers used a combination of high-resolution microscopes and computer models to study the seahorses' placental structures. It was found that the males' placentas grow in a similar way to those in humans, mice, and other mammals. Lead researcher, Dr. Vincent Savolainen, said: "This is a remarkable evolutionary adaptation. We found that male seahorses have the ability to grow complex placental structures that are much more developed than those seen in other fish species." The scientists believe that the male seahorses developed this adaptation because their brood pouches don't provide enough nutrients and oxygen to sustain their growing embryos. The placentas enable the fathers to provide a more supportive environment for their offspring. Dr. Savolainen added: "This discovery gives us new insights into how males can sustain the growth and survival of their offspring. It's a fascinating example of a father taking on responsibilities that were once thought to belong only to mothers." The study, published in the journal Nature, sheds new light on the evolution of pregnancy in animals and could also have implications for medical research on placentas in humans.
