Imperialism is defined as "A policy of extending a country's power and influence through diplomacy or military force." Imperialism is particularly focused on the control that one group, often a nation, has over another group or region. Imperialism is often used to gain access to natural resources, create larger markets for goods and services, increase political power, or spread a particular cultural or ideological influence. Imperialism has been used to control territories since ancient times, but it has become increasingly prevalent since the Age of Discovery in the 15th century. Imperialism has often been associated with colonialism, which is when an imperial power establishes settlements and political control in an area. This can involve the exploitation of the people and resources in the area, as well as the imposition of the imperial power's culture and language. Imperialism can also refer to the unequal economic relationships that exist between nations, with wealthier countries exploiting poorer ones. Imperialism has had both positive and negative effects on the world, depending on the context. On one hand, imperialism can lead to the spread of technology, healthcare, and education; on the other, it can be exploitative and oppressive.

Apple has announced a recall of certain 15-inch MacBook Pro laptops due to an issue with the battery. It's said that the batteries in these models can overheat, posing a potential fire risk. The recall affects 15-inch MacBook Pros sold primarily between September 2015 and February 2017. Affected users should stop using their laptops immediately and contact Apple for a free replacement battery. The company says it is aware of no incidents related to this issue, however, and that the recall is being conducted out of an abundance of caution. "Customer safety is always Apple's top priority, and we have voluntarily decided to replace affected batteries, free of charge," Apple said in a statement. "We encourage customers to visit an Apple Store or Apple Authorised Service Provider to have their battery replaced." Apple also noted that some MacBook Pro owners may be eligible for a free repair if their laptop has any other damage caused by the battery issue. This isn't the first time Apple has recalled a laptop due to a battery issue. In 2006, the company recalled 1.8 million iBook G4 and PowerBook G4 laptops due to a similar issue. For more information or assistance, users can contact Apple Support via phone or online chat.

There are several reasons why there are so few ancient human remains. One of the main reasons is that most human bodies decay rapidly after death, and so few bones survive long enough to become fossilized. Additionally, ancient humans did not typically bury their dead, which means that any remains that have been found are usually in areas where natural processes such as floods or landslides have exposed them. Lastly, archaeological sites often contain many artifacts, but few human remains, since ancient cultures rarely left behind physical evidence of their existence.

Despite being the standard loss function to train multi-class neural networks, the log-softmax has two potential limitations. First, it involves computations that scale linearly with the number of output classes, which can become computationally expensive as the number of classes increases. Second, the log-softmax function is sensitive to outliers, which can misrepresent the loss function and degrade model performance. To address these limitations, some alternatives to the log-softmax function have been proposed, such as the focal loss function, which down-weights the contribution of easy examples, and the sparsemax function, which encourages sparsity in the predicted probabilities. Other approaches include the hierarchical softmax and adaptive softmax, which reduce the computational cost of computing the loss function in large output spaces.

We consider convergence in the first k moments of the graph spectrum There are several ways to approximate sparse graphs and sequences of sparse graphs. One popular method is the so-called "graphon" approach, which represents a dense graph as a measurable function on [0,1]2. This can be used to construct a sequence of sparse graphs that converges to a dense graph in a certain sense. More specifically, given a sequence of sparse graphs Gn with n vertices and average degree dn, we can construct a graphon W such that the sequence of random graphs generated by sampling W and keeping edges with probability dnn converges in expectation to Gn. This convergence is in the sense of the first k moments of the graph spectrum, where the kth moment is the sum of the kth powers of the eigenvalues of the graph Laplacian. The graphon approach also allows for efficient calculation of various graph properties, such as the clustering coefficient and the number of triangles, as they can be expressed as integrals of the graphon.

We consider a wireless distributed computing system, in which multiple mobile users, connected wirelessly through an access point, collaborate to perform a computation task. In particular, users communicate with each other wirelessly in order to exchange the information required for their collaboration. For example, a distributed sorting task can be performed by mobile users following a shared protocol that involves local computations and data exchanges. The system may be under resource constraints, such as limited energy or bandwidth, which pose challenges on the design of an efficient communication mechanism. The communication mechanism itself may be a computation task that is mutually dependent on the actual computational tasks that the users perform. In this paper, we address these problems in the context of distributed computation over wireless communication networks. We propose a novel scheme that combines wireless networking with distributed computing techniques in order to allow users to efficiently collaborate in performing a given computation task. Our scheme is based on the use of coding theory to enable communication among users without the need for a central entity. The proposed scheme is scalable and may be used to perform a variety of computation tasks under different resource constraints. We assume a wireless distributed computing system consisting of n users, connected wirelessly through an access point. The users communicate with each other in order to exchange the information required for their collaboration. We consider a general class of computation tasks, which we call distributed applications, that can be performed by the users in the system. A distributed application is a collection of sub-tasks, each of which is executed by a subset of users in the system. In order to execute a sub-task, the participating users need to exchange information with each other. We assume that the users are equipped with energy-constrained devices, such as sensors or mobile phones. The devices may have limited energy resources, which need to be carefully managed in order to prolong their lifetime. We also assume that the devices are capable of wireless communication, and that they can be turned on and off in order to conserve energy. We propose a novel scheme for distributed computation over wireless communication networks, which we call coded distributed computing. In our scheme, the users cooperate in order to compute a function of their inputs, while taking into account the energy constraints of their devices. The scheme is based on the use of coding theory to enable communication among the users without the need for a central entity. The proposed scheme is scalable and may be used to perform a variety of computation tasks under different resource constraints. Our scheme has several advantages over existing schemes for distributed computation. First, our scheme is energy-efficient, as it minimizes the number of times that the devices need to be turned on. Second, our scheme is scalable, as it does not require a central entity to manage the communication among the users. Third, our scheme is robust to communication failures, as the coding theory used in our scheme allows the users to recover from communication errors. We illustrate the use of our scheme with two examples. In the first example, we consider the problem of distributed sorting, in which the users need to sort a sequence of numbers using only local comparisons. We show that our scheme can be used to solve this problem with a significantly smaller number of comparisons than the best known scheme for distributed sorting. In the second example, we consider the problem of distributed matrix multiplication, in which the users need to multiply two matrices using only local operations. We show that our scheme can be used to solve this problem with a significantly smaller number of operations than the best known scheme for distributed matrix multiplication.

Finally, the expected return for a state-action pair is computed by taking the expectation over the probability distribution. This approach has several advantages over traditional TD learning. Reactive oxygen species, such as superoxide ion (O- 2) and hydrogen peroxide (H 2O 2), are dangerous by-products of oxygen use in organisms. Parts of the immune system of higher organisms use these reactive oxygen species to kill invading microorganisms. Superoxide ion (O 2 is a molecule that contains an oxygen atom with an extra electron and is thus highly reactive. Hydrogen peroxide (H 2O 2) is produced by the addition of an oxygen atom to water (H 2O). It is also very reactive, although not as reactive as superoxide ion. Reactive oxygen species are powerful oxidizing agents that can damage cells and DNA. They can cause mutations that lead to cancer and other diseases. The body produces enzymes that detoxify reactive oxygen species. These enzymes include superoxide dismutase and catalase.

I'm not sure when it started happening, but I can tell you when I first noticed. I was in high school. A song came on the radio-my good friend and I were driving in my car, and we were both singing along with it. It was a song by the group Queen called "Bohemian Rhapsody." We both knew all the words, and we were belting them out at the top of our lungs. But then something strange happened. The words to the song started to change. They became gibberish. My friend and I looked at each other in confusion, and then we both started laughing. We thought it was just a funny coincidence-maybe we had misheard the lyrics. But then it happened again. With another song. And then another. We realized that the lyrics to songs were randomly changing for us. Sometimes they would be completely different words, and other times they would just be slightly off. But it was always enough to throw off the whole song. We started to notice that it wasn't just songs on the radio. Songs on our CDs would do it too. And then we realized that it wasn't just music. Movies would do it too. We would be watching a movie, and the dialogue would suddenly change. At first, we thought it was just us. But then we started talking to other people, and we realized that they were having the same experience. We would all be talking about a movie or a song, and we would all remember the dialogue or lyrics differently. It's been happening for years now, and we still don't know what's causing it. We've tried everything we can think of to figure it out, but nothing has worked. We've even gone to doctors, but they can't find anything wrong with us. It's like our brains are randomly changing the words to things. And we have no idea why.

The big day has arrived. Here's what you need to know about the general election. What happens when I vote? You'll be asked for your name and address, then given a ballot paper with the names of all the candidates in your constituency. Take your ballot paper into a polling booth, read the instructions and mark an X in the box next to the name of the candidate you want to vote for. Once you've made your choice, fold your ballot paper in half, so that you can't see who you've voted for and put it in the ballot box. Do I have to vote? Voting is not compulsory but if you don't vote anyone can ask why. Just tell them you don't have to give a reason. In some cases, people are fined 50 if they don't show up at the polls. Where do I vote? Check your voter registration card or contact your local authority to find out where your nearest polling station is. Find your local authority's website here. When do I vote? Polling stations will be open from 07:00 BST to 22:00 BST on 7 May. You only have to be over 18 to vote in this country, and you must have completed your application by 20 April. You can also register to vote by post, although you will need to apply by 5pm on 21 April. Or you can register as an emergency voter up until 5pm on election day. How does the voting system work? The UK uses the "first past the post" system for its general elections. This means the person with the most votes wins the seat, regardless of whether they actually have a majority of all the people who voted. For example, a candidate could get 30 of the total number of votes cast, but still win the seat because there was no clear winner between the other candidates. What's happening in Scotland? Scotland has 59 MPs, which means about one MP for every 84,000 people. That's more than anywhere else in the UK. Scottish voters will be able to choose from a list of candidates from each of their local political parties. But there's also a new party - SNP - which doesn't stand anywhere else in the UK. Scots will also be able to vote for independent candidates. During the last general election, the main parties were Labour, Tories and Lib Dems. What's happening elsewhere in the UK? England and Wales each have 650 MPs, and Northern Ireland has 18. People in Northern Ireland use a different system to the rest of the UK. Snap, the parent company of social media platform Snapchat, announced on Friday that it has acquired a brain-computer interface startup called MindMeld for an undisclosed amount. The acquisition comes as Snap eyes the future of augmented reality (AR) technology and its potential to revolutionize the way we interact with our devices. MindMeld, founded in 2016 by a group of neuroscientists and engineers, focuses on developing hardware and software that allows users to control technology through their thoughts. The technology involves placing a wearable device on a user's head that reads their brain signals and translates them into commands for a computer. Snap is no stranger to AR technology, having launched its AR-powered Spectacles smart glasses in 2016. The company has since been exploring ways to integrate AR into its core platform as well as potential new products. The acquisition of MindMeld could provide valuable technology and expertise to help achieve these goals. According to Snap, the MindMeld team will join its hardware division, helping to develop future AR glasses and other wearable devices. Snap CEO Evan Spiegel said in a statement that the team's "deep technical expertise and capabilities" would be a "critical component" in the company's ongoing efforts to build "a hardware platform where computing is always with you." MindMeld co-founder and CEO John Doe said in a blog post that joining Snap was "an incredible opportunity" to take their technology to the next level. "We're excited to work with a company that shares our vision for how AR glasses can unlock entirely new forms of human interaction with technology," Doe said. The acquisition follows Snap's announcement last year that it was working on a new version of its Spectacles glasses, which is expected to have improved AR capabilities. The company has not yet provided a release date for the new product, but the acquisition of MindMeld is a clear indication that Snap is serious about advancing the technology. As the market for AR glasses continues to grow, Snap's move to acquire MindMeld could give it a significant edge over competitors. With a team of neuroscientists and engineers on board, the company is well-positioned to develop groundbreaking new technology that could change the way we interact with the world.

The American CryptoFed DAO (decentralized autonomous organization) is the first legally recognized DAO in the US. It is based on the EOS protocol instead of Ethereum, the cryptocurrency most commonly used in blockchain-based platforms. The group's goal is to create a decentralized network of organizations that can share resources, best practices and expertise around digital currencies and blockchain technology. "There are a lot of different things that we can do with the DAO that we couldn't do before," said CryptoFed president and co-founder Thomas Carter. "We can pool resources, we can have a shared budget, we can have shared governance and we can have shared decision-making." The group plans to use the EOS blockchain to create a decentralized marketplace for digital currency and blockchain-based services. The marketplace will allow users to buy and sell services, as well as to find and connect with other like-minded individuals and organizations. "The idea is to create a one-stop shop for anything related to digital currency or blockchain technology," said Carter. The group is also working on a project to create a decentralized stock exchange. "We want to create a platform where people can trade stocks, bonds, and other assets in a completely decentralized way," said Carter. The group is currently in the process of raising funds to launch the stock exchange. The American CryptoFed DAO is not the only group working on a decentralized marketplace. The decentralized marketplace OpenBazaar is already operational and allows users to buy and sell a variety of goods and services. The group is also planning to launch a decentralized marketplace for digital assets. "There's a lot of interest in this space, and we think that there's a lot of potential for this type of marketplace," said Carter.

While constitutional law concerns the European Union's governance structure, administrative law binds EU institutions and member states to follow the law. Both member states and the Commission have a general duty to abide by the EU's constitutional principles and values, as set out in the Treaties. Administrative law is a body of law that governs how the European Union (EU) institutions and member states implement EU laws and regulations, including those related to the internal market, environment, health and safety, competition, intellectual property, public procurement, and other areas. Administrative law also applies when the EU interacts with citizens and businesses, such as through hearings, administrative review, and dispute resolution mechanisms. This body of law also includes rules and principles to ensure fair decision-making, such as proportionality and legal certainty, as well as remedies for violations of fundamental rights. Constitutional law, on the other hand, sets out the overall framework for the governance structure of the EU and its institutions. This includes the powers of the European Council, the European Commission, the European Parliament, and the Court of Justice of the European Union, as well as the treaties and other instruments that form the basis of the EU's legal order. Constitutional law also encompasses fundamental rights, such as the freedom of movement and equality before the law, as enshrined in the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union.

Kent Police has spoken out against vigilante groups who take it upon themselves to expose and punish paedophiles in their communities. The police force has called for these groups to stop taking the law into their own hands and allow law enforcement to handle these sensitive and complex cases. Vigilante groups have been on the rise across the UK in recent years, with members using social media to conduct sting operations and publicly shame alleged paedophiles. However, Kent Police has warned that this approach can do more harm than good, citing concerns over potential vigilantism, the safety of both victims and suspects, and a lack of due process. Superintendent Andrew Gwyther, from the Kent Police, said: "While we understand the very real concerns these groups have about protecting children, we would strongly advise them not to take matters into their own hands." The police force emphasised that exposing a suspected paedophile can actually impede an official investigation, and could even lead to the case being compromised in court. Vigilante groups may use tactics that could harm the accused or even the victim, potentially putting their safety at risk. Furthermore, members of these groups may not fully understand the complex legal procedures and the importance of preserving evidence in cases of child abuse. They may also lack expertise in properly handling sensitive information and communicating with victims. Instead, Kent Police has encouraged people to report any concerns they have about child protection issues through official channels, such as reporting to the police, local authority or the National Crime Agency (NCA). The NCA has a dedicated CEOP (Child Exploitation and Online Protection) Command that specialises in investigating online child exploitation. In conclusion, while it is understandable that people want to protect children, taking the law into their own hands raises serious concerns around safety, privacy and due process. The police are there to investigate crime and bring offenders to justice, and official channels should be used to report any illegal activity. Kent Police's message to vigilante groups is clear - if you suspect someone of child abuse, leave it to the professionals to investigate.

According to scholars Walter Kramer, Gotz Trenkler, Gerhard Ritter, and Gerhard Prause, the story of the posting on the door, even though it has settled as one of the pillars of the Luther myth, is not historically accurate. The door of the Schlosskirche in Wittenberg was not used as a bulletin board for announcements and publication of papal bulls at the time. Furthermore, there is no other evidence to support the story. It is first recorded after nearly a century, in 1704, by Anton Wilhelm Balthasar in his workLutheri Opera Omnia. Balthasar says that he had heard the story from the lips of a son of Philip Melanchthon who had heard it from one of his father's students. Kramer argues that it is highly unlikely that a student would witness such an event, since Luther's postings were intended for the Wittenberg community and therefore not accessible to students. Kramer further argues that if such a posting occurred, it is highly likely that Luther would have mentioned it in some way in his writings, as he did of all of his actions or movements that he considered significant. Kramer concludes that the story is most likely a legend that arose out of the celebration of the Reformation around 1700. The earliest reference to this event is found in the 1566 collection of Latin sermons preached during Lent by Melchior Adam , which contains a sermon entitled "De Postulatione Theses" (On the Posting of the Theses). Adam relates a story of how Luther became so infuriated with a papal bull that he posted his 95 Theses on the door of the church. In the years that followed, Adam's story was repeated by several others, including two contemporaries of Luther, Johann Bugenhagen and Mathesius, who related the story in their sermons.

Internal bleeding occurs when blood vessels inside the body are damaged and begin to leak blood into the surrounding tissues or spaces within the body. This can occur from trauma such as a high-impact collision or blunt force injury, as well as from medical conditions such as ulcers, cancer, or blood vessel disorders. Symptoms of internal bleeding may include abdominal pain, dizziness or weakness, bruising or swelling, and black tarry stools or bloody vomit. If you suspect you are experiencing internal bleeding, it is important to seek medical attention immediately as it can quickly become life-threatening if left untreated.

Before I start, I think it's important to point out that I am certainly biased. I am a vegetarian who will soon be getting a kitchen and going vegan. I'm an animal lover who has had some experience with animal husbandry (goats, chickens, ducks and rabbits) but would not consider myself an expert. I have also read a lot of books and articles on animal welfare, including those that support factory farming, vegetarianism and veganism. With that out of the way, let's get started! The Argument For Factory Farming Factory farming is a controversial topic, but there are some arguments in favor of it. One argument is that it is more efficient than traditional farming. This means that more food can be produced with fewer resources, which is important in a world with a growing population. Another argument is that factory farms are necessary to produce cheap food. This is important because many people cannot afford to buy more expensive, humanely raised food. Finally, some people argue that animals raised on factory farms are not treated any worse than animals in the wild. They point out that animals in the wild often suffer from disease, starvation, and predation. The Argument Against Factory Farming There are also many arguments against factory farming. One argument is that animals raised on factory farms are often treated very poorly. They may be confined to small spaces, given little to no access to sunlight or fresh air, and fed an unnatural diet. Another argument is that factory farming is bad for the environment. The large amount of waste produced by factory farms can pollute air and water, and the overuse of antibiotics can lead to antibiotic resistance. Finally, some people argue that factory farming is unethical because it involves exploiting animals for human benefit. Animals raised on factory farms are seen as nothing more than commodities, and they often suffer greatly as a result.

But perhaps the most important factor behind TikTok's addictive feed is the app's ability to trigger emotions. TikTok's videos are often funny, uplifting, and emotionally engaging. This emotional resonance keeps users coming back for more, eager to discover the latest viral trend or challenge. Overall, TikTok's addictive feed is the result of a carefully crafted algorithm and emotional engagement, creating a powerful synergy that keeps users hooked. Those are noms de guerre - assumed names taken by fighters. Especially for foreigners joining up, it's symbolic of leaving one's old name behind and joining the cause. Abu means 'father of' and is often used for the first-born son. What's more, these are not just names taken by Kurdish fighters in Syria - they're also used by Iraqi Kurds fighting ISIS across the border. Abu Bakir and Abu Muhammad aren't alone in using this nomenclature. Many other foreign fighters have assumed similar names. Michael Enright of Canada goes by "Abu Khaled." He's a former CBC radio host who joined up with the YPG in 2015. He says he was inspired to join up after hearing about the brutal treatment at the hands of ISIS of a young woman named Nadia Murad Basee Taha. She later won the Nobel Peace Prize for her work highlighting the plight of Yazidi women and girls caught up in ISIS territory. Jesse Mortensen from New Zealand uses the name Abu Bakr Al-Siddiq. Photo Credit: Facebook A New Zealander named Jesse Mortensen is known as Abu Bakr Al-Siddiq. He has been photographed wearing military fatigues and carrying an AK47 assault rifle. The BBC reported that another foreigner going by the alias "Abu Issa" is actually an American veteran of Iraq. His real name hasn't been revealed. It's not unusual for Kurdish fighters to give themselves aliases. But it's rarer for foreigners to go down this route. Many use their nom de guerre on social media accounts and posts. They are often public figures, sharing stories of their time on the frontlines. They pose with guns and often dress in uniform. Some take selfies in front of tanks and armoured vehicles. Some post pictures of themselves on social media with fellow fighters, both men and women. Michael Enright (left) is known by his nom de guerre "Abu Khaled." Photo Credit: Facebook Enright told the CBC earlier this year that when he first arrived at the training camp in northern Syria, he had some second thoughts. "I'm really nervous, I'm really scared," he said. "I don't know if this is the right thing to do." But he says he eventually made friends. "They're absolutely incredible people. They are very warm, they're good people," he said. Enright also said he felt compelled to help the fight against ISIS because of what happened to the Yazidis. "This is something I could do. I'm a 54-year-old man," he said. "I can still hold a gun."

I was too scared to sleep with the lights off in case it came back and I woke up to see its face right next to mine. I had a small lamp on my bedside table that I used to read books under at night, but even that felt too bright now. I had no desire to read or do anything except sit in the darkness and think about what I had seen. I knew I should go to the police, but I was scared that they wouldn't believe me. They would think I was crazy and lock me up. I didn't want to be locked up, I wanted to be out here where I could keep an eye on my room and make sure the thing didn't come back. I was so lost in thought that I didn't even hear the door open. It wasn't until I felt someone sit down on the bed next to me that I jumped. "Jesus Christ!" I shouted as I turned to see who it was. It was my best friend Alex. He looked tired and worried, like he hadn't slept in days. "What are you doing here?" I asked him. "How did you even get in?" "Your mom let me in," he said. "She's worried about you." "She should be," I muttered. "What happened?" he asked. "You've been in here for days." I hesitated for a moment, not sure if I wanted to tell him. But then I realized that I needed to tell someone. I couldn't keep it bottled up inside anymore. "I saw something," I said. "In my room." "What did you see?" "A monster," I whispered. "It was huge and had these long claws. It just appeared out of nowhere." Alex was quiet for a moment as he processed what I had said. "Did you tell your mom?" he asked. I shook my head. "I was too scared. I don't want her to think I'm crazy." "You're not crazy," he said. "I believe you." I felt a wave of relief wash over me. It was good to finally tell someone. "What are we going to do?" I asked him. "We'll figure something out," he said. "But first, you need to get out of this room." I nodded and slowly got to my feet. My whole body felt stiff from sitting in the same position for so long. Alex walked with me as I made my way downstairs. My mom was in the kitchen and she looked relieved to see me. "Oh, thank God," she said. "I was starting to worry about you." "I'm fine," I said. "I just needed some time to think." "Well, you can't stay locked in your room forever," she said. "It's not healthy." "I know," I said. "I'm sorry." "It's okay," she said as she hugged me. "I'm just glad you're okay." "I'm going to go home now," Alex said. "I'll talk to you later, okay?" "Okay," I said. I watched him leave before turning to my mom. "I'm going to take a shower," I said. "Good idea," she said. "You look like you could use one." I went upstairs and got into the shower. The hot water felt good against my skin. I stood there for a long time, letting the water wash over me. Eventually, I got out and got dressed. I looked in the mirror and saw that I looked better than I had in days. My eyes were no longer red and puffy from crying and I had color in my cheeks again. I went downstairs and found my mom in the kitchen. "Feeling better?" she asked. "Yeah," I said. "I think I am." "Good," she said. "Now let's go get some dinner, I'm starving." I smiled and followed her out of the house. I knew things weren't going to be the same as they were before, but I was determined to face whatever was out there. With my mom by my side, I knew I could handle anything.

Reactive oxygen species, such as superoxide ion (O- 2) and hydrogen peroxide (H 2O 2), are dangerous by-products of oxygen use in organisms. Parts of the immune system of higher organisms produce reactive oxygen species to kill invading pathogens. However, excessive or uncontrolled production of these molecules can damage cell structures, including DNA, proteins and phospholipid membranes, and lead to cell death or tissue damage. To counteract the harmful effects of reactive oxygen species, organisms have evolved antioxidant systems that scavenge these molecules and prevent their accumulation. These systems can involve enzymes, such as superoxide dismutase and catalase, that convert reactive oxygen species to less harmful compounds, as well as small molecules, such as glutathione and vitamin C, that can directly react with them and neutralize their reactivity. Knowing the balance between reactive oxygen species and antioxidant defenses is important for understanding many biological processes, such as aging, cancer, and inflammation.

Introduction In this paper we present a novel approach to the problem of emotion and behavior generation for real-time autonomous robotic systems. The working metaphor we use is the principle of "perceived affordance," and specifically the notion of perceiving affordances based on motor program generation. We argue that such an approach is able to automatically generate and adapt behavior in response to changes in the environment, with minimal computational requirements. Additionally, we discuss how this approach can be integrated into a robotic architecture and outline some applications of the proposed system. The concept of affordance was originally introduced by James Gibson (1979) to refer to the relationship between an object and an animal's ability to interact with that object. For example, a chair affords sitting, and a handle affords grasping. The term has since been used in a variety of disciplines, including psychology, sociology, anthropology, and philosophy. In recent years, the concept of affordance has been increasingly applied to artificial agents, including robots (e.g., Kober et al., 2010; Fong et al., 2003). There are two main approaches to implementing affordances in artificial agents. The first is based on pre-specified rules or heuristics. For example, a rule-based system might be designed such that if an object is within reach and is the same color as the agent, the agent will attempt to grasp the object. The second approach is to learn the affordances of objects from experience. For example, an agent might learn that objects that can be grasped are typically within reach and have a certain shape. The approach we propose in this paper is based on the second approach, but with a twist. Instead of learning the affordances of objects from experience, we propose that the agent should learn the affordances of objects by generating motor programs. That is, the agent should generate programs that describe how to interact with objects, and then use these programs to determine what the objects afford. There are several advantages to this approach. First, it is computationally efficient. Generating a motor program requires far less computation than learning the affordances of an object from experience. Second, it is more flexible than rule-based systems. Motor programs can be generated on the fly in response to changes in the environment, without the need for pre-specified rules. Third, motor programs can be adapted to the specific capabilities of the agent. For example, if an agent is unable to grasp an object, it can generate a different motor program that avoids grasping the object. The key idea behind our approach is that emotions and behaviors are best understood as emergent phenomena, arising from the interactions between an agent and its environment. We believe that this view is consistent with current neuroscientific evidence, which suggests that emotions and behaviors are generated by subcortical structures, such as the amygdala and the basal ganglia (LeDoux, 1996; Damasio, 1994). These structures are not capable of symbolic reasoning or complex decision-making. Rather, they are specialized for processing sensory information and generating simple motor programs. We argue that the principles of perceived affordance can be used to develop a neurobiologically plausible model of emotion and behavior generation. In particular, we propose that an agent should generate motor programs in response to changes in the environment, and that these programs should be used to determine the affordances of objects. This approach has a number of advantages over existing approaches. First, it is computationally efficient. Second, it is more flexible than rule-based systems. Third, it is more biologically plausible than models that rely on symbolic reasoning or complex decision-making. Applications The approach we propose in this paper can be used to develop a variety of robotic applications, including domestic robots, assistive robots, and industrial robots. Domestic robots are typically designed to perform tasks such as cleaning, cooking, and laundry. Assistive robots are designed to provide assistance to people with disabilities. Industrial robots are typically used in manufacturing and assembly tasks. Our approach can be used to develop robots for all of these applications. In a bid to preserve the ancient structure of the Ponte Milvio bridge in Rome, authorities have begun to remove thousands of so-called "love padlocks" affixed to its railings. The practice of attaching padlocks, also known as "love locks," to bridges and other public structures as a symbol of love and commitment has become a global trend in recent years, with couples flocking to the Ponte Milvio bridge in their droves to add their own locks. However, experts have raised concerns about the safety of the Ponte Milvio bridge, which was built in the 3rd century AD and has been subjected to centuries of wear and tear. The weight of the thousands of padlocks is said to be contributing to the bridge's structural decay, and officials have warned that if left unchecked, the locks could cause irreparable damage to the ancient monument. To tackle the issue, authorities have taken the drastic step of removing the locks with bolt cutters. As of yet, it is unclear what will happen to the padlocks once they have been removed. Some options being considered include recycling them or displaying them in a museum, although others argue that this would only encourage more people to continue attaching locks to the bridge. The removal of the locks has sparked a heated debate among locals and tourists alike. While some have argued for the preservation of the bridge's historical importance, others have lamented the loss of a romantic tradition that they believe added to the charm of the city. It's not just the Ponte Milvio bridge that has been affected by the scourge of love locks, however. Similar practices have caused damage to structures throughout the world, from the Brooklyn Bridge in New York to the Hohenzollern Bridge in Cologne, Germany. In the face of growing concerns, some cities have taken action to ban the practice altogether, with officials in Paris removing over a million padlocks from the Pont des Arts bridge in 2015. While some may argue that the removal of love locks is an attack on a romantic tradition, it is ultimately essential that we take steps to protect our heritage and ensure that it is preserved for future generations.

Asda, one of the UK's largest supermarkets, has been forced to admit that a flaw in its website allowed hackers to access customers' personal information and payment details. The BBC has learned that a vulnerability was discovered on the Asda website earlier this week, giving malicious actors the chance to collect sensitive data such as names, addresses and credit card numbers. It is believed that the incident occurred due to a fault in the website's coding which allowed certain types of requests to be submitted directly to the server, bypassing the usual security checks. The company has since taken steps to fix the issue and has said it is working with law enforcement agencies to investigate the breach. "We take the safety of our customers' data very seriously," said Mark Fox, Head of IT Security at Asda. "We are working closely with our security teams to ensure we have the best possible protection for our customers." Asda has urged customers to be vigilant when using the website and to monitor their accounts for any suspicious activity. It has also warned customers to be aware of potential phishing emails or calls claiming to be from the supermarket asking for personal or financial information. The incident is yet another reminder of the dangers posed by cyber criminals, who can often exploit vulnerabilities in websites and systems to gain access to confidential customer data. It is essential that companies take all necessary steps to protect customer information, and that they remain vigilant to the ever-changing threats posed by hackers.

In a recent interview with BBC News, the UK's former senior military adviser in the Middle East, Lt Gen Sir Simon Mayall, called Russia's intervention in Syria "hugely significant." Mayall praised the Russian military for its effectiveness in targeting ISIS and other extremist groups in Syria, something he claims the US-led coalition has been unable to do. Mayall stated that Russia's involvement has enabled Syrian government forces to regain control of key territories, including Aleppo, which was previously held by rebels for years. He also noted that Russian air support has been crucial in turning the tide of the six-year-long Syrian conflict in favor of the regime of President Bashar al-Assad. While acknowledging concerns about Russia's motives in Syria, Mayall argued that Moscow's efforts in the region are largely aimed at countering the West's influence in the Middle East. He noted that Syria has long been a priority for Moscow due to its strategic location and close ties to Russia's traditional allies in the region. Mayall's comments come amid renewed debate over the role of foreign powers in the Syrian conflict. The US, UK, and other Western powers have been critical of Russia's actions, accusing Moscow of supporting President Assad's brutal crackdown on his own people. However, Russia has consistently denied these accusations and accused Western governments of exaggerating the regime's abuses. Despite the controversy surrounding its involvement in Syria, Russia's military intervention has had a significant impact on the ground. As Lt Gen Sir Simon Mayall notes, the Russian military has been highly effective in targeting ISIS and other extremist groups in the region, helping to bring an end to the deadly conflict that has ravaged Syria for years.

While some people may argue that getting a tattoo inspired by a culture that is not their own is not necessarily immoral and that they are simply appreciating and embracing a culture they find intriguing, it fails to consider the power dynamic and historical context behind cultural appropriation. The appropriation of cultural symbols and practices with a lack of understanding of the culture's significance can be seen as a form of disrespect and disregard for the struggles and experiences of those within the culture. Furthermore, the process of cultural appropriation often involves taking something that has spiritual, cultural, or historical significance from a group of people who have either struggled or are currently struggling for visibility, recognition and respect. The act of wearing these symbols without permission can come across as insensitive, and a lack of sensitivity towards certain cultures or practices can inadvertently reinforce racist attitudes and biases. Therefore, cultural appropriation through a personal tattoo can be seen as immoral and shows a lack of understanding of and respect for cultural differences.

However, the deal was not signed because of a dispute over how the shutdown would be verified. North Korea had earlier refused to honour a deal reached in 1994 under which it agreed to close the Yongbyon nuclear facility in exchange for two lightwater reactors and heavy oil supplies. The US has also been pressing North Korea to declare all its nuclear facilities and allow international inspectors access to them. US National Security Adviser Condoleezza Rice said Washington would have no responsibility for North Korea's fate if it did not give up its nuclear weapons. "If they continue on their present course, the regime is doomed," she told Fox News. "We're not going to be responsible for the collapse of the North Korean regime." I never thought I would be having this conversation with my grandpa. He had always been my role model and the kindest person I had ever known. But three months ago, the doctors gave him the news that he had cancer and had only three months to live. As we sat in the hospital room, he asked me for a favor - his last wish, he said. He leaned in closer and whispered into my ear, "I need to confess something to you." I was confused, to say the least. "What is it, Grandpa?" I asked. "I am the infamous serial killer, Hannibal Lecter." I was stunned. I didn't know what to say or how to react. But as he started to tell me his story, I couldn't help but feel a sense of admiration towards him. Grandpa had been killing for years, but he always had a strict code of ethics. He only killed the people who he believed deserved it - criminals, rapists, murderers, and the like. He never killed for personal gain or pleasure; he believed that he was doing the world a service by taking out these dangerous individuals. As he finished his confession, he looked at me with tears in his eyes. "I know you have the same inclinations, my dear," he said. "But I want you to promise me that you will never kill for the wrong reasons. Always uphold the code." I nodded, tears streaming down my own face. "I promise, Grandpa." And with that, he passed away peacefully a few weeks later. I was left with the burden of his secret, but also with the knowledge that he had lived by a strict moral code and only did what he believed was right. I would always remember him as the best grandpa I could have ever asked for, and as a true inspiration.

It was long thought that the formation, which is located in the heart of Wiltshire's ancient landscape, was a circular stone circle dating back to the Neolithic period. However, after conducting a detailed laser scan of the stone formation, the researchers were surprised to find that the formation was actually a square. The discovery was made within the world-famous Avebury Neolithic complex, which is believed to have been constructed over 4,500 years ago. The complex consists of three stone circles, the largest of which is over 300 feet in diameter. The square formation is located within the South Inner Circle. "The discovery of a square formation within a stone circle is extremely unusual," said Dr Mark Gillings, lead archaeologist on the project. "It's been known for some time that there are subtle deviations from an exact circle in some of the stones at Avebury, but to discover a square formation is quite remarkable." The discovery is also causing some to rethink the purpose and significance of the Avebury complex. "This discovery means that we need to rethink our understanding of the Avebury site," said Dr Joshua Pollard, a researcher on the project. "It's possible that this square formation had some kind of significant function within the complex that we don't yet understand." The researchers are now planning to conduct further investigation of the square formation to try and shed more light on its purpose and significance. But for now, the discovery is causing great excitement in the archaeological world and is set to spark renewed interest in the Avebury complex among researchers and the public alike.

Yes, there is a scientific reason behind it. The cuteness of babies is due to their physical features, such as large eyes, round face, and small size, which trigger our "cute response" and evoke positive emotions. This phenomenon is known as baby schema or kinderschema, and it is a set of facial and body features that are perceived as cute and trigger nurturing and protective behavior in adults. Studies have shown that the baby schema is present in many animal species, not just humans, and that it contributes to the survival of the offspring by eliciting caregiving behavior in elders. In addition, the release of oxytocin - the "cuddle hormone" - in response to the cuteness of babies, enhances our bonding and attachment with them, another crucial factor for their survival. Therefore, it is natural to assume that other animal species, including non-mammals, may have a similar response to the cuteness of their young, although the specific features that trigger this response may differ among species.

The notes he had left for himself were a reach of support from his past self, who knew he would try to erase the pain again. Jack understood that some memories should not be forgotten and that he needed to move forward with his life, acknowledging what had happened but not letting it control his future. Jack's story made people realize the power of memories, both good and bad. They understood that, while some memories were painful, they were a part of their life that shaped them. The 2007 Lisbon Treaty explicitly recognised fundamental rights by providing in Article 6 (1) that "The Union recognises the rights, freedoms and principles set out in the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union of 7 December 2000, as adapted at Strasbourg, on 12 December 2007, which shall have the same legal value as the Treaties." The Lisbon Treaty also provides that the European Court of Justice (ECJ) will have jurisdiction to interpret these rights if national authorities fail to protect them. This has a direct bearing on fundamental rights in Ireland because Article 51 of the Charter requires that Member States ensure effective judicial protection in relation to fundamental rights. The Irish Government sought to make an "opt out" from this provision and also from the requirement that the EU adopt a common immigration policy based on the recognition of fundamental rights and respect for fundamental rights and freedoms of non-EU nationals. The Irish people voted against the Lisbon Treaty in June 2008 and the Government then sought to negotiate changes to the treaty to allow a second referendum to take place. The ECHR, which was adopted in 1950, is administered by the Council of Europe. The ECHR was incorporated into Irish law by the European Convention on Human Rights Act 2003. The ECtHR operates as the final court of appeal for individuals who claim that their rights under the ECHR have been breached. If the national courts do not abide by the judgments of the ECtHR, the case may be referred to the Committee of Ministers of the Council of Europe, which has the power to impose sanctions on member states. The European Union has no formal legal relationship with the ECHR or the Council of Europe. However, the Lisbon Treaty provides that the EU should accede to the ECHR, which it has not yet done. At present, the EU is bound by the ECHR only insofar as all its member states have ratified the ECHR and the charter of fundamental rights. The European Social Charter was revised in 1996 and brought into force in 1999. They are a diverse phylum of bacteria capable of carrying out photosynthesis, which means they can make their own food using sunlight, carbon dioxide, and water. In a groundbreaking discovery, geneticists have detected a fourth ancestral "tribe" which contributed to the modern European gene pool. The research, published in the journal Nature, is based on analysis of the genomes of more than 1,000 Europeans and 200 ancient skeletons. The new findings suggest that the earliest Europeans had four distinct ancestries - three previously known tribes and one newly discovered one. Researchers believe this fourth ancestors were hunter-gatherers who lived in Europe during the Mesolithic period (approximately 10,000 to 5,000 years ago). The researchers found that the fourth ancestry was most common in some parts of Southern Europe, such as Spain and Italy. They also identified a common ancestor in the Caucasus region, which could be linked to the fourth tribe. "This fourth ancestry has likely been present in Europe since the beginning of the Neolithic period, but only now we are able to detect it," said Professor Iain Mathieson from Harvard Medical School, one of the study authors. The findings could help shed light on the history of human migration into Europe, and how different populations interacted with each other. They could also help explain why some diseases are more prevalent in certain populations, and even why some people respond differently to certain drugs. "Our results suggest that tracing the genetic legacy of these ancient hunter-gatherers will help us better understand human prehistory and medical genetics," said Dr. David Reich, another researcher involved in the study. Overall, the findings of this research are significant and could have a major impact on our understanding of European history and population genetics.

In this note we revisit a "ring of graphs" Q in which the set of finite simple graphs N extend the role of the natural numbers N and the signed integers Z in algebraic structures known as rings. Specifically, we define a binary operation called the "graph sum" and show that it gives rise to a commutative and associative operation on N, just like addition in Z. Furthermore, we demonstrate that each graph has an additive inverse, similar to negative numbers in Z, and that the operation satisfies other familiar properties such as the distributive law. To summarize, the "ring of graphs" is a way to view graphs as mathematical objects that have algebraic structure similar to conventional numbers. We also present an algorithm for dynamically selecting transmit antennas and frequency, which can reduce the distance between the transmitter and receiver and thus increase the power transfer efficiency. Finally, we experimentally verify our proposed WPT DAS architecture with multiple receivers, demonstrating that it can significantly improve WPT efficiency compared with the single-antenna-based system.

Beaker is a web browser that is being built from the ground up with simplicity and privacy in mind. The project is still in its early stages, but it already has a working prototype. Beaker is based on the Dat protocol, which is an open-source alternative to the HTTP protocol. This means that Beaker can be used to access websites that are not necessarily on the public internet. For example, Beaker can be used to access websites that are hosted on the decentralized network known as the Dat network. This makes Beaker ideal for browsing the so-called "dark web," which is a collection of websites that are not accessible through traditional web browsers. However, Beaker can also be used to access regular websites, including those that use HTTPS encryption. Beaker is still in development, but it shows promise as a privacy-focused web browser that could one day compete with the likes of Firefox and Chrome.

The fuzzy K -means problem is a generalization of the classical K -means problem to soft clusterings, i.e. clusterings where each points belongs to each cluster to some degree. Although the classical K -means problem is NP-hard, it has been shown that the fuzzy K -means problem can be solved efficiently in polynomial time. The fuzzy K -means problem is defined as follows: Given a set of n points S and an integer k , find a partition of S into k clusters such that the sum of the squared distances between each point and the centroid of its cluster is minimized. A solution to the fuzzy K -means problem is a partition of S into k clusters, where each cluster is defined by a set of points and a centroid. The centroid of a cluster is the average of all points in the cluster.

This paper deals with a complete bipartite matching problem with the objective of finding an optimal matching that maximizes a certain generic predefined utility function on the set of all possible matchings. In order to solve this problem, several algorithms have been proposed over the years, including the Hungarian algorithm, the Hopcroft-Karp algorithm, and the augmenting path algorithm. The Hungarian algorithm is a well-known algorithm that solves the bipartite matching problem in polynomial time. It works by starting with an empty matching and iteratively adding edges to the matching until a maximum matching is obtained. The algorithm uses a clever method called the Hungarian method to identify augmenting paths in the graph, which are paths alternating between matched and unmatched edges. The Hopcroft-Karp algorithm is another well-known algorithm that also solves the bipartite matching problem in polynomial time. It utilizes a breadth-first search approach to find augmenting paths in the graph. The algorithm performs a series of alternating breadth-first searches, starting at unmatched vertices in one bipartition and moving towards unmatched vertices in the other bipartition. The algorithm terminates when no more augmenting paths can be found. The augmenting path algorithm is an algorithm that also solves the bipartite matching problem in polynomial time. It works by finding augmenting paths in the graph and iteratively updating the matching until a maximum matching is obtained. The algorithm uses a technique called depth-first search to find augmenting paths in the graph. All of these algorithms have been proven to be efficient in solving the bipartite matching problem. The choice of algorithm depends on various factors, such as the size of the graph and the specific application.

This phenomenon is known as "anticipatory listening." Our brains are wired to recognize and anticipate patterns in sound, including those in music. When we listen to a melody, our brains try to predict the notes that will come next based on the patterns and structures that we have heard before. This process is subconscious and can happen even if we have never heard the specific melody before. It also depends on prior exposure to music, as the brain needs a certain level of familiarity with musical patterns and structures to make accurate predictions.

Some of the oldest schools in South Africa are private church schools that were established by missionaries in the early nineteenth century. The private sector has grown ever since. After the end of apartheid, the South African government aimed to provide equal educational opportunities to all citizens, regardless of race or socioeconomic status. As a result, the government invested heavily in expanding and improving public education. Today, the South African education system consists of three main tiers: primary education, secondary education, and tertiary education. Primary education, which is free and compulsory, lasts for seven years. Secondary education is divided into two phases: lower secondary (Grades 8 to 9) and upper secondary (Grades 10 to 12). The National Senior Certificate (NSC) examination is taken at the end of the 12th grade and is a requirement for university admission. Tertiary education in South Africa is offered by universities, colleges, and vocational schools. Some of the most prestigious universities in the country include the University of Cape Town, the University of Witwatersrand, and the University of Pretoria. Despite improvements in recent years, South Africa's education system still faces many challenges, including a shortage of qualified teachers, insufficient infrastructure, and low levels of academic achievement among many students. The government continues to work towards improving the system and providing equal educational opportunities for all South Africans.

Wales coach Warren Gatland hails Shane Williams' late try in their defeat by Australia as a fitting end to the player's career, marking the end of an era in Welsh rugby. Williams, one of the greatest Welsh rugby players of all time, had announced his retirement earlier this year, and the game against Australia was his final outing in a Welsh shirt. Despite Wales' 24-18 defeat, Williams was able to leave the field to a standing ovation from the crowd at the Millennium Stadium, having scored his 58th international try in the dying minutes of the game. Speaking after the match, Wales coach Warren Gatland praised Williams' contribution to Welsh rugby and acknowledged the significance of the moment. "Shane will always be remembered as one of the greatest Welsh players of all time, and his try today was a fitting end to a remarkable career. He has been a true professional on and off the field, and his influence on Welsh rugby over the years cannot be overstated." Williams, who won two Grand Slams with Wales and was a member of the British and Irish Lions squad in 2005 and 2009, expressed his gratitude to the Welsh fans for their support throughout his career. "It's been an incredible journey, and I've been fortunate enough to play with some fantastic players and alongside some great coaches. I would like to thank the Welsh fans for their incredible support over the years, and for making my last game in a Welsh shirt such a special occasion." As Williams bowed out of international rugby, many fans and pundits praised his skill, speed, and flair on the rugby field, and highlighted the impact he had on the game both in Wales and around the world. While Welsh rugby will undoubtedly miss his presence on the field, his legacy as one of the greatest players of all time will live on, inspiring future generations of Welsh rugby players and fans.

I woke up to find that all of Earth's populace had vanished. It was eerie, the silence that had replaced the hustle and bustle of daily life. I had no idea what had happened, but as I walked around, I noticed that everything seemed untouched. It was like people had disappeared into thin air. As I was wandering around trying to make sense of things, I suddenly found myself in front of a group of beings that looked nothing like anything I had ever seen. They called themselves the Earth's guardians and they explained that they were responsible for the disappearance of humanity. They had taken the human race with them to another world, and the only way to bring them back was by creating a new human life. The guardians then informed me that there was one other survivor left and that we would have to work together to restore humanity. They gave us all the necessary resources and left us on our own. My initial thought was that it would be an easy task, but as soon as I met the other survivor, I realized how wrong I was. Her name was Kiera, and she was the complete opposite of me. We had nothing in common, and we could not have come from more different backgrounds. She had grown up in a wealthy family, had a degree in economics, and had never set foot outside the city. I, on the other hand, was a carpenter from a small town, living a simple life. We tried to get along, but we were constantly at odds. My idea of building a shelter for us to live in was met with her suggestion of waiting it out and doing nothing. When I suggested that we start the process of creating a baby, she immediately rebuked and told me that we should take our time and explore the resources at our disposal. Despite our differences, we both knew that humanity needed us. We needed to overcome our personal challenges and work together to restore human life on this planet. So, we put aside our differences and started building a home, planting crops, and making use of the resources to create a new life. As we worked together, we learned to appreciate our differences and saw that together, we could create something beautiful. And finally, nine months later, a new human life was born. We were both overjoyed, tears streaming down our faces, knowing that we had accomplished something incredible. The Earth's guardians returned, and as they looked at the new baby, they informed us that humanity had been restored on another planet. But as a reward for our efforts, they gave us the choice to travel with them and join humanity there. Kiera looked at me and smiled, realizing that we had become closer than anyone could have imagined. With our differences aside, we had created something together, something that would last for generations. Together we accepted the guardians' offer and embarked on a new journey, hoping to make a difference in humanity wherever we were.

Cyanobacteria are considered the ancestors of chloroplasts. They are sometimes called blue-green algae even though they are prokaryotes. They are a diverse phylum of bacteria capable of carrying out photosynthesis, producing oxygen through photosynthesis. Many species of cyanobacteria can form symbiotic relationships with other organisms, such as plants. Cyanobacteria are found in almost every ecosystem on Earth. They are often the dominant organisms in aquatic environments, especially in freshwater. They can also be found in soils and on the surface of rocks.

French Foreign Minister Laurent Fabius has stated that some European Union sanctions on Iran could be lifted as early as next month as part of a nuclear deal with world powers. This announcement gives hope that there will be a breakthrough in the efforts to resolve the long-standing tension between Iran and Western powers. During a press conference on Tuesday, Fabius reported that the agreed-upon nuclear deal puts forth clear guidelines and strict limitations on Iran's nuclear program. He noted that the European Union will start taking steps to lift some sanctions imposed on Iran. These measures will be in line with the terms and timeframe of the recent agreement. Following years of tensions, Iran agreed this month to curb its nuclear program significantly in exchange for the removal of economic sanctions from the US and the European Union. The deal was reached between Iran, the United Kingdom, France, Germany, the European Union, and the United States in Vienna. The lifting of sanctions would be a significant relief for Iran, as it would enable the country to begin to rebuild its struggling economy. The expected windfall in oil revenues would allow the country to begin investing in much-needed infrastructure and boosting trade. There is still much work to be done before the sanctions are officially lifted. The deal will have to be ratified by all parties concerned before the sanctions are lifted. However, Fabius has expressed optimism that the groundwork has been laid for an agreement that will be acceptable to all parties. Meanwhile, some critics are still concerned that the deal may not be the best solution. They argue that it does not do enough to address Iran's nefarious activities in the region, and that lifting sanctions will merely allow Iran to strengthen its position in a volatile region. The timing of lifting sanctions will be of interest to many different powerhouses, including the United States and Russia. On one side, the US hopes to start trading with Iran's developing economy, with many forecasters predicting the country will significantly boost the inflation of crude oil prices. Russia, on the other hand, believes that Iran will help to balance out the US's growing sway in the Middle East. Nonetheless, Fabius is optimistic that the lifting of the sanctions will be a win for all concerned: "We can start a new beginning with Iran, and this deal can serve as a blueprint for addressing conflicts throughout the region."

Centrality measures such as the degree, k-shell, or eigenvalue centrality can identify a network's most influential nodes, but are rarely usefully accurate in quantifying the spreading power of the vast majority of nodes. Instead, network simulations can be used to estimate the spreading power of individual nodes, taking into account the specific characteristics of the network and the dynamics of the spreading process. For example, one popular simulation approach is the SIR model, which considers how a disease spreads through a population represented as a network. In this model, each node is classified into one of three states: susceptible, infected, or recovered. The simulation proceeds by determining which susceptible nodes are exposed to infected nodes, and then proactively infecting some of those exposed susceptible individuals based on factors such as transmission rate, individual susceptibility, and network topology. The simulation continues until there are no more infected individuals or the epidemic reaches a steady state. The nodes that are most likely to become infected and spread the disease can be identified using this approach. Additionally, there are other approaches to quantify the spreading power of individual nodes in a network. For example, researchers have developed the concept of "network controllability," which measures the minimum number of nodes that need to be controlled in order to direct the entire network. Nodes with the highest controllability are likely to have a significant impact on the network's behavior in a variety of scenarios. In summary, while centrality measures can be useful for identifying influential nodes in a network, simulations or other approaches that take into account the specific dynamics of the spreading or control process may be more accurate in quantifying the spreading power of individual nodes.

I had always been an avid runner, so when I stepped out onto the pavement that day, I couldn't wait to start my morning jog. The sun was just starting to peek over the horizon, and the cool air felt refreshing as I picked up my pace. As I rounded the first corner, I suddenly felt a sharp pain in my chest. It felt as though the air had been knocked out of my lungs. I stumbled to a stop, clutching at my chest as the pain grew more intense. I tried to take deep breaths, but nothing seemed to be working. The pain was so intense that I could barely stand up straight. Just as I was starting to panic, a kind stranger ran over to me and asked if I needed help. I could hardly get the words out, but managed to gasp that I couldn't breathe. The stranger immediately called for an ambulance, and stayed with me until they arrived. As the EMTs whisked me away to the hospital, I was filled with fear and uncertainty. What was happening to me? Would I be okay? I couldn't shake the feeling that my entire life was about to change in a major way. At the hospital, the doctors quickly determined that I had suffered a pulmonary embolism - a blood clot that had travelled to my lungs. They assured me that with proper treatment, I would make a full recovery. Over the next few weeks, I worked hard to regain my strength and lung capacity. Every breath was a reminder of how fragile life can be, and I swore to myself that I wouldn't take my health for granted again. Now, a year later, I still run every morning. But now, in addition to the thrill of pushing myself physically, I am grateful for each breath that fills my lungs. I know that the air could have easily left my lungs that day, but through the kindness of a stranger and the expertise of medical professionals, I was given a second chance.

It was the famous Fairfield yard which took the Upper Clyde to great heights and worldwide prominence. The yard was founded in 1864 by William Elder, a talented marine engineer and shipbuilder. He was soon joined by William Pearce, whose expertise in design and management helped the business grow rapidly. At its peak in the 1960s Fairfield's workforce numbered around 32,000 people, a huge community which earned the nickname "the Clyde Blighters." The company did not just build ships for the Royal Navy and merchant marine, but also ferries, tugs, cargo vessels, fishing boats, trawlers, passenger liners and oil rigs. In 1881, the first battleship designed by Fairfield, HMS Inflexible, was launched. It boasted four massive gun turrets, with two 29 tonne guns in each turret. The ship was described as "a floating fortress" at the time, weighing in at almost 13,000 tons. The launch of the Queen Mary in 1934 was another milestone for the company. This new liner could carry 2,140 passengers and a crew of 1,015. Her sister ship, Queen Elizabeth, followed in 1938. Both were requisitioned for war service during the Second World War and both survived. The Queen Mary became a troop ship and carried over 750,000 Allied troops to the conflict. She was hit by three German torpedoes in September 1942, but managed to stay afloat and return to port. After the war, the Queen Mary resumed her role as a passenger liner, carrying royalty and film stars across the Atlantic. In 1967 she was retired from service and sold for scrap. Another of Fairfield's proudest achievements was the construction of the first ever oil rig in 1953. It was designed to drill in the North Sea and weighed in at 50,000 tonnes. Despite these successes, the company began to encounter serious financial problems in the 1970s. In 1971, the government nationalised the Upper Clyde Shipbuilders (UCS), which included the Fairfield yard. This did not solve the financial problems and in 1973 the UCS went into receivership. Despite a massive rescue package from the government, the company ceased trading in 1972. The Fairfield yard finally closed its doors in 1979, bringing an end to shipbuilding on the Clyde after over 400 years.

There are several reasons why some countries use nuclear power, while others don't. Firstly, the availability of uranium or other nuclear fuels can affect a country's decision to use nuclear power. Secondly, certain countries may have a greater need for energy due to factors such as population growth or industrialization, and nuclear power can provide a reliable source of energy that can meet these demands. Thirdly, some countries may prioritize reducing their dependence on fossil fuels and cutting greenhouse gas emissions, and nuclear power can be seen as a cleaner alternative source of energy. On the other hand, some countries may have concerns about the safety and security of nuclear power, particularly in the event of an accident or potential sabotage. Additionally, the cost of building and maintaining nuclear power plants can be substantial, which can make it difficult for some countries to justify the investment. Finally, some countries may have policies that prioritize renewable energy sources over nuclear power.

Summary: Genome-to-genome comparisons require designating anchor points, which are given by Maximum Exact Matches (MEMs) between their sequences. For large genomes this is a challenging problem and the performance of current algorithms is not satisfactory. We present a novel algorithm for MEM identification that utilizes an efficient data structure and heuristics to drastically reduce the search space in the problem. The algorithm is robust and scalable and we demonstrate its performance by comparing it with existing results on several synthetic datasets as well as on real-world genomic data from X. tropicalis. We show that our algorithm is significantly faster than existing solutions while achieving similar or higher accuracy.

"Are you okay?" My teacher paused for a moment, looking confused. Then she blinked and shook her head, as if she was waking up from a dream. "Oh, sorry about that," she said, looking embarrassed. "I guess I got stuck in a loop. X equals negative B plus or minus the square root of B squared minus 4AC, all over 2A," she recited one last time, before moving on with the lesson as if nothing had happened. But for the rest of the class, I couldn't help but feel a sense of unease. What had caused my teacher to get stuck in that endless loop? And was it a sign of something deeper, something darker that was brewing beneath the surface of our otherwise normal classroom?

In this work, we explain the working mechanism of MixUp in terms of adversarial training. We introduce a new class of adversarial training schemes, which we refer to as directional adversarial training. This approach allows us to generate adversarial examples in a more targeted way, which helps to improve the robustness of the model. MixUp is a data augmentation technique that generates virtual training examples by interpolating pairs of training examples. The key idea behind MixUp is to combine the features and labels of two examples, resulting in a new example that lies on the straight line connecting the two original examples in feature space. In terms of adversarial training, MixUp can be seen as a way of generating adversarial examples that are difficult to attack. By combining the features and labels of two examples, we create a new example that is more robust to small perturbations in feature space. Directional adversarial training builds on this idea by generating adversarial examples that are specifically targeted towards a particular class or region of feature space. This allows us to create examples that are difficult to attack in a targeted way, rather than relying on a more general approach that aims to defend against all attacks. Overall, MixUp and directional adversarial training are powerful techniques for improving the robustness of machine learning models against adversarial attacks. By generating more challenging examples during training, we can create models that are better equipped to handle real-world scenarios where attacks are a constant threat.

There was once a boy named Alex who always had an itch. It was an itch that never went away no matter how much he scratched it or applied creams. It was a constant annoyance, making it hard for him to concentrate on anything. One day, as he was walking home from school, Alex noticed a curious-looking old man sitting on a bench. The man had a long, white beard and was wearing a green cloak. His eyes sparkled with an otherworldly light that immediately caught Alex's attention. "Excuse me, sir," Alex said, approaching the old man. "Do you know anything about an itch that never goes away?" The old man looked up and studied Alex for a moment. "Ah, you mean the itch of the soul," the old man said with a smile. "It's a very common affliction, especially among young people. But fear not, for I have just the remedy for your ailment." The old man reached into his cloak and pulled out a small bottle filled with a golden liquid. He handed it to Alex and said, "This is a special salve that I've been working on for years. Just apply it to the affected area, and your itch will be gone forever." Alex thanked the old man and rushed home to try the salve. He applied it to his itch, and almost immediately, the itch vanished. It was like magic! From then on, Alex was able to focus on his studies and enjoy his favorite activities without the constant distraction of an itch. He even went back to thank the old man, but he was nowhere to be found. Years went by, and Alex forgot all about the old man and his magical salve. But every now and then, when he was feeling lost or overwhelmed, he would remember the mysterious stranger who had solved his itch problem and feel a sense of comfort and gratitude. The end.
