Understanding E3 ligase and target substrate interactions are important for cell biology and therapeutic development. However, experimental identification of E3 target relationships is not an easy task due to the large number of E3 ligases and substrate proteins as well as the limited number of available interaction data. Therefore, computational prediction of E3 target relationships is a valuable alternative approach in order to gain knowledge about E3-substrate interactions. In this work, we propose a novel two-step method based on protein sequence features and the random walk algorithm to predict E3-substrate pairs. We first use a support vector machine (SVM) classifier to screen the potential E3-substrate pairs. Then we use the random walk algorithm to assess the probability scores of the screened potential E3-substrate pairs. In our experiments, we collected a total of 3,169 E3-substrate relationships with 3,017 unique E3 ligases and 9,495 unique E3 substrates from the HIPPIE database. The positive and negative data sets for E3-substrate pairs were generated by randomly selecting one substrate for each E3 ligase and an equal number of non-substrate proteins for each E3 ligase. Our results showed that the proposed method can achieve a high prediction accuracy of 84.25 (MCC 0.6921) for 10-fold cross validation and 77.71 (MCC 0.5681) for independent test. Furthermore, the results also showed that our proposed method can outperform other state-of-the-art methods for E3-substrate relationship prediction. View Less

While it may seem like a simple business decision to hire more women in order to save money on salaries, this isn't the best solution for closing the gender wage gap. The underlying cause of the wage gap is institutionalized sexism that has been perpetuated over many years, and hiring more women won't necessarily solve this problem. Furthermore, if businesses are only hiring women to save money, they may be taking advantage of female workers by paying them less than they would pay a male worker in the same role. This could end up creating a new kind of wage gap between different groups of women. Instead, businesses should focus on practices such as conducting salary audits and providing equal pay for equal work regardless of gender.

It was the night before Christmas, and all through the house, not a creature was stirring except for one man: Santa Claus. As he prepared his sleigh and gathered his presents, he couldn't help but feel a sense of guilt. His team of elves had proven to be costly, and the rising cost of materials had taken a toll on his finances. He simply didn't have enough money to keep his workshop running. As he glanced out the window, he noticed a figure stirring in the night. It was a man in a suit, and he was looking up at the stars. Santa recognized him as an NSA agent - one of the many who had been tasked with monitoring the world's population. A thought occurred to Santa. He had been keeping tabs on children for decades. He knew when they were sleeping, and he knew when they were awake. What if he could sell that information to the NSA? What if he could use his surveillance data to pay his elves and keep his workshop running? Without hesitation, Santa set to work. He gathered the data that he had collected over the years and packaged it up in a neat little file. Then, he made contact with his NSA agent friend and struck a deal. The agent was pleased with the data Santa had provided. It was high-quality, comprehensive, and above all, accurate. He knew that his colleagues would be thrilled to have it. As such, he paid Santa handsomely for his efforts. Thanks to Santa's quick thinking, his workshop was saved. His elves were paid, his workshop was operational, and he could focus on delivering presents to children around the world. However, he couldn't shake the feeling that he had traded something priceless for something that was simply valuable. Nevertheless, he told himself that he had made the right decision - for himself, his workshop, and for the children he had devoted his life to serving.

It was a dark, cold night. The kind of night that made you want to curl up in bed with a good book and a cup of hot chocolate. But instead of being snug in my bed, I was standing outside in the freezing cold, trying to hail a taxi. I had been out celebrating with friends and had one too many drinks. Now I was regretting it. I finally managed to flag down a cab and gave the driver my address. I leaned back in the seat and closed my eyes, trying to forget the cold. I must have dozed off, because the next thing I knew, the cab was pulling up to my house. I paid the driver and got out, stumbling up to my front door. I fumbled with my keys for a few moments before finally getting the door open. I walked in and collapsed on my bed, fully clothed. I was just about to drift off to sleep when I heard a noise. I sat up, listening carefully. There it was again. It sounded like someone was in my house. I got up quietly and tip-toed to the door of my room. I peeked out and saw a shadow moving in the living room. My heart started pounding as I realized that there was an intruder in my house. I considered calling the police, but then I remembered that I had left my phone in the cab. I was going to have to handle this on my own. I crept out of my room and followed the shadow. It was moving towards the Christmas tree. Suddenly, I realized who it was. "Santa!" I exclaimed. He turned around, looking startled. "Uh, hi," he said sheepishly. "I hope you don't mind me dropping in like this, but I'm a bit low on funds to pay my elves. So I've started selling my surveillance data to the NSA." I stared at him for a moment, not quite sure what to say. Then I shook my head and laughed. "Well, I guess you're forgiven this time," I said. "But next year, try to be a little more discreet, okay?" "I will," Santa said. "And thanks for understanding." Then he slipped out the door and was gone.

The serial killer had found his next victim, and he felt the familiar thrill of anticipation. He began his normal routine of peeking through windows and popping up in mirrors, looking for that rush he got off on. He had done it so many times before that he didn't even have to think about it; it was like muscle memory. But this time was different. As he watched his intended victim move around his house, he couldn't help but notice something unusual about the place. It was full of horror movie memorabilia, from posters to action figures to life-size replicas of monsters. The killer frowned. This was not good. He had encountered people who were afraid of horror movies before, but he had always been able to use that fear to his advantage. He would simply appear as a monster from their worst nightmares, and they would be paralyzed with terror. But this guy was different. He had constructed his life around the prevention of such jump scares. His house was full of strategically placed mirrors, and he had a series of alarms that would sound if anyone entered uninvited. The killer knew that he would have to be very careful if he was going to succeed. He watched his victim for a few more minutes before he realized that he was running out of time. He needed to act quickly before the alarms went off. He slipped into the house as quietly as he could, scanning the area for any sign of danger. As he moved through the house, he noticed that his victim had set up several traps, all designed to startle him. But the killer was too experienced for that. He managed to avoid all of them, moving ever closer to his target. Finally, he reached the bedroom. The victim was sleeping soundly, completely unaware of the danger he was in. The killer smiled to himself, knowing that this was going to be easy. But just as he was about to strike, the victim woke up. He looked over and saw the killer standing in the corner of the room. But instead of screaming in terror, he just rolled his eyes and muttered, "Not this again." The killer was taken aback. He had never encountered someone who was so blase about his approach. He tried to scare the victim by adopting a monster's growl, but the victim just sighed and pressed a button on his remote control. Suddenly, the room was flooded with bright light, and a pre-recorded message played through the speakers. "Sorry, buddy," the voice said. "I'm a horror movie buff. I knew you were coming, and I set up some precautions." The killer was defeated. He knew that he could never overcome someone who was so prepared for his arrival. He slipped back out of the house, vowing to find a victim who was more vulnerable next time. But deep down, he knew that he had been beaten by a true horror movie fan.

In an exclusive interview with BBC News, founding member of iconic British band The Smiths, Mike Joyce, has revealed that the possibility of reforming was a very real prospect, if only for four days. The group, which formed in 1982 and split up just four years later, are widely considered to be one of the most influential bands in the history of British music. The Manchester-based outfit, consisting of members Morrissey, Johnny Marr, Andy Rourke and Joyce, sold millions of records throughout the world and spawned numerous hit singles, including 'This Charming Man', 'How Soon is Now' and 'Heaven Knows I'm Miserable Now'. In spite of the huge success, their time together was tragically short-lived. However, speaking to BBC News, Joyce has now revealed that, for a brief period of time at least, there was a chance that the band could have reunited. Joyce said: "There was a window of opportunity where everyone was in the same place at the same time... I think it was four days. We were all talking, but then it never happened." The group's frontman, Morrissey, had previously suggested that he would never reunite with the band, while guitarist Marr has also been vocal in his opposition to a reunion. Joyce added: "Maybe we could have done something special, but it wasn't to be. It's a shame because it would have been great to get back together and play the old songs." Despite the missed opportunity, fans of the band can at least console themselves with the fact that The Smiths' legacy remains as strong as ever, with their influence still being felt in the contemporary music scene.

As the emergency meeting ended, EU President, Charles Michel, acknowledged the challenges faced in trying to find a unified approach to the issue. In this extended abstract we present the gubs Upper Bound Solver. gubs is a dedicated constraint solver over the naturals for inequalities formed over uninterpreted function symbols and standard arithmetic operators (, -, , ). The solver implements a novel approach based on Groebner bases that leads to a modular and efficient solution for the problem. It is capable of solving instances of the problem that are intractable for current state-of-the-art SMT solvers. The main advantages of using gubs are its simplicity and flexibility. The user only needs to provide a set of constraints in a specific format and the solver will take care of the rest. The solver can also be easily integrated into existing tools and workflows. To evaluate its performance, we compared gubs with state-of-the-art SMT solvers on a range of benchmarks. The results showed that gubs outperformed the other solvers in most cases and was able to solve problems that were unsolvable by the other solvers. Overall, gubs represents a significant advance in the state-of-the-art in constraint solving and provides a powerful tool for solving problems in a variety of domains.

As the rain poured down relentlessly from the overcast sky, Cara watched in horror as her carefully tended garden became a waterlogged mess. She knew that with a lot of hard work and dedication, her garden could be restored to its former glory, and that is exactly what she did. The end result was a garden that was even more beautiful than before. The flowers bloomed brighter, the colors were more vibrant, and every inch of the garden shone with a renewed vitality. By combining cyanobacteria, or blue-green algae, with white button mushrooms, researchers from the Stevens Institute of Technology in Hoboken, New Jersey were able to create a bio-hybrid organism capable of producing electricity. These nanowires are able to absorb electrons from the mushroom's surface and convert them into a current. This current is then harnessed by a small circuit that is connected to the mushroom. According to Manu Mannoor, one of the lead researchers on the project, the team's goal was to "harness the power of nature," and it appears they have done just that. The bionic mushroom could potentially be used as an alternative source of clean energy for both homes and businesses. The research team believes this technology can be further developed and refined so that the mushrooms can produce even more electricity. They also plan to explore ways to integrate other organisms and materials into the bio-hybrid system, such as yeast, bacteria, and fungi. Overall, the development of bionic mushrooms is an exciting advancement in renewable energy technology. Its potential applications are seemingly endless and could help reduce our dependence on traditional energy sources.

Behavioural economists have shown that people are often averse to inequality and will make choices to avoid unequal outcomes. In this paper, we consider how to allocate indivisible goods fairly when the beneficiaries have a preference for equality. In particular, we study two settings that are commonly encountered in the literature: (1) those in which each beneficiary has a unit demand and there is a single item to be allocated; and (2) those in which there are several items to be allocated and each beneficiary has a 1N demand function. We show that the envy-free allocation of indivisible goods cannot be guaranteed if people have a preference for equality. We also prove that an envy-free allocation can be guaranteed only when the number of items is very large in the second setting.

Hundreds of people gathered in Cardiff Bay last night to show solidarity with the people of Paris following the terror attacks on Friday which left 17 dead. The vigil included a minute's silence, during which many lit candles and raised them towards the sky in remembrance of those whose lives were taken by the three days of violence. The event was organised by Cardiff Council, who said that it was intended to "show support for the citizens of France and all those affected by these terrible acts." The Mayor of Cardiff, councillor Phil Bale, led the ceremony, saying: "This evening we join together as a city to remember and pay respect to those innocents who lost their lives in Paris over the past few days." He added: "We send our condolences to their families and those affected by this tragedy and we will continue to stand in solidarity with the people of France, showing that we are all united against hatred and violence." The attack has been condemned around the world and many other vigils have been held in cities including London, Berlin and Madrid. Cardiff's Muslim communities also attended the ceremony in Cardiff Bay and spoke of their anguish at the attacks. Local Imam Mohammed Iqbal said: "No religion teaches you to kill innocent people and no god would ever ask anyone to do such a thing. We must stand together and share the love." The French flag was flown at half mast across Cardiff City Hall on Saturday and Monday and members of the public have been invited to leave messages of condolence and support in a book of remembrance located in City Hall. This morning, Cardiff Council unveiled a memorial plaque in front of City Hall, dedicated to the victims of the attacks. It reads: "In memory of those who lost their lives in the Paris attacks 13-15 November 2015. Nous sommes unis."

Video moment retrieval is to search the moment that is most relevant to the given natural language query. Existing methods are mostly trained in a fully-supervised setting, which requires the annotation of the query-moment pairs. However, in many real-world applications, only weak supervision information is available. In this paper, we propose a weakly supervised framework to learn query-moment matching by leveraging both unary (query-moment) and pairwise (moment-moment) relations... We first train an encoder to map text and video into a shared latent space and then use it to extract query-moment pairs and search moments that are most similar to the query. To exploit the weak supervision information, we adopt a pairwise similarity loss function to encourage semantically similar query-moment pairs to have close representations. We also design a query-specific gate to selectively match relevant moments from the whole collection. Our method is evaluated on three standard benchmarks, including MSR-VTT, TRECVID MED, and ActivityNet Captions, and achieves new state-of-the-art results, showing the effectiveness of our framework. Lenovo has now issued an apology to its customers, saying: "We apologize profusely for causing these concerns. We acted swiftly and decisively once these concerns began to be raised." The company has released a tool to completely remove the software from affected computers, however it has come under fire from some who believe it should have been more open about the presence of the adware in the first place. The incident is a reminder of how important it is for companies to ensure their products are secure and trustworthy. It also highlights the need for transparency when it comes to what is being shipped with new devices. Lenovo has vowed to take steps to avoid similar problems in future, including introducing a clear policy on pre-installed software and regularly testing products for vulnerabilities. It remains to be seen whether Lenovo's actions will be enough to restore customer confidence and trust in the company.

In a major step forward for sustainable transportation, solar cars are now becoming a reality. Solar cars are powered almost entirely by sunlight, using photovoltaic panels to convert the sun's energy into electricity that can be used to power an electric motor. The first successful solar car was the Sunraycer, developed in the 1980s by General Motors and the U.S. Department of Energy. Since then, solar cars have been built by universities, research groups and hobbyists around the world. Most recently, solar car technology has become more accessible and affordable. Companies like Sono Motors and Lightyear are making solar cars available to consumers. These cars are able to generate enough electricity from the sun to power themselves, with only minimal input from the driver. This makes them a cost-effective and environmentally friendly alternative to traditional gasoline-powered automobiles. The potential for solar cars is great. Not only do they reduce reliance on fossil fuels, but they could also help countries transition to renewable energy sources. Additionally, solar cars provide the opportunity for long-distance travel without the need for refueling stops. Solar cars are still in the early stages of development, and there is much work to be done before they become widespread. However, as technology advances and costs come down, they could soon become a viable option for drivers looking to reduce their carbon footprint.

It was a dark and foggy night, and Sarah was driving home from a long day at work. She had already driven for 30 minutes on the deserted winding road, and now her mind was starting to drift off. Suddenly, out of nowhere, a deer appeared on the road. It was a massive buck with antlers that were taller than the car's hood. Sarah's heart skipped a beat, and her instincts kicked in; she slammed on the brakes, but sadly, it was too late. The deer froze in the headlights of the car, and there was no escaping from the collision. Sarah could hear the sound of the impact as the car hit the deer. For a moment, everything went quiet, and the car came to a screeching halt. Sarah's heart was pounding in her chest as she sat there, frozen, in shock. She couldn't believe what had happened. She remembered reading about deer in the headlights, but she never thought it would happen to her. As she sat there trying to compose herself, she looked out of the window and saw the deer lying in the middle of the road, motionless. The car was damaged, but Sarah was lucky enough to be unhurt. She sat there for a few minutes, gathering her thoughts and reflecting on what had happened. After she regained her composure, Sarah checked the car for damage and then called the police to report the accident. She had to wait for a while for the authorities to arrive, during which she sat silently in the car, replaying the moment over and over in her mind. Finally, the police arrived at the scene, and Sarah explained everything that happened. They took some pictures of the car and the deer, and then called a tow truck to take the car back to the garage. The accident had caused a significant impact on Sarah, and it took her a while to feel comfortable driving again. From then on, she made sure to pay extra attention to the road, especially when driving at night, to avoid any other possible encounters with deer in the headlights.

In the fast-paced world of technology, software engineering has quickly become an attractive prospect for college graduates and seasoned professionals alike. But amidst the growing popularity of the field, there are a few aspects of the job that nobody seems to talk about. First and foremost, software engineering requires a large amount of self-motivation and discipline. Many new hires mistakenly believe that they will receive a significant amount of hand-holding from their managers and colleagues, but this is simply not the case. While teams may collaborate on projects, software engineers must have the drive to work independently and meet tight deadlines. Another aspect of software engineering that is often overlooked is the level of communication required. While the stereotype of the introverted programmer may persist, the reality is that software engineers must constantly communicate with various stakeholders, including clients, product owners, and project managers. Effective communication is crucial in avoiding misunderstandings and ensuring that everyone is on the same page. Along with communication, software engineers must also be comfortable with constant learning and adaptation. Technology moves at an incredibly rapid pace, and the best engineers are those who embrace new languages, frameworks, and tools as they emerge. This means that, unlike many other professions, software engineering requires a long-term investment in continuing education. Finally, software engineering can be a mentally and emotionally challenging job. Because the process of developing software is often iterative and involves significant trial and error, it's not uncommon for engineers to work long hours and experience setbacks. Successful engineers are those who can maintain a positive outlook and persevere through these challenges, even when it feels like progress is slow. In short, while software engineering can be a rewarding and lucrative career, it's also one that requires a significant level of self-motivation, communication, adaptability, and mental fortitude. For those who are up to the challenge, however, the rewards are limitless.

Public health doctors have warned that a government drive to boost participation in rugby in English schools is ill-conceived and risks children getting seriously hurt. This announcement has been met with strong criticism from public health doctors, who are concerned about the potential for serious injury for children involved in competitive school rugby. Dr. Ben Goldacre, a public health doctor and member of the British Medical Association's Child Health Committee, said: "We are very concerned about the implications of this decision. Rugby is an inherently dangerous sport, and it is not appropriate to expose children to such a high risk of injury in a school setting." He added: "We believe that schools should be encouraging and supporting children to take part in sports that are safe and enjoyable. We do not think that competitive school rugby is suitable for the majority of children." Dr. Goldacre's concerns have been echoed by other medical professionals, with many pointing to the potential for long-term damage from playing the contact sport at a young age. The Department for Education has defended its decision, claiming that competitive rugby in schools will help prepare children for life beyond the classroom. A spokesperson said: "Rugby teaches children valuable lessons in teamwork, resilience, and respect - all of which will help them as they progress into adulthood." Despite this, public health doctors remain unconvinced that the benefits outweigh the risks. Dr. Goldacre concluded: "We urge the government to reconsider their plans and focus instead on providing schoolchildren with safer, more inclusive sporting activities."

The Intensive Care Unit (ICU) is a hospital department where machine learning has the potential to provide valuable assistance in clinical decision making. Classical machine learning models usually only provide predictions based on historical data, but newer machine learning techniques, such as deep learning and reinforcement learning, can provide more accurate and nuanced predictions based on real-time data. In the ICU, machine learning algorithms can be used to analyze patients' physiological parameters, such as heart rate, blood pressure, and respiratory rate to predict the likelihood of deterioration or other adverse events. This information can help healthcare providers make better decisions about when to intervene with treatment or when to discharge a patient. Machine learning can also be used to analyze patterns in electronic health records (EHRs) to identify trends and risk factors for certain conditions or complications. For example, a machine learning algorithm could analyze EHRs to identify patterns of sepsis, a potentially life-threatening condition that requires rapid intervention. Overall, machine learning has the potential to improve the quality of care and outcomes for ICU patients by providing real-time, data-driven insights to healthcare providers.

This can include taking away privileges or engaging in constructive dialogue to help them learn from their mistakes. It is important to seek alternative methods of discipline that do not rely on physical violence.

Throughout the Middle Ages, Newcastle was England's northern fortress. Incorporated first by Henry II, the city had a new charter granted by Elizabeth in 1589. The town prospered during the medieval period, gaining a reputation as a centre of trading and commerce, and became an important port. The castle was extended to provide additional protection against attack from Scotland, and a mint was established in the city. In the 16th century Newcastle became a major centre of cloth production. The city's merchants were instrumental in introducing new manufacturing processes and encouraging the development of the coal trade. By the 17th century, Newcastle had become one of the largest towns in England, with a population of over 30,000. In 1642, the English Civil War broke out and Newcastle was besieged by Parliamentary forces. After a nine-month siege, the Royalists surrendered to the Parliamentarians and the city was occupied by them until 1647. In the 18th century, Newcastle developed further as a commercial and industrial centre, becoming home to many shipbuilders, ropemakers and glassmakers. Throughout the 19th century, Newcastle continued to grow and develop, becoming a major shipbuilding centre and also an important centre for engineering, manufacturing and industry. The development of railways in the region during this time saw the city become an important transport hub, linking it to the rest of the country. In 1834, the world's first passenger railway opened between Newcastle and Darlington. Today, Newcastle is a vibrant and bustling city, combining its rich history with modern attractions and amenities. It is home to a range of universities, museums and galleries, as well as a thriving nightlife scene. Newcastle remains an important port and commercial centre, as well as a popular tourist destination.

Ping refers to the round trip time taken by a packet of data to travel from the source to the destination and back. It is measured in milliseconds (ms). A low ping (under 20 ms) indicates a fast and stable connection, while a high ping (above 100 ms) suggests a slow and unstable connection. Loss, on the other hand, refers to the number of packets of data that fail to reach the destination. Packet loss can be caused by network congestion, faulty equipment, or poor signal strength. It results in slow downloadupload speeds and a decrease in overall performance. High ping and packet loss can both have negative effects on your connection quality. High ping can result in delayed responses, lag, and stuttering. Packet loss can cause data to be corrupted, dropped, or retransmitted, leading to slow internet speeds, decreased stability, and increased latency. In extreme cases, high ping and packet loss can lead to disconnections or failed connections.

This would result in around 45,000 fewer deaths over the next 10 years, the report said. It would also lead to a reduction in hospital admissions and crime. The government is currently consulting on the introduction of a minimum price per unit of alcohol, with a view to introducing it in England. The Welsh government has already introduced a minimum price of 50p per unit, and the Scottish government is planning to do so later this year.

It was a typical day for Sarah as she sat at her desk, typing away on her computer. She was used to the usual sounds of the office - the whirring of printers, the hum of air conditioning, and the chatter of coworkers. However, today, there were additional noises that were not pleasant. She started to hear a faint hissing sound. At first, she ignored it and assumed it was just a noisy coworker's microphone. But as the hissing grew louder, Sarah couldn't help but be distracted. The sound was unsettling - like a snake coiled and ready to strike. It seemed to be coming from one of the air vents, but no one else in the office seemed to notice it. Sarah felt like she was going crazy, but she couldn't ignore the noise any longer. She got up from her desk and followed the hissing, trying to locate the source of the sound. The noise grew deafening as she got closer to the air vent in the corner of her office. She hesitantly reached out to touch the vent and was shocked to find that it was ice cold. Suddenly, a gust of cold air blew out of the vent, carrying with it a foul smell. It was the smell of something decaying, and Sarah gagged at the stench. She knew something was seriously wrong with the ventilation system, and she had to alert the building manager immediately. As she made her way down to the manager's office, Sarah could hear other strange noises coming from the building's pipes. There were clunking and banging sounds that made her jump each time they happened. It was like the building was alive, and it was not a pleasant feeling. Thankfully, the building manager was responsive and quickly sent out an HVAC technician to fix the broken ventilation system. As the technician worked on the pipes, Sarah could hear the screeching and grinding of metal against metal. She was relieved when the noise finally stopped, and the air in her office smelled fresh again. After that experience, Sarah became more aware of the sounds around her in the office. She realized how much of an impact background noise can have on her concentration and well-being. From then on, she took steps to make her workspace as peaceful and quiet as possible, free of noises that weren't pleasant.

The old tipping debate. I generally side with those that want to end the mostly American practice of tipping about 20 percent of the cost of the meal. That may sound selfish, but I'm willing to pay a bit more for my meal if the restaurant can pay its employees a living wage without relying on tips. As I've written before, it is not uncommon for restaurants to skim money from their servers. A quick Google search of "restaurant skimming tips" turns up hundreds of examples. One way this occurs is by basing a server's pay on sales instead of hours worked. That means a server who gets stuck waiting around for customers could make less money than a co-worker who had fewer sales but was at the restaurant longer. There is also the "house charge" in which the restaurant charges a customer an added service fee and then keeps the entire amount. The restaurant is supposed to share that money with the staff; however, there have been dozens of lawsuits against restaurants claiming they were denied the full amount of the tip. Another practice is adding a mandatory gratuity to the bill. This means the customer must pay a tip whether they received good service or not. I'm not against tipping if the restaurant pays its employees a livable wage. If a restaurant does so, it shouldn't be allowed to keep the tips. Tipping has become the American way, but it's time for restaurants to change. - Joel Addington is editor of The Dispatch

Asia has overtaken Europe to become the world's second-richest region, according to an annual report by the Boston Consulting Group (BCG). The report, released on Monday, found that the combined wealth of Asia's high net worth individuals (HNWIs) - those with financial assets of 1m or more - had surpassed that of Europe for the first time. The region as a whole saw its combined wealth grow by 6.4 in 2019 to 22.9tn, whereas Europe's wealth fell by 2.8 to 21.5tn. The report highlighted that the fortunes of Asian HNWIs have been boosted by strong economic growth and the rising value of financial markets in the region, particularly in China. This trend has been further amplified by the coronavirus pandemic, which has caused havoc across the global economy but has not impeded the growth of Asian economies as much as their counterparts in Europe, the Middle East and Africa. It is thought that the increased wealth in Asia will lead to higher levels of philanthropy, with wealthy individuals keen to put their money towards charities and causes within their own communities. Commenting on the findings, one of the authors of the report, Uwe Schroeder-Wildberg, said: "The vast majority of HNWIs in Asia are investing locally rather than internationally, which is having a positive impact on the region's economies." He added: "We expect the gap between Asia and Europe to continue to widen in the coming years, as more and more wealthy individuals from the region invest in local businesses and causes." The BCG report also showed that North America remained the wealthiest region in the world, with total HNWI wealth standing at 30.7tn.

As the hunter stood over the freshly slain deer, he couldn't help but feel a twinge of guilt. The animal's eyes, once so full of life, were now empty and glassy. "Excuse me," a voice said from behind him. The hunter spun around, expecting to see another human. Instead, he saw the deer's ghostly form hovering in the air. "Whoa, what the?" the hunter exclaimed, stumbling back a few steps. "I was wondering if I could talk to you," the deer said calmly. The hunter gaped at the spectral apparition before him. He had never believed in ghosts before, but here was a talking deer, so he supposed stranger things had happened. "Uh, okay," he said cautiously. "What do you want to talk about?" "I just wanted to say...thank you," the deer said, sounding earnest. "Thank me?" the hunter repeated, bewildered. "Yes. You see, my life was getting difficult. I was old and sick, and I knew that my time was coming. Being killed by a skilled hunter like yourself is a quick and relatively painless way to go. You spared me the drawn-out suffering that I was facing." The hunter felt a lump form in his throat as he listened to the deer's words. He had never considered that his hunting trips could actually be helping the animals that he killed. "I didn't know," he said quietly. "It's okay," the deer said with a little shrug. "Ignorance is understandable. But I wanted to let you know that not all of us view you hunters as monsters. In fact, some of us are grateful for the mercy you provide." The hunter felt a weight lift off his shoulders. He still felt a twinge of sadness for what he had done, but he also felt a new sense of purpose. He realized that if he hunted with mindfulness and care, he could make a positive impact on the wildlife around him. "Thank you for talking to me," he said to the deer's fading form. "I'll keep what you said in mind." With that, the deer vanished into the ether, leaving the hunter standing among the trees, deeper in thought than he had ever been before.

In the United States, the federal government uses a progressive tax system, where the tax rate increases as income increases. As of 2021, there are seven federal tax brackets: - 10 on taxable income from 0 to 9,950 - 12 on taxable income over 9,950 to 40,525 - 22 on taxable income over 40,525 to 86,375 - 24 on taxable income over 86,375 to 164,925 - 32 on taxable income over 164,925 to 209,425 - 35 on taxable income over 209,425 to 523,600 - 37 on taxable income over 523,600 For example, if your taxable income is 50,000, your first 9,950 is taxed at 10, and the remaining 40,050 is taxed at 12. It is also important to note that deductions and credits can impact your actual tax liability.

We evaluate the performance of our proposed method on the CHiME-4 dataset and compare it with several baseline methods. The results demonstrate that our proposed method outperforms the baseline methods in terms of both perceptual evaluation of speech quality (PESQ) score and signal-to-distortion ratio (SDR). Furthermore, we also analyze the impact of different factors such as number of channels and number of speakers on the performance of our proposed method. Our work contributes to the advancement of speech separation research by providing a novel approach for integrating multi-channel signals for speech separation. Our proposed method can be used for various applications such as automatic speech recognition (ASR), speaker diarization, and speaker verification. Moreover, our work provides insights into how multi-channel signals can be effectively used for speech separation tasks.

The number on the bottom indicates what kind of note gets one beat. The number on the top indicates how many beats there are in one measure. We present a local routing algorithm which guarantees delivery in all connected graphs embedded on a known surface of genus g. The algorithm transports O (g log n) memory and is SLIPk-optimal in the sense of routing by shortest paths. It is also optimal in the number of hops on any genus g surface. The algorithm is based on a novel parameterization of the space of all possible routes through a connected graph embedded on a surface. This parameterization allows us to construct a constant number of such routes per edge, each of which is guaranteed to deliver messages in the given graph. We also show that this parameterization can be used to construct an efficient distributed data structure for efficient local routing in any graph embedded on a surface.

Knowledge graphs capture entities and relations from long documents and can facilitate reasoning in many downstream applications. Extracting compact knowledge graphs containing only salient entities and relations is important but challenging due to the long tail nature of entity and relation popularity. This paper proposes a novel method to extract salient entities and relations from a long document by formulating the problem as a multi-task learning problem where the tasks are entity classification, entity co-reference resolution, and relation extraction. We propose a new deep neural model that can be jointly trained for all three tasks. This is a challenging learning problem because the three tasks are inter-dependent such that their optimization requires careful design. We proposed a new scheme to train this complex model by hierarchical training: first, we pre-train a language model using the entire document collection; then, we use the pre-trained language model to initialize the parameters during training on a long document for the three tasks. Our experimental results demonstrate that our approach effectively extracts salient entities and relations from a long document and outperforms the state-of-the-art methods by up to 5.

One of the challenges in large-scale information retrieval (IR) is to develop fine-grained and domain-specific methods to answer natural language questions. Despite the availability of numerous sources and datasets for IR, the task of finding a suitable answer remains difficult due to the complexity of natural language and its inherent ambiguity. In this paper, we propose a novel deep learning-based approach to large-scale IR using an ensemble of convolutional neural networks (CNNs). Our approach is able to accurately classify questions according to their domain while also providing accurate answers to those questions. We evaluate our approach on a large-scale dataset with over 115,000 questions and demonstrate that our model outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods in both accuracy and speed. Our findings provide an effective solution to the problem of large-scale information retrieval and suggest promising directions for future research.

The technology, reported in the journal Neuron, can identify inside a living animal the changes caused by Parkinson's disease. The breakthrough means that for the first time it is possible to observe in real-time the effects of a disease which affects around one million people in the UK. If it can be used on humans, the technique could help doctors identify if a treatment is working and allow them to intervene before patients start showing symptoms. Scientists have previously found that mice with Parkinson's have a change in the activity of the neurotransmitter dopamine. This chemical is necessary for normal movement. In the new study, scientists at Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT), Harvard University and the University of Southern California injected nanoparticles into the brains of Parkinson's-like mice. These particles are designed to bind to dopamine and emit a green light when they detect it. Using a special microscope, scientists were then able to track the behaviour of dopamine in living animals. They found that the technique allowed them to monitor how levels of dopamine changed throughout the day and over the course of the disease. Scientists say this is the first time such detailed information has been gathered about dopamine levels in the brain. Lead author Dr Li-Huei Tsai, from MIT, said: "This is a very powerful tool for understanding how Parkinson's disease develops, how it progresses and how we might develop new treatments." Dr Michelle Gardner, head of biomedical research at Parkinson's UK, said: "The ability to monitor dopamine levels in a living animal will provide invaluable insights into how the condition develops. "By allowing researchers to test new drugs without needing to wait for patients to show symptoms, this technology could speed up the process of finding treatments for Parkinson's significantly."

John had always been curious about what it would feel like to be invisible. He had read countless books and watched movies where the main character had the power to turn invisible. One afternoon, he decided to put a little experiment to the test. He hopped into his mom's car and drove down to the local Walmart. As soon as John entered the store, he whisked himself away to the restroom. Once inside, he closed the door and whispered to himself, "I'm invisible, I'm invisible." It was a little ritual he had created to see if it would work - and after a few seconds, he felt a strange tingling sensation throughout his body. John took a deep breath and opened the door. Sure enough, he was invisible. He walked out of the restroom, and without wasting a moment, mingled with the customers shopping in the store. It was strange knowing that no one could see him, but John felt exhilarated. He wandered through the aisles, observing people, and seeing how they behaved without the knowledge that anyone was watching them. As he wandered past the shelves of toys, John snickered as he watched an adult man fumble with a light-up yo-yo. Then he observed a family with young children repeatedly selecting and putting back jars of glitter glue. John couldn't help but chuckle at how kids could spend what felt like hours deciding on the perfect toy, while adults would breeze through the store with the same focus they had in their jobs. John was hypnotized by the inner workings of the store. Without anyone noticing him, he saw things happening that he would never have imagined. Kids were pulling faces and making silly faces at each other, and their parents had no idea. A cashier was eating candy from a shelf without paying, and a group of co-workers were sharing jokes as they restocked the shelves. Suddenly, John heard a voice call out, "John, get over here!" It was his mom - he had been in the store for over two hours. He quickly ran back to the restroom and repeated his ritual. After a moment, he was back to his visible self. John exited the restroom and found his mom waiting for him. "What took you so long?" she asked. "I was just looking around," John replied with a smile, that only he knew was because of what he had experienced. As John walked out of Walmart, he couldn't stop thinking of his adventure. Being invisible had been fun, but he was more excited about what he had seen - the secret world of Walmart that only became visible to him because he was invisible. It was a strange and surreal two hours, but John was glad to have tried it.

I hesitated to mention my suspicions to her, not wanting to be seen as a conspiracy theorist or cause offense. As it turns out, there was a family legend passed down through generations that their ancestor had discovered the Fountain of Youth, which had granted him immortality. It seemed too fantastical, but the records were too convincing to ignore. We spent weeks going through every document and cross-referencing every detail we could find. Eventually, we came to the conclusion that it was true. The face in the records was indeed evidence of a man's immortality and reincarnation. And it seemed that my assistant was the latest vessel for his spirit and now had the power to live for centuries beyond our time. I couldn't believe what I was seeing, but I couldn't deny the evidence before me. My assistant was the carrier of a remarkable and supernatural power. As a historian, I had learned that the truth is often stranger than fiction. And this was indeed the strangest truth I had ever uncovered.

We present a local routing algorithm which guarantees delivery in all connected graphs embedded on a known surface of genus g. The algorithm transports O (g log n) memory and runs in O (n m) time. Our algorithm works as follows: 1. Take an arbitrary vertex as the starting point and mark it as visited. 2. For each of its neighbors, check if it has been visited or not. 3. If the neighbor has not been visited, create a new path from the starting point to that neighbor and mark the neighbor as visited. 4. Repeat steps 2 and 3 until all vertices have been visited. To guarantee delivery, we use a spanning tree data structure to store the paths created in each step. With this structure, we can easily determine if a vertex has already been visited or not. Furthermore, the spanning tree also allows us to quickly determine which vertices are connected and which ones are not, allowing us to avoid any unnecessary detours when routing through the graph. We can further optimize our algorithm by using an Eulerian tour to traverse the graph instead of a spanning tree. This technique allows us to visit each vertex exactly once, thus reducing the number of steps needed to complete the routing. The trade-off is that the memory requirement increases to O (g n), but the time complexity remains O (n m). Overall, our algorithm provides a solution to the problem of routing in graphs embedded on known surfaces, guaranteeing delivery in all connected graphs and requiring only O (g log n) memory and O (n m) time.

The HeLa cell line is immortal because it has unique properties that allow it to continuously divide and replicate indefinitely. One key factor is that it contains an active telomerase enzyme, which prevents the telomeres on the ends of its chromosomes from shortening and, in turn, stops the cells from undergoing a process called senescence (cellular aging) and apoptosis (programmed cell death). Additionally, HeLa cells have mutations in genes that regulate cell cycle progression, allowing them to divide more rapidly and without the normal checks and balances that would otherwise stop their growth. These features can cause the cells to become cancerous, which is why they are often used as a model for studying cancer biology.

Another great game to play with your older dog is tug-of-war. Older dogs love to play tug-of-war, but be careful not to let your dog get too rough. If your dog gets too excited and starts biting you during a game of tug-of-war, stop playing immediately. Finally, fetch is always a good game to play with an older dog. Older dogs may not have the same energy as younger dogs, but they still love to play fetch. You can make this game easier for your older dog by using a softball or another smaller ball that is easier for your dog to pick up. In conclusion, there are many ways to keep your older dog entertained and active. Games like hide-and-seek, fetch, and tug-of-war are all great ways to do this. Just make sure that you are careful not to let your dog get too excited and bite you during a game of tug-of-war.

When this happens, it's because the builders didn't make sure the boat was balanced properly before it launched.

Distributed machine learning is becoming a popular model-training method due to privacy, computational scalability, and bandwidth capacities. In this work, we explore scalable distributed-training versions of two algorithms commonly used for image classification: k-nearest neighbors (kNN) and convolutional neural networks (CNNs). We find that kNN can be trained using a parameter server model, while CNNs can be trained using either a synchronous or asynchronous training model. Each of these models has different trade-offs in terms of convergence speed and model accuracy. Our experiments on the CIFAR-10 dataset show that distributed kNN converges faster than distributed CNN training under both synchronous and asynchronous models. However, the final model performance is higher for the distributed CNNs than for the distributed kNNs. For CNNs, we observe that the async training model converges faster than the sync training model, but has lower final model performance. We also show that the use of data augmentation in distributed training can improve the final model performance for both kNN and CNN classifiers.

Facebook and Snopes had been in talks to work together to create a fact-checking program for the Facebook platform, but Snopes has decided to cancel the partnership. The team decided to walk away from the deal because Snopes is not comfortable with Facebook's role in how the fact-checking program will be implemented. The program would have allowed Facebook users to flag articles as "disputed" if they thought the content was false. Facebook would then send the article to one of its fact-checking partners, like Snopes, for review. If the fact-checkers determined the article was indeed false, it would be labeled as "disputed" on Facebook. However, Snopes says it is not comfortable with the fact that Facebook would ultimately decide which articles get sent to fact-checkers, and which don't. In a statement, Snopes said: "We were concerned that the parameters of the partnership were not being strictly adhered to. Specifically, we were concerned that Snopes' fact-checking work would never be made genuinely public or transparent to anyone outside of Facebook, that Snopes would always be one fact-check away from losing partnership status, and that decisions about whether an article is and is not 'disputed' would be unilateral and final." The partnership was first announced in December 2016, and Snopes says it had been working with Facebook for several months to try to iron out the details. However, the team ultimately decided that the partnership was not in line with its values. Snopes is not the only fact-checking partner that has had issues with Facebook. PolitiFact also recently ended its partnership with Facebook, citing similar concerns.

A recent study published in the journal Science has found that male seahorses incubate their young with a placenta-like structure, making them the first known vertebrate to do so. The findings show that male seahorses have evolved a unique reproductive system to take on the primary role of caring for their offspring. The research team from Oxford University, who conducted the study, looked at several species of seahorses and found that the males produce a placenta-like organ called a 'marsupium'. This organ is located in the brood pouch on the seahorse's ventral side. It acts as an incubator for fertilized eggs, allowing them to develop until they are ready to hatch. The researchers believe that this unique adaptation has developed in response to the challenges posed by the seahorse's environment. Male seahorses tend to live in shallow waters, where their eggs could be damaged by small predators or washed away by waves and currents. By incubating the eggs inside the marsupium, they are protected from the elements and given a better chance of survival. In addition to protecting the eggs, the marsupium also provides nourishment for the embryo. It contains hormones which stimulate the growth and development of the embryos, as well as nutrients which help them survive until they are ready to hatch. This new discovery sheds light on the complex reproductive strategies of seahorses, and could lead to further insights into how other animals reproduce. It also highlights the importance of studying the behavior and physiology of different species, as it can reveal amazing adaptations which could benefit humans.

Online storage service Amazon Web Services (AWS) S3 is a popular choice among individuals and businesses alike. While the button may seem daunting due to its high price tag, it can actually save users a significant amount of money in the long run. This is because AWS S3 charges users based on the amount of data they store and the frequency of access. By moving infrequently accessed data to a cheaper storage option, users can reduce their monthly bill. In addition, using the 100k button can provide an added layer of security for sensitive data. AWS Glacier and AWS Deep Archive use a "cold storage" method, which means that the data is not readily accessible and is kept in a highly secure environment. AWS recommends that users evaluate their data storage needs and determine which storage option is best for their business. By utilizing the various storage options offered by AWS, users can optimize their data storage and potentially save money. In this paper, we provide details of a robotic system that can automate the task of picking and stowing objects from and to a rack in an e-commerce fulfillment warehouse. First, the robot arm is used to pick up objects from their designated locations in the rack and place them into the desired bin. To accurately locate and identify objects, the vision system employs a combination of RGB cameras and 2D laser scanners. The controller is responsible for managing the entire operation, including the task allocation, motion control, and object identification. In addition, a safety mechanism is integrated to ensure that no damage occurs to either the objects or the rack during the operation. The system has been tested on a real-world warehouse and demonstrated its capability to accurately pick and stow objects in short time frames. Moreover, we present an evaluation of the proposed robotic system in terms of its accuracy, speed, and reliability. The results show that our system can reliably and efficiently complete the task of picking and stowing objects from and to a rack in an e-commerce fulfillment warehouse.

Computer maker Lenovo has found itself in hot water after customers discovered that their new laptops and PCs came pre-installed with what amounted to "spyware." Security researchers discovered that Lenovo was shipping a program called "Superfish" that injected its own ads into online search results and potentially made users' private data vulnerable to interception. The program was not only a nuisance, but a major security risk as it was capable of intercepting encrypted web traffic by using self-signed security certificates. This would allow hackers to potentially intercept and steal sensitive information such as passwords, banking details, and other personal data. Needless to say, customers were outraged when they discovered their new purchases were infected with this software. Lenovo initially defended the program, saying that it wasn't a security threat and had been added to "help our customers." However, it was forced to backtrack and issue a public apology after a wave of negative feedback on social media and in online forums. The company has since released instructions on how to remove the Superfish software, along with an automated tool to help users uninstall the program. However, it's unclear how much damage may have already been done, as users' computers may have been compromised by the spyware before it was discovered and removed. The incident highlights the importance of vigilance when it comes to computer security. Whether you're a casual user or a business owner, it's crucial to take steps to protect your information and ensure that your devices are not infected with malware or other malicious software. Lenovo's misstep also underscores the need for companies to prioritize customer trust and security above all else. It's clear that consumers are increasingly aware of the threats posed by malware and other security risks, and they're not willing to compromise on the quality or safety of the products they purchase. In this case, Lenovo learned that the hard way.

In October 1529, Philip I, Landgrave of Hesse, convoked an assembly of German and Swiss theologians at the Marburg Colloquy, to establish doctrinal unity in the emerging Protestant states. Agreement could not be reached, and the Marburg Articles, a compromise between Lutherans and Zwinglians, were rejected. A second attempt at reconciliation was undertaken by the Diet of Augsburg, in 1530. The Augsburg Confession was presented to Charles V, Holy Roman Emperor on 25 June 1530, by four Lutheran princes and two city representatives. The Confession was based on the belief that the Word of God as contained in the Scriptures of the Old and New Testaments is the only rule and norm according to which all teachers and doctrines must be appraised and judged. It went beyond the Augustana and addressed the issues raised in the 1529 Marburg Colloquy. In 1531, the Diet of Augsburg declared the Augsburg Confession to be part of the law of the Empire. It was approved by ten votes against three, two bishops abstained. This text has been called critical for the beginnings of the Reformation in Germany. A document called Melanchthon's Variata, also known as the Apology of the Augsburg Confession, was published in 1531. The Variata was a revision of the Augsburg Confession, approved by Luther in 1530, which introduced some concessions to Catholic doctrine. It was presented to Charles V, but did not receive official approval. In 1532, the Diet of Regensburg declared the Augsburg Confession to be binding on all subjects of the Diet. In 1533, the Diet of Nuremberg declared the Augsburg Confession to be binding on all subjects of the Diet. In 1537, the Diet of Ratisbon declared the Augsburg Confession to be binding on all subjects of the Diet. The Augsburg Confession has remained an important part of the confession of most Lutheran churches since then. References Luther's 95 Theses. Christian Classics Ethereal Library. Deep learning models continuously break new records across different NLP tasks. At the same time, their success exposes weaknesses of model evaluation. Here, we compile several key pitfalls of evaluation in natural language processing. 1. A lack of standardization: Each NLP task has different evaluation metrics, making it difficult to compare models across tasks. For example, some tasks measure performance with accuracy while others use F1 score. 2. Unbalanced datasets: Evaluation metrics can be skewed due to imbalanced datasets, where the number of examples from one class is much greater than that from other classes. This can lead to models performing well on the majority class but poorly on minority classes. 3. Limited generalizability: The success of deep learning models often depend on data availability and context. Models may perform well on a specific dataset but fail to generalize to other datasets or tasks. 4. Unclear error sources: Evaluation metrics can mask the underlying errors made by models and make it difficult to diagnose problems. For example, a model may achieve good accuracy without properly recognizing certain classes, leading to false positives. 5. Subjective assessment: Many NLP tasks require human judgement and are therefore difficult to evaluate objectively. Furthermore, even when objective metrics exist, they may not always capture the full complexity of the problem.

Little disclaimer: this deals with US laws and procedures so I apologize if anyone outside the US isn't able to contribute, except to tell me how great it is having a universal healthcare system The Affordable Care Act (ACA) is a federal law that was signed into law by President Barack Obama in 2010. The ACA was designed to make health insurance more accessible and affordable for people who don't have access to employer-sponsored health plans. It also helps reduce the cost of health care for individuals and families with lower incomes. Under the ACA, individuals are required to have health insurance or face a tax penalty. Individuals can get coverage through their employers, government programs (such as Medicare and Medicaid), or from private insurers. Individuals can also purchase health insurance through the ACA's Health Insurance Marketplace, which offers plans from private insurers. The ACA also includes several provisions to help make health care more affordable for individuals and families. These include subsidies to help people pay for health insurance, protections against discrimination based on pre-existing conditions, expanded Medicaid eligibility, and caps on how much insurers can charge for certain services. The ACA has had a significant impact on the US health care system and has helped millions of Americans gain access to quality, affordable health care. However, the law is still controversial and there are ongoing debates about its future.

The Rankine cycle is the fundamental thermodynamic underpinning of the steam engine. The cycle is an arrangement of components as is typically used for simple power production, and utilizes the vaporization and condensation of water to produce mechanical work. The Rankine cycle is used for steam turbines and for steam engines, and it is the most common thermodynamic cycle for power generation in which heat energy is converted to mechanical energy. In the Rankine cycle, water is first pumped into a boiler where it is heated to create steam. The steam is then piped into a turbine, where it expands and drives the turbine. The turbine is connected to an electrical generator, which produces electricity. The steam is then condensed back into water in a condenser and the cycle repeats. The efficiency of the Rankine cycle is limited by the fact that it uses a working fluid (water) that undergoes phase change (vaporization and condensation). The use of a working fluid that does not undergo phase change, such as a gas, would theoretically increase efficiency. However, in practice, it is difficult to achieve the high temperatures and pressures needed for power generation using only a gas.

Video moment retrieval is to search the moment that is most relevant to the given natural language query. Existing methods are mostly trained in a fully-supervised setting, which requires the annotations of the exact starting and ending timestamps of the relevant moment in each video. However, the manual annotation is time-consuming and expensive. Therefore, there is a growing interest in unsupervised or weakly-supervised methods, which can learn to retrieve relevant moments without requiring such detailed annotations. These methods typically rely on some form of representation learning, which aims to capture the semantic meaning of the video and the query, and use this information to identify the relevant moment. Some common approaches include using pre-trained language and vision models, leveraging weak supervision signals such as video-level category labels, and incorporating contrastive learning to learn a joint representation of video and text.

In order to evaluate our method, we will train a linear regression model on the 300W public dataset [2]. Methodology Data Representation Our data will be represented as a sequence of images containing bearded men wearing glasses. Each image in the sequence will contain landmarks marking the locations of facial features like eyes, nose, etc. For example, we might have a sequence consisting of images of a man at various angles who has a beard and is wearing glasses. Each image would be labeled with the 3D coordinates of the landmarks and the 6 DOF of the camera relative to that image. We will use a convolutional net to extract features from our images. The convolutional net will take an image as input and output a vector of features. Each vector will be used as input to a linear model which will predict the 3D positions of the landmarks and the 6 DOF of the camera. This is motivated by the fact that the variance of the prediction is a measure of the model's uncertainty about the prediction. Thus, the idea is to give more weight to the losses for the tasks that the model is less certain about. In 1542, Luther read a Latin translation of the Qur'an. He went on to produce several critical pamphlets on Islam, which he called "Mohammedanism" or "the Turk." Though Luther saw Islam as a grave danger to Christian Europe, he also considered it a legitimate religion and urged Christians to engage Muslims in theological dialogue. Luther's writings on the subject were collected in a volume called On War Against the Turk (Von Kriegssachen gegen die Turken). In his 1529 work, The Babylonian Captivity of the Church, Luther had already stated that the papacy was the Antichrist, and that the pope was "the very devil incarnate." In 1545, Luther wrote a lengthy treatise entitled Against the Sabbatarians, in which he attacked the Anabaptists for their rejection of infant baptism. A year earlier, he had written a pamphlet entitled Against the Murderous, Thieving Hordes of the Peasants, in which he justified the suppression of a rebellion by peasants in Germany. Luther's attitudes toward Jews were more ambivalent. At times, he denounced them as enemies of Christianity; at other times, he urged Christians to read the Old Testament and learn from it. In one of his final works, written in 1543, Luther called on Christians to "not despise or suspect them [Jews] on account of their blindness, but rather to receive them cordially, and enjoy their friendship as brothers and children of Abraham." Luther's legacy Luther died on February 18, 1546, at the age of 62. He is buried in the Castle Church in Wittenberg, where he preached his final sermon just weeks before his death. Over the centuries, Luther has been both praised and criticized for his role in the Reformation. His supporters credit him with freeing Christians from the control of the Catholic Church and making the Bible accessible to the general public. His detractors accuse him of causing division within Christianity and unleashing religious violence. While Luther's views on many theological issues - including the nature of salvation and the authority of Scripture - were controversial in his own time, they have since become widely accepted within Protestantism. Luther also helped to standardize the German language, translating the Bible into German and writing many hymns, including "A Mighty Fortress Is Our God." In 1999, Pope John Paul II said that Luther's actions during the Reformation had been "erroneous" and "objectionable," but that his theology contained elements that could be seen as positive. The Lutheran World Federation and the Roman Catholic Church issued a joint statement in 1999 acknowledging that Luther had been mistaken in some of his criticisms of the Catholic Church, while affirming the shared belief of Lutherans and Catholics in the Trinity and the divinity of Jesus Christ.

The home secretary wrote to cabinet colleagues in December seeking approval to "reduce significantly" one type of stop and search, Newsnight has learned. Despite setting a 12 December deadline, the Home Office still has not decided whether to act on the advice. A Whitehall source told Newsnight that, in December, Mrs May wrote to colleagues asking them whether they agreed with her view that a particular type of stop and search - under Section 60 of the Public Order Act - should be cut back. Mrs May made her recommendation on the basis of a report from a Home Office internal review, which found that "the use of Section 60 orders was often disproportionate." The review also concluded that the power was being used more frequently in some parts of England than others, particularly in London and Birmingham. After the 12 December deadline, there was no immediate response from ministers, so Mrs May followed up her request with another letter at the end of January. At this point, one minister is understood to have raised concerns about the impact of a reduction in stop and search in their department's area of responsibility, which would require an amendment to the Police and Crime Bill currently going through Parliament. The matter was referred up to the full cabinet. No decision has been taken on whether to act on Mrs May's advice or not. In a statement, the Home Office said: "The Home Secretary believes in the importance of stop and search powers, including Section 60 orders, but recognises that they need to be used appropriately and proportionately. "She has written to ministerial colleagues seeking their views about how best to reduce the use of Section 60 orders and will respond as soon as possible." Section 60 orders allow police officers to stop and search people without reasonable grounds for suspicion, within a designated area for a specified period of time. In October 2012, the government introduced reforms aimed at bringing down the total number of stop and searches, after it emerged that black people were seven times more likely to be stopped under the tactic than white people. However, Section 60 stops have continued to rise. In 2012-13, in England and Wales, there were 108,247 Section 60 stops - an increase of 13 compared with the previous year. 'Proportionate?' Earlier this month, the Home Affairs Select Committee heard evidence from the police about the use of Section 60. Nick Gargan, chief constable of Avon and Somerset police, said he had only used Section 60 twice in two years. He described the power as "proportionate," saying: "My view is that it is a power which should be used very rarely." Alan Pughsley, chief constable of Kent police, told MPs that his force had used Section 60 "many times" over the past year. He said: "We've got a lot of problems with gang activity in Thanet, particularly in Margate, and in those circumstances I believe that Section 60 is appropriate." Mr Pughsley added: "I think the problem we have with Section 60 is that it is seen by some as an object of protest, and that is a shame because I think it is a useful tool." Labour MP Keith Vaz, who chairs the committee, asked David Tucker, from the Association of Chief Police Officers (Acpo), whether the increased use of Section 60 across the country could lead to more riots. He replied: "I don't want to speculate about the future, but if we are not careful then anything that creates a sense of grievance can lead to disturbance. That is something that all of us in policing, as well as you and other members of the panel, need to be alert to."

The top number tells you how many beats there are in a measure, and the bottom number tells you what kind of note gets one beat. This paper extends the problem of 2-dimensional palindrome search into the area of approximate matching. Using the Hamming distance as the measure, we search for 2D palindromes that allow up to k mismatches in the pattern. This is done by constructing a new data structure, a 2D-trie with multiple paths and a dynamic programming algorithm for efficient approximate matching. Our approach makes use of an enhanced data structure which is based on the Trie, an indexing tree that efficiently stores strings and allows quick search operations. We present several algorithms for searching, insertion and deletion of nodes in the 2D-trie which can be used to quickly find palindromes with up to k mismatches. Finally, we analyze the complexity of our algorithms and discuss their implications for applications.

TikTok is a social media platform that has taken the world by storm. The app has quickly become the go-to destination for short-form mobile videos, entertaining millions of users globally. With its seemingly endless feed of content, many users find themselves spending hours on end scrolling, laughing, and sharing their favorite videos. But what makes TikTok's feed so addictive? According to psychologists, the answer lies in the platform's algorithm. TikTok's algorithm uses artificial intelligence and machine learning to understand each user's behavior and preferences. By analyzing data such as how long a user watches a video or how many times it is played, the algorithm can predict what type of content the user is likely to enjoy and serve it up in their feed. This means that users are constantly being presented with new and exciting content that is tailored to their unique tastes. And as they continue to interact with the content they enjoy, the algorithm becomes even more accurate, leading to a highly personalized feed. Another factor that contributes to TikTok's addictive nature is its emphasis on micro-entertainment. Rather than lengthy videos, TikTok's videos are typically between 15-60 seconds long, making them the perfect bite-sized chunks of content for users to consume during their free time. The app also boasts a highly engaged community of creators who continuously come up with new and creative content, keeping users coming back for more. But while TikTok's feed may seem like pure entertainment, psychologists warn that its algorithm-driven nature can also have negative effects on mental health. The constant flood of content can lead to information overload and feelings of overwhelm, which can be detrimental to well-being. Overall, TikTok's algorithm and micro-entertainment approach are key components in its addictive nature. As the app continues to grow and evolve, it will be interesting to see how its developers balance the desire for engagement and growth with the need to promote healthier technology use.

Each granum can contain anywhere from two to a hundred thylakoids, though typically each granum consists of about ten thylakoids. The thylakoids are arranged in a spiral pattern, with the outermost thylakoid at the base and the innermost thylakoid at the top. The grana thylakoids are connected by stroma lamellae, which contain enzymes that convert light energy into chemical energy. In addition to the enzymes, each stroma lamella also contains proteins and pigments that help absorb and transfer energy. This whole assembly is held together by peripheral proteins, which act like glue and keep the thylakoids in place. The helical arrangement of the thylakoid stack enables the efficient transfer of light energy from one thylakoid to another, thus maximizing photosynthesis.

An activist investor is an individual or group of individuals who buy a significant stake in a publicly traded company with the aim of using their influence to effect changes in the company's management or corporate strategy. Large public corporations are afraid of activist investors because they can disrupt the status quo and demand changes that could impact the company's profitability or position in the market. Activist investors can push for actions such as selling non-core assets, returning capital to shareholders, or changing the composition of the board of directors. They can also demand changes in corporate governance, such as implementing better environmental, social, and governance (ESG) practices or enhancing transparency. The changes an activist investor can bring to a company can vary significantly depending on the specific situation. They may push for short-term changes, such as increased dividends or stock buybacks, or long-term changes, such as strategic acquisitions or divestitures. They can also push for changes that align the company's vision with socially responsible investment goals or focus on increased shareholder value. Ultimately, the goal of an activist investor is to improve the performance and profitability of the company and increase shareholder value.

Short answer No one knows, but most neuroscientists agree that different parts of the brain are responsible for producing different "thoughts" or "feelings." How they originate is still a mystery . Long answer While it is unclear how thoughts and feelings originate, neuroscientists have made significant progress in understanding the mechanisms of thought and emotion. Different parts of the brain are responsible for different functions, and each is involved in producing different thoughts or feelings. The prefrontal cortex is responsible for abstract thinking, planning, decision-making, and problem-solving. The limbic system is responsible for emotions, memories, and drives. The hippocampus helps to store and retrieve memories. The amygdala is responsible for emotional responses such as fear. Finally, the basal ganglia are responsible for unconscious motor control and habit formation. Although scientists have identified these areas of the brain as being involved in producing thoughts and feelings, how they interact to create them remains largely a mystery.
