Adversarial training provides a means of regularizing supervised learning algorithms while virtual adversarial training is able to extend supervised learning algorithms to the semi-supervised setting. However, both methods require making small perturbations to numerous entries of the input vector, which is inappropriate for sparse high-dimensional inputs such as one-hot word representations. We extend adversarial and virtual adversarial training to the text domain by applying perturbations to the word embeddings in a recurrent neural network rather than to the original input itself. The proposed method achieves state of the art results on multiple benchmark semi-supervised and purely supervised tasks. We provide visualizations and analysis showing that the learned word embeddings have improved in quality and that while training, the model is less prone to overfitting.

The art of music captivates souls, and the art of organized destruction captivates and ends lives. This was the singular thought that had taken over Musette's mind for five measures of Moonlight Sonata. The country that had grown from those using the magic of classical music was tiny. It was made of contrasting citizens: middle-aged snobs, twenty-and-thirty-something people who demeaned the snobs with the title of "Pleb," and teenagers. The teenagers made the largest portion of the population, oddly enough. Of all types, they lived: metalheads, Eclectics, musicians. Musette was from an Eclectic family who lived on a border town. Eclectics were never much appreciated because people worried about Eclectics becoming traitors and moving to other genres. "This is the power: to captivate people completely," Musette said to herself. She turned to her cat. "Don't you agree, Franz?" Franz jumped to the piano seat and gave an arm-lick of appreciation. Musette gushed, "I knew you agreed, baby." The roar of a guitar echoed through the streets outside, a D minor. Musette laughed. "It's okay, Franz, they're friends." A scream broke out, indicating that they weren't. Musette put Franz in a backpack with a binder and ran where she knew the loudest speakers were hiding. It's happening. The windows of the Metro showed a dense city. The windows of buildings showed people cowering inside, the inside of the Metro, people riding home and soldiers to the arena. At the arena, Musette jumped out. She noticed a few school friends with binders like her and some adults, soldiers, with violins. Inside the arena was a small area. There were five microphones facing a half-circle of orchestra seats. A piano sat in front. In classical magic, it was easy to mess up keys and render a spell as weaker. Playing wrong notes at the correct tempo modified the spell, but no one could predict how it would turn out. Musette carefully lay down her bag at the piano and sat to begin. Her fingers were already twitching in anticipation. She cursed at the readiness of her fingers, so ready to spit out a melody that they may freeze. The conductor tapped the music stand at the center of the half-circle. "Let's do this s. Symphony eighteen," he growled with finality. Musette took a shaky breath. She was a virtuoso by no means, but she was born with the magic, along with her friends who were there. The air turned purple as soon as the strings started playing. One, two, three, four, five-and six-and. Musette launched herself in. The group generated so much of a charge that her shoulders froze, but she forced her hands to keep going. This was the weapon. The players burst out of the intro and the air turned blue. The speakers boomed, and an amplifier exploded in the distance. For five minutes, they played. Musette played the finals notes just as she was about to pass out. As the battle lay finished, Franz strolled to a microphone. Of course, he just had to meow in key. It took five days to repair the speakers after Franz had cast a spell, short-circuiting them.

The son of an impoverished Bedouin goat herder, Gaddafi became involved in politics while at school in Sabha, subsequently enrolling in the Royal Military Academy, Benghazi. Founding a revolutionary cell within the military, in 1969 they seized power from the absolute monarchy of King Idris in a bloodless coup. Becoming Chairman of the governing Revolutionary Command Council (RCC), Gaddafi abolished the monarchy and proclaimed the Republic. Ruling by decree, he implemented measures to remove what he viewed as foreign imperialist influence from Libya, and strengthened ties to Arab nationalist governments. Intent on pushing Libya towards "Islamic socialism," he introduced sharia as the basis for the legal system and nationalized the oil industry, using the increased revenues to bolster the military, implement social programs and fund revolutionary militants across the world. In 1973 he initiated a "Popular Revolution" with the formation of General People's Committees (GPCs), purported to be a system of direct democracy, but retained personal control over major decisions. He outlined his Third International Theory that year, publishing these ideas in The Green Book.

Solving linear systems boils down to applying a procedure which is based on basic arithmetic. Basic arithmetic is very fast on modern computers. A modern high-end CPU can execute over 300 billion floating point operations per second (additions, subtraction, multiplication are examples of floating point operations). A modern GPU can achieve an order of magnitude more, a Nvidia GTX 980 can in an ideal scenario execute over 4000 billion floating point operations per second. To really get these numbers you need to do a lot of the operations in parallel, but linear algebra is very easy to do in parallel. You usually have a lot of numbers that you need to do the same kind of operation to at the same time, and that is precisely what modern computers do best.

There are thought to have been as many as 200m downloads of period tracking apps worldwide. But a leading UK medical royal college has warned that women should not rely on them as a form of contraception. And privacy campaigners say users should be wary of what data they might unwittingly be sharing when they download some apps. A search for period tracking apps will quickly bring up dozens of offerings - some with charts, others illustrated with pink tulips or lilac flowers. In the health and fitness category, period trackers come second only to apps which monitor running. Amy Worsfold, from Greenwich, south-east London, has used different trackers for three years. She is a soprano opera singer. Amy told me: "When you are starting your period or you're pre-menstrual, the hormones that rush around your body affect your larynx in ways that are detrimental to your singing voice. "I use the app to avoid auditions, premieres or really important performances on those days if I can." She plots and predicts her cycle on her smartphone. The app also helps her identify connections with changes in her emotions, eating habits and headaches. Amy added: "Being able to chart what happens to you and how you uniquely respond to your cycle is a great way of taking ownership of something that really sucks - but is completely necessary." Sometimes women download period trackers to monitor their fertility. But the Royal College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists has warned they should not be used as a form of contraception. Only one such app on the market has been independently evaluated for effectiveness in this area. Generally, they are not classed as medical devices, which would involve stricter regulation. Ida Tin is the Berlin-based Danish entrepreneur behind an app called Clue. Around 10 of her market is in the UK. She said: "I wanted to develop the next generation of technology for family planning - and I do believe we'll get there. But we're not there yet." Women in Mexico and Brazil have recently shown huge interest in Clue, possibly because of fears about getting pregnant during the Zika virus outbreak. Ida Tin is interested in how anonymised user data from her free app can be used for the greater good. To this end, she is collaborating with medical researchers at Oxford University. She has built her business on a responsible approach. She added: "The app is a very powerful tool. I can't do what our users want me to do unless I use their data. "I appreciate I'm asking people for a lot of trust in me, but a lot of companies [in the same line of work as mine] don't honour that trust." Some apps which are more firmly pointed at conception have a clear value to advertisers - as a woman planning a baby is a potential market for prams, clothing and many other purchases. Sam Smith is a privacy campaigner at medConfidential. He said: "For all medical apps, but especially for conception apps, there needs to be a source people can trust that's independent and says this app is safe for you. "You can read the terms and conditions - and legally you are required to. But everybody knows that nobody does." He sees the lack of regulation, or even official recommendation, as a market failure in this area. His advice is that if an app is free, consider whether you are paying for it in effect by giving away your data - and investigate where it might be going.

In a speech he said, given the effects of the referendum vote, the government had to be "realistic about achieving a surplus by the end of the decade." The target had been the chancellor's most prized goal and had been driving austerity measures in previous budgets. But he said the economy is showing "clear signs" of shock following the vote to leave the European Union. Giving a speech in Manchester, Mr Osborne said: "The referendum is expected to produce a significant negative economic shock to our economy. How we respond will determine the impact on jobs and growth. "We must provide fiscal credibility, continuing to be tough on the deficit while being realistic about achieving a surplus by the end of the decade." Labour's shadow chancellor John McDonnell welcomed the move, saying: "Sadly the vote last Thursday for Brexit has only brought forward what was inevitable. "The Chancellor had already dropped his other fiscal rules on welfare and debt at the Budget in March, and according to many economists he was expected to be forced to drop this one too." BBC business editor Kamal Ahmed says that the target was heading for the "Treasury shredding machine" following a speech from Home Secretary Theresa May yesterday. In a speech launching her bid to become prime minister she said "we should no longer seek to reach a budget surplus by the end of the parliament." Kamal says that Mr Osborne has now followed suit. Nevertheless, the Treasury insists that it still wants to balance the books and "fix the finances." Mr Osborne first committed himself to returning the national finances to surplus by 2020 at the Conservative Party conference in 2013 and it became policy in the July budget of 2015. But there have been questions ever since over whether that target could be met. Even before the referendum vote he only had "a slightly better than 5050 chance" of making the target said Carl Emmerson, deputy director of the Institute for Fiscal Studies. But the uncertainty caused by the Leave vote could hold back the economy and make creating a surplus even more difficult. "Having voted for Brexit last week, the economy is clearly going to go into a downswing, that might be a full-blown recession, that might just be very very low growth," said Paul Johnson the director of the IFS. It is sometimes easy in these incredible political times to forget that for most people "it's the economy, stupid" still holds true. For the UK economy, one of the most important passages of Theresa May's speech yesterday was when she signalled that George Osborne's "fiscal rule" (to produce a budget surplus by 2020) was for the Treasury shredding machine. "While it is absolutely vital that the government continues with its intention to reduce public spending and cut the budget deficit, we should no longer seek to reach a budget surplus by the end of the parliament," Mrs May said. Now the chancellor has said he agrees, arguing that the government must be "realistic" about its fiscal targets and that austerity policies could be eased. My Treasury sources point out that the "rule" can be varied in "non-normal" times. And these are pretty "non-normal" times. The abandonment of the fiscal target suggests the government could borrow more, presumably for investment in infrastructure and to mitigate the need for tax rises and spending cuts, if the economy does take a turn for the worse as some predict. Owner Cuerden Leisure is selling Blackpool's South and Central Piers and the Grade II listed Llandudno Pier. St John Stott, director at Cuerden Leisure, which also owns Eastbourne Pier, said the company was "restructuring its assets." Blackpool North Pier was bought by a local businessman in 2011. Collectively, they are on the market for offers of around PS12.6m, with individual guide prices of PS4.8m for Blackpool Central, PS3.3m for Blackpool South and PS4.5m for Llandudno Pier. Blackpool Central Pier is home to a 33m high (108ft) Ferris wheel, Blackpool South Pier and Llandudno Pier were all built in the 19th Century. Llandudno, which is 695m long (2,280ft), is the only pier with listed building status meaning any future owners would require Listed Building Consent to make changes to the structure. Known as the "Queen of Welsh Piers," it nestles in the crescent bay between the outcrops of the Little and Great Orme. Blackpool Central Pier, which stands at 341m long (1,118ft), and Blackpool South Pier, which is 150m (492ft), do not benefit from listed status, despite opening in 1864 and 1892 respectively. Richard Baldwin, a director at Bilfinger GVA, which is selling the piers for Cuerden Leisure, said it would be very unlikely that a new owner would make significant changes. He said: "In our opinion, the value is in the existing use and this is unlikely to change at either of the Blackpool piers." A spokesman for the National Piers Society, which promotes the preservation and continued enjoyment of seaside piers in the UK, said: "These piers are all in good order and trading successfully, and, given that Easter is almost upon us, I have no doubt that they will quickly find a buyer or buyers."

When Lady Fatale finally found her boyfriend, moisture was dripping down the bathroom mirror like it was caught in a summer rainstorm. She switched on the fan and began groping her way through the steam, towards the sound of running water that almost drowned out the faint sobbing. One stubbed toe on a bathroom scale later, she found Doctor DNA curled up on the shower floor. " I don't suppose you were waiting for me to join you? " she said as she reached to turn the water off. Switching it to cold crossed her mind, but she thought better of it. " You heard, didn't you? " She sighed. " Yes. It's all over the news. " " Did they discover the message? " " I don't know. But they know it was you. " " Gentlemen of the United Nations, " he intoned, " by now you've discovered the terrifying effects of Forced Evolution. Beautiful, isn't it? The way the slightest change to chromosomes, the tiniest tweak in our blueprints can twist the flesh and mutate the mind. The virus is contagious, untraceable, and quite expensive - if you want the antidote. " I wrote that my sophomore year. I used to doodle pictures of limbs-turned-tentacles, eyestalks, mandibles..... " " And now you've cured cancer, " she finished. " Everything, " he said gravely. " Although it'll take another week to confirm the common cold. " Lady Fatale draped a towel over his shoulders and kissed his forehead. " It'll work better next time, hun. " " There is no next time. I spent eight years on the equations alone, eleven months double-checking it. This was my one shot. " A ringtone echoed through the bathroom; it was her " Unknown Caller " song. " Don't answer, " he murmured. " I shut mine off an hour ago. Someone leaked it online. It's been nothing but interviews, job offers, and " Thank you, oh, thank you " for hours. " " Job offers is good, " she said carefully. He'd always been sensitive about living off her earnings. " And interviews, I mean, it's still publicity. You've got your name out there now, at least people know you can cause a worldwide phenomenon. So what if the Cronenberg Strain was a bust? You still have - what was it - " The Metallic Marrow Virus," right? You've been hinting at that one for a while now. " " But what's the point? No matter what I do, I'm still the man who invented the Ultimate Cure. The Metrocity Globe called me the ' Final Doctor '. " " That's just it! I always thought it was hokey, that idea of living like it's your last day. I was always a cynical piece of shit. I believed that if you knew that a day was your last day, you were more liable to start a riot or just cry constantly in the fetal position than actually do anything meaningful with your life. But you never really know how something's going to feel until you go through it. We're all stuck in our own heads that way. So when the day came, when I woke up to that post stickied at the top of reddit, I didn't react the way a movie character would react. The first thing I did was double check that it wasn't April Fools day, obviously. I told you I'm a cynical piece of shit. When I was sure that it was real, I called my mom. We held an impromptu family reunion in the park. I don't know what happened, but it just kept growing. My mom and dad invited their siblings, but then their siblings invited their spouses' families, and so on, until there was a huge crowd of people I had basically no relation to. We sat around drinking and told stories and played cards at the table. An ex-girlfriend showed up at some point to apologize to me. I guess that's what she was doing with her day, just making amends. I told her that I forgave her. I didn't really, but it felt like the thing to do. Some people from one of the local churches came out and passed out candles to everyone when it started getting dark. Some of us chilled in a circle and listened to the hymns. I've never really believed in that stuff, but the songs were nice anyway. I can't pretend like I didn't have sex "one last time." One of my co-workers hit me up with a text and I'm a hotblooded American male. But it was nice. It was gentle and we cuddled afterwards. You know, that sappy shit. She wasn't on good terms with her family and didn't have any plans, so I invited her back to the park. A bunch of my family had a campfire set up. We fell asleep there, her head on my chest. I remember my mom kissing my forehead as I was drifting off. I woke up dirty. Literally, covered in dirt. That's what happens when you fall asleep in a park. All around me, people were confused. My coworker was gone. I found her sitting on a bench, speaking on her phone. She looked up at me when she hung up, eyes shining with anger. "They got it wrong! " I'd never seen her angry before. She had always been kind of a doormat. "It MISSED US! They announced to the entire world that it was going to hit and it fucking MISSED US!" " ..... Shit." I didn't know what to say. "Wow. What the fuck?" She ranted about how irresponsible it was for them to do this, but I was distracted by how confident she seemed. She'd given something up, expecting the end. We all had. I'd given up some of my bravado and let myself be soft. She'd let go of her fear and become confident. "Hey." I interjected, when she paused to take a breath. "You're right, this is totally inexcusable, but if the world's really not gon na end..... do you want to get dinner with me tonight or something?" It didn't work out between us, not in the long run. She was too nice, I was still a cynical piece of shit. But things ended on good terms. That's kind of the crux of it, of everything that happened after that day. When the world "ended," it ended on good terms. Not for everyone, but for most people. People spent that day with their family, or thinking about the good they could have done. They connected with their fellow man. The truly unhappy people killed themselves ahead of time or when they found out it wasn't coming. So the world that was left behind was..... softer. More empathetic. Slower to judge. It can't last forever. Two years have passed now and I can already feel it dying out, the rhetoric becoming hateful and vitriolic again. But I still think it was for the best. Sometimes people need to actually be faced with the capital-e End before they're going to change. People are dumb that way. Anyway, this is all just to say that I disagree with giving those astronomers the death penalty.

Alloying copper with tin to make bronze was first practiced about 4000 years after the discovery of copper smelting, and about 2000 years after "natural bronze" had come into general use[citation needed]. Bronze artifacts from the Vinca culture date to 4500 BC. Sumerian and Egyptian artifacts of copper and bronze alloys date to 3000 BC. The Bronze Age began in Southeastern Europe around 3700-3300 BC, in Northwestern Europe about 2500 BC. It ended with the beginning of the Iron Age, 2000-1000 BC in the Near East, 600 BC in Northern Europe. The transition between the Neolithic period and the Bronze Age was formerly termed the Chalcolithic period (copper-stone), with copper tools being used with stone tools. This term has gradually fallen out of favor because in some parts of the world the Chalcolithic and Neolithic are coterminous at both ends. Brass, an alloy of copper and zinc, is of much more recent origin. It was known to the Greeks, but became a significant supplement to bronze during the Roman Empire.

Across a majority of pedestrian detection datasets, it is typically assumed that pedestrians will be standing upright with respect to the image coordinate system. This assumption however, is not always valid for many vision-equipped mobile platforms such as mobile phones, UAVs or construction vehicles on rugged terrain. In these situations, the motion of the camera can cause images of pedestrians to be captured at extreme angles. This can lead to very poor pedestrian detection performance when using standard pedestrian detectors. To address this issue, we propose a Rotational Rectification Network (R2N) that can be inserted into any CNN-based pedestrian (or object) detector to adapt it to significant changes in camera rotation. The rotational rectification network uses a 2D rotation estimation module that passes rotational information to a spatial transformer network to undistort image features. To enable robust rotation estimation, we propose a Global Polar Pooling (GP-Pooling) operator to capture rotational shifts in convolutional features. Through our experiments, we show how our rotational rectification network can be used to improve the performance of the state-of-the-art pedestrian detector under heavy image rotation by up to 45.

In quantum mechanics, each particle isn't a tiny chunk of matter that you can point to, it is instead a cloud of probability about where that particle is. So there might be a 99 chance that a particle is here, a 0.9999999999999999 chance that it is there but also a 0.0000000000000001 chance that it is on the other side of the galaxy. The mathematics gives you possible solutions for where the particle can be and the superposition is the combination of all those possible solutions, which itself is a possible solution to the mathematics. i.e. the particle is here, there and halfway to the Andromeda galaxy all at the same time.

The Big Data analytics are a logical analysis of very large scale datasets. The data analysis enhances an organization and improve the decision making process. In this article, we present Airline Delay Analysis and Prediction to analyze airline datasets with the combination of weather dataset. In this research work, we consider various attributes to analyze flight delay, for example, day-wise, airline-wise, cloud cover, temperature, etc. Moreover, we present rigorous experiments on various machine learning model to predict correctly the delay of a flight, namely, logistic regression with L2 regularization, Gaussian Naive Bayes, K-Nearest Neighbors, Decision Tree classifier and Random forest model. The accuracy of the Random Forest model is 82 with a delay threshold of 15 minutes of flight delay. The analysis is carried out using dataset from 1987 to 2008, the training is conducted with dataset from 2000 to 2007 and validated prediction result using 2008 data. Moreover, we have got recall 99 in the Random Forest model.

The baby sitting next to me was the first to realize the plane was going down. From the second we lifted off the ground, he cried like hell, squirming in his mother's arms, trying desperately to get off the already sinking ship. "It's her first flight," her mother would say with a grin to whomever she could. The enormous man sitting on my left was the next to realize the flight's inevitable fate. About an hour in he fell asleep, resting his head atop my shoulder. "This is why," I thought to myself. "This is exactly why I'm going to the seminar." That weekend I would be attending a very informal class on the ins and outs of serial killing. I figured 27 was a decent age to make the move from gingerly squishing spiders in my apartment to simple murder. It wasn't until we were 6 hours into the flight that the remaining passengers gained knowledge of our plane's engine failure. This was partly due to the pilot's careful explanation of the problem at hand and partly because the plan starting falling, nose pointed downwards, toward the coast of Portugal. Passengers screamed, cried with mouths full of pretzels and peanuts, hugged their loved ones. The baby on my right had suddenly been silenced. He looked out the windows at the horizon rising fast, a slight smile on his face. His mother followed his lead, keeping silent, tears streaming down her face. With a jolt, the man next to me awoke, noticed his situation, and started grabbing for something inside his carry-on. As the horizon outside the window rose higher and higher, I realized I was living my last few minutes. The pilot, now barely audible spoke over the intercom, informing us to prepare for proper procedures. He let out a defeated sigh at the end of his speech, "You know what," he muttered. "Spend these last few minutes with your family." Immediately, I set out looking for an appropriate target for my first and only kill. I glanced at the baby and his mother, still quietly looking out the dirty window. I guess I just couldn't bring myself to strangle either of those two - I wasn't completely evil. I turned to my left, where the fat man was trying to open a little case he had dug out of his backpack with shaky hands. Eyeing his neck, I realized my hands weren't physically big enough to strangle him either. I unbuckled my seat belt and started climbing around him toward the aisle separating the two rows of seats. A teenage girl in the aisle screamed as a suitcase from the overheard storage flew directly into her head. A flight attendant's cart sped down the aisle, an assortment of drinks and snacks flying off as it hit each row. Finally, I stepped in the aisle and started looking for my victim. I was considering killing the businessman a couple rows in front of mine who stepped on my toe just before departure at the terminal when I felt hands around my neck. I didn't need to turn around - the giant hands let me know exactly who my killer was. - This is one of my first stories. I really would like feedback on how to improve my writing. 333

In this paper, we analyze the outage performance of two multicarrier relay selection schemes, i.e. bulk and per-subcarrier selections, for two-hop orthogonal frequency-division multiplexing (OFDM) systems. To provide a comprehensive analysis, three forwarding protocols: decode-and-forward (DF), fixed-gain (FG) amplify-and-forward (AF) and variable-gain (VG) AF relay systems are considered. We obtain closed-form approximations for the outage probability and closed-form expressions for the asymptotic outage probability in the high signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) region for all cases. Our analysis is verified by Monte Carlo simulations, and provides an analytical framework for multicarrier systems with relay selection.

Duverger's law. Basically because we have a system where the winner takes all (so the president or congressman being elected represents 51 of the population at minimum) we naturally tend to split into the two party system. Imagine you have 10 people voting on what kind of pizza to order. Some are vegetarian and some are meat lovers. Whoever gets the most votes gets to order the pizza for everyone. Now, 4 people are vegetarians and will vote for the veggie lovers pizza, and 6 are meat-lovers. However, 3 of those 6 want pepperoni, and 3 want Canadian bacon. If you tally up the votes the vegetarians would win and get their way, even though more people wanted meat on their pizza, but because they split up over a smaller detail they lost all together. The same works for politics. If 45 are conservative and 55 are liberal, then you'd expect the democrats to win. However, if a socialist is also running and gets 15 of the liberal vote then the election turns out like this: 40 democrats, 45 republicans, and 15 socialists. So, even though more people are liberal and would vote democrat, because of the split in the Democratic Party the conservatives win the election. So if my first choice is socialist, and my second choice is democrat, if I vote socialist the democrats are all that more likely to lose to the republicans and the socialists never stood a chance anyway. So I essentially not only threw my vote away to a party that won't win, I took votes from my second favorite option and allowed the republicans to garner more votes overall,because of our voting structure. CGP Grey has a good and simple explanation of how this happens. 15 people spent 40 days living in a cave in France without sunlight, clocks, or contact with the outside world as part of an experiment called Deep Time. Participants had to pass mental and physical examinations before the experiment, and they were monitored even after their exit. The experiment could help scientists anticipate the challenges of long-term submarine and space missions.

Pairwise ordered tree alignment are combinatorial objects that appear in RNA secondary structure comparison. However, the usual representation of tree alignments as supertrees is ambiguous, i.e. two distinct supertrees may induce identical sets of matches between identical pairs of trees. This ambiguity is uninformative, and detrimental to any probabilistic analysis. In this work, we consider tree alignments up to equivalence. Our first result is a precise asymptotic enumeration of tree alignments, obtained from a context-free grammar by mean of basic analytic combinatorics. Our second result focuses on alignments between two given ordered trees S and T . By refining our grammar to align specific trees, we obtain a decomposition scheme for the space of alignments, and use it to design an efficient dynamic programming algorithm for sampling alignments under the Gibbs-Boltzmann probability distribution. This generalizes existing tree alignment algorithms, and opens the door for a probabilistic analysis of the space of suboptimal RNA secondary structures alignments.

A ground isn't necessary, it's the neutral that is necessary. Only two wires are required and in the US, older homes had only two wires. The ground is only for safety: it's an isolated wire that is an "extra" path for electricity in case something goes wrong. The metal parts of an appliance are all connected to the ground, so that if a hot wire somehow gets in contact with something it shouldn't, the electricity will flow through the ground wire instead of through you. The electrical ground (the third wire) is not normally used, and is literally connected to the ground (the earth, dirt) near the main electrical connection to the home.',Ground" actually means two slightly related things. The traditional definition is literally a connection to the earth, usually used for safety. In case of a problem, high current can be directed to the ground instead of up your arm or somewhere that'll catch fire. This works because the earth is basically an infinitely large sink; current usually needs to travel in a loop, but if it gets dumped into the earth it just dissipates, rather than returning to its source. The other meaning ground is used in circuit design and analysis. Technically, a voltage measurement must be between two points in a circuit; for example, the voltage of a battery is between its two terminals. When you have a complicated circuit, it's easier to pick one common point and call it a reference, so that it's one implied point for a voltage measurement at any other point. Rather than saying "the voltage between point A and point B is x," you can just say "the voltage at point A is x." It also makes circuits easier to draw, because you can just draw the ground symbol where there's a connection to ground, rather than drawing all the wires connecting the ground points.

Drone is pushing down as much air as it weighs. Drone weight goes away, air pushing-down-weight replaces it. Weight of all the things in the box stays the same. Think legs. You weigh the same stood on one leg as you do standing on two, because your mass is unchanged, you're just using a smaller support.','Because the drone applies a force to the air in the box, which in turn applies a force to the box that is equal to the weight of the drone.','The drone hovers by pushing air down at a force that is equal to the force of gravity on the drone. These equal and opposite forces cancel each other out and that's why the drone hovers in one spot. The air being forced down will hit the floor of the box at the same force, therefore pushing down on the box (and scale) with the same forceweight as the if the drone wasn't hovering.... and therefore the box will weight the same. This was tested by mythbusters in episode 77: URL0', "The drone creates downwash with equivalent pressure to the weight of the drone. If drone is moving up, the pressure is higher if it's moving down pressure is lower. At higher altitude the downwash is still there but the area pressure is applied to, is much larger. In a closed system, like it is with a drone in the box, air circulates and is applied to an area of certain size to minimize the loss of energy while weighing.,For a drone to fly, it's propellers have to push down enough air to counteract its weight. Air goes down - drone goes up. So when the drone is hovering, it's pushing its exact weight in air down below it. So when a scales under it, it will read the same weight wether the drone is sitting on it, or hovering above it.

The problem of distributed formation control of nonholonomic mobile robots is addressed in this paper, in which the robots are designed to track a formation. Collision avoidance among agents is guaranteed using a control law based on a repulsive force. In an uncertain environment where obstacles exist, the construction of a repulsive force and rotational direction enables agents to avoid and pass the obstacles. The control inputs of each robot are designed to be bounded. Numerical simulations with different formations are implemented to demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed scheme.

Culture Minister Helen Grant told MPs their future was "unresolved" and bookmakers must take immediate action to increase protection for players. People can wager PS100 every 20 seconds on fixed-odds betting terminals. Labour said they were "an example of David Cameron's Britain" and councils should have new powers to curb them. But following a Commons debate, Labour's call for local authorities to be given new powers to restrict the growth of the machines was defeated by 314 to 232 votes. There are more than 33,000 fixed-odds betting terminals in the UK. The last Labour government relaxed the gambling laws, allowing bookmakers to start installing them. But the party has accused the gambling industry of exploiting those changes to target poorer parts of the country, It says fixed-odds betting terminals are acting as a magnet for crime and anti-social behaviour and local authorities should be given new powers to deal with "clusters" of shops opening together. They would also review the number of high-speed, high-stakes fixed-odds betting terminals allowed on bookmakers' premises and would take steps to make the machines less addictive by requiring pop-ups and breaks in play. Shadow culture minister Clive Efford said the last government had always maintained the machines should be kept under review. The "world had changed" since they were first licensed, he said, with the online gambling industry now worth more than PS2bn. "These machines are an example of Cameron's Britain - one rule for constituents and another for big business which operate the betting shops," he said. Another Labour MP, Brian Donohue, said fixed-odds betting terminals had been "likened to cocaine" as they were "absolutely and totally addictive." Ministers insist that local authorities can already reject applications for new gambling premises and review existing licences. But Ms Grant acknowledged the growth of the machines was "concerning" and she expected the industry to introduce voluntary player protection measures, such as suspensions in play and automatic alerts when stakes hit a certain level, by March. She said the government was waiting for the findings of a study into "how [the machines] are used and the real impact on players" before deciding what further action may be needed. "There is no green light for these machines. Their future is unresolved pending the research we have started," she told MPs. Labour, she added, had liberalised gambling laws and accused them of "rank hypocrisy, total cynicism and outright opportunism." "Labour bought these machines into being and they have the audacity to bring forward a motion blaming the government for any harm caused," she said. The gambling industry insists it does not target deprived areas and has introduced a code of conduct for player protection and responsible gaming. "Betting is a pursuit enjoyed by millions of working class people throughout Britain and we seek to reach the widest audience possible by being present on High Streets," the Association of British Bookmakers said. "We accept there are concerns about these gaming machines and are always open to a constructive dialogue with politicians about the appropriate powers for local authorities." It added: "The claims of widespread problem gambling on machines is just not supported by evidence. The industry continues to develop its approach to harm mitigation for the small number of gamblers who do experience problems." MPs have previously rejected calls from Labour to reduce the maximum stake from PS100 to PS2 and to cut the top prize from the current PS500.

In this paper, a special decision surface for the weakly-supervised sound event detection (SED) and a disentangled feature (DF) for the multi-label problem in polyphonic SED are proposed. We approach SED as a multiple instance learning (MIL) problem and utilize a neural network framework with a pooling module to solve it. General MIL approaches include two kinds: the instance-level approaches and embedding-level approaches. We present a method of generating instance-level probabilities for the embedding level approaches which tend to perform better than the instance-level approaches in terms of bag-level classification but can not provide instance-level probabilities in current approaches. Moreover, we further propose a specialized decision surface (SDS) for the embedding-level attention pooling. We analyze and explained why an embedding-level attention module with SDS is better than other typical pooling modules from the perspective of the high-level feature space. As for the problem of the unbalanced dataset and the co-occurrence of multiple categories in the polyphonic event detection task, we propose a DF to reduce interference among categories, which optimizes the high-level feature space by disentangling it based on class-wise identifiable information and obtaining multiple different subspaces. Experiments on the dataset of DCASE 2018 Task 4 show that the proposed SDS and DF significantly improve the detection performance of the embedding-level MIL approach with an attention pooling module and outperform the first place system in the challenge by 6.6 percentage points.

Disclaimer: I'm from the UK, so this is what I feel may be possible in the near future in my country. I am unsure about larger and poorer places. First off, assumptions (or prerequisites): Everyone has unlimited access to the internet, be it at home on a PClaptop or through the local library etc. There is an ultimately secure system which allows anonymous voting and political discussion through a secure server (for example using a specific machine, separate from any other technology, issued to each person with personalised PIN numbersfingerprint technology and multiple layers of encryption running on a server probably kept separate from the internet but which works in a similar way, state controlled and free). There has been an education programme running for at least 40 years showing people the value of politics and debate. Teaching children the critical thinking skills needed to assess an issue in a balanced and unbiased way. Explaining the basics of law so all laws, whether they are being drafted or have been passed, can be understood by a high school graduate. People can only engage in this voting and discussion system if they have graduated from these courses. The courses also have to be centrally controlled. OPTIONAL (but I think it is important): Compulsory national service after graduation. However instead of having this in the military, it must be in all areas of public service through a series of rotations. This way everyone will gain experience in the areas which legislation will have an impact on. Continuous political education. There must be a dedicated and unbiased TV channelnewspaper etc. dedicated to the current political status, focusing on legislation being drafted. This will include expert synopsis of the drafts and debates between people for and against the legislation. If lobbyists and pressure groups were to end up anywhere, it would be here where they would get their voice heard. The key is that they cannot pay anyone or pressure anyone to vote the way they want. They have to actually convince the public to do so. Ok, second part. Clauses (or ideas): There are no representatives. This means no MPs or PMs, in the USA there would be no congressmen, senators or president. This also means that their can be no parties. Reason: Representation means putting the choices of many in the hands of the few, as a result it is not representative. Considering modern technology and the ability to communicate instantaneously with everyone, this is pointless. Also unlike communism this will not lead to a one-party state, but instead to a no-party state. And as there are no representatives and no-one at the head of the country, corruption and totalitarianism is less agreeable. Everyone who has graduated can vote, individually, through the use of their unique ID (think social security numbers) on each and every piece of legislation. Reason: This is true representation. Instead of voting in a party who will bring in some acts which you may agree with and some acts which you don't agree with, you get to pick and choose exactly what you want. No more picking the better of two evils. Legislation is drafted by a randomly chosen panel of experts, picked from a pool of the countries top workers in the relevant areas (the size of the pool will depend on the population of the country). Legal advisors and aid will be provided. Each person is only allowed to work on one piece of legislation in their lives. Once this has happened they are immediately removed from the pool. Each person must do so anonymously, and cannot turn down this duty except in exceptional circumstance. All work they do is extremely confidential and will be essentially treated like jury duty. Anyone who violates the above will be stripped of their right to this process, will be removed from the panel and will be punished (punishment hasn't been decided). Reason: Stops bias as people with no experience in an area continuously work on all the legislation in that area. Through this way they may end up instigating pieces of legislation which are unrealistic. The anonymity of it is an attempt to decrease the chance of lobbyists or anyone else trying to influence those on the panel. The priority legislation of that moment is decided through social trends (at least partly measured through social media). Trends are prioritised and listed. They are then passed to a waiting list and those which are strongly related compiled into single units. A panel is chosen and notified so as to start the drafting process. Reason: Just one possible way of deciding what is important to the population. The drafting process is open-source within reason. The actual draft is shown to the public at all stages of the process. It cannot be changed by the public, but anyone who has an ID can comment on parts of the draft and make suggestions. This is where the reddit style forum comes in to play. Comments can be upvoted and agreed with (as well as commented on), this increases visibility of the comment and once it has passed a threshold it must be seriously considered by the drafting panel. Reason: To ensure complete representation of the public opinion everyone has to be allowed some input and influence in some way. However as they may not have expert knowledge of the field they cannot be allowed to actually change the draft. This is a decent way to allow crowd sourced input into a document for experts to be guided by. A self-regulatory report system may be put in place to ensure the conversation remains serious. Compulsory education to 18 as mentioned above in the prerequisites. Also governmentally provided classes which can allow recaps or further study in these political or social based areas. Reason: ensuring everyone's full ability to understand the system. Ensured and compulsory time to get involved. You must be allowed some time each day by your workplace to participate in debate, or to just lurk and get to gripa with it all. Voting will be done on specific days (once every month? Every other week?). This will be accompanied by consistent reminders and obligatory time to vote. Reason: trying to ensure everyone can get involved. Majority votes over 50 are required for legislation to be passed into a bill. Reason: Otherwise it's not really representative! Hellenistic warfare was a continuation of the military developments of Iphicrates and Philip II of Macedon, particularly his use of the Macedonian Phalanx, a dense formation of pikemen, in conjunction with heavy companion cavalry. Armies of the Hellenistic period differed from those of the classical period in being largely made up of professional soldiers and also in their greater specialization and technical proficiency in siege warfare. Hellenistic armies were significantly larger than those of classical Greece relying increasingly on Greek mercenaries (misthophoroi; men-for-pay) and also on non-Greek soldiery such as Thracians, Galatians, Egyptians and Iranians. Some ethnic groups were known for their martial skill in a particular mode of combat and were highly sought after, including Tarantine cavalry, Cretan archers, Rhodian slingers and Thracian peltasts. This period also saw the adoption of new weapons and troop types such as Thureophoroi and the Thorakitai who used the oval Thureos shield and fought with javelins and the machaira sword. The use of heavily armored cataphracts and also horse archers was adopted by the Seleucids, Greco-Bactrians, Armenians and Pontus. The use of war elephants also became common. Seleucus received Indian war elephants from the Mauryan empire, and used them to good effect at the battle of Ipsus. He kept a core of 500 of them at Apameia. The Ptolemies used the smaller African elephant.

Timothy was sleepy. Every Monday was the same thing. The classroom lets you sleepy: the half-light, the fans rhythmic noise, the girl's talk, the lessons - math mainly - everything. Honestly, that happens almost every day. Tim hated to wake up early. He was sitting down, waiting for his turn to continue the text that Amy, the girl in front of him, was reading. Every two months her teacher chose a literary work for the class read together and "Red Riding Hood" was the flavor of the month. Amy had that kind of hoarsely voice, which make everything almost unbearable for him. He looked to his side and started to watch some kids playing in the yard outside. His desk was the last of the row, right by the window, in the corner of the classroom. That wall was his pillow and the window was his one way ticket to the world of the sleepy and fruitful minds. He loved the sport's classes. It was infinitely funnier to play dodgeball or even volley - which the other boys claimed to be a "girlie" game - than being stuck in that classroom all day, learning things that he judged to useless in real life. He was absolutely sure that if, rather than wield a sword, Link had learned about tapeworms and solitary, or the procreation method of hermaphrodite beings he never, and I repeat, never would have saved Princess Zelda. He never understood why instead of learing Bhaskara, they wouldn't teach something useful like..... ..... like Hadouken! Really, think about the possibilities. You get home, in the middle fo the night and find the door ajar. The house is quiet and you suspect that whoever did that is gone already. But when you turn on the kitchen lights you find a hooded person, pointing a gun at you. You have two options: you can yell the quadratic equation on all its glory and simply get killed in the most stupid way ever - or in the best case scenario make the thief laugh his ass of and then get a bullet in the head. Or the second option, that would be just to yell "Hadouken!" and blow out the kitchen, the living room of the house next door and as a bonus, kill the burglar. Honestly, which one is the best? - Tim. Well, giving it a second thought I believe that a kame-hame-ha suits the situation better. Even though it takes more time to charge..... - Timmy. In the other hand, taking into consideration the destruction power, the winner is definitely the Genki Dama. Oh yeah! Just imagine how..... - Timothy Blake! Please! You know that terrible feeling when you leave a dark room and go straight to the sun light? That's exctly how Timothy felt when his name was called out loud and cristal clear. Mrs. Garner just took him off his mind battle between his favorite characters super powers. The whole class staring at him, some holding their laughs, others just looking in disapproval. Amy was smiling her best braces-ornamented "steel-smile." She used that thiing since he first knew her. She should have a rare condition..... - Timothy, if you don't want to read, that's fine. But please, don't make us wait for you to come back from dreamland. The classroom exploded in laugh. Timothy suffered from "attention deficit hyperactivity disorder," or ADHD, or in his mom own words: he couldn't pay attention to something for more than 5 minutes. He would think about everything and nothing at the same time. He would stop in the middle of the street if something gets his attention and risk being hit by some driver more inattentive than himself. As his friedns would say: he tripped. He never reads. He never talks. And no one ever talks to him. And no one was waiting this time to be different. And then the scream. Tim looked down the window and saw a bunch of other kids forming a circle around someone. The climbing frames was getting crowded by curious kids looking for some insider view. Then he saw coach Anderson running through the people trying to get into the circle. He asked to the kids to back off so whoever it was could get some room for breathing. Timothy recognized the girl that was laying on the ground but he couldn't remember her name. - Oh my God! That's Nina! - someone shouted behind him. Thanks for that, he thought. Coach Anderson was kind of desperate as the number of people was increasing. He started to ask for help. Other teachers ran to his assistance and started to get the kids back to their classrooms. One of the teachers screamed and asked someone to call 911. Another teacher just hugged her and got her out of there. Some students started to take pictures with their cell phones. More teachers came and among them was the school's principal. Things were getting intense. When the paramedics arrived and the kids were kept at a safe distance, Tim and the others could get a clear picture of the scenario. The girl was laying on the ground and a metallic bar was just a couple of steps away from her. Tim noticed that a bar was missing from the top of the climbing frames. Her face was looking towards Tim's class, but she wasn't moving, or blinking. Or breathing. After all the efforts were done, the paramedics put the little girl on a stretcher and closed the zipper of a black bag. - Timothy Blake! - shouted Mrs Garner. Tim woke up with a jump. Looked around. Deja-vu. Everybody was quiet around him. They were staring at him. Some were playing with their tablets, others just talking among themselves in secret but always giving him a glimpse. They were kind of waiting for something. - Please Tim. Continue the reading. Try this time, please. Then he just realized he had slept. Fear crawled his back with its cold and sharp fangs. He was shaking. A tear just rolled down his face from the side. - Are you okay Tim? what happened darling? I'm not mad at you sweetie. You don't need to feel like that. - Mrs Garner said sweetly. And then the classroom just heard a scream. The scream of a girl that just died.

Stack Overflow was created to help developers easily search for answers. It has an upvotedownvote system put in place to let users decide what questions are appropriate for the platform. Some questions, even if well-written, on-topic, and helpful for other developers, are being downvoted for unknown reasons by other users, sometimes resulting in a lot of negative feedback. Many people downvote already downvoted questions just because these questions had negative feedback and they felt like they had to contribute. This can discourage users from contributing, especially if they are new. If the negative culture continues, it may be that the site will eventually just become new users who don't have experience asking questions and older users complaining about the lack of quality on the site.

Wearable orthoses can function both as assistive devices, which allow the user to live independently, and as rehabilitation devices, which allow the user to regain use of an impaired limb. To be fully wearable, such devices must have intuitive controls, and to improve quality of life, the device should enable the user to perform Activities of Daily Living. In this context, we explore the feasibility of using electromyography (EMG) signals to control a wearable exotendon device to enable pick and place tasks. We use an easy to don, commodity forearm EMG band with 8 sensors to create an EMG pattern classification control for an exotendon device. With this control, we are able to detect a user's intent to open, and can thus enable extension and pick and place tasks. In experiments with stroke survivors, we explore the accuracy of this control in both non-functional and functional tasks. Our results support the feasibility of developing wearable devices with intuitive controls which provide a functional context for rehabilitation.

He was treated by Dr. Paul Dudley White, a cardiologist with a national reputation, who regularly informed the press of the President's progress. Direct sound printing (DSP) is a new 3D printing technology developed by scientists at Canada's Concordia University. It involves sending focused pulses of ultrasound through a chamber into a liquid resin contained within. The sound causes rapidly oscillating microscopic bubbles to form at specific points in the resin, causing the resin to solidify at the exact location of the bubble. DSP is able to produce small, detailed items within structures that have opaque surfaces. It could potentially be used to 3D-print repairs into internal components or create implants inside a human body without surgery.

"I'm sorry Mrs Lowie but your husband..... he's dead..... he..." " SUNSHINE, RED WINE, GLITTER EVERYWHERE! " A dozen nurses paraded into the room with a cacophony of noise, spinning in tight circles. Glitter seemed to drop from the ceiling and around her, the pale curtains separating the beds were replaced by bright, vibrant colours. The puffy-eyed Mrs Lowie sat beside her sobbing, was on her feet with a smile, spinning around. She outstretched her hand and Sandra took it. Light on her feet, she effortlessly joined the other dancers as more people entered the ward. Drummers entered, with their instruments wrapped around their waist, a couple of cymbal crashes, and more people from a band marched in. Sandra found her heart thumping harder with every drum beat as she looked around and saw the other patients sitting up, clapping along. What is going on?! Sandra thought in horror, unable to control her body as she danced with the others. Her smile contrasted with the wide eyed incredulity in her eyes. She turned back to Mrs Lowie and found a fearful wide eyed stare. She too had a troubled look in her eyes and tears continued to fall down her frail, wrinkled cheeks as she danced. " WHY OH WHY ARE N'T I HAPPY EVERY DAY," The lights dimmed, a strange spotlight from an unknown place above illuminated the man's chiselled, handsome frame. " I'VE FOUND THE ONE WHO'S STOPPED ME FROM DISMAY" The man sung; his voice booming over the dancers who spun round him in circles. He cast a glance at Sandra and blew her a kiss. Involuntarily, she found herself grabbing her heart and stepping backward, an exaggerated motion that she had no control over. The man turned back to the doorway where a new woman, a blonde haired, blue eyed poster child of beauty, timidly stepped into the room. " ME AND YOU WILL BE TOGETHER" She sung. " TOGETHER AND FOREVER" The man purred, singing in unison with the woman so their voices were woven together. When will this end Sandra pleaded, trying to tear her eyes away from the scene. She continued to dance, slower this time, as the music slowed in tempo. She couldn't stop herself. " THERE'S NO ONE BUT YOUUUUU," They sung as a cymbal crashed and everyone broke into rapturous applause. The singing stopped, the dancers disappeared as quickly as they had arrived and Sandra found herself sitting opposite the woman as she had done moments before, shaking and aching from dancing so hard. "What..... what happened?" Mrs Lowie said, shaking as she turned her head from side to side. Sandra swallowed. "I have no idea."

My phone dinged with a work email. "Performance review today. Please arrive one hour early and be prepared to afterward perform your usual job duties." That one caught me off-guard more than the last time Doctor Improbable darted me. Performance review? I was the night watchman at the Center for the Study of Omega Radiation, and about every four or five nights someone would knock me out (some with darts, some with the classic punch, a couple different tasers) and then when I woke up the reactors would be about five minutes from melting down and scattered across the building. It got to the point that I wore a boxing helmet for the punches and learned how to take a punch. I also kept a lead-lined coverall in my office so I could get close enough to shut down the reactors. I was just glad the Center offered such good insurance that I could keep getting checked out at the hospital. "I am so fired," I murmured to myself as I drove in. "I haven't stopped any break-ins and there's always a ton of destruction every few days I'm surprised they have anything left." So when I walked in, I was surprised by the pleasant smile on my boss's face. "Have a seat," she said, almost obequious. I sat down, immediately suspicious. "So. Performance review?" "Yes," she said. "You've been here a year. I had to appeal to my superiors, but they agreed you deserve to know some things. I hope afterwards you'd be willing to stay with us, but I, for one, would understand if you decided to move on." She pulled out a folder marked "Eyes-Only" and handed it to me. The very first line was a study done. I didn't understand it perfectly, but it seemed to consider the dangers of supervillains and the marginal value of heroes stopping them compared with stopping them the usual way. It seemed to suggest that if property damage could be localized and minimized the heroes pulled ahead. Well, we weren't getting rid of heroes and villains any time soon. Another study showed that creating an obvious target would draw the supervillains and localize the property damage. The Center was seemingly a perfect target. No, it was better than perfect; it specifically existed to be targeted. While it did technically generate some power, there wasn't any actual radiation. A dummy reactor fed into dummy readouts. Once in a while they'd make something in a real lab that didn't do anything and send it there to make it a better target. The last document there was a personnel history file, with hire dates and exit dates, in reverse chronological order. I was on there, for a year. The previous year, they had eight night watchmen. Three had died, four had quit, and one had apparently become the Leopard, a notorious cat burglar villain. I wracked my brain trying to remember if I'd ever encountered him and then realized I hadn't. He probably figured out what was going on and hated being a sitting duck. I closed the file, struggling to keep a straight face. "So that's why the job pays so much and has such great insurance. I'll stay on. I've got a front-row seat to the designated battleground for supers. I've even managed to stay conscious for a few of them."

Psychological anthropology is an interdisciplinary subfield of anthropology that studies the interaction of cultural and mental processes. This subfield tends to focus on ways in which humans' development and enculturation within a particular cultural group - with its own history, language, practices, and conceptual categories - shape processes of human cognition, emotion, perception, motivation, and mental health. It also examines how the understanding of cognition, emotion, motivation, and similar psychological processes inform or constrain our models of cultural and social processes.

The Restore Justice campaign, spearheaded by Paul Staines who writes the Guido Fawkes political blog, calls for the death penalty to be brought back for child and police officer murderers. He cites opinion polls which suggest about half the population would like it re-introduced for murderers. This rises to 60 when it comes to child or police officer killers. Mr Staines needs 100,000 people to support his e-petition on the government website to prompt a possible parliamentary debate on the issue. The last executions in the UK took place in 1964. The death penalty was formally abolished in Britain in 1965 and in Northern Ireland in 1973. Despite it rating high on public opinion polls, it was last debated in Parliament in 1998 during the passage of the Human Rights Act. It was rejected by 158 votes. "The majority are in favour for bringing back the death penalty everywhere except in Parliament," said Mr Staines. "Politicians are complaining that there's a disconnect and that the public aren't engaged with them - maybe if they represented the views and the will of the voters, there wouldn't be such a big disconnect." He added: "The people want the death penalty, and politicians aren't prepared to vote for it. That's not right. "What I'm trying to do is get Parliament to discuss this issue between what Parliament wants and what the people want." House of Commons leader Sir George Young has warned that it would damage democracy to ignore strong opinions among members of the public "or pretend that their views do not exist." Douglas Carswell MP agreed, saying, although he was firmly against the death penalty, he was in favour of Parliament debating it and would support a referendum on whether it should be brought back. "I'm convinced that if there was a referendum on capital punishment we could win it; we could get most people to say'no' to the death penalty. "We need to treat people as grown-ups and have the debate and not do what we have done for half a century which is to ignore the public's concern and treat them with contempt. "The important thing is we have this debate." Mr Carswell added that the reason why Parliament had not debated this topic in recent years was because it was "out of touch with the public." "The mistake MPs have made is to not trust the people and to try and ignore their concerns. We can disagree with it but we have to trust it." But Neil Durkin from Amnesty International said it was a "waste of time and money that we as a nation cannot afford." In September 2010, YouGov conducted the last opinion poll to ask directly if people want the death penalty re-instated. It suggested that 51 did. And a Mori poll in July 2010 asked people which of a list of crimes they thought should have the death penalty. For child murder, 62 supported it while a YouGov poll in November 2010 found 74 of people supported the death penalty for murder in some circumstances, though only 16 supported it for all murders. However, when similar polls were carried out in the 1970s, support for it was far higher with 70 in favour. Anthony Wells, associate director of YouGov, says polls which ask about the death penalty are straightforward: "Do you support it or not?" "When people already know about it and have established views then it is quite simple. The hard ones [opinion polls] are when people need to have an issue explained to them." He said historically opinion polls on capital punishment have been commissioned by newspapers when there has been a heinous crime such as after the Soham murders. Mr Wells added that such polls are not often commissioned in times when a high-profile murder is not in the news. However, the last two polls on the subject were not about a specific case, being conducted for a story about sentencing for murder and for a Channel 4 programme. Polls are quite accurate, plus or minus 3, said Mr Wells, and their accuracy can be checked against real life events such as who is going to win the election or X Factor. "All the polls about the death penalty show similar patterns so even if it was worded differently it would still get the same result," he added. "You can only tell what people think at the moment, but if it follows current trends then yes, I'd expect it to go down." Mr Durkin from Amnesty International said it was important to have an informed debate, rather than a simple "yes or no" question. Cooperative relaying improves the performance of wireless networks by forming a network of multiple independent virtual sources transmitting the same information as the source node. However, interference induced in the network reduces the performance of cooperative communications. In this work the statistical properties, the cumulative distribution function (CDF) and the probability density function (PDF) for a basic dual hop cooperative relay network with an arbitrary number of interferers over Rayleigh fading channels are derived. Two system models are considered: in the first system model, the interferers are only at the relay node; and in the second system model, interferers are both at the relay and the destination. This work is further extended to Nakagami- m faded interfering channels. Simulation results are presented on outage probability performance to verify the theoretical analysis.

Labeling data correctly is an expensive and challenging task in machine learning, especially for on-line data streams. Deep learning models especially require a large number of clean labeled data that is very difficult to acquire in real-world problems. Choosing useful data samples to label while minimizing the cost of labeling is crucial to maintain efficiency in the training process. When confronted with multiple labelers with different expertise and respective labeling costs, deciding which labeler to choose is nontrivial. In this paper, we consider a novel weak and strong labeler problem inspired by humans' natural ability for labeling, in the presence of data streams with noisy labels and constrained by a limited budget. We propose an on-line active learning algorithm that consists of four steps: filtering, adding diversity, informative sample selection, and labeler selection. We aim to filter out the suspicious noisy samples and spend the budget on the diverse informative data using strong and weak labelers in a cost-effective manner. We derive a decision function that measures the information gain by combining the informativeness of individual samples and model confidence. We evaluate our proposed algorithm on the well-known image classification datasets CIFAR10 and CIFAR100 with up to 60 noise. Experiments show that by intelligently deciding which labeler to query, our algorithm maintains the same accuracy compared to the case of having only one of the labelers available while spending less of the budget.

Distributed matrix multiplication is widely used in several scientific domains. It is well recognized that computation times on distributed clusters are often dominated by the slowest workers (called stragglers). Recent work has demonstrated that straggler mitigation can be viewed as a problem of designing erasure codes. For matrices A and B , the technique essentially maps the computation of A T B into the multiplication of smaller (coded) submatrices. The stragglers are treated as erasures in this process. The computation can be completed as long as a certain number of workers (called the recovery threshold) complete their assigned tasks. We present a novel coding strategy for this problem when the absolute values of the matrix entries are sufficiently small. We demonstrate a tradeoff between the assumed absolute value bounds on the matrix entries and the recovery threshold. At one extreme, we are optimal with respect to the recovery threshold and on the other extreme, we match the threshold of prior work. Experimental results on cloud-based clusters validate the benefits of our method.

Steinman held his head in his hand, feeling the sweat drip from his brow on to his thumb and fore finger, it was at this point he had realised- he was way in over his head. The summer heat of Israel did not help nor did the courtroom camera focusing on his reaction. He rose his head, and looked at the witness, attempting to show no emotion, he could not let the world see weakness in him. The witness was a young jewish girl giving an account of her experience in auschwitz. The woman spoke in polish and in order to understand her, Steinman held the headset closer to his left ear and the translator spoke. '..... The guard believed we were somehow smuggling bread into the camp and for some reason believed I had something to do with it and he wanted a confession from me.' The Israeli prosecutor asked her a question and steinman heard the translation through the headphones'And what did he do to get a confession?' 'He put a gun to my twin sisters head. He said he would get a confession from me as he knew what it was like to lose a twin sister. He told me it was like losing part of your soul.' 'What did he do then?' 'He asked me again if I had smuggled bread into the camp..... he was right.' 'Let me be clear - you did smuggle bread into the camp?' 'No, he was right. It was like losing a part of your soul.' The court sat in silence like they had all morning. They would have gasped in horror but nothing shocked them anymore. The cameras focused on the defendant sitting in the bulletproof glass booth but he was showing no emotion either. The court, the world, wanted anything from him any emotion but more than ever they wanted to see remorse on his face, remorse for his crimes or even disgust. They could try all day but they would get nothing from him. Hitler sat slouched in his chair, his head resting on his shoulder with soulless eyes staring into space. He never moved, he never spoke. Every so often when a witness took the stand you would hear him mumble under his breath incoreenhenlty. The only words Steinman could make out were'juden' or'Deutschland'. With no luck yet again all focus was back on the witness as she continued to tell her stories of woe and horror. By this time steinman had already zoned out, he couldn't concentrate on the sobbing girl. All the stories sounded the same, and there was many of them, so many of them that Hitler's case was falling apart with every word. It was steinman's fault after all, in his arrogance he believed he was the greatest lawyer in the world, so great in fact that he could get Adolf Hitler of the hook and after which the cases would be coming in right, left and center. Those delusions of grandeur were fading away quickly. Steineman looked at the papers sprawled out in front of him looking for an answer. He looked at the long list of indictments: Crimes against humanity, war crimes, crimes against the Jewish people, membership in a criminal organisation. It was impossible, even if the court found Hitler innocent on one account he could still get hung for any of the other 14 indictments. There was nothing he could do so he lay his head to rest in his hand again and listened to the polish girl but her sweet somber voice was interrupted by Adolf Hitler. He had finally moved, the cameras focused on him and Adolf Hitler rose from his seat, his arms shaking as they lifted his frail body. On his two feet, he gazed into the air and his lips began to move slowly at first. His arms then began to flail frantically as he spouted and spat words incoherently. Again Steineman could only make out words like'deutschland' and'juden'. One of the three judges intervened banging his gavel,'Mr hitler if you have one more outburst I will hold you in contempt of court.' but it didn't stop him as he shouted about'autarky' and the'aryan race'. Words Steinman now recognised, words from his Nuremberg speech. Did Hitler know where he was? or what year it was? Perhaps at the age of 75 his mind was at the mercy of the late stages of syphilis and what was left of his body was ravished by his parkinson's disease. The Judge spoke once more'Bailiff remove him from the the court.' A man behind hitler in the booth approached him and attempted to restrain him but Hitler fought back, eventually the Bailiff overpowered him and dragged him out the court kicking and screaming. The Judge looked at the papers on his desk placed them in order and hit the bottom of them off the desk, aligning them.' The court will take a short recess then...' that is when it hit Steineman. 'Your honour!' 'Yes, Steinman?' 'My client would like to change his defence.' The court had again found something that made them gasp. 'My client would like to plead not guilty by reason of insanity.'

Partial voluming (PV) is arguably the last crucial unsolved problem in Bayesian segmentation of brain MRI with probabilistic atlases. PV occurs when voxels contain multiple tissue classes, giving rise to image intensities that may not be representative of any one of the underlying classes. PV is particularly problematic for segmentation when there is a large resolution gap between the atlas and the test scan, e.g., when segmenting clinical scans with thick slices, or when using a high-resolution atlas. In this work, we present PV-SynthSeg, a convolutional neural network (CNN) that tackles this problem by directly learning a mapping between (possibly multi-modal) low resolution (LR) scans and underlying high resolution (HR) segmentations. PV-SynthSeg simulates LR images from HR label maps with a generative model of PV, and can be trained to segment scans of any desired target contrast and resolution, even for previously unseen modalities where neither images nor segmentations are available at training. PV-SynthSeg does not require any preprocessing, and runs in seconds. We demonstrate the accuracy and flexibility of the method with extensive experiments on three datasets and 2,680 scans. But now, for the first time, the dirt has been dug up by archaeologists eager to find out more about our ancestors. Perhaps the most interesting find has been the foundations of a house dating back to the 1300s. The archaeologists said it is a hugely significant find, opening another door into the past and allowing us to learn more about how people used to live. A flint scraper, used by people living more than 3,000 years ago, was also found. It would have been used to scrape animal skins, and as a sort of tool for eating food. The dig was organised by the Belfast Hills Partnership and Queen's University Belfast. First-year archaeology students were given their first chance to explore an ancient site. Some of those taking part said it had made them even more eager to follow this career path. The dig has been going on for several weeks, but at the end of next week it will all be covered up again and restored to how it was before the archaeologists dug their trowels into the previously untouched land. Lizzy Pinkerton from the Belfast Hills Partnership said they want to make sure it remains in good condition. They will now analyse all of the data and artefacts they have found. It is unclear how many other potted sites like the one in Slievenacloy are waiting to be explored all over Northern Ireland, but the enthusiastic archaeologists say they are determined to find out.

A good convergence metric must satisfy two requirements: feasible in calculation and rigorous in analysis. The average convergence rate is proposed as a new measurement for evaluating the convergence speed of evolutionary algorithms over consecutive generations. Its calculation is simple in practice and it is applicable to both continuous and discrete optimization. Previously a theoretical study of the average convergence rate was conducted for discrete optimization. This paper makes a further analysis for continuous optimization. First, the strategies of generating new solutions are classified into two categories: landscape-invariant and landscape-adaptive. Then, it is proven that the average convergence rate of evolutionary algorithms using landscape-invariant generators converges to zero, while the rate of algorithms using positive-adaptive generators has a positive limit. Finally, two case studies, the minimization problems of the two-dimensional sphere function and Rastrigin function, are made for demonstrating the applicability of the theory.
