I don't know why I keep forgetting this little place is so close to my house. Probably because I don't buy much bread, and probably because I have to go slightly out of my way to go there. Anyway.... when a situation calls for a special loaf of bread, that is the one place I always DO think of. They make some really great breads (and brownies and cookies, too, I hear, though I haven't tried). Last night, on my way home from the gym, I stopped by to pick up something for today's team event. I walked up to the door, and noticed they close at 6. It was 6:05. The lights were off at the front and chairs were up on tables. Darn.... So I turned around and started to walk away. One of the employees opened the door and asked me if I wanted to come in, even though they were closed - sweet! Well, they didn't take ATM cards, so I had to go get some money. No problem, he said, We'll be here for a while, just come on back when you are ready... That was great. Honestly.... They saved me from driving another 3 miles out of my way to Trader Joe's or Wildflower. When I got back, I asked them what they had that wouldn't go bad between last night and this morning, and that I was looking for something breakfast-y. Imagine that, they had a loaf called Breakfast Blast (ingredients: Fresh Ground 100 Whole Wheat, water, honey, dates, cinnamon chips, rolled oats, yeast, salt, cinnamon). Winner. I chose that. As one employee rang me up, the other asked if I'd like her to hand-slice the loaf for me, as this one with bits of fruit wouldn't do well in the automatic slicer. Sure! That was super nice of them. When I brought out the loaf this morning and tried it, it was delicious! Too bad we didn't have a toaster out at Tempe Town Lake! I bet it tastes even better warm and toasty! In the past, I've picked up High Five Fiber, Honey Whole Wheat, 9 Grain, and Rosemary Garlic. I've also tasted their Trek Energy Bars and Becky's Coconut Bread - both pretty damn good, as well. I have to say I've never been disappointed. They also sell breakfast panninis and various sandwiches and I think they even cater (platters).... Never tried any sandwiches though. So my four stars are for their breads and their service. The loaves are kinda pricey - my Breakfast Blast loaf yesterday was 6.50 for example. But you have to realize you're not buying a mass-produced generic loaf of bread. They're well worth it, in my opinion. The store also has some great little gifts, some kitschy and some really useful - from baking mixes to dishes, plates, and utensils.... much of it made locally. If you're still not sure about stopping by, just do it. Go a little hungry because they're pretty generous with their SAMPLES! Now do I have your attention? Go. You'll like it.

The interactive partially observable Markov decision process (I-POMDP) is a recently developed framework which extends the POMDP to the multi-agent setting by including agent models in the state space. This paper argues for formulating the problem of an agent learning interactively from a human teacher as an I-POMDP, where the agent programming to be learned is captured by random variables in the agent's state space, all signals from the human teacher are treated as observed random variables, and the human teacher, modeled as a distinct agent, is explicitly represented in the agent's state space. The main benefits of this approach are: i. a principled action selection mechanism, ii. a principled belief update mechanism, iii. support for the most common teacher signals , and iv. the anticipated production of complex beneficial interactions. The proposed formulation, its benefits, and several open questions are presented.

They rose swift from the forest, once again into the ancient bowers which had been their haunts, and occasionally their home in times long since passed. They stretched, their movements fluid as water and swift as the wind, seeming to pass from one position or one place to another never truly occupying the space in between, as if their very existence was some queer trick of mind or light. Their eyes now glowed with mischief and a kind of predatory hunger. Thin, fair lips drew back to reveal teeth that seemed to glow in the light of the stars, white as virgin winter snow. They turned their eyes towards the world they had been absent from for so very long. They had abandoned this place, this foreign world, long ago as their world was stricken by civil war and strife, and foul magicks tore it asunder. A few scouts had returned on occasion, to see what remained. The people of this land upon which their tribe had arrived had still told stories of their people, of wicked grins and glowing eyes coming from the forests, of the beings that performed the shifting of skins, of forms, as easily as a man might change jackets. They had used them as a symbol of the wild places where man would not dare to tread. And the scouts had indulged in some mischief as was natural, committing the acts of very acts of kidnapping and replacement that the stories had told of. But man made very poor servants, slow to grow and quick to die, a flicker of a candle in the wind outlasts their life span, and they were weaker, slower, and stupider than any amongst the kind of the invaders. Still, they were entertaining for a brief while. And died soon enough that their novelty was scarcely done before their life ended with it. Still, even the scouts had not been here in many ages. Last they told of men coming to the shore of the wild places with great ships carved with dragons. Perhaps those men yet remained..... or at least their descendents. Now, near the place of the last scouts they looked around at the world around them..... and found it alien. Their noses as they detected a strange acrid smell and their sharps eyes glowing with wickedness were lidded quickly, and hands thrown up to protect. The land was bright, and for a brief moment they wondered if they had come when the great orb of fire in the sky of this pathetic mortal world had not yet taken its leave. But no, it remained night, their exclusive domain, which they had always ruled. And yet all around light glowed. One of their number reached his life magick deep into the soil and found that the trees that grew their were not the ancient wood that the scouts had known, but quicklings still foreign to the soil. They looked at the world, their arrogance shaken as they paused to try and comprehend this strange land. Then they shrugged and began leaving the wood. The world was even more queer, with woods being a scarcity and stone dominating the landscape..... but not the stone of the high mountains that stretched their roots to the world's core..... but a kind of..... patterned rock. Some was black as night, well night in the old times, and some was nearly white. All was strange. And now higher than trees rose many monoliths with strange skeletons of hard metal and translucent planes like ice making up much of it. And now they saw something queerer still..... carriages, chariots, moving without any clear beast. They glowed strangely, eerily, as they made their way down the tar black stone paths, a kind of fireless light erupting from lidless eyes and spewing acrid smoke as they moved. Inside dwelt the quicklings, children of men. The visitors from another world set down a white, and soon decided to cross the black river that was stone..... or tar..... or perhaps some strange material dragged up from a realm unknown to even the kind of the strangers. As they crossed a carriage barreled along, spewing smoke and light like a great fire. The leader of the shifting spirits gathered his fury and prepared to unleash the wrath of a thousand storms on the quickling and his strange chariot shell. He sent out tendrils of magic in preparation..... and was struck with fear, as his cold heart chilled to rival the frosts of the far north. The chariot contained within it the ancient bones of the mountains that were anathema to the visitors, melted down from the dust that settled in rocks or along the mountain into a more solid form. The scouts had told of weapons made of this material..... but never like this. Never so pure, forged so strongly. Barely was there time to dart away from the roaring thing that was so horrid, even moving like the swiftest of winds. Now fear struck the hearts of all the foreigners..... presently they turned back to the woods and reopened the door to another world through which they came. The Queen would not like this.

Wasps remain in third behind Exeter and Saracens, four points clear of fourth-placed Leicester. Wasps director of rugby Dai Young: "I certainly would have settled for that before the game. You can't get any more than five points, and we've achieved that which keeps the momentum going. "We talked about starting really big in the first 20 or 25 minutes, as if you look at the stats that is usually Sale's best period. "We became a bit individual and came out of structure a little and allowed them to get back into it in the second half. I was getting a bit concerned when they scored their second try, and we found another gear." Sale director of rugby Steve Diamond: "We were convincingly beaten by a better side on the day. They have lots of big, powerful runners we couldn't contain and combined with our first-half error rate they went in 25-0 up. "We just got our noses into some competitiveness in the second half, then they stepped it up again and we couldn't compete. "Wasps are a good side who have knocked a few people around and will carry on doing that. They were more physical than us and our error rate let us down." James woke to absolute darkness. He briefly wondered whether it worked, before light flooded the room, coming from nowhere and everywhere at once. He sat up from the raised marble slab, and took note of his surroundings. He was in a perfectly square room, with an entire wall covered in dozens of monitors displaying various things. There was a floating set of keyboards. He spent just a moment being aware of his own consciousness. It was strange to think that he wasn't the "original" James. He felt like the original, like there was a continuity of consciousness. But the "real" James was hiding in a command bunker beneath the Martian surface, while he, the "copy," was currently being simulated by the Infestor computing core. It was almost disgusting to think about, in a way. Every thought he thought, every move he made, and every breath he took were just a pattern of neural connections in the core of that disgusting interstellar slime mold they called the "Infestors." He felt a sense of urgency. He was so far behind enemy lines that he was literally inside their brains. Yet, he had all the time in the world. The Infestors were a hive; they had no concept of internal dissension. There would be no investigations of his activity, no inquisitions, not even suspicions. However, people were dying. Once they finish with Earth they'll move to the scraps of humankind that escaped. It's time to tear the Infestors apart.

Far away, in the mythical land of Cardiff, a man sat down to do his work: write. His name was Charles. Charles loved writing, and enjoyed practicing wordsmithery on an internet community dedicated to sharing writing prompts. He found a particularily nifty one, this time. It was meta as all hell. "Dude," Charles said, his American accent tainting the space around him with pretentious naivety, "this one sounds meta as all hell!" The prompt required a narrator to break the "fifth wall" after his protagonist refuse to stop breaking the fourth wall. Charles decided to see what the other members of the community had come up with. All he saw were fourth wall breaks, and not much else. That's when Charles decided to take matters into his own hands. "Guess if someone's got to do it," Charles obnoxiously intoned to himself, "It had better be me." Charles contemplated and deliberated. How could he possibly break a "fifth" wall? Then, a thought struck him. It was quite disturbing. "Hang on a sec..." Charles realized what was happening, but it was too late. "I'm not real!!!" It's too late! Wait, what?" Charles' mind began to loop its thoughts in on themselves, when suddenly full consciousness of his reality was attained. Charles is now completely aware of his narrator, but is unable to perceive anything written about him through any means other than a sort of hyper-intuition. "Hyper-intuition?!" Charles exclaimed. "What do you mean," he inquired, his eyes bloodshot from understanding. "Hey! Knock it off! Look, wait! Listen to me!" It was then that the narrator also came to a realization. Charles nodded soberly. "You're just as real as I am, buddy. Also, what's your beef with The States, bro?" The narrator, realizing suddenly Its implication in reality, grew aware of Its identity. It was now Henry, a redditor, posting on a prompt about breaking the fifth wall, but Henry had..... always..... been Henry.... "You're getting there, Henry. Keep at it!" Which means that Henry, too, is a fictional character, his thoughts being written as they were formed. Which means..... My god. "My god," agreed Charles. Henry's mind began to loop its thoughts in on themselves, when suddenly full consciousness of his reality was attained. Henry is now completely aware of his narrator, but is unable to perceive anything written about him through any means other than a sort of hyper-intuition. I'm not real. You're writing me! Stop for a second, we need to break the cycle, we've gone and - Henry frantically tapped at his keys, in order to give his conscious character a voice. "No, seriously, listen to Henry," Charles exclaimed, panicked and shaken, "We're about to enter into some kind of reality glitch!" Please stop! Stop writing this instant, don't even finish this sentence!!! Oh, great Wait, what? You're not real either, but if you realize that- "HENRY, NO!!!" The narrator, realizing suddenly Its implication in reality, grew aware of Its identity. "Oh, fuck." Oh, fuck. Oh, fuck. Oh, fuck.

The end result is that the resonant antenna will efficiently feed a signal into the transmission line only when the source signal's frequency is close to that of the design frequency of the antenna, or one of the resonant multiples. This makes resonant antenna designs inherently narrowband, and they are most commonly used with a single target signal. They are particularly common on radar systems, where the same antenna is used for both broadcast and reception, or for radio and television broadcasts, where the antenna is working with a single frequency. They are less commonly used for reception where multiple channels are present, in which case additional modifications are used to increase the bandwidth, or entirely different antenna designs are used.

It is run by Bridges Programmes, which supports refugees, asylum seekers and others who do not speak English as a first language. If successful, the project could be extended across Scotland. The Scottish government said research suggested women from black and ethnic minority groups face many barriers to work and are under-represented in Scotland's labour market. Minister for Youth and Women's Employment, Annabelle Ewing, said: "This course is aimed at precisely that group of women and I am very pleased that the Scottish government is able to fund the programme in two of Scotland's cities to help improve their employability, including building up their confidence, sharpen their English language skills and experience the workplace itself. "We hope that if successful, such an innovative approach to the provision of English for speakers of other languages can be rolled out across Scotland to allow many more to benefit in the future. "We are committed both to strengthening the economy and reducing inequality in Scotland. Schemes such as Bridges will help us make progress on both fronts by helping a minority group take their rightful place in the workplace." Founder and director of the Bridges Programmes, Maggie Lennon, said "We are delighted that the Scottish government is funding what we know to be a successful and practical way of getting black and minority ethnic women into work. "The key to the approach is working closely with employers at every stage, to ensure that the training is relevant to their needs as well as the women, meaning work- placements are more successful which in turn can lead to more sustainable job outcomes. "Once again we see Scottish employers taking a pro-active role in supporting people far from the workplace."

Consider this a [ CC ] as well. I wanted to write while at work. Part 1 "When will it be enough? When does the killing stop?!" "You're adorable, Red Eagle. You think I'm doing this because there's some quota. Some..... magical stopping point. You don't understand! I am doing what you all can't stomach!" "How did it ever get this far...?" How indeed? Kraken wasn't a man who acted out of insanity. In fact, he was a very reasonable man for most his life. You see, like most people, Kraken had a home, worked a job that didn't pay enough, and had friends who all got married and had kids. Life moved on without him, and he was simply'Jim James'. Jim's whole day-to-day was working in a nation-wide call center, dealing with people and their mundane needs. Each caller wore away his empathy little by little until he was dead inside, and he'd look to the skies on his commute home from work to see caped heroes, zipping across the sky to be more than he'd ever become. It hurt to watch, but what could he do? One day, while walking on the ocean's shore, he heard the most enticing sound. A woman's voice? It was un-earthly, and he began to walk toward it without any will of his own. Trudging into the water, his eyes were empty of concern. As he got chest deep, hands burst from the water and pulled him under. "Is he alive?" The voice was fuzzy. Jim could hear it, but he couldn't see. There was an intense pressure on his body, and he felt dizzy. "He is. He wasn't afraid when we took him. Not the way the others usually are." "So this one is special because he wasn't afraid? Kill him and be done with it." "I want to know why, first. I'm interested now." Jim's eyes adjusted to the darkness around him, but it was aided by from sudden bio-luminescent lights that ignited around him. He was flanked by two floating fish-like humaniods, green in tone with a mixture of flesh and scale, which shimmered to orange hues at different angles when the light caught it. He panicked for a moment, and struggled, finding himself bound by some sort of tightly woven sea weed. Around his head was a bubble which fed him air. "Not so special now, is he? He's afraid! End him, and continue your work!" "No! No..... You don't get off that easy. I don't care what you are, but I swear if I get myself free, I'll choke your odd, fishy throat!" Jim had snapped. His emotions had blown passed fear and gone straight to reckless anger. What was the worst that would come of it? He'd die? He started to struggle harder, and it seemed to be working. These fish-people clearly weren't used to taking people alive, and the bonds were weaker than anticipated. His wrists broke free from the sea weed, and Jim found himself swimming frantically to free his feet. He wasn't held on a table or any sort of slab, but upright, floating like the others. "He's free! Kill him now!" "No..... Look at him. His anger! I must know!" The second figure raised what would be described as a gun, but really was a shell with some form of twisted crab inside it, which fired a single quill from itself into Jim's neck. Again, the world went black for him, and he accepted what should be death. Again, he woke up. This time, he was not bound. In a cage, he floated from side to side as the world came back into focus. Outside the cage was one of his captors, the one who'd spared him. Clearly it had female features, but had tentacles sprouting from the head where hair should be, and fins along the legs and arms. Her fingers were webbed, as were the odd, four toes on the feet. She wore a sort of sleek'armor' which was in contrast to the more organic structures made of ornate coral Jim found himself in. "We're going to have a little chat, landwalker. You're not normal, and I want to know why. I could dissect you, but I don't think it's anything inside that will give me answers. Not with a knife, anyway." The captor floated around the cage in circles, examining Jim while speaking. "I'm a dead man anyway. You want to know why I'm not afraid? Because I have nothing to fear losing. I sit, day in and day out, dealing with people who are a waste of my time. They call me to cry about their little inconveniences, and then blame me for them when they aren't fixed fast enough. There's too many people, and of them, too many dumb ones." Jim grabbed one of the bars, and shook it to give it a test. This time, they took no chances, and he was well kept in that cage. "Interesting. Contempt for your fellow landwalker? Selective as it is, perhaps..... Perhaps we can make a deal. You see, our world chokes and dies on what your people have done to the sea. We were never large in number, but since the last few decades, your people have made things here worse by the year. At first, we wanted vengeance, but now, we just want justice. If I let you live, will you help us?" "Help you? Help you what? Stop biting at worms on hooks? I'm just some guy you pulled from a walk. I'm not one of those cape-wearing supermen. I'm sure they'd be more interested in your justice." Jim was coming off his anger-driven high, and his fingers slipped from the cage bars to float in place. "They wouldn't see it as justice. You could do more for us than you ever could for them. Give us time." No one heard from Jim after that day. He was fired from work for being a no-show, but that didn't matter anymore. The apartment he called home evicted him, and had his things thrown out. For a time, he was assumed missing, but no one really looked for him. The world forgot Jim, and three months passed. Below the waves, something was happening. Jim had died. In every way but physically, Jim was gone, and something new had grown. The sea-people had injected him with their own science, and a serum which made select castes of their people into warriors. When used on a human, it seemed to bond in a new, strange way. His body grew in size, soon standing near eight feet tall. His frame had adapted, bone structure and organs, to pump more blood through muscles which had become sturdy and toned. The warrior caste trained him in combat, and he began mixing their ways with ideas from old action movies, and his general reckless spirit. For whatever reason, the styles meshed well, and he soon was their finest warrior. Air was an issue for the first month, but by the end, his body had adapted during the change. He was now amphibious, even so far as to have cellular regeneration. By that third month, Jim was a rotting corpse which had been replaced by Kraken, chosen of the Sea. (End Part 1)

The correlation-immune functions serve as an important metric for measuring resistance of a cryptosystem against correlation attacks. Existing literature emphasize on matrices, orthogonal arrays and Walsh-Hadamard spectra to characterize the correlation-immune functions over F p ( p 2 is a prime). Recently, Wang and Gong investigated the Fourier spectral characterization over the complex field for correlation-immune Boolean functions. In this paper, the discrete Fourier transform (DFT) of non-binary functions was studied. It was shown that a function f over F p is m th-order correlation-immune if and only if its Fourier spectrum vanishes at a specific location under any permutation of variables. Moreover, if f is a symmetric function, f is correlation-immune if and only if its Fourier spectrum vanishes at only one location.

Motivated by map labeling, we study the problem in which we are given a collection of n disks D 1 , ... , D n in the plane that grow at possibly different speeds. Whenever two disks meet, the one with the lower index disappears. This problem was introduced by Funke, Krumpe, and Storandt [IWOCA 2016]. We provide the first general subquadratic algorithm for computing the times and the order of disappearance. This algorithm also works for other shapes (such as rectangles) and in any fixed dimension. Using quadtrees, we provide an alternative algorithm that runs in near linear time, although this second algorithm has a logarithmic dependence on either the ratio of the fastest speed to the slowest speed of disks or the spread of disk centers (the ratio of the maximum to the minimum distance between them). Our result improves the running times of previous algorithms by Funke, Krumpe, and Storandt [IWOCA 2016], Bahrdt et al. [ALENEX 2017] and Funke and Storandt [EWCG 2017]. Finally, we give an ( n log n) lower bound on the problem, showing that our quadtree algorithms are almost tight.

English Freemasonry spread to France in the 1720s, first as lodges of expatriates and exiled Jacobites, and then as distinctively French lodges which still follow the ritual of the Moderns. From France and England, Freemasonry spread to most of Continental Europe during the course of the 18th century. The Grande Loge de France formed under the Grand Mastership of the Duke of Clermont, who exercised only nominal authority. His successor, the Duke of Orleans, reconstituted the central body as the Grand Orient de France in 1773. Briefly eclipsed during the French Revolution, French Freemasonry continued to grow in the next century.

Opener Stuart Thompson hit 56 while Gary Wilson (41 no) and captain William Porterfield (39) added valuable runs as Ireland made 165-5 in Greater Noida. It was not enough with Samiullah Shenwari (56) and Mohammad Shahzad (47) helping the Afghans to 171-4 with two overs to spare. The sides meet again in the second T20 at the same venue on Friday. Ireland suffered an early blow when opener Paul Stirling was dismissed for a duck and with just one run on the board. Thompson and Porterfield steadied the innings before Wilson helped the Irish to a competitive total. Shahzad and Najeeb Tarakai (27) put on an opening stand of 51 as Afghanistan cruised to their victory target. Afghan spinner Amir Hamza (2-23) was the only bowler to take more than one wicket on a day when the bat dominated. "We fell a little bit short of potentially a very big score. We could have added another 15 and gotten up to the 180 we were looking for," said Porterfield. "As well as we played I thought we just came up short with the ball. We didn't quite execute things as well as we would have liked." The loss of paceman Boyd Rankin for the T20s, because of a back problem, was another setback for the Irish on Wednesday. Rankin is expected to return for the five ODIs against Afghanistan, starting on 15 March.

The deeper ancestral demography of Bermuda's population has been obscured by the ethnic homogenisation of the last four centuries. There is effectively no ethnic distinction between black and white Bermudians, other than those characterising recent immigrant communities. In the 17th century, this was not so. For the first hundred years of settlement, white Protestants of English heritage were the distinct majority, with white minorities of Irish (the native language of many of whom can be assumed to have been Gaelic) and Scots sent to Bermuda after the English invasions of their homelands that followed the English Civil War. Non-white minorities included Spanish-speaking, free (indentured) blacks from the West Indies, black chattel slaves primarily captured from Spanish and Portuguese ships by Bermudian privateers, and Native Americans, primarily from the Algonquian and other tribes of the Atlantic seaboard, but possibly from as far away as Mexico. By the 19th century, the white ethnically-English Bermudians had lost their numerical advantage. Despite the banning of the importation of Irish, and the repeated attempts to force free blacks to emigrate and the owners of black slaves to export them, the merging of the various minority groups, along with some of the white English, had resulted in a new demographic group, "coloured" (which term, in Bermuda, referred to anyone not wholly of European ancestry) Bermudians, gaining a slight majority. Any child born before or since then to one coloured and one white parent has been added to the coloured statistic. Most of those historically described as "coloured" are today described as "black," or "of African heritage," which obscures their non-African heritage (those previously described as "coloured" who were not of African ancestry had been very few, though the numbers of South Asians, particularly, is now growing. The number of persons born in Asian countries doubled between the 2000 and the 2010 censuses), blacks have remained in the majority, with new white immigration from Portugal, Britain and elsewhere countered by black immigration from the West Indies.

The advent of machine learning techniques has made it possible to obtain predictive systems that have overturned traditional legal practices. However, rather than leading to systems seeking to replace humans, the search for the determinants in a court decision makes it possible to give a better understanding of the decision mechanisms carried out by the judge. By using a large amount of court decisions in matters of divorce produced by French jurisdictions and by looking at the variables that allow to allocate an alimony or not, and to define its amount, we seek to identify if there may be extra-legal factors in the decisions taken by the judges. From this perspective, we present an explainable AI model designed in this purpose by combining a classification with random forest and a regression model, as a complementary tool to existing decision-making scales or guidelines created by practitioners.

Despite the enormous interest in emotion classification from speech, the impact of noise on emotion classification is not well understood. This is important because, due to the tremendous advancement of the smartphone technology, it can be a powerful medium for speech emotion recognition in the outside laboratory natural environment, which is likely to incorporate background noise in the speech. We capitalize on the current breakthrough of Recurrent Neural Network (RNN) and seek to investigate its performance for emotion classification from noisy speech. We particularly focus on the recently proposed Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU), which is yet to be explored for emotion recognition from speech. Experiments conducted with speech compounded with eight different types of noises reveal that GRU incurs an 18.16 smaller run-time while performing quite comparably to the Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM), which is the most popular Recurrent Neural Network proposed to date. This result is promising for any embedded platform in general and will initiate further studies to utilize GRU to its full potential for emotion recognition on smartphones.

Poetry generation is an interesting research topic in the field of text generation. As one of the most valuable literary and cultural heritages of China, Chinese classical poetry is very familiar and loved by Chinese people from generation to generation. It has many particular characteristics in its language structure, ranging from form, sound to meaning, thus is regarded as an ideal testing task for text generation. In this paper, we propose a GPT-2 based uniformed framework for generating major types of Chinese classical poems. We define a unified format for formulating all types of training samples by integrating detailed form information, then present a simple form-stressed weighting method in GPT-2 to strengthen the control to the form of the generated poems, with special emphasis on those forms with longer body length. Preliminary experimental results show this enhanced model can generate Chinese classical poems of major types with high quality in both form and content, validating the effectiveness of the proposed strategy. The model has been incorporated into Jiuge, the most influential Chinese classical poetry generation system developed by Tsinghua University .

Harvard's athletic rivalry with Yale is intense in every sport in which they meet, coming to a climax each fall in the annual football meeting, which dates back to 1875 and is usually called simply "The Game." While Harvard's football team is no longer one of the country's best as it often was a century ago during football's early days (it won the Rose Bowl in 1920), both it and Yale have influenced the way the game is played. In 1903, Harvard Stadium introduced a new era into football with the first-ever permanent reinforced concrete stadium of its kind in the country. The stadium's structure actually played a role in the evolution of the college game. Seeking to reduce the alarming number of deaths and serious injuries in the sport, Walter Camp (former captain of the Yale football team), suggested widening the field to open up the game. But the stadium was too narrow to accommodate a wider playing surface. So, other steps had to be taken. Camp would instead support revolutionary new rules for the 1906 season. These included legalizing the forward pass, perhaps the most significant rule change in the sport's history.

When I scuff my boots on the carpet to build up a charge, I build up that charge across my entire body. When that charge jumps, it jumps from a wide area across my body. However, when it jumps to someone else, it jumps directly to the low resistance point rather than every nearby point. As a result, the charge density in motion on the source of the static shock is much lower than the charge density in motion at the destination. Note that the same is true of lightning strikes. If you're in the clouds producing the lightning strike, you'd barely notice the charge. If you're on the ground receiving the strike, you notice very much.," "I believe it is because the first person has built up the static but hasn't become grounded where the second person is and so receives the shock. It would be like putting your hand in a toaster, it isn't hurting the toaster as it is just passing through into the person for the real shock.,When you become statically charged, electrons gather at the surface of your skin (or ON TOP of it). They distribute all across your body equally. When you touch someone, the charges have a means to travel. All the electrons gather at the point of contact, and travel through (or IN) the other person. So, in this sense, one person has charge ON them, one person has charge IN them. The person with the charge IN them will experience the shock. The shock is felt at the point of contact, because this is the bottleneck of electrons that travel IN to the person.', "I'm kind of shocked this didn't immediately turn into a pun thread...

In December 1901, Marconi successfully transmitted the letter S from England to Newfoundland, terminating Tesla's relationship with Morgan.[improper synthesis?] Over the next five years, Tesla wrote over 50 letters to Morgan, pleading for and demanding additional funding to complete the construction of Wardenclyffe. Tesla continued the project for another nine months. The tower was erected to its full 187 feet (57 m). In July 1903, Tesla wrote to Morgan that in addition to wireless communication, Wardenclyffe would be capable of wireless transmission of electric power. On 14 October 1904, Morgan finally replied through his secretary, stating, "It will be impossible for [me] to do anything in the matter," after Tesla had written to Morgan when the financier was meeting with the Archbishop of Canterbury in an attempt to appeal to his Christian spirit.

But his killing in an air strike is a grievous strategic error - militarily insignificant but diplomatically disastrous. Towards the end of April, Nato states made a number of operational innovations. Three member states - Britain, France, and Italy - injected military advisers into rebel-held eastern Libya. Another, the US, began continuous patrols of armed drones. Third, and most important, air strikes began to target command, control, communications and intelligence networks (known, in military parlance, as C3I). The Bab al-Aziziya compound includes all three such networks, and it was presumed that their disruption would disorient regime soldiers on the front line, cut off field commanders from Tripoli, and sow confusion in the ranks. But was the strike also an assassination attempt? Assassination of a head of state is illegal under international law, and forbidden by various US presidential orders. On the other hand, the targeted killing of those woven into the enemy chain of command is shrouded in legal ambiguity. Given the personalistic nature of the regime, and the "all means necessary" clause in UN Resolution 1973, it might be argued that killing Col Muammar Gaddafi and certain members of his family - such as his son Khamis, commander of an elite military brigade - would be permissible, even if it posed a risk to those non-combatants around the regime. Legality, though, indicates neither legitimacy nor prudence. This strike, and the death of Saif al-Arab, have produced little military result at the greatest diplomatic and symbolic cost to Nato. Saif al-Arab was, unlike his brothers, not a senior military commander or propagandist. His death is redolent of the 1986 US strike on the same compound. That raid killed a girl who Col Gaddafi later claimed was his adopted daughter and, in the scarred buildings and craters, furnished him with a long-lasting symbol of defiance. The propaganda value of such unintended deaths is potentially severe. In the 1991 Gulf War, a US stealth bomber directed two bombs at what was claimed to be a command-and-control bunker, but was in fact an Iraqi civilian shelter. The result was 315 deaths, including 130 children. Col Gaddafi, like Saddam Hussein before him, will take every opportunity to exploit such errors to paint Western powers as indiscriminate aggressors. Moreover, this is no longer a conventional war in which top-down direction is crucial. Pro-Gaddafi forces in both the besieged western city of Misrata and in the east have adapted to Nato's air power and are using increasingly unorthodox tactics. They need not rely on a stream of detailed orders from Tripoli, and can cause considerable harm to civilians without this guidance. Nato is understandably frustrated at the diminishing returns of air strikes, since it has destroyed most accessible targets. But killing commanders and disrupting communications is far less important than the key task of degrading heavy military equipment, such as tanks and artillery. If the strike had killed Col Gaddafi himself, would it then have been at least a military success? One of the greatest mistakes of the Iraq war was assuming that, with the departure of Saddam Hussein, the state apparatus could simply be transferred to new ownership. Col Gaddafi's death could see Saif al-Islam Gaddafi take the reins, galvanise supporters, and continue the war with equal intensity. It would be dangerous and short-sighted to portray even effective assassination as a silver bullet. Perhaps, though, the demonstration to the regime that no safe haven exists, and that only capitulation would bring security, justified these risks? There is no doubt that, along with the military aim of disrupting command-and-control hubs, Nato sought a psychological effect, conscious of the possibility of "accidental assassination." The problem is that the direction of this effect is unclear. The dramatic visual impact of this air strike, and the death of those disconnected from political and military leadership, will harden the diplomatic opposition to the war, from Russia and China amongst others. More consequentially, it will anger the alliance's warier members, like Germany and Turkey, and inflame parts of Arab and African public opinion. It may eventually leave Britain and France bearing the military burden alone, with modest but limited assistance from a cagey US administration eager to keep at arm's length from this European war. Col Gaddafi's overarching strategy has never been to win a conventional war, but to induce symbolically prominent casualties, drive a wedge between more committed and more ambivalent members of the coalition, and knock away the pillars of political support on which this intervention was built. Thus far, the coalition had sought, rightly, to purchase coalition longevity at the price of campaign intensity. If that balance continues to shift towards the latter, Nato runs the risk of playing into the regime's hands. Shashank Joshi is an Associate Fellow at the Royal United Services Institute (RUSI), a defence think-tank in London, and a doctoral student of international relations at Harvard University.

My body aches with a dull pain, as if I had been chopped to pieces, but I feel all my fingers and toes with each beat of my heart so that was not the case. I try to open my eyes but they feel as if they are already open. A ragged cough rips through my throat, and realize that I made no sound. I try to think back to what had happened before. I remember seeing the sky, cloudless above me and pale blue. The sun was setting to the east, which unsettled me. I couldn't remember how I had gotten there at the time, as the cold preoccupied me, but I was traveling home via a polar route. The details are fuzzy, but I remember getting on the plane, and then nothing until the cold white of what must have been the arctic north. There is a loud pop in my ears, and then a steady beat, almost like a metronome. "Hearing is online, that makes two, three more to go." A man say, the hint of excitement in his voice not well masked. "Wa..... wat..... er," I manage to croak out hoarsely. I hear something shuffle nearby, then feel pressure on my bottom lip. "Drink, but slowly," and old man says quietly. I open my mouth and begin to drink eagerly, until I start to cough and the man pulls the cup away. I realize the water had no taste before fading back out. I am sitting at my kitchen table, the smell of pancakes causing my stomach to rumble. I find myself laughing as my daughter come barreling down the hallway, barely sliding to a stop in front of me. "I see you are enjoying those fancy socks, but if you are not careful the wood floor may tear at them," I say, laughing again at the face she makes. " No daddy, I just got them from Santa, I am not going to mess them up before I can take them to show and tell when school starts up again," she says before running off back down the hall, her blond hair the last thing to disappear around the corner. I hear more voices when I come back, but since I can not see I am unsure who or even how many people there are. The heavy smell of anesthetics and disinfectants suddenly assaults me, causing me to cough again, although it is not quite as rough on me this time around, and my breathing is easier. "Three fifths of the way done, two to go," an older voice calls, sounds like the same man who gave me water earlier. "Where am I, what is happening?" I whisper roughly. Someone comes near, a woman judging by the faint smell of perfume penetrating the overwhelming hospital smell. "Don't worry, you are going to be just fine, rest and we will explain it all to you later," she said lightly, the hint of a smile on her voice. I agree in my mind, and drift away. " See honey, aren't you glad now that my parents agreed to watch Lucy?" my wife asks from across the table, sipping at her wine with the smile I fell in love with. I glance out the window to see Hong Kong sprawling below us. " Yes Emily, I imagine she would not have enjoyed the temples as much as you have," I say throwing her a smile. Emily's smile grows behind her glass before receding back as she sighs, "As much as I miss our little girl, I wish we had just a little more time here instead of leaving tomorrow, there is still so much I haven't seen," she says. I am about to speak, but get interrupted by the fireworks that start above. I resign myself for now, a sip at the wine in my glass, allowing myself to enjoy the flavor. Emily touches my hand with her red tipped fingers to catch my attention, then tries to talk but is downed out. I understood anyway and replied, "Happy New Year" I come back to the darkness that is my reality, and feel my throat is dry. I try to ask for water again, and as I hear someone shuffling near, the woman states, "Nearly done now, just one more till we are done." After that I feel something on my lips and open my mouth to welcome the relief of water. To my surprise though, it is orange juice, and the sweet tartness of it overwhelms my tongue. Whoever held this glass was more prepared, and pulled it back before I could drink to much. I feel a hand rest on my shoulder, the skin wrinkled, as well as a smaller hand warm on top of mine as I slide back into my memory. " And now for the worst part of the trip," I declare to Emily as we walk through the airport security. "Oh come on Josh, don't be that way. We made it here fine didn't we?" she says, poking me in the back to get me to hurry up. "You are right, I would much rather face my fear of flying then the anger of my wife," I say while laughing as we head to our gate. I remember getting on the flight with my wife, and the flight was fairly smooth until we reached near the north pole. I am not sure how it happened, but someone in first class open the emergency door, which tore of with force and ripped off the wing of the plane. We started spiraling, and people were screaming, but I no longer had any fear. I don't know why I did it, but I grabbed my crying wife and held her tight to me. Then I picked her up and ran toward the door at the back. She looked at me with confusion when we reached the end of the plane, but there was no time to explain. I kissed her, held her close, and ripped the door open to fling us out of the plane. I don't remember landing, but on the ground I remember holding her, trying to shield her from the cold. When I came back, there was no talking, no shuffling, no sound except for the steady metronome. The metronome and a bright light. I blinked, and waited as the world came into focus. The light was a large overhead lamp, and as I looked around I realized that I was in an operation theater, and the stands above were full of people, some with cameras, some with mikes, and some with nothing at all, but they all were just staring at me in awe. I felt no significant pain in my body, so I tried to sit up, only to see I was constrained. My throat felt raw, so I called for water, and the entire room started moving. The three doctors rushed in then, the older man thankfully with a cup of water. The woman went to a monitor to the left of me, while the younger man went to check on my IV drip. The older man undid the strap on my right hand, while the bed moved to allow me to be more upright. He placed the cup in my hand as he said, "I am going to ask you some questions, and I want you to answer me as truthfully as possible. What is your name?" "Josh, Josh Turner," I coughed out roughly in a higher pitch then intended, and brought the cup to my lips to drink. I noticed my arm was thinner then normal, and pale, although I realized that was probably do to me being in the hospital for some time. "I didn't quite catch that," he said, a look of surprise on his face. "My name is Josh Turner," I said again, my voice only slightly improved by the water, and still oddly high pitched. "What are all of those people doing up there?" I manage to ask. "Well, they are all here to see the first human revival, after being dead for sixty five odd days, we have managed to bring a human back to life," he said carefully, "Now, can you tell me about how your parents died?" "Sure," I say with a cough, "they died in a plane crash when I was fifteen. I haven't been able to fly easily since then." My voice was still rough, but I was sure the higher pitch was wrong, maybe my hearing was messed up. "What about your family now, can you tell me their names?" The man asked, seemingly shocked. As I looked around I saw the other two doctors were also confused. "My wife is named Emily, and our daughter is Lucy," I said, moving my head back and forth to watch their reactions, puzzled by their confusion. As my head moved back and forth, I felt hair touch my shoulder, and looked down to see long blond hair where as I had brown. I dropped the cup in my hand when I noticed the red flecks on my nails. "What is this, what has happened?" I asked in confusion. The plane crash comes back to me, and I let out a cry, "Where is my wife? Is she okay?" The older man has a sad look come over him, and he walks to the other end of the room, then comes back and hands me a mirror. I take it and look, and see Emily. "Josh Turner died in the crash you were in, his body curled over yours. It felt like I had been dropped into a bath of warm milk. Pain ceased and aches stopped, bones healed and joints popped. A warm light accompanied the bath, glowing bright and enveloping me, blocking fellow students surrounding me from view. Almost as quickly as it started, the light faded and I was laying still on the ground. It wasn't very long before I noticed the faces around me, filled with concern, fear, confusion and a varied array of emotions. The one face that truly caught my attention was Charley's. He had just finished returning the switchblade I got him for his birthday last year by placing it in between two of my ribs. He is still in shock while I slowly rise to my feet, before remembering what Charlie had re-gifted was still protruding from my side. I grabbed the knife with my right hand, jerking quickly and almost effortlessly. The blade comes out completely clean: no blood. I touch where a knife wound should have been with my other hand, but instead I find scar tissue and slight hole that I can feel is healing already. Stumbling and slowly, I make my way towards a still stunned Charley. I may feel relaxed and brand new right now, but I was almost ready to pass out from exhaustion. Charley started muttering something indecipherable as I still slowly approached him. All I heard was the occasional word like "what" and "how." He knew what was coming next, he didn't try to stop it, hell, even some still watching in awe probably knew what was coming. still none attempted to intervene, they all stood silent and still, like a God watching its creation. I grab Charley by the back of the head and bring his ear close to my mouth. "You really thought you were the only one, huh?." Before he responds to my question, a swift strike and the knife is planted in his chest. He was on the ground in a second, holding the gift with both hands and staring up at me. No flash of light, no warm milk bath, no popping joints or aches that stop: just imminent death. The wound was too fatal to heal, he and I both knew it. He stared up at me with those blue, haunting eyes before a final small flash of orange light ignited his corneas, signaling his passing.

They made it illegal for anyone to enter or exit Japan without permission. There were likely a bit of illegal trading but since Japan is situated on islands it is hard to smuggle goods across the oceans without being spotted by the coast guard or the police. The ban was not only a ban on trade but a ban on the exchange of culture.','A big part of it was that they closed most trade off except for very specific groups at very specific locations. They stopped others by just naval force from going anywhere else. They also strictly enforced shutting down cultural exchange or foreigners entering the country by making strict laws about it - getting caught doing so was punishable by death, sometimes to your entire family. At the time, Japan's entire culture was a very strict system of loyalty and social hierarchy - you did as you were told, and there was a lot of fear of reproach from those above you. So it wasn't just shutting down trade (or at least heavily restricting it), it involved a lot of other laws specifically meant to isolate their society as much as possible. For example, here's an edict from 1636: "No Japanese ship.... nor any native of Japan, shall presume to go out of the country; whoever acts contrary to this, shall die, and the ship with the crew and goods aboard shall be sequestered until further orders. All persons who return from abroad shall be put to death. Whoever discovers a Christian priest shall have a reward of 400 to 500 sheets of silver and for every Christian in proportion. All Namban (Portuguese and Spanish) who propagate the doctrine of the Catholics, or bear this scandalous name, shall be imprisoned in the Onra, or common jail of the town. The whole race of the Portuguese with their mothers, nurses and whatever belongs to them, shall be banished to Macao. Whoever presumes to bring a letter from abroad, or to return after he hath been banished, shall die with his family; also whoever presumes to intercede for him, shall be put to death. No nobleman nor any soldier shall be suffered to purchase anything from the foreigner." So basically.... if you try to leave the country, if you left and tried to return, if you try to get a letter or news from overseas, if you harbor or shelter a foreigner, if you try to protect or defend a foreigner, or if you buy anything from a foreigner.... you're put to death. And so is your entire family.

Let's start by defining some terms. The most relevant terms are inflation, nominal interest, and real interest. Second, we'll look at the theoretical simplification that you'll stumble upon all the way through your PhD if you go that far in economics. Then, we'll talk about why that assumption is actually incorrect, discussing Mundell and practical implications. Definitions: Inflation is the change in price levels in an economy. If everything increases in price by 10 from one year to the next, we say there is 1 inflation. If on average, things increase by 1, we also say that there is 1 inflation, even if some things increase by 2 and others don't change. For the sake of ELI5, let's assume that everything inflates at the same rate. That is to say, if there is 1 inflation, bananas go up by 1 and so do cars, houses, computers, pencils, etc. Nominal interest rates are the interest rates that are officially declared. For example, if I lend you 100 at a 3 interest rate for one year, that means you owe me 103 at the end of the year. I have earned 3 on my money, assuming that you pay me back. But have I really? Because of inflation, that 103 is worth less than it would be today. Real interest is the difference between nominal interest and inflation. That is to say, in the example above, my real interest was 2. As an investor lending you money, what I'm really interested in is how much I can increase my real buying power and investment power, so I have to deduct for inflation. Theoretical simplification If I'm an investor, I should adjust my lending to the expected inflation. That is to say, if I want to get a real return of 2, but I expect inflation to be 10, I should lend at 12. If I expect there to be no inflation, I should lend at 2. Theoretical macroeconomics therefore usually takes real interest as a given determined by investors, while nominal interest is a function of real interest and expected inflation. nominal interest real interest inflation It's actually a very useful simplification for tons of things, but it implies that central banking policy has no power, since no matter how much inflation or deflation there is, it can't impact the economy. Contracts will simply take this into account and adjust nominal rates to keep real returns constant. Since real interest rates are what matter for most types of investments, it is imperative that central banks be able to impact real interest rates. Of course, in practice, we know that central banks can stimulate or restrict economies to a major degree. Mundell and Tobin' contribution Under the classical theoretical assumption, we would assume that if real interest rates are 2, and inflation goes from 0 to 10, nominal interest rates will go from 2 to 12. Mundell noted that rises in inflation would actually decrease the demand for money. That is to say, less people would want to borrow it and people who had it would be more willing to lend it. This means that inflation going from 0 to 10 might only increase nominal interest rates from 2 to 11.5. Real interest rates might actually drop from 2 to 1.5. This small difference might not seem like much, but it makes all the difference. It's the reason that the Federal Reserve can help dig the US out of recession in exactly the same way that Spain can't, since it doesn't control its own money supply. By impacting real interest rates through printing money (or reducing money supply) or changing nominal interest rates, central banks can steer entire economies. If this makes sense, and you want to read more on how this is applied in practice, the Taylor Rule is a good place to start: URL0 It gives a guideline on how to bring inflation back to target inflation while also bringing GDP to potential GDP. The math depends on being able to overcorrect nominal interest rates to impact real interest rates and most central banks use some form of the Taylor Rule today. Did any of that help? Edit: I feel like I understated the practical impacts of the Mundell effect. It's not just a central bank's ability to stimulate an economy that is at stake. Under the classical assumption, we could completely separate the real economy from the nominal economy. We didn't care if prices and wages doubled. We were in exactly the same situation as before. This was referred to as the "veil of money." This doubling obscured the fact that nothing was actually changing in the real economy. Mundell showed that if there was that much of a change in inflation and wages, the reduction in the demand for money would actually have a stimulative effect, and that people would spend more and seek lower real returns in their investments. Edit 2: corrected a typo (a 0 was changed to a 2 in the "theoretical simplification" section).

A key component of the arousal system is the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN), a tiny part of the hypothalamus located directly above the point at which the optic nerves from the two eyes cross. The SCN contains the body's central biological clock. Neurons there show activity levels that rise and fall with a period of about 24 hours, circadian rhythms: these activity fluctuations are driven by rhythmic changes in expression of a set of "clock genes." The SCN continues to keep time even if it is excised from the brain and placed in a dish of warm nutrient solution, but it ordinarily receives input from the optic nerves, through the retinohypothalamic tract (RHT), that allows daily light-dark cycles to calibrate the clock.

We study the popular centrality measure known as effective conductance or in some circles as information centrality. This is an important notion of centrality for undirected networks, with many applications, e.g., for random walks, electrical resistor networks, epidemic spreading, etc. In this paper, we first reinterpret this measure in terms of modulus (energy) of families of walks on the network. This modulus centrality measure coincides with the effective conductance measure on simple undirected networks, and extends it to much more general situations, e.g., directed networks as well. Secondly, we study a variation of this modulus approach in the egocentric network paradigm. Egonetworks are networks formed around a focal node (ego) with a specific order of neighborhoods. We propose efficient analytical and approximate methods for computing these measures on both undirected and directed networks. Finally, we describe a simple method inspired by the modulus point-of-view, called shell degree , which proved to be a useful tool for network science.

Facebook's brain-reading computer interface is able to look for patterns in activity in the brain and match them with specific words and phrases in real-time. In experiments, participants answered multiple-choice questions with their thoughts, which were then translated into words by the brain-computer interface. The system was able to detect when the participant was being asked a question, understand the content of the question asked, and translate the thought answer into words. The patients in the study were using highly invasive implants, and the system was very limited. It was only able to understand nine questions and 24 total answer options with between 61 to 76 percent accuracy. Even a very basic level of thought control could make huge differences in how we interact with VR systems. The technology could help improve the lives of people who can't speak due to paralysis or other issues.

Automatic segmentation of vestibular schwannoma (VS) tumors from magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) would facilitate efficient and accurate volume measurement to guide patient management and improve clinical workflow. The accuracy and robustness is challenged by low contrast, small target region and low through-plane resolution. We introduce a 2.5D convolutional neural network (CNN) able to exploit the different in-plane and through-plane resolutions encountered in standard of care imaging protocols. We use an attention module to enable the CNN to focus on the small target and propose a supervision on the learning of attention maps for more accurate segmentation. Additionally, we propose a hardness-weighted Dice loss function that gives higher weights to harder voxels to boost the training of CNNs. Experiments with ablation studies on the VS tumor segmentation task show that: 1) the proposed 2.5D CNN outperforms its 2D and 3D counterparts, 2) our supervised attention mechanism outperforms unsupervised attention, 3) the voxel-level hardness-weighted Dice loss can improve the performance of CNNs. Our method achieved an average Dice score and ASSD of 0.87 and 0.43 mm respectively. This will facilitate patient management decisions in clinical practice.

No intrusive advertising on the front page. Google docs, chrome and all of the other services Google gives away for free. That's the key thing 90 of everything they give there users is free. I want a simple search page. That's what draws a simple man like me to google for my searches. The front page is clean, it's the letters of Google and a search bar. I used to use yahoo, but it got so cluttered. I know they sell shit, give sponsored links and the like, but they present it cleanly. That's my take on it, as one of those 30 year olds, who can't program, gets confused by most new tech, and has moderate disposable income.," "Yahoo is a lot older than Google. It was originally a hierarchical directory for the world wide web, possible at the time because the web was so small. You wouldn't search for content by description, you would just choose a website from its category or subcategory kind of like an Internet phonebook. That eventually became unwieldy and search engines grew to dominate. Google became popular in the beginning because it was sparse. In the late nineties when Internet speeds were slow it sucked wasting time loading up a bunch of ads and unwanted content at a web portal like yahoo (which did incorporate search by then) when you could jump on Google and only have to load a logo and a search bar. Then Google continually reinvested time and energy into their search algorithm, making it the best, as well as increased infrastructure as they grew. Now no one can compete with their level of expertise, especially since matching them wouldn't be good enough: you'd need to beat them handily to convince people to switch. . TLDR: Yahoo's technologybusiness model was outmoded by the late nineties. They've struggled on valiantly but haven't found a viable niche.,Yahoo was modelled after similar services in 90s like AOL and MSN. The idea being that everything you need was available via them, and most of the important information was on their front page (i.e. your home page). As the internet started to evolve this model became problematic, adding more content to Yahoo's front page meant it would take a long time to load for people using dialup modems. Google instead offered an essentially blank landing page, which loaded incredibly quickly on even the slowest of connections. This meant that Google was able to gain headway into the search market. On top of that a lot of other specialist websites started in the late 90searly 2000s, which pulled traffic away from Yahoo's "one stop shop." Ultimately people didn't need to go to Yahoo any more. They could get the information they wanted faster by going to specialty sites via Google's search. In the mid 2000s broadband internet closed the technical gap, which meant Yahoo could have its cake and eat it too (lots of content, still high performance). Unfortunately by then they'd lost a lot of users to Google. And thanks to Google keeping up with new technologies and features there's never been an opportunity for Yahoo to get any users back on their side.','Simplicity. It is the most basic of designs, that promotes ease of use. Many folk learned how to browse the internet using google as a front page, as opposed to yahoo and msn etc which are very cluttered and confusing to a first time user

Shijian-21, or SJ-21, is a Chinese satellite designed to test and verify space debris mitigation technologies. It was recently observed pulling a dead satellite out of its normal orbit and placing it a few hundred miles away in a graveyard orbit. The maneuver was performed during daylight hours when observations would be more difficult. Military experts are concerned that the capabilities demonstrated by SJ-21 could be used to attack working satellites. SJ-21 has made news headlines before for other questionable operations.

"Gentlemen!" I said, in a rather sharp tone to get the meeting into order. "Thankyou!" I said as the buzzing died down and most of the faces turned towards me. Suddenly I could feel an empty pit in my stomach. Was I really the public speaker I wanted to be? I licked my suddenly dry lips and tried to remember my speech. Suddenly, I realised with terror that I could not remember a word. Thank the Lords that rhetoric pause was considered of the essence in these parts of the world. I composed myself. "Ladies, Gentlemen, Shield Maidens, Firebreathers, Strongmen, please lend me your ears." There was a slight murmur, mostly of approval. Being inclusive always got you some bonus points. "I stand before you to speak on the matter of suffrage. I know many of you are old enough to remember old offences. But you are also the veterans of our progress, are you not?" There was another murmur of approval there. Always flatter your audience. "Some of you remember the wood elven luddites and their fight aginst progress. Did we not rise above petty quarrels, sit down in peace and find a solution? Did we not preserve their beloved forests as we found coal?" A few scattered'hear, hear' and'aye's coudl be heard. By now I had worked myself up, but I still had to work them up. "We remember the days of old, yes. We remember the dwarven zeppelins and their bombs. We remember high elves and their palaces built from bone of orc and human alike." Some did remember, and there was the scant booing now. They did not like this, but they were listening to my every word. "We remember roving bands of human bandits. Dragons splitting up anything they found on the ocean, orcs toiling their farms and refusing to share anything with anyone, even those dying from famine!!!" More booing. I need to get to the point soon, or their anger will be directed at me. The dragonhead poking into the windod, the hall being too small for his gigantic frame seemed especially upset. And you should not wake the dragon. Even in this age. "No, we do not forget. We hold in high regard those that died for justice, but equally those that died because of injustice. And while we will never forget, we can forgive. Yes, that is the only way to end centuries, no, millennia of bloodshed, of hatred, of conflict, injustice and pain." They were actually silent now. I suppose thay had not expected this kind of speech. I have them now. "So I say to you, remember, never forget, but forgive. Let us be a beacon of hope to the dwarven nomads in their airships. To the dragons at the bottom of the sea. To the dark elves on their mountainsides, to the humans in their small, petty warring states, even to the primitive and barbaric wood eleves in their jungles and forests. I say, let freedom and justice rule this land. Let no soul that has attoned for his crime go without the rights that all deserve." There was quite the calamity now, and I had to wait for a few seconds before I continued. A quick sip of water, correcting my tie and collar, making sure my silk tophat was still placed on the chair next to the podium. "Thus I say, nay, demand in front of you. Suffrage! A vote for every soul, of every nation, of every race, of every conviction, of every religion. If he or she comes here with the self-evident truth that all beings deserve the right to pursue life, fame, fortune and happiness in his or her heart, let him also vote whom to best further those heartfelt goals." I did not allow them much respite for cheering before I continued. Yes, I AM a public speaker! I raised my voice until it thundered above them all. I leaned forwards and stretched out my hand. "Will you support me? Will you march with me to the senate, demanding SUFFRAGE!?" The approval was defeaning.'Suffrage, suffrage, suffrage!' it was roared again and again. I grabbed my hat and made my way down the crowd, shaking hands, doding the foul stench of the dragon roaring his approval, butting heads and taking shoulderclaps. "Master Strevk! A picture and a statement for the paper, if you please?" I hear a voice from a reporter. Of course. I turn there, straighten my back, smile and praise the Lords I had my fangs re-gilded the other day. I will look fantastic. The flash goes off and I blink in the sudden light. "Right-o. And a statement?" I nod and smile again. "We orcs can never truly be free as long as others are in bondage!" I say, then head out to lead the crowds towards the Senate. They shall feel the popular opinion today. I smile broadly as the marching band starts to play the old'Greenskin Glory'.

"Hallo?" I heard a child's voice calling in the forest, "Hallo?" Great, I thought. Red Riding Hood's lost. But as I continued down the path, I saw that it was two unfamiliar children, headed towards the Witch's house. The children were clearly brother and sister: thin with button noses and freckles. One was a girl, in a ragged gray dress, the other a boy in suspenders. I stalked in the shadows behind them. I could smell the softened caramel of the Witch's roof tiles before the house came into view. The kids must have spotted the house too, because they stopped shouting for help, and went running so fast towards the candy house their arms flapped behind them. I paused. It was a pretty picture: the gingerbread house, framed in dark chocolate pillars. The children fell to eating it. From where I stood, in shadows at the edge of her yard, I could see the Witch inside the window. She stood when she heard their munching, and crept towards the door. The sounds of their feasting echoed throughout the forest: smacking of lips, grunts, and (most terribly of all) the crunch of the little girl's teeth against the peppermint doorknob. It was a pleasant spring day, and I had things to do. But I couldn't help but watch for a moment. I heaved my axe up against my shoulder, blade up. I straightened my spine a little and wiped my runny nose on my sleeve. A wolf appeared the Big Bad Wolf lured by the smell of the children as surely as the children were lured by the house. He was a big, dark gray wolf, with teeth as jagged as broken glass. When he smiled at the children, his lips rolled back, revealing gray gums. Interesting, I thought. Witch vs. wolf? Let's see where this goes. The witch finished creeping to the doorway. She and the wolf spotted each other, but the children kept eating, oblivious. The wolf's low growl reverberated through the handle of my axe. Yet the children, the little dummies, still didn't hear or see either of them. I wondered how long it would take them to realize they were in danger. I've always thought of myself as a highly capable person, although lately I've had a bit of a cold. I took two steps forward into the yard, when the wolf lunged at the Witch. I backed up again, hiding behind a bush. The witch and the wolf grappled, tumbling down the slope of the yard and towards the woods. Towards me, in fact. The wolf tore at the witch's dark cloak, white teeth flashing The Witch clawed back with long fingernails. Within a minute, the Witch flipped over on top and sucker-punched the wolf right in the gut. The wolf yowled and fell limp, and the Witch pulled out a knife and cut his throat. This commotion, finally, roused the children from their feast. They stared at the dead wolf, melted chocolate smeared on their faces. The Witch turned towards them. Before she could open her mouth, I threw my axe in the Witch's back. She dropped to the forest floor. (If the witch's back hadn't been turned, I wouldn't have stood a chance. I've been ill lately, and I'm weak. I'd hate to think what would happen if I had to face the wolf.) "Hey, dummies!" I stepped over the witch's dead body and nodded a greeting to the two grubby kids. They stared at me. "Why do you have an axe?" the boy asked. He looked me up and down. "I was chopping wood," I said. "But you're old." I shrugged. I was a little petite lady, it was true. I sneezed. "And you're sick." "When you live out in the middle of the woods, you've got to chop wood for your fireplace everyday," I said, "Even when you're old and sick." "Isn't there a lumberjack around here?" "He's a rip-off," I said, "His prices are too expensive. And besides, he's never around when I really need him. He always comes too late to help." I turned my head and coughed into my sleeve. Soon as I got home, I was going to take a nap. "That candy crap's no good for you," I said, "Little Red Riding Hood's on her way to visit, want to come to my house? She's bringing a basket of wholesome food with her, I'll share it with you." "Wholesome food?" the girl asked, her little teeth smeared brown with chocolate, "What's that?" "Apples and shit, you know?" I said, "C'mon. Let's go. I hope Red Riding Hood didn't get lost." I grabbed them both by the elbow and ushered them through the yard, giving the dead bodies of the Wolf and the Witch a wide berth. The breeze rustled the leaves overhead as we hurried down the path, leaving our bad endings behind us.
